summary: The prose is genuinely good: definitions match Edexcel wording (adding value, risk vs uncertainty, segmentation vs targeting), misconceptions are ones students actually make, and the real examples are mostly accurate. But as a Learn Mode section it is inert: zero recall widgets, zero diagrams (even for market mapping, whose own examMatters says exam questions come with a diagram), only 5 of 25 MCQs used inline, and the final block has no quiz or practice at all. The practice set is not IAL-shaped (a 4-mark 'Define', a 6-mark 'Explain two', an 'Outline' command word, point-based guidance for levels-marked 10/20-markers) and three of the five are attached to the wrong blocks. A whole block is spent on four sampling methods that are not on the IAL spec while in-spec bullets (market size/share, brands, ICT in research, online retailing) are missing from Learn Mode and only exist in the Notes tab. A strong IAL teacher would happily use the notes text but would not set the practice questions as written.

accuracyIssues.issue: IAL WBS11 numbers this topic 1.1 Meeting customer needs (1.1.1 The market, 1.1.2 Market research, 1.1.3 Market positioning). The content actually covers all of 1.1.1-1.1.3, not a sub-point. Students cross-referencing the spec or past-paper grids will not find '1.3.1'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Relabel as 1.1 and either split into 1.1.1/1.1.2/1.1.3 or keep as one section titled '1.1 Meeting Customer Needs'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Random/stratified/quota/convenience sampling are not IAL spec content; 1.1.2c only requires 'limitations of market research, sample size and bias'. A full block (2 of 15 subsections, 1 inline MCQ) is spent on out-of-spec taxonomy while in-spec bullets are absent.
accuracyIssues.fix: Compress to one subsection 'Sample size and bias' (keep the Literary Digest example) and reallocate the space to market size/share and ICT in research.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'response bias — where the way you phrase a question leads respondents toward a particular answer' is a description of leading-question / questionnaire-design bias. Response bias normally means respondents answering inaccurately (social desirability, acquiescence). Terminology is muddled.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rename to 'question bias (leading questions)' and, if keeping response bias, define it as respondents giving untrue or socially acceptable answers.

accuracyIssues.location: Market Positioning and Orientation > market-mapping > realExample (Under Armour)
accuracyIssues.issue: Claims Under Armour 'positioned itself as performance-focused but more accessible than premium brands'. Under Armour is priced at parity with Nike/Adidas; its actual gap was performance fabric (moisture-wicking compression) vs cotton. The assertion that it 'used market mapping' is also unsupported. Example is stylised to fit the concept.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a defensible example: e.g. a market map of the UK/HK supermarket sector (Aldi/Lidl vs Waitrose on price vs range) or budget airlines; or say 'a market map would show...' rather than claiming the firm used one.

accuracyIssues.location: The Market: Mass vs Niche > dynamic-markets > FLOW ['Consumer tastes shift','New technology emerges','Business fails to adapt']
accuracyIssues.issue: Rendered as a causal arrow chain but the three items are not causally linked (taste shift does not cause technology to emerge). Flows elsewhere in the section are genuine chains, so this one teaches a false causation pattern.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a real chain: 'New technology emerges → consumer expectations shift → firm that fails to adapt loses share (Nokia)'.

accuracyIssues.location: The Market: Mass vs Niche > mass-markets, body paragraph 1
accuracyIssues.issue: 'A mass market is the largest segment of a market' conflates mass market with a segment; a mass market is a market where products have mass appeal / are aimed at the general population without segmentation. Later section on segmentation then contradicts this framing.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'A mass market is one where a standardised product is aimed at the whole (or a very large part of the) market rather than a specific segment.'

accuracyIssues.location: Competition, Risk and Uncertainty > risk-vs-uncertainty body + block takeaway 3
accuracyIssues.issue: 'You cannot plan for what you cannot foresee' and 'uncertainty cannot be insured against' overstate the point. IAL mark schemes credit contingency planning, cash reserves and flexibility as ways to reduce the IMPACT of uncertainty. As written, a student may argue nothing can be done.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add: 'Businesses cannot predict uncertainty but can build resilience against it — contingency plans, cash reserves, flexible cost structures.'

accuracyIssues.issue: '5,300 homes' — BARB's panel was ~5,100 homes for most of the 2010s and has been expanding toward ~7,000 since 2023. Minor number drift.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'around 5,000+ homes' or update to current figure.

accuracyIssues.location: Multiple realExamples and body: Persil, ONS, Mintel, BARB, Pret A Manger, Innocent, 'UK cereal manufacturer', Starbucks 'few pence ... three pounds'
accuracyIssues.issue: Examples and currency are heavily UK-centric for an audience in HK, Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the Middle East. Not wrong, but reduces relatability and IAL papers use international case studies.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap at least half for international/regional examples (e.g. Grab, Shopee, Samsung, Jollibee, Emirates; statistics offices generically 'government statistics').

quizIssues.question: Which sampling method divides the population into subgroups before selecting a proportionate sample from each?
quizIssues.issue: Quota sampling ALSO divides the population into subgroups and fills proportionate targets from each; the only real discriminator (random vs non-random selection within groups) is absent from the stem. Options B (quota) and C (stratified) are both defensible. Explanation's 'without the same systematic approach' does not resolve it.

quizIssues.question: A mobile phone manufacturer discovers through surveys that customers want longer battery life. This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Stem contains no numerical data; surveys can be qualitative (open questions). 'Primary qualitative research' (option B) is equally defensible. Needs a numeric cue (e.g. '68% of 2,000 respondents').

quizIssues.question: A start-up clothing brand uses Instagram analytics to understand the age and spending habits of its followers. This data is best described as:
quizIssues.issue: Classification as 'secondary' is contested: a firm's own social-media analytics about its own followers is commonly treated as primary data gathered via ICT (spec 1.1.2d), which this section never teaches. Also Instagram analytics does not report 'spending habits'.

quizIssues.question: Adding value is best defined as:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option is worded 'Increasing the selling price above the cost of inputs', which is exactly the misconception the adding-value subsection warns against ('confuse adding value with increasing price'). Should read 'the difference between selling price and the cost of bought-in inputs'.

quizIssues.question: Dyson develops products based on its engineering expertise rather than direct customer requests. This approach is best described as:
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 'Asset-led marketing' is never taught in the section and is a defensible answer for Dyson (leveraging internal strengths/assets). A student who has read the wider textbook may pick C and be marked wrong.

quizIssues.question: What is a niche market?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q0 (same answer, near-identical options). With the PreTest drawing 3 random MCQs from this bank, duplicates inflate the chance of testing the same fact twice.

quizIssues.question: What is the main purpose of market mapping?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q5.

quizIssues.question: Luxury watchmaker Patek Philippe produces limited quantities and charges premium prices. Which market type best describes its approach?
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q9 (luxury handmade watch = niche with premium pricing).

quizIssues.question: Dyson initially struggled to sell its bagless vacuum cleaner because retailers were reluctant to stock it. This most closely illustrates:
quizIssues.issue: Second Dyson/product-orientation item (with Q4); bank over-samples one example.

quizIssues.question: To what extent is market research likely to guarantee the success of a new product launch?
quizIssues.issue: Evaluative command phrasing in an MCQ; three distractors use absolutes ('eliminates all risk', 'guarantees', 'only'), making the answer trivially the hedged option. Tests test-wiseness, not content.

quizIssues.question: Evaluate the claim: 'Market orientation is always superior to product orientation.'
quizIssues.issue: 'Evaluate' as an MCQ stem; distractors with 'always'/'always fail'/'only useful' are transparently wrong. Same test-wiseness problem as Q22 and Q20.

quizIssues.question: A UK cereal manufacturer notices sales falling as consumers switch to high-protein breakfasts. This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 'A supply-side shock' is Economics jargon not in the Business spec; harmless but odd. UK-specific framing.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term niche market (4 marks)' — IAL Business definitions are 2-mark 'What is meant by...' items. The guidance pads to 4 by crediting an example and 'premium pricing', neither of which is part of a definition. Teaches the wrong exam shape.
'Explain two benefits ... (6 marks)' — IAL uses 'Explain one ...' for 4 marks (K1/A1/An2 chain). There is no 6-mark explain-two format on WBS11. Guidance also has no application requirement.

'Outline two features of a dynamic market (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Business command word (it is GCSE/other boards). Should be 'Explain one feature...' (4) or 'What is meant by a dynamic market?' (2).

'Assess ... (10 marks)' allocation is correct, but the guidance is point-marked ('Define... 2 marks; FOR 2+2; AGAINST 2+1; conclude 1') whereas IAL 10-mark Assess is levels-marked (Knowledge 2 / Application 2 / Analysis 3 / Evaluation 3). No case-study context is given although IAL Assess questions are always contextual.

'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' allocation correct, but guidance again allocates points (2+3+2+2+2+2+2+3+2) instead of the levels grid (K4 / App4 / An4 / Ev8); students will think listing more points earns more marks. Generic stem with no stimulus material, unlike the real Section C question.

Coverage: 3 of 5 practice questions are niche/mass/dynamic market. Nothing on market research methods, orientation, market mapping, segmentation, competitive advantage, adding value or risk vs uncertainty — i.e. 10 of the 15 subsections have no written practice.

structureIssues: Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) across 15 subsections — the spaced/immediate retrieval mechanic that defines Learn Mode never fires; the section is read-only plus one MCQ per block.

Zero diagrams. Market mapping is the canonical diagram of this topic and its own examMatters says 'questions often provide a diagram' — yet no market map is shown. Adding value (input cost vs price bar) and mass/niche positioning are also natural diagrams.

practiceIndices are attached to the wrong blocks: block 1 'Competition, Risk and Uncertainty' → practice[0] (define niche market); block 2 'Market Research Methods' → practice[1] (benefits of niche market); block 4 'Market Positioning and Orientation' → practice[2] (market research in a dynamic market). Block 0, where all the niche/mass/dynamic content lives, gets no practice. Correct mapping: practice 0,1,3,4 → block 0; practice 2 → block 2.

Block 5 'Segmentation and Competitive Advantage' has no quizIndices and no practiceIndices even though quiz[6] (segmentation bases) and quiz[7] (adding value) exist. The section ends on three subsections with no check for understanding.
Only 5 of 25 MCQs are used inline (one per block); 20 sit unused except via random PreTest/PostTest draws.

Spec ordering is scrambled: product vs market orientation (spec 1.1.2a, market research) is placed in the 'Positioning' block; segmentation (1.1.2e) is placed with competitive advantage/adding value (1.1.3). A student following the spec cannot map blocks to spec bullets.

Weighting: a full block (2 subsections + 1 inline MCQ) on sampling methods that are not on the IAL spec, while spec bullets market size/share, brands, ICT in research and online retailing are absent from Learn Mode (they exist only in the Notes tab as 'Market Size, Share & Growth' and 'Branding').

2-per-step pairing: block 0 pairs (mass, niche) then leaves 'dynamic-markets' alone; block 2 leaves 'qualitative-vs-quantitative' alone; block 5 leaves 'adding-value' alone as the final step with no quiz — a weak finale. Pairings themselves are coherent.
Takeaways match their blocks well (good). Block 4 has 4 takeaways vs 3 elsewhere; fine.

Some FLOW chains are filler rather than causal: 'Research customer needs → Design product to match → Launch with confidence'; 'Identify existing data sources → Analyse data for your purpose' (2-step). The dynamic-markets flow is non-causal (see accuracy).
Misconceptions are genuine student errors (risk=uncertainty, segmentation=targeting, adding value=raising price, gap=opportunity, bigger sample=better) — this is a strength, not filler.

Difficulty ramp is flat: every subsection follows the identical template; there is no build from definition → application → evaluation within the section, so the 20-mark evaluate question at the end has no scaffolding step before it.
ialSpecGaps: 1.1.1a Market size and market share — definitions and the share/growth calculations are not in Learn Mode content (only in the Notes tab).
1.1.1a Brands — branding as a characteristic of mass markets is mentioned in one clause; no teaching of brand, brand loyalty, or brands as barriers to entry (Notes tab has it, Learn Mode does not).

1.1.1b Dynamic markets: online retailing; innovation and market growth; adapting to change — only one passing sentence ('Online retailing, streaming services and electric vehicles are all examples'); no treatment of how online retailing changes markets or of innovation driving market growth.
1.1.2b Market research used to quantify likely demand — not covered; research is framed only as identifying needs and gaining insight.

1.1.2c Limitations of market research (as a topic) — only implied via sampling bias; no explicit treatment of cost, time, consumers not doing what they say, research becoming outdated (the practice[2] guidance expects these).
1.1.2d Use of ICT to support market research: websites, social networking, databases — not taught at all, yet quiz[17] tests it.
1.1.3a Market mapping — taught in text but the spec skill (interpreting/drawing a map) is untested because there is no diagram.
strengths: Definitions are Edexcel-accurate: adding value as selling price minus cost of bought-in materials/components; risk (quantifiable) vs uncertainty (not); segmentation vs targeting; market map = two variables, gap ≠ demand.
Misconceptions are real ones with a corrective 'Instead write:' sentence in mark-scheme language — the best part of the section.
examMatters paragraphs consistently push context-dependent evaluation ('generic answers score poorly', 'link to budget, time, information needed'), which matches how IAL levels are awarded.
Real examples are mostly accurate and dated correctly (Nokia 2007→2013, Literary Digest 1936, McPlant UK trial, Coca-Cola scale, Morgan volumes, Marriott brand portfolio).
Inline MCQs 0-4 are correctly matched to their blocks and quiz[2], [8], [21], [23] are well-constructed application items with plausible distractors.
Block takeaways faithfully summarise their block content.
topFixes: Rewrite the practice set to IAL shape and re-map it: 'What is meant by a niche market? (2)', 'Explain one benefit of operating in a niche market (4)', keep Assess (10) and Evaluate (20) but replace point-based guidance with the levels grid (K/App/An/Ev) and a short stimulus; add one 4-mark and one 8/10-mark item each for market research, market mapping/positioning and adding value; set practiceIndices so block 0 gets the niche/dynamic items, block 2 the research item, block 5 the adding-value item.

Add recall widgets that are genuinely orderable/unambiguous: fillin for the adding-value and risk-vs-uncertainty definitions (word banks with non-interchangeable terms), a reorder for the market-mapping procedure (choose variables → plot competitors → identify gap → test demand in the gap) and for the primary-research process; do NOT add reorders for the four sampling methods or segmentation bases (parallel lists).

Add a market-map diagram (ideally interactive: drag a brand onto price/quality axes) and an adding-value bar (input cost vs selling price); attach quiz[6]/[7] and a practice item to block 5 so the section does not end unchecked.

Fill spec gaps inside Learn Mode: market size/share/growth with a worked calculation, brands and brand loyalty, ICT in market research (websites, social media analytics, databases), online retailing as a driver of dynamic markets; shrink the sampling block to a single 'sample size and bias' subsection.

Clean the quiz bank: delete duplicates (10, 12, 15, one of 4/18), fix ambiguous items 3 (add 'random selection within each group'), 16 (add a numeric cue), 17 (reclassify or teach ICT-sourced data first), 7 (reword correct option as a difference, not a price rise), and remove absolute-word distractors in 20/22/24.

summary: The expository text is genuinely good: definitions match Edexcel wording ("willing and able", ceteris paribus), the movement-vs-shift distinction is hammered consistently, the shift-outcome table and PED/TR logic are correct, and the misconceptions are real ones markers see. A strong IAL teacher would happily use the prose. But the assessment scaffolding around it is broken: the section has zero diagrams despite three dangling diagramRefs on a topic whose spec bullet is literally "supply and demand diagrams"; the inline quiz/practice wiring is off by one for 4 of 5 blocks (the Supply block ends with a PED question, the YED block with an equilibrium question); 2 of 5 practice questions (market positioning, market share) belong to 1.1 Meeting Customer Needs and all 5 tariffs are non-IAL (Define 4, Explain 6, Analyse 10, Outline 4); quiz Q18 is internally inconsistent with an unfinished explanation; three "real examples" are factually wrong or backwards (UK strawberries illustrate a seasonal supply shift, not the law of supply; UK tobacco duty has been falling since 2021-22; the memorable 2024 PS5 story is price rises, not cuts); and every fillin hint gives away the answer's first letters. Extras (chains + evaluation) are entirely about market research/segmentation/mapping, i.e. the previous section. Fix the wiring, diagrams and practice set and this is a B+.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the demand logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'ab__', 'mov_____', 'down____' give the first 2-4 letters plus exact length; combined with templates that literally quote the section's bolded phrases ('willing and ___', 'a ___ along the demand curve') this is a copy task, not recall. Also trivial: 'able' and 'downward' test nothing conceptual.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin with no letter hints, targeting the concept: 'A rise in the good's own price causes a ___ along the demand curve, whereas a rise in income causes a ___ of the curve' (answers: movement, shift) plus 'Demand that is backed by the ability to pay is called ___ demand' (effective).

recallAudit.prompt: Order these from cause to effect for a rightward demand shift:
items: Consumers willing to buy more at every price
Demand curve shifts right from D1 to D2
Equilibrium price and quantity both increase
recallAudit.reason: Cause (income) -> behavioural effect -> diagrammatic representation -> market outcome is a real causal chain a student can reconstruct. shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. Minor: steps 2 and 3 are the same fact stated twice (behaviour vs its drawing), so only the first/last positions are truly discriminating; note the equilibrium outcome is taught in block 3, after this recall appears.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the supply logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'ab__', 'up____', 'al___' leak the answers; 'able' is a straight repeat of the demand fillin one step earlier; 'along' in 'a movement ___ the supply curve' is a grammar completion, not a knowledge check.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin without letter hints: 'Higher prices raise ___ margins, so firms ___ output' (profit, increase); 'A change in the good's own price causes a ___ along the supply curve; a change in production costs causes a ___' (movement, shift).

recallAudit.prompt: Order these from cause to effect for a leftward supply shift:
items: Government imposes a new indirect tax
Production costs increase for all firms
Supply curve shifts left from S1 to S2
Equilibrium price rises and quantity falls
recallAudit.reason: Tax -> cost -> shift -> new equilibrium is a genuine causal chain and mirrors how a 4/6-mark IAL answer is structured. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid, not identity.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the equilibrium logic:
recallAudit.reason: 'sup_____', 'sur____', 'lo___' give the answers. 'supplied' in 'quantity demanded equals quantity ___' is a formulaic completion. Without the hint 'lower' would be ambiguous with 'cut'/'reduce' in 'Firms then ___ their prices'.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin without hints using the surplus/shortage pair: 'A price above Pe creates a ___ (excess ___); a price below Pe creates a ___ (excess ___)' with answers surplus/supply/shortage/demand, forcing the student to pair each disequilibrium with its cause.

recallAudit.prompt: Order these steps when demand shifts right:
items: Demand curve shifts from D1 to D2
At the old price there is now excess demand
Price rises to a new equilibrium Pe2
recallAudit.reason: This is the best recall in the section: it includes the intermediate mechanism (excess demand at the old price) that students usually skip, so the order is a real test of understanding the price mechanism. shuffled [1,3,0,2] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the PED calculation logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'qu______', 'pr___', 'ela____', 'ine______' leak all four. The formula line 'PED = % change in ___ demanded / % change in ___' has two blanks in one template string while the other two strings have one each (4 answers vs 3 templates) — check the renderer handles a double-blank template. The elastic/inelastic pair is trivial once one is filled.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A numeric fillin: 'Price rises 8%, quantity demanded falls 12%. PED = ___ ; demand is ___ ; a price cut would ___ total revenue' (answers -1.5, elastic, increase) — tests calculation, interpretation and application in one item.

recallAudit.prompt: Order these goods from most inelastic to most elastic demand:
recallAudit.reason: This is a ranking, not a cause-effect sequence, and the middle of the ranking is not determinable from the content taught. Brand-level PED for a branded cereal (many near-identical rivals and own-label) is commonly estimated as elastic (|PED| well above 1), plausibly more elastic than leisure flights; the section gives no data to settle it. Only insulin-first is unambiguous. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Either supply PED values on each card (e.g. Insulin -0.1, Petrol -0.3, Branded cereal -1.8, Holiday flights -2.5) so the ranking is fully determinable, or replace with a causal reorder: 'Many close substitutes exist -> price rises 5% -> consumers switch to rivals -> quantity demanded falls 15% -> |PED| = 3, demand is elastic'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the PED-revenue link:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'inc_____', 'inc_____', 'pr___' leak; 'raise' would also fit both first blanks without the hint. Two of three answers are the identical word, and 'Total revenue = ___ multiplied by quantity sold' is trivial. Also the exercise cannot catch the misconception the section warns about (assuming a price cut always raises revenue) because it never asks the inelastic-price-cut case.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin with the four-cell matrix: 'Elastic demand: price cut -> TR ___ ; price rise -> TR ___ . Inelastic demand: price cut -> TR ___ ; price rise -> TR ___' (rises, falls, falls, rises) — this directly targets the stated misconception.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the YED classification:
recallAudit.reason: 'inc___', 'nor___', 'inf_____' leak the answers; the formula blank 'income' is given by the section title. Without hints the items would be fine.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Remove letter hints and add magnitude: 'YED = +0.4: ___ good, income-___ (necessity); YED = +2.1: ___ good, income-___ (luxury); YED = -0.6: ___ good' (normal, inelastic, normal, elastic, inferior).

recallAudit.prompt: Order the impact of a recession on different product types:
items: Economy enters recession and incomes fall
Demand for luxury goods (high YED) drops sharply
Demand for inferior goods (negative YED) rises
Diversified firms weather the downturn best
recallAudit.reason: Items 2 and 3 are parallel, simultaneous consequences of item 1 — there is no reason luxury demand falling must precede inferior demand rising, so a student who understands YED perfectly can still be marked wrong by swapping them. Item 4 is a conclusion, not a step. Only first and last positions are determinable. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. This is exactly the founder's 'ordering things with no real order' complaint.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Replace with a sort/classify exercise: given products with YED values (e.g. designer handbags +2.4, bread +0.3, own-label beans -0.7, restaurant meals +1.6), classify into 'demand rises in recession' vs 'demand falls in recession', or a fillin: 'In a recession incomes ___, so demand for goods with YED > 1 ___ while demand for goods with YED < 0 ___' (fall, falls, rises).

accuracyIssues.location: Supply and Factors Affecting Supply > what-is-supply > realExample (UK strawberry farmers)
accuracyIssues.issue: Backwards and teaches the wrong concept. UK strawberry retail prices are LOWEST in summer because that is peak season; farmers supply more in summer because of growing conditions (seasonality = a supply SHIFT), not because 'retail prices are highest'. Presented as 'the law of supply in action' (movement along the curve), it is a textbook example of the opposite. Also UK-centric for an international cohort.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a genuine own-price response, e.g. US shale oil producers bringing rigs back online when crude rose above ~$80 in 2022, or ride-hailing drivers logging on during surge pricing. Move seasonality to the shift-factors list where the spec puts it.

accuracyIssues.location: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > ped-and-revenue > realExample (UK government tobacco taxation)
accuracyIssues.issue: Claims 'total tax revenue increases each year'. HMRC tobacco duty receipts peaked around 2021-22 (~£10.3bn) and have fallen since (~£8.8bn 2023-24, lower again 2024-25). Also conflates government tax revenue with a firm's total revenue (TR = P x Q), which is the concept being taught; the addictive-good framing is Economics 2.x/market failure territory.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a business example: e.g. Netflix's 2022-2024 price rises with subscriber numbers still growing (inelastic, TR up) vs. a supermarket price cut on a highly substitutable own-label line. Keep the numbers checkable.

accuracyIssues.location: Demand and Factors Affecting Demand > what-is-demand > realExample (Sony PS5)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Sony cut the price of the PS5 in several markets to boost sales in 2024. As the price dropped, quantity demanded rose sharply.' Sony's headline 2024 move was a ~19% price RISE in Japan (Sept 2024), followed by rises in Europe/UK/Australia (Apr 2025) and the US (Aug 2025); 2024 saw only short promotional discounts, and PS5 shipments fell year-on-year in FY2024. The example as written is not true and will confuse students who read the news.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either flip it (Sony raised PS5 prices in Japan in Sept 2024 -> contraction in quantity demanded, movement along the curve) or use a clean documented price cut (e.g. Tesla's Jan 2023 Model 3/Y cuts of up to 20% followed by record Q1 deliveries).

accuracyIssues.location: Market Equilibrium > equilibrium-price-and-quantity > realExample (UK housing markets)
accuracyIssues.issue: Muddled: says excess demand pushes prices 'above the level most buyers can afford, demonstrating disequilibrium in action'. If price rises to ration the shortage that IS the price mechanism working towards equilibrium; 'prices too high to afford' is not disequilibrium. Also UK-centric.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a genuine price-below-equilibrium case (concert tickets selling out in minutes and reselling at multiples on secondary markets — excess demand at the face-value price) and say explicitly that the resale price is the market moving to equilibrium.

accuracyIssues.location: Demand and Factors Affecting Demand > what-is-demand > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Examiners deduct marks if you say demand shifts…' IAL Business mark schemes are positive-marking (marks awarded for creditworthy points); nothing is deducted. The movement/shift precision point is valid but the framing is wrong and needlessly frightening.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rephrase: 'Marks for a movement along the curve are only awarded if you describe a change in quantity demanded caused by the good's own price; writing demand shifts for a price change earns nothing for that point.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Half the marks come from the diagram itself' is invented. In WBS11 papers the diagram is either a specific 4-mark 'Draw a supply and demand diagram to show…' item or supports an Explain/Analyse; there is no fixed 50% weighting.
accuracyIssues.fix: State the real pattern: a standalone diagram question is typically 4 marks (axes labelled, original curves and equilibrium, correctly shifted curve, new equilibrium shown), and in longer answers a correct diagram supports knowledge/application marks.

accuracyIssues.location: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > factors-affecting-ped > realExample (UK energy suppliers)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'British Gas raised prices by 54% in April 2022' — the 54% was the Ofgem price cap increase for the average dual-fuel customer; British Gas raised in line with the cap. Imprecise attribution; also the example sits in a price-capped, regulated market, which is an odd exemplar for free-market elasticity. UK-centric.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'The Ofgem price cap rose 54% in April 2022 and household energy consumption fell only marginally' — or use a globally recognisable case (petrol demand after the 2022 oil spike).

accuracyIssues.location: Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) > calculating-yed > realExample (Aldi and Lidl)
accuracyIssues.issue: Reasonable, but the emoji is a noodle bowl and the example again is UK-only. Minor: 'Their budget products have negative YED' is asserted, not evidenced; the section elsewhere warns students to evidence such claims.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap for a regionally portable example (instant noodles/own-label brands in Asian supermarkets during 2022-23, or Uniqlo vs luxury during downturns) and fix the emoji.

accuracyIssues.issue: In the IAL Business (WBS11) specification, 'The market' (demand, supply, markets, PED, YED) is topic 1.2 (1.2.1-1.2.5); 1.3 is Marketing mix and strategy. The app's numbering 1.3.1-1.3.5 is offset from the spec. Unsure whether this is a deliberate app scheme, but students cross-referencing the spec/textbook will be confused.
accuracyIssues.fix: Verify against the current WBS11 spec and align numbering (1.2 The market) or drop spec-style numbers.

quizIssues.question: A local gym charges a monthly fee of $40 and has 500 members. It raises its fee to $50 and membership falls to 400. What does this imply about PED?
quizIssues.issue: Internally inconsistent and the explanation is unfinished. Revenue is exactly unchanged (500x$40 = $20,000; 400x$50 = $20,000), yet the keyed answer [0] says 'demand is inelastic so revenue rises'. The explanation literally contains 'Revenue rises from $20,000 to $20,000... actually revenue = ... However…' — a visible authoring note. A numerate student who checks the arithmetic will (correctly) reject the keyed answer.

quizIssues.question: Which factor is most likely to make the supply of a product more elastic?
quizIssues.issue: Price elasticity of SUPPLY is not in the IAL Business specification (only PED and YED in 1.2.4/1.2.5) and is not taught anywhere in this section. Out-of-spec question; explanation does not address the distractors.

quizIssues.question: Which statement best evaluates the impact of a rise in interest rates on the housing market?
quizIssues.issue: Off-topic for this section (interest rates belong to economic influences in Unit 2/3 content) and answerable purely by test-wiseness: the only hedged option ('…but the effect depends on…') is correct, the other three are absolutes. Same pattern in Q21 and Q24 — students learn 'pick the longest option with but/depends'.

quizIssues.question: Evaluate the usefulness of supply and demand diagrams for explaining real-world market changes.
quizIssues.issue: 'Evaluate' is a 20-mark essay command word; as an MCQ it degenerates into spotting the hedged option. Distractors 'useless because no business uses diagrams' and 'only applicable to agricultural markets' are not plausible.

quizIssues.question: To what extent is knowledge of PED useful for business decision-making?
quizIssues.issue: Same test-wiseness flaw: [2] is the only non-absolute option; [0] 'PED values never change', [3] 'businesses cannot measure percentage changes' are not credible distractors.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following would cause the supply curve to shift to the left?
quizIssues.issue: Explanation refers to options as '(A)', '(B)', '(D)' but options are rendered unlabelled/indexed; same in Q6 ('Luxury goods (A)'), Q8 ('option D'), Q9 ('Options A and B'). Cosmetic but confusing in the InlineQuiz UI.

quizIssues.question: A product has a YED of +2.3. This means the product is:
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 'A Giffen good' (also Q13) is not IAL Business content; harmless as a wrong answer but signals Economics content leaking in.

quizIssues.question: A business has a product with inelastic demand (PED = -0.3). A manager proposes raising prices by 20%. Which concern is most valid?
quizIssues.issue: Keyed answer [1] is a speculative scenario rather than a knowledge item, and [0] is arguably 'a concern' too (fewer units sold is a real, if not decisive, concern). Wording 'most valid' invites debate. Acceptable but weaker than the rest.

practiceIssues.issue: OFF-TOPIC: 'Evaluate the factors that determine the market positioning of a new product… (20 marks)' is 1.1.3 Market positioning, not The Market. Also a 20-mark IAL Business Evaluate is always case-study based with stimulus data; none is provided. The guidance is points-based ('3 marks' per factor, '2 marks' for intro) whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (Knowledge/Application/Analysis/Evaluation, Levels 1-4) — the model answer teaches the wrong marking model.

OFF-TOPIC: 'Outline two ways a business could increase its market share (4 marks)' is 1.1.1 The market (market share), not demand/supply/elasticity. 'Outline' is not an IAL Business command word (Define/State/Explain/Calculate/Draw/Analyse/Assess/Discuss/Evaluate).

'Analyse … (10 marks)': in IAL Business, Analyse is a 6-mark command; 10/12 marks are 'Assess'. The guidance awards 2 marks for 'Judgement on how useful YED is' — evaluation is not credited under Analyse. Points-style '(2 marks)' allocations again misrepresent levels marking. Content-wise the question is on-topic and good.

'Define PED (4 marks)': Define is a 2-mark command in WBS11; a 4-mark tariff does not exist. The guidance pads to 4 by adding elastic/inelastic interpretation, which is not part of a definition. Also wired as the inline practice for the Market Equilibrium block (practiceIndices [0]), so students meet a PED definition question before PED is taught.

'Explain two factors… (6 marks)': Explain is 4 marks in IAL Business; 6-mark tariffs are Analyse. The two-part 'explain two' format is not used. Guidance for Factor 2 ('government grants… increasing the quantity demanded at every price level') blurs the movement/shift language the section insists on — say 'shifts demand to the right'. Wired as inline practice for the PED block (practiceIndices [1]) although it is a demand-shift question.

Coverage: no Calculate question (4 marks, the single most predictable PED/YED item on WBS11), no 'Draw a supply and demand diagram to show…' (4 marks), no Assess (10/12) on pricing strategy given PED. The set tests the section's two weakest links and none of its strongest.

structureIssues: ZERO DIAGRAMS: blocks 0-2 carry diagramRef 'demand-curve', 'supply-curve', 'equilibrium-diagram' but diagrams[] is empty (meta.diagrams: 0), so InlineDiagram never renders. The prose repeatedly says 'on a diagram…', examMatters demand D1/D2, S1/S2, Pe/Qe labelling, and spec 1.2.3(b) is literally 'supply and demand diagrams'. Highest-impact gap in the section; PED/YED blocks have no diagramRef at all (a TR-under-elastic/inelastic diagram would help ped-and-revenue).

INLINE QUIZ WIRING OFF BY ONE: quizIndices are [0],[1],[2],[3],[4] but quiz[1] is PED/revenue (shown at end of Supply block), quiz[2] is a supply shift (shown at end of Equilibrium block), quiz[3] is YED (shown at end of PED block), quiz[4] is equilibrium (shown at end of YED block). Only block 0 gets an on-topic inline MCQ. Suggested map: block0->Q0 or Q12; block1->Q2 or Q17; block2->Q4 or Q11 or Q19; block3->Q7/Q9/Q15; block4->Q6/Q16/Q23.

INLINE PRACTICE WIRING: practiceIndices [0] (Define PED) on the Equilibrium block, [1] (demand-shift Explain) on the PED block. Both are one block out of place; blocks 0, 1 and 4 get no practice at all despite on-topic candidates existing.

EXTRAS ARE THE WRONG SECTION: all 4 chains (market research, segmentation, market size/growth/share, market mapping) and all 3 evaluation points (primary research cost, segmentation oversimplifies, data becomes outdated) belong to 1.1 Meeting Customer Needs. Nothing in extras touches demand, supply, equilibrium, PED or YED. Flashcard 22/25 ('Trace how high competition in a market affects…') and duplicated flashcards 20-22 = 23-25 show the same copy-paste origin.

2-per-step pairing: block 3 (PED) has 3 subsections, so calculating-ped + factors-affecting-ped form one step and ped-and-revenue sits alone on the block's last step with the inline quiz (currently the YED Q3), practice, ExplainItBack and takeaway — the heaviest concept in the section is the most cluttered step. Consider splitting PED into two blocks (calc+factors / revenue) each with its own quiz.

Recall placement: factors-shifting-demand's reorder ends with 'Equilibrium price and quantity both increase', which is not taught until block 3 (Market Equilibrium). Served as the 'spaced' recall at the top of the Supply step, it references a concept the student has not yet met.

Difficulty ramp is sensible (definition -> shift factors -> equilibrium -> PED -> YED) and matches the spec order. Takeaways match their blocks accurately. Misconceptions are real ones (movement vs shift, equilibrium != fair, PED sign, price cut != more revenue, inferior != low quality) — not filler. Only factors-affecting-ped's misconception ('students list factors without applying') is a study-skills note rather than a conceptual misconception.
Fillin hint design is systemic: all 16 hints across 6 fillins are first-letters-plus-length ('mov_____'), making every fillin a copy exercise. This is a component-level pattern, not a per-item slip.

Exam-tips in common_mistakes ('extension/contraction in demand') use terminology the main content never introduces (content only says 'movement along'); flashcard 2 also uses extension/contraction. Align: introduce extension/contraction once in what-is-demand.

Regional skew: 7 of 11 real examples are UK-based (Sony aside: Oatly ok, UK strawberries, UK housing, UK energy/British Gas, UK tobacco tax, Aldi/Lidl UK, Ryanair). Target students are in HK/SG/MY/PK/LK/ME; at least half should be regional or global.
ialSpecGaps: 1.2.1 Demand — factors leading to a change in demand: 'advertising and branding' (only alluded to inside 'tastes'), 'external shocks' and 'seasonality' are not taught for demand (seasonality appears nowhere; it is arguably the mis-described strawberry example).
1.2.2 Supply — covered fully (costs, technology, indirect taxes, subsidies, external shocks).

1.2.3 Markets — (b) 'supply and demand diagrams': no diagrams exist in the section; (c) 'operation of market forces to eliminate excess demand and excess supply' is explained in prose but the shortage-side flow is not drawn or given its own flow block (only the surplus flow is).

1.2.4 PED — (b) interpretation of numerical values: perfectly elastic/inelastic and unitary values are not defined in content, yet Q10 uses 'Perfectly elastic' and Q7/Q18 hinge on unit elasticity; (c) factors: brand loyalty and habit/addiction (used in Q5 and the tobacco example) are not in the taught factor list; (d) significance for pricing strategies is covered via TR only — no explicit link to price skimming/penetration or pricing decisions in a case context.

1.2.5 YED — (c) 'factors influencing YED' (nature of the good, income levels of target market, perceptions/branding) is entirely absent: the block teaches calculation and significance only. (b) interpretation: numeric thresholds are taught; fine.

Movement terminology: Edexcel mark schemes accept 'extension/contraction' — used in common_mistakes and flashcards but never taught in content (unsure whether the IAL scheme requires it; the GCE scheme does credit it).
strengths: Definitions and law statements are exam-accurate: 'willing and able… at a given price in a given time period', ceteris paribus, PED and YED formulas with correct sign conventions, luxury/necessity/inferior thresholds (what-is-demand, what-is-supply, calculating-ped, calculating-yed).

Movement-vs-shift discipline is enforced consistently across keyIdea, body, examMatters, misconception and takeaways in both demand and supply blocks — this is the number-one marking issue on this topic and the section drills it well.

shifts-and-new-equilibrium correctly handles simultaneous shifts (one variable determinate, other depends on relative magnitudes) with a sound 2022 oil example; the four-outcome bullet list is exactly what students need to memorise.

Three of five reorders (factors-shifting-demand, factors-shifting-supply, shifts-and-new-equilibrium) are genuine causal chains that mirror IAL 'chain of reasoning' analysis marks; shifts-and-new-equilibrium's inclusion of 'excess demand at the old price' is exactly the step weak students omit.
Misconceptions are real ones markers see, not filler: equilibrium != fair, price cut != always more revenue, inferior != low quality, forgetting YED's sign.
Quiz calculations (Q7, Q15, Q16) are correct and cleanly explained; Q12/Q17/Q19 apply concepts to fresh contexts (EVs, minimum wage, solar subsidy) at a suitable IAL level.
Flow blocks (price rise -> real income falls -> switch to substitutes; tax -> costs -> shift) are concise and well-targeted, and takeaways faithfully summarise each block.
topFixes: Add the three referenced diagrams (demand shift D1->D2, supply shift S1->S2, equilibrium with surplus/shortage and Pe/Qe) so InlineDiagram actually renders; add a TR/elasticity diagram for ped-and-revenue. This is the spec's own bullet (1.2.3b) and currently absent.

Re-wire quizIndices/practiceIndices so each block's inline MCQ and practice question are on-topic (e.g. block1->Q2, block2->Q4, block3->Q9, block4->Q6), and replace the two off-topic practice questions (market positioning 20-marker, market share Outline) with on-spec IAL-tariffed items: Calculate PED/YED (4), Draw a diagram to show… (4), Explain (4), Analyse (6), Assess a pricing decision given PED (10/12), Evaluate with a short case (20) — with levels-based guidance.
Fix or delete quiz Q18 (revenue is unchanged at $20,000; explanation contains an unfinished authoring note) and drop Q14 (price elasticity of supply is not in the IAL Business spec).

Correct the false/backwards real examples: UK strawberries (illustrates a seasonal supply shift, not the law of supply), UK tobacco duty (receipts have fallen since 2021-22; also tax revenue != firm TR), Sony PS5 2024 (Sony raised, not cut, prices); and rebalance the UK-heavy example set toward the app's Asian/Middle-East cohorts.

Remove first-letter hints from all six fillins (or make them optional after a wrong attempt) and replace the two non-causal reorders (PED goods ranking; recession/YED parallel outcomes) with classify/sort or numeric fillin exercises; move the extras chains/evaluation (all 1.1 market research content) to meeting-customer-needs and write on-topic ones (e.g. 'Cost-push shock -> supply shifts left -> price up, quantity down -> firms with inelastic demand pass costs on').

summary: The prose is competent and mostly accurate: key ideas are crisp, the 15 misconceptions are real student errors rather than filler, and the examMatters notes are generally the right advice for IAL levels-based marking. A strong IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is, for four reasons. (1) The interactive layer is broken: all 9 fill-in recalls are trivial with hints that spell the answer ("SM___", "lo_", "ty__"), and the block→inline-quiz mapping is off by one so blocks 2 and 4 quiz students on pricing and distribution before those are taught. (2) The two most diagram-dependent models in Unit 1, the PLC curve and the Boston Matrix, have zero diagrams. (3) Practice mark allocations do not match IAL Business command words (Define is 2 marks not 4; Explain is 4 not 6) and the 10/20-mark model answers are written as point-per-mark rather than levels. (4) The section is labelled 1.3.3 but covers spec 1.3.1-1.3.5, and several spec bullets (types of branding, design-mix social trends beyond ethical sourcing, price-comparison sites, mass vs niche, product-to-service) are missing while quizzes test untaught terms (USP, intensive/exclusive distribution).

recallAudit.blockTitle: Marketing Objectives, Strategy and Product Life Cycle
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the marketing objectives logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'SM___', 'cor______', 'awa______' plus template line 1 literally lists 'specific, measurable and time-bound' next to the blank. All three are copy-the-hint. 'awareness' could otherwise be 'image/loyalty' but the hint removes any thought.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin without letter hints: give a vague objective ('increase sales') and ask the student to supply the missing SMART components (a number, a deadline, a metric); or a short-answer 'rewrite this objective as SMART' with AI grading.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Marketing Objectives, Strategy and Product Life Cycle
recallAudit.prompt: Order the product life cycle stages:
items: Introduction — low sales, high costs, building awareness
Growth — sales rise rapidly, profits begin
Decline — sales fall, product may be withdrawn
recallAudit.reason: Chronological and canonical. shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. Weakness: each item begins with the stage name, so a student who can alphabetise the four words gets it without reading the descriptors.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep as reorder but strip the stage names: order the four descriptors only ('sales low, costs high, profit negative' etc.), which forces reasoning about sales/profit patterns.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Marketing Objectives, Strategy and Product Life Cycle
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the Boston Matrix logic:
recallAudit.reason: Template line 1 says 'high market share and high market ___' and line 3 says 'market ___ against market growth'; each line contains the other line's answer. 'products' in 'fund investment in other ___' is filler (could be Stars/Question Marks but hint 'pro_____' forces it).
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A 2x2 classification drag-drop: given four named products with share/growth data, place each in the correct quadrant and pick the matching strategy (invest/hold/harvest/divest).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the marketing mix logic:
recallAudit.reason: 'Product, Price, ___ and Promotion' with hint 'Pl___' is a GCSE-level gap; 'affects all the ___' = 'others' tests nothing. Zero cognitive load for an A-level student.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Consistency check exercise: show a mini mix (e.g. luxury product, penetration price, supermarket distribution, TV ads) and ask which P is inconsistent and why; or fillin where the blanks are the *reasoning* words (e.g. 'a premium price with mass distribution sends a ___ brand message').

recallAudit.prompt: Order these B2B purchase stages from start to finish:
items: Places order and builds ongoing relationship
recallAudit.reason: Items 2 and 3 can defensibly swap: in real procurement you request proposals and THEN evaluate suppliers on them. 'Researches and evaluates' before 'Requests proposals' is the author's choice, not a logical necessity. shuffled [3,1,0,2] is valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reword to make each step strictly dependent: 'Identifies need and writes specification' → 'Shortlists suppliers and requests proposals' → 'Evaluates proposals on spec, price and reliability' → 'Negotiates contract and places order' → 'After-sales service builds long-term relationship'. Or replace with a B2B-vs-B2C classification (sort 8 tactics into B2B or B2C).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the customer loyalty logic:
recallAudit.reason: Answer 3 is 'loyalty' inside an exercise titled 'customer loyalty logic' with hint 'loy_____'. 'retain' could be 'keep' but hint 'ret___' fixes it. No understanding tested.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin on the economics: 'Retaining a customer costs roughly ___ than acquiring one because there are no ___ costs' with answers 'less' / 'acquisition', no letter hints; or a short calculation on customer lifetime value vs acquisition cost.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the design mix logic:
recallAudit.reason: Line 1 'balances function, ___ and cost' then line 2 'prioritise aesthetics and function over ___': each line leaks the other's answer; hint 'co__' spells cost.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Given three products (Ryanair seat, Dyson vacuum, Primark T-shirt) rank the three design-mix elements for each; or a triangle-drag widget placing products in the design-mix triangle.

recallAudit.prompt: Order these from cause to business effect:
items: Business adopts ethical sourcing and sustainable design
Production costs rise but brand reputation strengthens
Premium pricing and loyalty offset the higher costs
recallAudit.reason: Real causal chain a student can reconstruct. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. Caveat: it hard-codes the happy ending ('offset the higher costs') whereas the section's own misconception says the net profit effect 'depends on the market context'; the recall contradicts the nuance the section teaches.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep, but change item 4 to 'Business decides whether premium pricing and loyalty can offset the higher costs' so it does not assert the outcome.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the promotion logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hint 'ty__' for 'type' and 'ma__' for 'mass' are the founder's exact 'P______' complaint. 'targeted and ___ methods' = 'direct' is a definition-copy. Tests reading of the previous paragraph only.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification: sort 8 promotional activities (TV ad, BOGOF, trade show, sponsorship, PR story, email campaign, billboard, personal selling) into ATL vs BTL. Sponsorship and PR would also plug the spec gap.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the branding value chain from investment to outcome:
items: Business invests in consistent brand identity
Brand loyalty reduces price sensitivity (lower PED)
Business gains premium pricing power and market share
recallAudit.reason: Genuine causal chain and correctly links branding to lower PED (a spec point). shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Weakness: identical to the section's own flow diagram (steps + result) shown moments earlier in the same step, so 'immediate' recall is pure copying.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep but remove the flow block from the section body, or move this recall to the 'spaced' slot only.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the viral marketing logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'con______', 'lo_', 'unp__________' give the answers outright; 'lo_' for 'low' is absurd. 'consumers' could also be 'users/people' without the hint.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Two-sided evaluation drag: sort statements into 'advantage of viral marketing' vs 'risk of viral marketing'; or fillin with no letter hints on the cost mechanism ('the business pays only for ___ of the content; ___ is done by the audience').

recallAudit.prompt: Order the price skimming process from launch to maturity:
items: Launch innovative product at a high price
Early adopters buy despite the premium
Competition enters and price is gradually reduced
Product reaches mass market at a lower price
recallAudit.reason: Chronological and causally tight; a student who understands skimming reconstructs it. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. Best recall in the section.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the pricing factors logic:
recallAudit.reason: 'brand ___' could be image/strength, 'the ___' could be market/law, 'Pricing must be ___' could be flexible/reviewed; only the hints 'pos________', 'eco____', 'dyn____' disambiguate, so the exercise reduces to word completion. Also 'economy' is not one of the IAL spec's listed factors.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Scenario-to-strategy matching: four mini cases (new innovative gadget, entering crowded market, strong brand, high dev costs) matched to the spec's factors (USPs/differentiation, competition, brand strength, PLC stage, costs/profit) and a recommended strategy.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the distribution channel logic:
recallAudit.reason: All three are definitional word-completions with letter hints; 'consumer' in 'manufacturer sells to ___ with no intermediaries' is given by the phrase 'direct distribution' in the same line.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Build-the-channel drag: given product types (fresh fish, Coca-Cola cans, industrial machinery, handmade jewellery), assemble the appropriate channel (direct / one-level / two-level / agent) and justify.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the e-commerce distribution transformation:
items: Costs fall and customer data becomes directly available
Business must invest in logistics and fulfilment capabilities
recallAudit.reason: Items 3 and 4 are parallel consequences of item 2, not sequential; and 'must invest in logistics' realistically precedes launching a DTC channel (you need fulfilment before you can sell direct), so a thoughtful student could put item 4 first or second. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Replace with an opportunities-vs-challenges classification of e-commerce impacts (wider reach, customer data, lower intermediary margin, returns handling, logistics investment, loss of in-store service), which is what the examMatters note says the exam asks.

accuracyIssues.issue: States the iPhone price 'gradually falls over the following 12 months as newer models are released'. Apple holds the list price fixed for the model year and cuts it in one step when the next model launches; it is not gradual and new models do not appear within those 12 months. Misdescribes the example used to define skimming.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'the new model launches at a premium; roughly a year later, when the next model is released, the price is cut in a step, capturing more price-sensitive buyers'. Or use a cleaner skimming example (games consoles, new-generation TVs).

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims Warby Parker grew 'to a $3 billion valuation through direct distribution alone'. Warby Parker opened its first physical store in 2013 and now operates 200+ stores; its IPO valuation (2021) was ~$6bn and it is a multi-channel retailer. 'Direct distribution alone' is false and the number is unmoored from a date.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reframe as a DTC-then-omnichannel example: 'started online-only to cut out opticians, then added its own stores once customers wanted to try frames' — which also illustrates the section's own point that physical retail still matters.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'access to over 100,000 UK stores' is unverifiable and implausible as a count of outlets stocking Cadbury via Booker; UK convenience stores number ~50k and total grocery outlets are well under 100k.
accuracyIssues.fix: Drop the figure: 'reaching tens of thousands of independent retailers Cadbury could never serve directly'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'recognised by 97% of consumers globally' is a widely circulated unsourced statistic; no reliable global survey supports it.
accuracyIssues.fix: Remove the percentage; the premium-over-unbranded-shoe point stands on its own.

accuracyIssues.location: Marketing Objectives, Strategy and PLC > boston-matrix > realExample (Cadbury Plant Bar)
accuracyIssues.issue: Cadbury Plant Bar was discontinued in 2023, so it is a poor example of Cash Cow money funding 'innovation' unless the failure is acknowledged (which would actually be a better teaching point about Question Marks).
accuracyIssues.fix: Either update to a live product or reframe: 'Dairy Milk cash funded the Plant Bar (a Question Mark) which was withdrawn in 2023 — showing not every investment becomes a Star'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Lists 'B Corp' alongside Fairtrade and Rainforest Alliance as an ethical-sourcing certification. B Corp certifies a whole company's governance/impact, not the sourcing of materials.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace B Corp with FSC (timber) or Fairtrade/Rainforest Alliance only.

accuracyIssues.issue: The factor list (costs, objectives, brand positioning, competition, PED, economy, legal) does not match the IAL spec list for 'factors that determine the most appropriate pricing strategy': number of USPs/amount of differentiation, PED, amount of competition, strength of brand, stage in the PLC, costs and need for profit. USPs/differentiation and PLC stage are missing; 'state of the economy' is not on the spec. A student revising to this list would miss two mark-scheme-listed factors.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rebuild the factors paragraph around the six spec factors, then optionally add economy/legal as 'other'.

accuracyIssues.issue: The promotion methods list omits public relations and sponsorship, which the IAL spec names as types of promotion (and which quiz Q5's explanation cites as BTL, so quiz and content disagree).
accuracyIssues.fix: Add PR and sponsorship bullets to the BTL list.

accuracyIssues.location: Marketing Objectives, Strategy and PLC > product-life-cycle > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Examiners penalise guesses' — IAL mark schemes do not deduct marks for unjustified claims; they simply award no application/analysis marks. Slightly misleading about how marking works.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'An unjustified classification earns knowledge marks only; application marks require evidence from the case.'

accuracyIssues.location: Marketing Mix and Customer Loyalty > b2b-vs-b2c > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Office 365' was renamed Microsoft 365 in 2020; dated.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'Microsoft 365'.

accuracyIssues.location: Marketing Objectives, Strategy and PLC > marketing-objectives > realExample (Nike DTC 60% by 2025)
accuracyIssues.issue: Target is real (announced 2021) but Nike publicly reversed course in 2024, returning to wholesale partners; presented without that context the example implies the objective succeeded.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add one clause: 'Nike later rowed back on the target in 2024 — objectives must be reviewed when market conditions change.'

quizIssues.question: Which element of the design mix is most important for a budget airline?
quizIssues.issue: Design mix is taught for physical products ('how economically it can be manufactured'); applying it to an airline service and then explaining with 'minimising manufacturing and operational costs' is conceptually muddled — airlines do not manufacture. Also this MCQ is attached to block 3 (Promotion), not block 2 (Design).

quizIssues.question: In the Boston Matrix, a 'cash cow' is characterised by:
quizIssues.issue: Exact duplicate of Q1 (same concept, same answer). With only 25 MCQs in the bank and the PreTest sampling 3 at random, duplicates waste bank capacity.

quizIssues.question: Penetration pricing involves:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q2; and Q15 near-duplicates the skimming content of Q2's distractor. Three of 25 items test the same skimming/penetration distinction.

quizIssues.question: What is meant by a 'unique selling point' (USP)?
quizIssues.issue: USP is never defined or mentioned anywhere in content[] (only in notes). Quiz tests untaught material.

quizIssues.question: Which distribution strategy involves selling products through a limited number of carefully chosen outlets?
quizIssues.issue: Intensive/selective/exclusive distribution are not taught in content[] (selective appears once in passing in the 4Ps section). Untaught material.

quizIssues.question: A premium handbag brand sells only through its own flagship stores and its website. This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Same untaught intensive/selective/exclusive taxonomy as Q14. Additionally, 'own stores + website' is arguably 'direct distribution' (taught) rather than 'exclusive distribution' (untaught); a student who learned the section would pick the taught concept and be marked wrong. Distractor 3 does not offer 'direct'.

quizIssues.question: A budget airline uses social media advertising, low fares, online-only booking, and no-frills service. Which element of the marketing mix is most critical...
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 2 reads 'Promotion (celebrity endorsements)' but the stem says the airline uses social media advertising, so the option contradicts the stem rather than testing judgement.

quizIssues.question: Evaluate the usefulness of the Boston Matrix for a business making strategic decisions.
quizIssues.issue: 'Evaluate' MCQ where the one hedged, balanced option is correct and the other three are absolutist ('always', 'useless', 'only'). Answerable by pattern-matching without any Boston Matrix knowledge. Same flaw in Q22 and Q24.

quizIssues.question: To what extent is branding the most important element of the marketing mix for a luxury fashion house?
quizIssues.issue: Same 'pick the hedged option' construction as Q20; options 0, 2, 3 are strawmen no student would choose.

quizIssues.question: Evaluate the view that social media is now the most effective form of promotion for all businesses.
quizIssues.issue: Same construction; option 1 ('False, because social media is free and therefore has no value') is nonsensical rather than plausibly wrong.

quizIssues.question: A company repackages an existing product and targets it at a new demographic. This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Targeting a new demographic is textbook Ansoff 'market development' — it is not offered as an option, so 'extension strategy' is correct by elimination, but Q16 offers 'Market development' as a distractor for a sugar-free variant (which is really 'product development'). The two items use the Ansoff vocabulary inconsistently; Ansoff is not in this section's content.

quizIssues.question: A firm considers switching from cost-plus to competitive pricing. Which argument against this change is most persuasive?
quizIssues.issue: Only option 1 is a coherent argument at all; 0, 2, 3 are false statements, not weaker arguments. 'Most persuasive' framing promises a judgement item but delivers a spot-the-only-true-sentence item.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term USP (4 marks)'. In IAL Business (WBS11) 'Define' is a 2-mark command; the 4-mark command is 'Explain'. The model answer pads a definition with an example and a benefit to reach 4 points, which is not how a define question is marked. USP is also never taught in content[] yet this is the inline practice for block 3.

'Explain how a business might use extension strategies... (6 marks)'. IAL Business 'Explain' is 4 marks; 6 marks is 'Analyse'. Model answer gives 6 point-marks including a definition mark, which mismatches IAL's KAA levels for 6-markers. Also via practiceIndices=[1] on block 4 this PLC question is served at the end of the Pricing block, three blocks after PLC was taught.

'Assess the factors... pricing strategy for a new technology product (10 marks)'. Command/marks pair is valid for IAL (Assess 10). But the model answer is written as '2 marks per factor + 2 for judgement' — IAL 10-markers are levels-marked (K/App/An/Ev) with a required two-sided argument and a contextual judgement; the guidance teaches the wrong structure. No case context given, and the factors listed (innovation, competition, brand, costs) omit the spec's PED and PLC stage. Not attached to any block via practiceIndices.

'Evaluate the importance of an integrated marketing mix... (20 marks)'. Command/marks valid. Model answer again assigns point-marks ('3 marks', '2 marks') which misrepresents levels marking; no case-study stimulus although IAL 20-markers are always context-based. Content is reasonable. Not attached to any block.

'Explain how the Boston Matrix could be used by a food manufacturer (6 marks)'. Same Explain/6-mark mismatch as P1 (should be 'Analyse' at 6 or 'Explain' at 4). The 'food manufacturer' context is not used in the model answer at all. Not attached to any block, so the block that teaches the Boston Matrix (block 0) has no inline practice.

structureIssues: Inline quiz mapping is off by one relative to teaching (content[].quizIndices = [0],[1],[2],[3],[4],[5] look auto-assigned sequentially, and LearnModeTab.jsx:106-108 indexes them straight into quiz[]): block 1 (Marketing Mix/Loyalty) shows the Boston Matrix Q1; block 2 (Design) shows the penetration-pricing Q2 BEFORE pricing is taught in block 4; block 3 (Promotion) shows the design-mix Q3; block 4 (Pricing) shows the distribution-channel Q4 BEFORE distribution is taught in block 5; block 5 (Distribution) shows the BTL Q5. Only block 0 is correct. Fix: block0 [0,1,11,10,6,16,18,20], block1 [9,19], block2 [3], block3 [5,13,22,24], block4 [2,8,12,15,21], block5 [4,7,14,17,23].

Inline practice mapping is wrong: practiceIndices [0] on block 3 and [1] on block 4 index into practice sorted by marks ascending (LearnModeTab.jsx:82,110-113), giving the Promotion block a USP 'Define' (untaught) and the Pricing block an extension-strategies question. P2 (pricing, 10 marks) is the obvious fit for block 4 and P4 (Boston) for block 0; P3 (integrated mix, 20 marks) for block 1. Three of five practice questions are never surfaced inline.

diagrams[] is empty (meta.diagrams = 0). The PLC sales/profit curve and the Boston Matrix 2x2 are the two models in this section that IAL papers expect students to sketch or read; teaching them as bullet lists only is the single biggest pedagogical gap. A distribution-channel ladder diagram would also help block 5.

Section is numbered '1.3.3' but its scope is the whole IAL topic 1.3 (1.3.1 Product/service design, 1.3.2 Branding and promotion, 1.3.3 Pricing strategies, 1.3.4 Distribution, 1.3.5 Marketing strategy). In the spec, 1.3.3 is 'Pricing strategies' alone. Students cross-referencing the spec or past-paper labels will be confused. Either rename to '1.3 Marketing mix and strategy' or split into five sections matching the spec.

Block order does not follow the spec: block 0 is 1.3.5 (strategy: PLC, Boston) and block 1 mixes an untethered '4Ps' intro with 1.3.5 items (B2B/B2C, loyalty), then 1.3.1-1.3.4 follow. Better: 4Ps overview first, then design → promotion/branding → pricing → distribution → strategy (PLC/Boston/B2B/loyalty/mass-vs-niche), so that pricing and promotion can reference the PLC as prior knowledge and the strategy block can synthesise.

'Marketing Objectives' (SMART etc.) is not an IAL 1.3 spec item; it is a reasonable primer but occupies the first step of the section, which given the 75% step-0 abandonment rate is the most expensive real estate in the section. Consider moving it into the 4Ps step or cutting it.

2-per-step pairing produces two orphan single-section steps with heavy widget stacks: 'Boston Matrix' alone (with quiz + takeaway + spaced recall from PLC + its own immediate fillin) and 'Customer Loyalty' alone, 'Viral Marketing' alone. The branding reorder recall duplicates the branding flow block visible on the same step, so 'immediate' recall is copying.

Block 2 title 'Product/Service Design' covers only the design mix and ethical sourcing; the block's takeaway ('Social trends toward sustainability are reshaping product design') is not supported by content on waste minimisation / re-use / recycling / resource depletion, which the spec lists explicitly.

Block 3 takeaway 'ATL reaches mass audiences; BTL is targeted and measurable' is fine, but block 3 never teaches types of branding (individual/family/corporate) or ways to build a brand beyond 'consistent identity', so a student cannot answer the 'types of branding' knowledge questions IAL papers set. Takeaways otherwise match their blocks accurately.

Misconceptions are genuinely good: all 15 describe real student errors (vague objectives, rigid PLC, always-divest Dogs, 4Ps in isolation, points = loyalty, design-mix as separate decisions, ethical = less profit, advertising is best, brand = logo, virality on demand, penetration for everything, cost-only pricing, direct is best, e-commerce kills retail). Not filler.

Difficulty ramp is flat: every section follows the identical template (definition paragraph → flow → paragraph → example), analysis/evaluation lives only in examMatters text, and the only evaluation exercises are the three 'pick the hedged option' MCQs. No section escalates to an applied mini-case.
ialSpecGaps: 1.3.2 Types of branding: individual brand, brand family (family branding), corporate/own brand — not taught anywhere in content[].
1.3.2 Ways to build a brand: USPs/differentiation, advertising, sponsorship, use of social media — USP and sponsorship absent from content (USP appears only in quiz Q13 and practice P0).
1.3.2 Changes in branding and promotion to reflect social trends: 'emotional branding' is named in the spec and only appears in the B2B section as a contrast; not taught as a concept.
1.3.2 Types of promotion: public relations and sponsorship omitted from the ATL/BTL list.

1.3.1 Changes in the elements of the design mix to reflect social trends: concern over resource depletion, designing for waste minimisation, re-use and recycling — only 'ethical sourcing' is covered; the circular-design bullets are missing.

1.3.3 Factors that determine the most appropriate pricing strategy: 'number of USPs / amount of differentiation' and 'stage in the product life cycle' are not in the factors section (PLC is mentioned once in passing in the methods intro).

1.3.3 Changes in pricing to reflect social trends: online sales and price comparison sites — not taught (EasyJet dynamic pricing example gestures at online pricing but price-comparison sites are absent).
1.3.4 Changes to distribution to reflect social trends: 'changing from product to service' (e.g. streaming replacing physical media, subscription models) — not taught.
1.3.5 Marketing strategies appropriate for different types of market: mass markets vs niche markets — not taught as a topic ('niche' appears only inside two misconceptions).
1.3.5 Consumer behaviour: how businesses develop customer loyalty — covered; but the spec framing 'consumer behaviour' (e.g. rational vs emotional decision-making) is only touched via B2B/B2C.

Unsure: whether the current IAL spec wording for distribution channels uses the '4-stage / 2-stage / direct' terminology; content uses 'zero-level / one-level / two-level', which is fine conceptually but may not match mark-scheme vocabulary.
strengths: keyIdea lines are genuinely good one-sentence summaries a student could memorise (e.g. product-life-cycle, branding, distribution-channels).
All 15 misconceptions are authentic A-level errors with an 'Instead write:' correction; no filler.

examMatters notes consistently push application and evaluation over description, which is exactly what IAL levels-based marking rewards; the branding note correctly links strong brands to reduced PED (a spec point).
Three of six reorder recalls (PLC stages, price skimming, branding value chain) are real sequences; the skimming one is a model of what the exercise type should be.
Quiz bank distractors are mostly plausible and correctIndex is right on all 25 items; explanations are present and accurate.

Real examples are current-ish and internationally recognisable (Apple, Nike, Starbucks, Patagonia, IKEA, Ice Bucket Challenge), appropriate for an international-school audience rather than UK-only brands, with the exceptions of Tesco Clubcard, Lucozade and Booker.
Practice P2 and P3 use the correct IAL command-word/mark pairs (Assess 10, Evaluate 20) and P3's argument structure (for / against / 'necessary but not sufficient' judgement) is a sound skeleton.
topFixes: Fix content[].quizIndices and practiceIndices so each block's inline quiz/practice tests what that block taught (currently 5 of 6 blocks show a mismatched MCQ, two of them on untaught material; the Promotion block's practice is an untaught USP question). Suggested mapping is in structureIssues[0]/[1].

Rewrite all 9 fill-in recalls: remove letter-pattern hints ('SM___', 'lo_', 'ty__'), stop putting the answer in an adjacent template line, and replace at least the Boston Matrix, design mix, promotion and distribution fillins with classification/placement exercises (quadrant drag, ATL/BTL sort, build-the-channel). Fix the two weak reorders (B2B stages, e-commerce transformation) per recallAudit.
Add diagrams: PLC sales+profit curve with extension-strategy bump, Boston Matrix 2x2 with cash-flow arrows, and a distribution-channel ladder; wire them via diagramRef on blocks 0 and 5.

Correct practice command words to IAL Business conventions (Define = 2, Explain = 4, Analyse = 6, Assess = 10/12, Evaluate = 20) and rewrite P2/P3 guidance as levels descriptors (KAA + evaluation with contextual judgement) instead of point-per-mark; add a short stimulus to the 10/20-markers.

Close the spec gaps with four short subsections: types of branding + ways to build a brand (incl. USP, sponsorship, emotional branding); design-mix social trends (resource depletion, waste minimisation, re-use/recycling); pricing social trends (online sales, price-comparison sites) and the spec's six pricing factors; mass vs niche marketing strategy and product-to-service distribution shift. Rename the section '1.3 Marketing mix and strategy' or split to match 1.3.1-1.3.5.

summary: The prose is mostly accurate and the misconceptions are largely real ones (overdraft for fixed assets, shares = debt, limited liability = no loss), so a teacher would not be embarrassed by the explanations. But the section would not be put in front of IAL students as-is: the inline quiz/practice mapping is misaligned with the blocks (block 1 'Business Planning' gets an internal-finance MCQ; block 3 'External Sources' gets 'Define cash flow', a term the section never teaches), every fill-in leaks its answer via first-three-letters hints, one 'reorder' is a matching exercise with nothing to order, three of five practice questions use non-IAL mark allocations or command words with point-based rather than levels-based guidance, the Tesla example is factually wrong, and the spec's own bullets (cash-flow forecast interpretation, business angels, peer-to-peer, leasing, trade credit, grants, finance appropriate to limited vs unlimited liability) are missing while Unit-1 'forms of business' content is bolted on. Examples are almost entirely UK companies with UK institutions (HMRC, Companies House) for an international audience.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the business plan logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'for______', 'inv______', 'upd_____' give the first three letters plus length; template 'financial ___' / 'lenders and ___' leaves only one plausible completion. Also 'upd_____' is 8 chars but 'updated' is 7 (hint/answer length mismatch).
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in without letter hints, or a 2-item reorder: 'Entrepreneur researches market -> writes plan with forecasts -> presents to bank -> bank assesses repayment capacity -> loan approved'. Better: a short 'which stakeholder cares about which section' drag-match.

recallAudit.prompt: Order these business plan steps logically:
items: Research the target market and competitors
Produce financial forecasts and cash-flow projections
Write the executive summary as an overview
recallAudit.reason: Research must precede strategy, forecasts depend on marketing/ops costs, and the body explicitly teaches that the executive summary is 'written last'. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] is a valid non-identity permutation.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the retained profit logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'div______', 'int______', 'pro___' leak the answers; without hints 'kept after ___ are paid' could be 'taxes' (the body says 'after all costs, tax and dividends'). 'int______' is 9 chars but 'interest' is 8. Third blank ('making a ___' -> profit) is trivial.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Scenario judgement: 'Firm A: 3 years of losses; Firm B: Ltd with £2m retained earnings; Firm C: start-up. Which can use retained profit and why?' or a fill-in on the opportunity-cost point the misconception makes (shareholders forgo ___).

recallAudit.prompt: Order the sale and leaseback process:
items: Business identifies an asset it owns outright
Asset is sold to a finance company for cash
Business leases the asset back for ongoing use
Cash is reinvested but lease costs are now incurred
recallAudit.reason: A genuine procedural chain (own -> sell -> lease back -> consequence) that follows from understanding the mechanism. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the owner's capital logic:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'sav____', 'com_______', 'wea___' leak the answers. Without hints, blank 2 ('It signals ___ to potential lenders') is ambiguous — the body itself says it 'signals confidence'; blank 3 could be 'savings'.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Drop letter hints and accept synonyms, or replace with a reorder of the start-up funding ladder the body implies: owner's savings -> family/friends -> bank loan once trading history exists -> retained profit once profitable.

recallAudit.prompt: Order these from shortest to longest term finance:
recallAudit.reason: Each label carries its duration in brackets, so the task is reading numbers, not applying understanding (trivial).
