Add recall widgets — fillin on formulas (ROCE, gearing, capital employed, labour turnover) and one reorder with a genuine causal chain (borrow → gearing rises → fixed interest → downturn cuts profit → insolvency risk) — and set quizIndices/practiceIndices on each block so inline items match what was just taught.

summary: The four subsections that exist (decision trees, CPA, moving averages/extrapolation, correlation) are accurately written and the examMatters advice is genuinely exam-relevant, but the section is structurally broken as an IAL 3.3 unit. Investment appraisal (payback, ARR, NPV - the most-examined calculation topic in WBS13 3.3.2) is absent from content[] and notes[], yet 5 of 10 MCQs, 4 of 5 practice questions, 7 flashcards and 2 common_mistakes test it; two further MCQs test Unit 2 break-even/contribution and one practice question tests sensitivity analysis, which is not in the IAL spec at all. With 0 diagrams for the most diagram-dependent topic in the course (tree, network, time-series, scatter), no worked CPA or moving-average calculation, and 0 recall widgets in the one section where procedural reorders would be legitimate, a strong IAL teacher would not put this in front of students without a rewrite of scope and assessment.

accuracyIssues.issue: Pearson IAL numbering: 'Decision-making techniques' is topic 3.3 with sub-points 3.3.1 Quantitative sales forecasting, 3.3.2 Investment appraisal, 3.3.3 Decision trees, 3.3.4 Critical path analysis. In the spec, 3.3.3 is Decision trees only. Same mislabelling pattern across the unit (3.3.1 = spec 3.1 etc.), so students cross-referencing past papers/spec will be confused.
accuracyIssues.fix: Relabel as '3.3 Decision-making techniques' and structure blocks as 3.3.1-3.3.4.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Each branch carries a probability and a financial payoff' - only chance branches carry probabilities; decision branches carry costs, not probabilities.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Chance branches carry a probability and a payoff; decision branches carry the cost of that option.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Roll-back procedure (work right-to-left, calculate EMV at chance nodes, then pick highest net gain at each decision node) is never stated in Learn Mode; it only appears in common_mistakes[2], which is a paywalled/other-tab area. The flow step 'Calculate EMV at each chance node' omits the decision-node comparison.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add a body sentence and a flow step: 'Roll back from right to left: EMV at chance nodes, then choose the highest net gain at each decision node.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Presented as a real example but is a hypothetical (no company, invented 20%/£500m/£80m figures). Arithmetic is correct.
accuracyIssues.fix: Label as a worked example, or cite a documented case (e.g. typical Phase III success rates ~50-60%, overall ~10% from Phase I).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Each activity has an EST ... and LFT' - in Edexcel activity-on-arrow networks EST and LFT are node values (the circle node shows node number / EST / LFT); an activity's EST is its tail node's EST and its LFT is its head node's LFT. Students who think EST/LFT belong to activities mislabel the network in the exam.
accuracyIssues.fix: State that ESTs/LFTs are written in the nodes and explain how an activity reads them; pair with an Edexcel-style node diagram.

accuracyIssues.issue: London 2012 claim that 'the critical path for the main stadium determined that steel frame erection and roof installation had zero float' is an unverifiable invented specific presented as fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either keep it generic ('the ODA used critical path scheduling across venues') or use a documented case with published critical-path detail.

accuracyIssues.issue: Only one limitation offered (duration estimates). Spec 3.3.4 requires 'limitations of CPA'; standard mark-scheme points also include: complex for large projects, dependencies may change, does not guarantee completion, needs management commitment/monitoring, ignores costs/resource availability.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add 3-4 limitations to body or examMatters.

accuracyIssues.issue: A 4-quarter moving average must be centred (average of pairs) to align with time periods; not mentioned. IAL 3.3.1 lists 'three period/four period'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add one sentence on centring even-period averages, or a small table showing a 3-period calculation.

accuracyIssues.issue: Asserts Blockbuster 'extrapolated steady DVD rental growth' through the mid-2000s - no evidence; Blockbuster launched Total Access in 2006 specifically in response to Netflix DVD-by-mail (from 1998), and Redbox kiosks were a major factor. Streaming (2007) to bankruptcy (2010) is 'within five years' only loosely; the causal story is oversimplified.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rephrase as illustration: 'a firm extrapolating Blockbuster's 2004 revenue peak would have missed the shift to DVD-by-mail, kiosks and streaming; Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy in 2010.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Netflix/House of Cards example does not illustrate the subsection's key idea (spurious correlation misleading investment); it illustrates quant+qual blending. 'Predicted the success ... before production began' overstates the popular account (data supported the 2011 bid decision).
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a spurious-correlation business case, or move this example to the 'limits of forecasting' paragraph and soften the claim.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'ask you to calculate a moving average and plot it' - IAL papers ask for calculation and interpretation; plotting is not a typical requirement.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'calculate a moving average and use it to identify/extrapolate the trend.'

accuracyIssues.location: flashcards[16] 'When should a firm accept a special order?'
accuracyIssues.issue: Special-order/contribution pricing is not in IAL Business 3.3 (nor Unit 3).
accuracyIssues.fix: Remove or move to a Unit 2 section.

quizIssues.question: An investment of £120,000 generates annual cash flows of £40,000 for 5 years. The payback period is:
quizIssues.issue: Tests payback (spec 3.3.2), which is never taught in this section's content[] or notes[]. Because PreTest samples 3 random MCQs from this bank, a learner can be gated on wholly untaught material.

quizIssues.question: A project costs £200,000 and generates total net profit of £80,000 over 4 years. What is the ARR?
quizIssues.issue: ARR never taught in Learn Mode content or notes. Question itself is correct (10%).

quizIssues.question: A project has an NPV of −£15,000. The firm should:
quizIssues.issue: NPV never taught in Learn Mode content or notes. Question correct (reject).

quizIssues.question: Which investment appraisal method accounts for the time value of money?
quizIssues.issue: NPV untaught in this section; also distractor 'Contribution analysis' is not an investment appraisal method, making the item incoherent.

quizIssues.question: A product sells for £30 with variable costs of £18. The contribution per unit is:
quizIssues.issue: Contribution is WBS12 Unit 2 (2.2.3 break-even) content, not IAL 3.3 Decision-making techniques. Off-spec for this section and untaught here.

quizIssues.question: Fixed costs are £60,000 and contribution per unit is £15. The break-even point is:
quizIssues.issue: Break-even is Unit 2 content, off-spec for this section and untaught here.

quizIssues.question: A firm calculates a 3-period moving average using sales data of £40,000, £50,000, and £60,000. What is the result?
quizIssues.issue: Trivial arithmetic (mean of three numbers); does not test understanding of why/when moving averages are used. Correct and harmless.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Explain how sensitivity analysis can improve business decision-making' (4 marks) - sensitivity analysis is not in the IAL Business spec (3.3.2 lists simple payback, ARR, NPV and their limitations only). Off-spec.
NPV 'Explain' 4-marker: mark allocation matches IAL 'Explain' (4), guidance usable, but NPV is never taught in this section's content or notes.
'Analyse the limitations of payback' 6 marks: allocation matches IAL 'Analyse' (6) and guidance is a fair mark-scheme sketch, but payback is untaught in this section.

20-mark 'Evaluate' matches IAL, guidance is a reasonable outline, but the context gives cost of capital with no cash-flow data so no calculation is possible (real IAL 20-markers come with case data), the stem is generic ('a business') rather than the logistics company, and the whole topic is untaught here.

Only practice item matching taught content; 10 marks fits IAL 'Assess' (8/10/12) and calculations in guidance are correct (EV resort $1.6m vs renovation $1.5m). Minor: stem should reference the hotel chain, as IAL stems do. No practice question exists for CPA or sales forecasting at all.

structureIssues: Scope mismatch: content[] and notes[] cover decision trees, CPA, moving averages/extrapolation, correlation - but investment appraisal (payback/ARR/NPV, spec 3.3.2) is absent while quiz (4/10), practice (4/5), flashcards (7/20), common_mistakes (2/6) and extras chains (1/4) are dominated by it. The Learn Mode never teaches what its own assessments test.

Block order does not follow the spec (3.3.1 sales forecasting, 3.3.2 investment appraisal, 3.3.3 decision trees, 3.3.4 CPA); block 1 title 'Quantitative Techniques' is a misnomer since block 2 (sales forecasting) is equally quantitative.

Only 2 blocks -> 2 learn steps, each pairing two calculation-heavy topics (decision trees + CPA; moving averages + correlation). Each step carries ~6 paragraphs, 2 flows, 2 examples, 2 misconceptions, 2 examMatters plus inline quiz/practice/explain-back - cognitive overload for 'introduce and practise a calculation' content. Should be 4 blocks (one per spec sub-point).

Neither block sets quizIndices or practiceIndices, so InlineQuiz/InlinePractice cannot be block-matched; a learner finishing the decision-trees/CPA step may be served an NPV/payback practice question they have not been taught.

0 diagrams for the most diagram-dependent topic in WBS13: no decision-tree diagram (spec: 'construct and interpret simple decision tree diagrams'), no Edexcel-style network with node circles (spec: 'complete and interpret simple networks'), no time series with trend line, no scatter graph for correlation. InlineDiagram renders nothing on either step.

0 recall widgets, despite this section containing the course's most genuinely procedural sequences (roll-back: EMV at chance nodes -> net gain -> choose at decision node; CPA: list dependencies -> forward pass ESTs -> backward pass LFTs -> float -> critical path; MA -> trend -> extrapolate). These are the rare cases where reorder recalls would be legitimate, and formula fill-ins (Float = LFT - duration - EST) would be non-ambiguous.

No worked numerical CPA example (network, EST/LFT table, float) and no worked moving-average table; examMatters tells students to 'practise the forward and backward pass' and 'practise the arithmetic' but the section gives nothing to practise on. The decision-trees pharma example is the only numerical walkthrough.

Quiz coverage: all 10 MCQs are calculation/definition; none test extrapolation's continuity assumption, correlation vs causation, decision-tree limitations or CPA limitations - i.e. none test block 2's second subsection or any evaluation content the examMatters emphasise.

Misconceptions: decision-trees ('EMV is the actual outcome') and correlation ('strong correlation proves causation') are real student errors; moving-averages ('MA predicts the future') is acceptable; CPA ('critical path is the most important path') is soft - the observed student errors are 'shortest path' or 'path with most activities' (which quiz Q6 correctly uses as distractors).
Takeaways accurately match their blocks (no issue).
ialSpecGaps: 3.3.2 Investment appraisal: simple payback (calculation incl. part-year formula), average rate of return, net present value with discount factors, limitations of each - entirely absent from content[] and notes[] (only present in flashcards/quiz/practice/common_mistakes/extras).

3.3.1 Quantitative sales forecasting: calculation of moving averages (3-period/4-period incl. centring) from a data table, plotting/identifying the trend and extrapolating from it - no worked calculation shown.

3.3.1 Correlation as examined in IAL: scatter graphs and line of best fit, positive/negative/no correlation, using a correlation to forecast (e.g. advertising spend vs sales) - content gives the coefficient range but not the scatter-graph interpretation skill papers use.
3.3.3 Decision trees: constructing the diagram and rolling back through multiple decision nodes; treating option cost on the decision branch - no diagram, roll-back procedure not in Learn Mode body.

3.3.4 Critical path analysis: completing a network diagram (node number/EST/LFT), dummy activities (unsure whether IAL requires them), calculating EST/LFT on a given network, and the fuller set of CPA limitations - no network shown, one limitation only.
Sensitivity analysis and contribution/break-even (assessed in practice[3] and quiz[7],[8]) are NOT part of 3.3 - reverse gap: off-spec material being taught/tested.
strengths: Core definitions are correct and IAL-aligned: EMV = sum(prob x payoff), net gain = EMV - cost; critical path = longest route with zero float; Float = LFT - EST - duration; forward pass for EST, backward pass for LFT; correlation coefficient range; extrapolation's continuity assumption.

examMatters entries give genuinely mark-scheme-relevant evaluation points (decision trees: probabilities are estimates, one-off decision, risk attitude; forecasting: continuity assumption; correlation: confounding variables).
The pharma decision-tree example is a numerically correct EMV/net-gain walkthrough that also makes the 'average vs single outcome' point.
common_mistakes are real, correct and exam-useful (roll back right-to-left; Forward=Highest/Backward=Lowest; ARR uses profit; include Year 0 in NPV).
Practice[2] (decision trees, 10-mark Assess) has correct calculations and a realistic Assess structure with a context-specific judgement about risk vs the $0.1m EV difference.
Mark allocations on all five practice questions match IAL Business command-word conventions (Explain 4, Analyse 6, Assess 10, Evaluate 20).
Takeaways summarise their blocks faithfully; flow steps in each subsection are genuine procedures.
topFixes: Add an Investment Appraisal block (simple payback incl. part-year formula, ARR, NPV with a discount-factor table and worked example, limitations of each) so the 5 MCQs, 4 practice questions and 7 flashcards that test it are actually taught; add a matching notes[] entry.

Add diagrams for every subsection: a decision tree (squares/circles, roll-back arrows, worked figures), an Edexcel-style CPA network with node circles showing node/EST/LFT plus a float table, a time-series chart with 3-period moving average and extrapolated trend, and a scatter graph showing positive/negative/spurious correlation.

Replace off-spec assessment items: quiz[7] and quiz[8] (Unit 2 contribution/break-even) and practice[3] (sensitivity analysis) with items on extrapolation limits, correlation vs causation, CPA limitations and decision-tree limitations; add a CPA calculation practice (e.g. 'Calculate the float of activity X and identify the critical path', 4-6 marks) and a sales-forecasting one ('Calculate the 3-period moving average and comment on the trend').

Introduce recall widgets where the sequence is genuine: reorder for decision-tree roll-back (assign probabilities/payoffs -> EMV at chance nodes -> subtract cost -> choose highest net gain at decision node), CPA (list dependencies -> forward pass ESTs -> backward pass LFTs -> float -> critical path), forecasting (collect data -> moving average -> trend -> extrapolate); fillin for Float = LFT - duration - EST and EMV formula.

Restructure to 4 blocks in spec order (3.3.1 Sales forecasting, 3.3.2 Investment appraisal, 3.3.3 Decision trees, 3.3.4 CPA), fix the section number/title to Pearson's '3.3 Decision-making techniques', and set quizIndices/practiceIndices on each block so inline quiz/practice match what the step just taught.

summary: A strong IAL teacher would use the prose in the two blocks (drivers/impact; FTA-customs union-single market; trade creation vs diversion) as a decent starting point, but would not put the section in front of students as-is. The "Trade Creation, Trade Diversion" realExample (Scottish salmon post-Brexit) is factually wrong on two counts and mislabels the concept it is meant to illustrate; the CET example uses "UK buyers" inside the EU. More seriously for exam prep, the section is titled to cover the whole 4.1 Globalisation topic but teaches only ~40% of it: no growing/emerging economies or growth indicators, no international trade/specialisation/FDI, no protectionism, no ASEAN, and only 3 of the spec's 7 globalisation factors. Six of the ten MCQs (and two of five practice questions) test that untaught content, so the pre-test gate and inline quiz will feel unfair, and 3 of 5 practice questions are Economics-style macro essays rather than case-based IAL Business questions. It is a low C: correct core definitions and real firms, but a critical example error, large spec gaps, and assessment misaligned with the teaching.

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims 'Post-Brexit, UK fisheries lost tariff-free access to the EU single market' and calls the EU switching to Norwegian salmon 'trade diversion ... (Norway has an EEA arrangement)'. Under the EU-UK TCA (2021) UK-origin goods including Scottish salmon are tariff-free and quota-free; what changed is non-tariff barriers (customs declarations, export health certificates). Norway's EEA membership excludes fisheries and Norwegian salmon actually pays an EU tariff, so this is not trade diversion caused by a CET at all. Scottish salmon exports to France/EU hit records in 2023, so the 'increasingly switch' claim is also unsupported. The example teaches the concept wrongly.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a genuine diversion example, e.g. EU CET on bananas historically favouring ACP/EU-territory producers over cheaper Latin American bananas, or ASEAN Free Trade Area preferences shifting Malaysian/Indonesian sourcing away from cheaper non-ASEAN suppliers. If keeping Brexit, describe it as new non-tariff barriers (customs checks, SPS paperwork) raising costs, not lost tariff-free access.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'If the EU's CET makes Brazilian orange juice costlier than Spanish juice, UK buyers switch to Spain' — the UK left the EU customs union in 2020, so a UK buyer is not subject to the EU CET. Students in 2026 will be confused or repeat a wrong example.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change 'UK buyers' to 'German buyers' (or any current EU member).

accuracyIssues.location: Trade Blocs > trade-creation-vs-diversion > body[1] and flow steps
accuracyIssues.issue: Diversion is presented as something 'the CET forces' and the flow says 'External barriers raised (trade diversion)'. Trade diversion also occurs in FTAs with no CET (preference alone shifts sourcing), and a CET does not necessarily raise external barriers — diversion arises from the relative preference given to members. Imprecise mechanism.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword: 'Trade diversion occurs when tariff-free access for members makes a less efficient member supplier cheaper than a more efficient non-member supplier who still pays the external tariff.' Flow step 3: 'Non-members still face external tariff (trade diversion)'.

accuracyIssues.location: Globalisation & Business > drivers-of-globalisation > body[1] and keyIdea
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Three forces drive it' (technology, trade liberalisation, deregulation). The IAL Business spec lists ~7 factors contributing to increased globalisation: reduction of trade barriers, political change, reduced transport/communication costs, increased significance of global companies (MNCs), increased investment flows (FDI), migration, growth of trading blocs. A student who learns 'three' will under-answer a 'factors' question.
accuracyIssues.fix: Teach the full spec list; keep the three as a grouping but name political change (China/India opening, end of Cold War), MNCs, FDI flows, migration and trading blocs explicitly.

accuracyIssues.issue: Walmart India sequence is muddled: the 2007 Bharti Walmart JV was itself the wholesale cash-and-carry business (Best Price, first store 2009); Walmart did not 'then shift' to cash-and-carry. The actual sequence is JV (cash-and-carry) → JV dissolved 2013, Walmart continued wholesale alone → 2018 acquired 77% of Flipkart for c.$16bn to reach consumers via e-commerce, which is the more relevant point for strategic flexibility.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'FDI rules barred Walmart from multi-brand retail, so it entered via a wholesale cash-and-carry JV with Bharti (2007-13), then bought a majority of e-commerce firm Flipkart in 2018 to reach Indian consumers — strategic flexibility, not just cost-cutting.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'A strong pound makes UK exports expensive abroad; a weak pound makes imported inputs costly' — UK-centric for an international (HK/SG/MY/KR/PK) audience, and the section also covers transfer pricing, which is not in IAL 4.1. Not wrong, but off-audience and off-spec.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a generic 'a stronger home currency ...' formulation or a local currency example (e.g. Malaysian ringgit, Korean won); drop transfer pricing or move to 4.4 MNCs.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'For businesses inside the bloc, the impact is overwhelmingly positive' — one-sided. Firms inside also face more competition from member firms, bloc-wide regulation/compliance costs and loss of protection; IAL 4.1.5(b) 'impact on businesses of trading blocs' expects balanced analysis.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add the downside for insiders: increased competition from member firms, compliance with bloc regulations, loss of national protection; keep the outsider/tariff-jumping FDI point.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Examiners test your ability to rank the levels of integration' overstates how IAL Business papers assess this; Business questions ask about the impact of a named bloc (EU, ASEAN, NAFTA/USMCA) on a business, not to rank FTA/CU/single market (that is more an Economics Unit 4 question).
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword to: 'Business questions ask how membership of a named bloc (EU, ASEAN, USMCA) affects a specific firm's costs, markets and competition — use the level of integration to explain why.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Coaches a generic evaluative line: 'Always consider: It depends on the firm's size, industry, and risk appetite.' IAL mark schemes reward context-specific judgement; a formulaic 'it depends' without case evidence sits at the bottom of the evaluation level.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with guidance to tie the judgement to case data (e.g. share of revenue overseas, currency of costs vs revenue, supplier concentration).

accuracyIssues.issue: IAL Business Unit 4 (WBS14) numbers Globalisation as topic 4.1 (4.1.1 growing economies ... 4.1.5 trading blocs); 4.3 is Global marketing. Unsure whether 4.3.1 is an internal app numbering, but if students see it they will mis-map to the spec.
accuracyIssues.fix: Confirm app numbering convention; align to spec 4.1 if it is meant to mirror Pearson.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best describes an emerging economy?
quizIssues.issue: Tests 4.1.1 growing/emerging economies, which the section content never teaches. If drawn in the 3-question pre-test it is unanswerable from this section.

quizIssues.question: Which indicator combines income, health and education to measure development?
quizIssues.issue: HDI is not mentioned anywhere in content[]; untaught. Correct answer and explanation are fine.

quizIssues.question: What is a key risk of over-specialisation in international trade?
quizIssues.issue: Specialisation/competitive advantage (4.1.2) is not taught in this section. Correct answer fine; distractor A 'Reduced efficiency in production' is weak.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason for protectionism?
quizIssues.issue: Protectionism (4.1.4) is entirely absent from the content, yet this and two other MCQs test it. Question itself is sound.

quizIssues.question: Which organisation's primary role is to promote free trade and resolve trade disputes?
quizIssues.issue: WTO is mentioned only in passing ('the WTO and bilateral agreements reduce tariffs'); dispute resolution role is untaught. Minor.

quizIssues.question: A government provides subsidies to domestic steel producers ... This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Option C wording 'A domestic subsidy as protectionism' is clumsy and semi-leaks the answer by being the only option with a qualifier; subsidies as protectionism are untaught in the content.

quizIssues.question: What is the most likely impact of retaliatory tariffs on exporting businesses?
quizIssues.issue: Retaliation/protectionism untaught in content[] (only in extras). Question is sound and correctIndex correct.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Explain two causes of increased globalisation over the past 30 years' for 4 marks: IAL Business 4-mark Explain questions ask for ONE point developed with two linked strands; 'two causes' for 4 marks is not the IAL format. Guidance is a list, not a mark scheme (no Knowledge/Application/Analysis breakdown).

SolarTech 6-mark Analyse is well-formed and realistic (EU tariffs on Chinese solar panels did exist 2013-2018). But the guidance sprawls beyond an Analyse (strategic responses, EU consumers) and gives no levels-based mark scheme; a 6-mark Analyse needs 2 developed chains, not 8 points.

'Assess the extent to which free trade benefits developing countries' (10 marks) is an Economics macro question; IAL Business Assess questions are anchored to a business in the case ('Assess whether joining the FTA benefits [named firm]'). The context describes a country, not a business. Guidance is a macro list (comparative advantage, profit repatriation) and has no mark scheme.

'Explain the role of the WTO' (4 marks) is a pure-knowledge recall question with no business application; IAL Business does not set it in this form and the WTO is not taught in the section beyond one clause.

20-mark 'Evaluate the view that globalisation creates more winners than losers' has context: null. Every IAL Business 20-marker is case-based; the guidance is Economics-flavoured (income inequality, cultural homogenisation, government redistribution) rather than business decision-making. No model answer or level descriptors.

structureIssues: Zero recall objects (0 reorder, 0 fillin) so the Learn Mode's spaced/immediate recall mechanism never fires here; the FTA -> customs union -> single market ladder is a genuine orderable sequence that would make a good reorder, and trade creation vs diversion a good fillin.
Zero diagrams: the integration ladder (FTA/CU/single market) and the inside-vs-outside-the-bloc effect are natural simple visuals; InlineDiagram slot renders nothing.

Blocks carry no quizIndices/practiceIndices, so the inline MCQ and inline practice shown after the 'Globalisation & Business' block can be about protectionism or HDI (untaught), and the 20-mark macro essay can appear as the block's written question.

Content[] vs quiz[]/practice[]/common_mistakes[] mismatch: 6 of 10 MCQs, 2-3 of 5 practice questions and 3 of 6 common_mistakes (developing vs emerging, protectionism, FDI limitations) cover material absent from the taught content — the pre-test/post-test comparison is therefore not measuring what the section teaches.

Section 2 'Impact of Globalisation on Business Strategy' drifts into 4.2/4.4 material (offshoring, outsourcing, transfer pricing, hedging) while the 4.1 spec items that belong here (growing economies, indicators, trade/FDI, protectionism) are missing; the block would be better titled and scoped to the spec.
Notes[] (3 notes) define MNC and FDI and list 'capital market deregulation'; content[] never defines MNC or FDI though it uses 'FDI' in body text — Learn Mode and Notes tab are inconsistent.

Both blocks are exactly one 2-section step each, so every step ends with the full stack (quiz + practice + ExplainItBack + takeaway); with only two steps the section is very short for a topic with five spec sub-bullets.

UK/Brexit-centric examples (pound, UK fisheries, BMW UK pre-Brexit, UK buyers) in three of four subsections; no ASEAN, RCEP, CPTPP, GCC or SAFTA despite the target audience (SG/MY/HK/KR/PK/Middle East) and ASEAN being named in the spec.
Takeaways do match their blocks and the misconceptions are real student errors (customs union vs single market; 'always produce in the cheapest country'; 'only big firms benefit') — no filler here.
ialSpecGaps: 4.1.1 Growing economies: growth of emerging economies (China, India, Brazil etc.) vs developed economies; implications of economic growth for individuals and businesses — not taught (but quizzed in MCQ 0).
4.1.1 Indicators of growth: GDP per capita, literacy, health, Human Development Index — not taught (but quizzed in MCQ 1).
4.1.2 International trade and business growth: exports and imports; link between business specialisation and competitive advantage; FDI flows — not taught (MCQ 2 tests specialisation).

4.1.3 Factors contributing to increased globalisation: political change, increased significance of global (transnational) companies, increased investment flows (FDI), migration, growth of trading blocs — only technology, trade liberalisation and deregulation are taught.
4.1.4 Protectionism: tariffs, import quotas, other trade barriers (government legislation, domestic subsidies) — entirely absent from content[] though covered by MCQs 3, 7, 9, practice Q1 and extras.

4.1.5 Trading blocs: expansion of trading blocs — EU, ASEAN, NAFTA/USMCA named in spec; ASEAN never mentioned. Impact on businesses of trading blocs is only partially covered (insider view one-sided).
(unsure of exact lettering) 4.1.3 'reduced cost of transport and communication' is only implied via 'containerised shipping'; not developed as a named factor.
strengths: Core definitions are correct and IAL-appropriate: FTA vs customs union (CET) vs single market (four freedoms), and trade creation/diversion in the Viner sense; the 'Trade Blocs > types-of-trade-blocs' misconception ('customs union vs single market') is exactly the error students make.

Real firms with broadly accurate facts: Zara/Inditex 12 supplier clusters and fast lead times, BMW's EU supply chain, USMCA setting independent tariffs on China; the tariff-jumping FDI point is a good business-level consequence of blocs.
All 10 MCQ correctIndex values are correct and explanations are concise and accurate (e.g. HDI composition; not all EU members use the euro).
Practice Q2 (SolarTech, 6-mark Analyse) is a well-formed, realistic IAL Business case question tied to a real EU-China solar tariff episode.
Block takeaways faithfully summarise each block; flow diagrams in each subsection are coherent cause-effect chains; examMatters for trade creation vs diversion gives a usable essay structure.
extras[] chains and evaluation prompts are balanced and would support the missing protectionism content if promoted into content[].
topFixes: Replace the Scottish salmon realExample (factually wrong: UK salmon is tariff-free under the TCA; Norway's EEA deal excludes fish; this is not trade diversion) with a correct diversion example, and change 'UK buyers' to an EU-member buyer in the orange juice CET example.

Close the spec gaps or move the assessment: add a block on 4.1.4 protectionism (tariffs, quotas, subsidies, legislation, retaliation) and a block on 4.1.1/4.1.2 (emerging economies, GDP per capita/HDI, specialisation, FDI) — or relocate MCQs 0-3, 7, 9 and practice Q1/Q3/Q5 to sections that teach them so the pre-test and inline quiz only test taught content.

Expand 'Three forces drive it' to the spec's full factor list (trade barriers, political change, transport/communication costs, MNCs, FDI flows, migration, trading blocs) with an ASEAN/RCEP/GCC example for the target audience.

Rewrite practice Q3 and Q5 (and Q4) as case-based IAL Business questions with a named firm and levels-based mark scheme (Knowledge/Application/Analysis/Evaluation), and trim Q2's guidance to two developed chains.

Add recall widgets (reorder: FTA -> customs union -> single market; fillin: trade creation vs diversion) and a simple integration-ladder diagram; set quizIndices/practiceIndices on each block so inline assessment matches the block.

summary: The prose is clean, mostly accurate and well-structured, but the Learn Mode content[] does not teach the IAL WBS14 topic it is labelled as. The spec's "Global markets and business expansion" (4.2.1-4.2.5) is about push/pull factors, off-shoring/outsourcing, extending the product life cycle, assessing a country as a market and as a production location, reasons for global mergers/JVs, and global competitiveness (exchange rates, cost vs differentiation, skill shortages). Instead the two blocks teach generic entry-mode theory, Ansoff and PESTLE (Unit 3 content) and Bartlett & Ghoshal, which is an AQA framework not on the Edexcel IAL spec at all. The quiz, flashcards and common_mistakes DO cover the real spec bullets, so 8 of 10 MCQs (and therefore the pre-test gate and the inline quizzes) test material the section never teaches; a student who reads every word would still fail the pre-test on push factors, off-shoring, repatriation, exchange rates, Porter and natural hedging. A strong IAL teacher would not put this in front of students as their 4.2 revision without a rewrite of content[] to match the assessment items and the spec.

accuracyIssues.location: Strategic Analysis for Global Expansion > pestle-bartlett-ghoshal > body[1], body[2], examMatters, takeaway[2], takeaway[3]
accuracyIssues.issue: Bartlett & Ghoshal (international / multi-domestic / global / transnational) is not in the Pearson Edexcel IAL Business specification (it is AQA A-level 3.7.7 content). Presenting it with 'Link PESTLE to Bartlett-Ghoshal ... the firm needs a multi-domestic or transnational strategy' as if IAL examiners expect it misdirects revision time and would earn no spec-specific credit on a WBS14 paper.
accuracyIssues.fix: Remove the framework from the core section (or tag it clearly as non-spec extension). Replace with the actual 4.2.5 bullets: impact of exchange-rate movements, competitive advantage via cost competitiveness vs differentiation, and skill shortages.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'both require significant commitment and capital' contradicts the standard IAL point (and this section's own flashcard 'Joint ventures require less capital, share risk') that a JV reduces the capital burden versus a wholly owned subsidiary/acquisition.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'A JV shares capital, risk and local knowledge with a partner; FDI gives maximum control but requires the full capital commitment and bears the full risk.'

accuracyIssues.location: Strategic Analysis for Global Expansion > ansoff-global-context > body[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Market penetration (existing product, existing market) means growing share domestically' is imprecise: penetration is about any existing market. An MNC already trading in Korea pursuing more share there is market penetration, not a domestic strategy.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'means growing share in a market the firm already serves (which may be home or an existing foreign market)'.

accuracyIssues.location: Market Entry Methods > joint-ventures-fdi > body[2] vs examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: body says the choice 'depends on three factors: resources, market characteristics, speed'; examMatters says 'Always use the framework: control vs risk vs resources vs speed' (four, different). Students get two inconsistent frameworks in the same subsection.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use one framework consistently (control, risk, cost/resources, speed, market knowledge) in body, flow, examMatters and takeaway.

accuracyIssues.issue: Flow mixes three different decision criteria as if one decision tree: 'High control needed -> FDI', 'Moderate risk tolerance -> Joint venture', 'Low capital -> Exporting or franchising'. A firm with high control needs AND low capital gets contradictory outputs.
accuracyIssues.fix: Make the flow a single-variable ladder (commitment/control rising: export -> license/franchise -> JV -> FDI) and leave the multi-factor trade-off to the prose.

accuracyIssues.location: Strategic Analysis for Global Expansion > ansoff-global-context > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Examiners love asking which Ansoff quadrant a firm is using' is an overclaim for a Unit 4 (WBS14) section; Ansoff is Unit 3 (theories of corporate strategy). It can be used as an analytical tool in Unit 4 answers but is not what 4.2 questions target.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reframe as: 'Ansoff is Unit 3 content; in Unit 4 use it as one line of analysis when assessing the risk of entering a new country, not as the answer itself.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'roughly 93% run by franchisees' is dated (that was end-2019); McDonald's has reported ~95% franchised since 2021 and 40,000+ restaurants only from 2022 onward.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'over 40,000 restaurants ... about 95% franchised (2023)'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Ireland's low corporation tax rate (12.5%)' — since 2024 Ireland applies the OECD 15% minimum to groups with revenue over EUR 750m, which is exactly the US tech cohort the question is about. Historically correct, currently misleading.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'historically low 12.5% corporation tax (15% for the largest groups since 2024)'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Toyota Burnaston is a UK-centric example for an international-school audience (HK, Korea, SG, MY, PK, LK, Gulf) and its Brexit framing needs extra context these students lack.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use e.g. Samsung's FDI in Vietnam (Bac Ninh/Thai Nguyen) or Hyundai in Chennai; keep tariff-avoidance logic.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a 'push' factor for international expansion?
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer (index 1) is right, but push/pull factors are never taught in content[]; this can appear in the pre-test gate and the inline quiz for a block that does not mention them. (Indices are 0-based.)

quizIssues.question: A UK manufacturer moves its factory to Vietnam to take advantage of lower wages. This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Correct (off-shoring), but off-shoring vs outsourcing is not taught anywhere in content[] (only in flashcards/common_mistakes).

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best explains why a firm might extend its product life cycle through international expansion?
quizIssues.issue: Not taught in content[]. Distractors are throwaways ('reduce the quality', 'avoid domestic taxation') so the item tests nothing; the correct option is the only sensible sentence.

quizIssues.question: When assessing a country as a production location, which factor relates to the ability to move profits back to the home country?
quizIssues.issue: Not taught in content[]. 'Repatriation of profits' is not one of the listed IAL 4.2.3 bullets (closest is 'likely return on investment'); the question is answerable from vocabulary alone since only one option contains 'profits'.

quizIssues.question: How does a strengthening domestic currency affect an exporting business?
quizIssues.issue: Correct (index 1) and a genuine spec point (4.2.5 exchange rates), but exchange-rate effects are absent from content[]. Distractor 3 ('Domestic wages fall') is implausible filler.

quizIssues.question: Which of Porter's Five Forces would a firm consider when assessing whether it is easy for competitors to enter a new foreign market?
quizIssues.issue: Explanation contradicts the stem's framing: it says high barriers 'make a market more attractive for existing firms', but the firm in the question is itself the entrant, for whom high barriers are a deterrent. Porter's Five Forces is also not in content[] and is Unit 3 material.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is the BEST reason for a firm to acquire a foreign company rather than start from scratch?
quizIssues.issue: Two distractors are absolutes ('eliminates all risks', 'guarantees higher profit margins') that any student eliminates on wording alone; only option 0 is a real distractor. The reasons for global mergers (4.2.4) are not taught in content[].

quizIssues.question: How can a firm use 'natural hedging' to manage exchange rate risk?
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but hedging/natural hedging is not in content[] and is not an explicit IAL 4.2.5 bullet; fine as stretch, wrong as a pre-test item for this section.

practiceIssues.issue: 6-mark 'Analyse the advantages and disadvantages...' is not an IAL Business tariff (papers use 4 Explain / 8, 10, 12 Assess / 20 Evaluate). Also the stem ignores its own context ('a new overseas market' rather than 'the Indian market for this company'), so application marks cannot be targeted. (Indices 0-based.)

20-mark Evaluate is the right tariff, but (a) the stem is generic ('a new international market') while IAL 20-markers are anchored to the case ('...for this South Korean company entering Europe'), and (b) the guidance tells students to 'Apply Porter's generic strategies' which is irrelevant to entry-mode choice and is Unit 3 content. Guidance is a bullet list, not a levels-based mark scheme (knowledge/application/analysis/evaluation), so students cannot self-mark.
'Explain two reasons' for 4 marks does not match the IAL 4-mark format ('Explain one reason...' with knowledge + 3 linked development). No mark scheme, only a list of possible points.

4-mark 'Explain the difference between FDI and licensing' is answerable from definitions only; IAL 4-markers require a developed chain of reasoning. Guidance is a model answer without mark allocation.

10-mark Assess is well-formed and realistic, but the stem drops the context ('a European luxury goods company' rather than the Italian brand in Brazil/India/Nigeria) and the guidance gives no levels descriptors or indication that a supported judgement is required for Level 4.

structureIssues: Content[] vs assessment mismatch: content teaches entry modes, Ansoff, PESTLE, Bartlett-Ghoshal; quiz[]/flashcards[]/common_mistakes[] cover the real IAL 4.2 bullets (push/pull, off-shoring, PLC extension, country as market/production location, exchange rates, Porter, hedging). Pre-test (3 random MCQs from this bank) and inline quizzes therefore test untaught material for ~80% of items.

Neither block sets quizIndices or practiceIndices, so InlineQuiz/InlinePractice fall back to default selection; with quiz[0] = push factors and quiz[1] = off-shoring, the first block's inline MCQ is almost certainly on something the block does not mention.

Zero recall widgets in the whole section (0 reorder, 0 fillin): the only retrieval practice inside Learn Mode is two inline MCQs. This section has natural fillin material (push vs pull, off-shoring vs outsourcing, five reasons for global mergers/JVs) that is currently unused.

Each block has exactly 2 sections, so every step is the 'last step of a block': each of the two steps stacks NoteSection x2 + InlineQuiz + InlinePractice + ExplainItBack + TakeawayCard, making two very long steps with no lighter step in between.
0 diagrams for a section whose core idea (entry modes rising in control and risk) and secondary idea (Ansoff 2x2) are both inherently diagrammatic; InlineDiagram never renders.

Section numbering '4.3.2' does not match the IAL spec where 'Global markets and business expansion' is topic 4.2 (4.2.1-4.2.5); 4.3 is Global marketing. Students cross-referencing the spec will be confused (unsure whether the app uses its own numbering scheme deliberately).
Notes[] (2 notes) duplicate the same off-spec material (entry methods, Ansoff) rather than covering the spec bullets, so Notes tab and Learn tab reinforce the gap instead of filling it.

Misconception quality: franchising control (genuine), FDI always best (genuine but repeated verbatim in notes[0].misconception), Ansoff market development vs diversification (genuine); pestle-bartlett-ghoshal misconception is exam technique rather than a conceptual misconception (filler).

Flow blocks in exporting-licensing-franchising and ansoff-global-context are descriptive three-step restatements ('Firm wants international revenue -> Low capital -> Licenses IP'), not causal mechanisms; they add length without teaching anything the paragraph did not.
ialSpecGaps: 4.2.1 Conditions that prompt trade: push factors (saturated markets, competition) and pull factors (economies of scale, risk spreading) — only in quiz/flashcards, not taught in content[]
4.2.1 Possibility of off-shoring and outsourcing (and the distinction) — not taught in content[]
4.2.1 Extending the product life cycle by selling in multiple markets — not taught in content[]
4.2.2 Assessment of a country as a market: levels of disposable income, ease of doing business, infrastructure, political stability, exchange rate — not taught in content[]

4.2.3 Assessment of a country as a production location: costs of production, skills and availability of labour force, infrastructure, location in trade bloc, government incentives, ease of doing business, political stability, natural resources, likely return on investment — not taught in content[]

4.2.4 Reasons for global mergers or joint ventures: spreading risk over different countries/regions, entering new markets/trade blocs, acquiring national/international brand names/patents, securing resources/supplies, maintaining/increasing global competitiveness — content[] gives generic JV pros/cons only; the five spec reasons are not listed
4.2.5 Global competitiveness: impact of movements in exchange rates on exporters/importers — not taught in content[]
4.2.5 Competitive advantage through cost competitiveness and differentiation — not taught
4.2.5 Skill shortages and their impact on international competitiveness — not taught (only a flashcard)
strengths: Entry-mode ladder (exporting < licensing/franchising < JV < FDI by control and risk) is correct, clearly stated and consistently echoed in takeaways, notes and extras chains.

Franchising misconception ('trades direct operational control for contractual control') and the Ansoff market-development-vs-diversification misconception are real, well-phrased student errors with usable 'Instead write' lines.
Real examples are factually sound (McDonald's franchising, Netflix 190 countries, Toyota Burnaston tariff logic, Uber TfL/UberPop) and each is tied back to the concept rather than decorative.
Quiz correctIndex values are all correct; no double-correct options.
Practice[2] (10-mark Assess on luxury brand in Brazil/India/Nigeria) and practice[4] (20-mark Evaluate) have realistic, international contexts and guidance that pushes toward a judgement.

Flashcards and common_mistakes are well aligned to the actual IAL 4.2 spec (off-shoring vs outsourcing, ease of doing business index, exchange rates on both revenue and cost sides, listing-without-evaluating) and would be a good seed for rewriting content[].
topFixes: Rewrite content[] to teach IAL 4.2.1-4.2.5: block 1 = conditions that prompt trade (push/pull, off-shoring vs outsourcing, PLC extension) + assessing a country as a market; block 2 = assessing a country as a production location + reasons for global mergers/JVs; block 3 = global competitiveness (exchange rates, cost vs differentiation, skill shortages). Reuse the existing flashcards/common_mistakes as the source.
Remove Bartlett & Ghoshal (AQA-only) from the section; demote Ansoff and PESTLE to one-paragraph 'link to Unit 3' callouts rather than full subsections with examMatters claims.
Set quizIndices/practiceIndices on each block so inline quiz and practice match what the block teaches, and ensure every quiz item is covered by content[] so the pre-test gate is fair.

Fix practice tariffs and schemes: replace the 6-mark Analyse with an 8-mark Assess, make 4-markers 'Explain one...', anchor the 10- and 20-mark stems to their contexts, delete the Porter's generic strategies instruction, and add levels-based mark schemes (K/App/An/Ev) with a short model answer.

Add retrieval and visuals: fillin recalls for push vs pull and off-shoring vs outsourcing, a reorder recall on a genuine sequence (e.g. staged entry: export -> licence -> JV -> FDI as commitment rises), and a diagram of the control/risk ladder or the country-assessment factor comparison.

summary: The four prose subsections are well written, mostly accurate and pitched at the right level, with a good standardisation/glocalisation pair and a sensible 4Ps-through-culture lens. But the section does not teach half of what its own quiz and flashcards examine: ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric approaches, Ansoff, Porter's Strategic Matrix and global niche markets appear in 5 of 10 MCQs and in practice questions yet in no content[] section, so the PreTest gate (3 random MCQs) will regularly test untaught material. A full subsection is spent on Hofstede (not on the IAL spec) while spec bullets (marketing approaches, Ansoff, Porter, niche-market features, social media) are absent. There are zero recall exercises and zero diagrams, so Learn Mode here is two steps of reading plus one MCQ each. A strong IAL teacher would use the prose but would not consider this section spec-complete or exam-aligned.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] 'Cultural Influences on Global Marketing' > hofstede-dimensions > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: The KFC 'eat your fingers off' story is an unverified marketing legend (hedged with 'reportedly' but then built on as fact). More importantly it is presented as the Hofstede example yet applies no Hofstede dimension; it invokes 'high-context' (Edward Hall's framework, not Hofstede's) and asserts a translation error was inappropriate 'in a collectivist culture', which is a non-sequitur. Students copying this into an exam would show confused theory.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with an example that actually uses a dimension, e.g. high uncertainty-avoidance Japan and the emphasis on guarantees/detailed information in car or appliance marketing, or collectivist family-centred advertising by Coca-Cola/McDonald's in China; move the KFC translation anecdote (clearly labelled as anecdotal) to the cultural-mistakes section if kept at all.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] 'Cultural Influences on Global Marketing' > hofstede-dimensions (whole section)
accuracyIssues.issue: Hofstede's cultural dimensions are not in the Pearson IAL Business WBS14 spec (4.3.3 Cultural/social factors lists cultural differences, different tastes, language, unintended meanings, inappropriate translations, inappropriate branding and promotion, social media). A full 25% of the section's teaching time goes to off-spec theory while spec bullets are untaught. Not wrong, but misleading about what is examinable.
accuracyIssues.fix: Keep Hofstede as an optional 'extras' evaluation chain (it already exists in extras.chains[2]) and replace the content section with spec-listed cultural/social factors, including social media.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'glocalisation is usually the strongest evaluative point' teaches a stock conclusion. IAL levels-based mark schemes reward a judgement justified from the case context; an examiner will not credit 'glocalisation' as a default answer, and for some cases (luxury, B2B components, commodities) standardisation is the better-supported judgement.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword: 'Your judgement should depend on the case: product type, cultural distance between markets, and the firm's resources. Often the strongest answer specifies which 4Ps elements to standardise and which to adapt, and why for THIS firm.'

accuracyIssues.issue: The Chevrolet Nova 'no va' failure is a well-documented myth: the car sold adequately in Venezuela and Mexico, and 'nova' as one word reads as 'new star' in Spanish. common_mistakes[4] even builds a recommendation on it ('demonstrates that even large, well-resourced firms can fail'). A knowledgeable examiner would mark this as a false example.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a verified case (e.g. Pepsi's 'Come alive' slogan issues in Taiwan is also contested; safer: HSBC's 2009 'Assume Nothing' rebrand after it translated as 'Do Nothing' in several markets, or Ikea product names needing renaming in Thailand).

accuracyIssues.issue: Context describes 'a major American fast-food chain' with 'significant difficulties in India'. Every recognisable candidate (McDonald's, KFC, Domino's, Subway) is a well-known Indian success story precisely because of menu adaptation, and this section's own glocalisation example (McSpicy Paneer) says so. The scenario contradicts the taught content and would confuse students who bring real knowledge.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either make the firm explicitly fictional with a stated cause of difficulty, or flip it to match reality (success in India after heavy adaptation; difficulties in, say, Bolivia/Iceland where McDonald's actually withdrew).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Beverly in Italy' was discontinued by Coca-Cola in 2009; presenting it in the present tense ('offers local flavours like ... Beverly in Italy') is out of date.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use Thums Up (India), Georgia coffee (Japan) or Inca Kola (Peru, majority-owned by Coca-Cola) instead.

accuracyIssues.issue: Content lists four dimensions and the takeaway says 'Hofstede's dimensions (individualism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity)'; notes[1] lists five (adds long-term orientation); the framework has six. Minor inconsistency across surfaces.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either state 'Hofstede's original four dimensions (later extended to six)' in content, or align notes to the same list.

accuracyIssues.issue: Takeaway 'Adaptation: tailored to each market — higher relevance but higher costs and complexity' summarises a strategy that has no section of its own in the block; adaptation is only mentioned as a foil inside standardisation/glocalisation. Takeaway does not match what was taught.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either add a short 'Local adaptation' section (ideally merged with the ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric approaches) or drop this bullet.

quizIssues.question: Unilever sells single-use sachets of shampoo in India instead of full-sized bottles. This is an example of adapting which element of the marketing mix?
quizIssues.issue: Two options are defensible. Sachets are a packaging/size change (Product) that enables a lower price point (Price); Edexcel textbooks describe sachet strategies under product adaptation as often as under pricing. The explanation itself says 'by selling smaller quantities' (a product change). correctIndex=1 (Price) will be marked wrong for a student who reasonably answers Product.

quizIssues.question: Why might comparative advertising (naming competitors) be problematic in Asian markets?
quizIssues.issue: Distractors 'Asian consumers do not watch television' and 'Competitors in Asia do not have brand names' are absurd rather than plausible; the item cannot discriminate. Also 'Asian markets' is an over-generalisation (comparative advertising is legal in e.g. Singapore and Hong Kong).

quizIssues.question: Which marketing approach involves fully adapting the strategy to each local market with local teams making key decisions?
quizIssues.issue: correctIndex=2 (Polycentric) is correct, but the ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric terminology is never taught in content[]; it exists only in flashcards. As a PreTest item it tests untaught material.

quizIssues.question: According to Ansoff's Matrix, a firm selling its existing products in a new geographical market is pursuing:
quizIssues.issue: Correct (Market development) but Ansoff is not taught anywhere in content[]; only a flashcard covers it.

quizIssues.question: Which of Porter's generic strategies would best describe Ryanair's global approach?
quizIssues.issue: Ryanair is a European short-haul carrier, not a global business, so 'global approach' is odd wording. Porter's Strategic Matrix is not taught in content[]. Option 'Stuck in the middle' is not one of Porter's generic strategies (it is the failure state) and 'Focus (differentiation)' is awkwardly phrased. Correct answer (Cost leadership) is right.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic of global niche markets?
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but global niche markets (spec 4.3.2) are not taught in content[]; students only meet them in flashcards/extras.

quizIssues.question: A luxury watch brand uses the same marketing strategy worldwide with no local adaptation. This best describes which approach?
quizIssues.issue: Ethnocentric is correct per spec terminology, but the term is untaught in content[]. Distractor 'Glocal' is not a recognised approach name (spec uses domestic/ethnocentric, mixed/geocentric, international/polycentric) and looks like a filler option.

quizIssues.question: In China, the colour white is associated with:
quizIssues.issue: Pure trivia recall; a student who knows the concept (colour symbolism varies, so audit packaging) can still get it wrong, and one who gets it right has shown no business understanding. Not the kind of item IAL papers ask.

quizIssues.question: KitKat offering matcha flavour in Japan and dulce de leche flavour in Argentina demonstrates:
quizIssues.issue: Fine and correct, but it is conceptually the same item as index 0 (brand-with-local-product = glocalisation/product adaptation); the bank has two items on one idea and none on language/translation/social media.

practiceIssues.issue: 4-mark 'Explain what is meant by X and give one example' is a GCSE/UK-style define-and-example item. IAL Business 4-markers are 'Explain one reason/benefit/way...' marked Knowledge 2 + Application 2. Guidance is prose, not a mark scheme (no K/A split).
6-mark 'Analyse' is a valid IAL tariff, but the guidance is a bullet-dump of ten points with no levels descriptors (Level 1-3, K/A/An), so a student cannot self-mark. Context is fine and realistic.

10-mark 'Assess the extent to which' matches the IAL tariff and the Swiss-watch context is usable, but the question stem is generic ('for an international business') rather than tied to the given firm as IAL 10-markers are; guidance has no levels (K/A/An/E) descriptors. Also tests niche markets, which content[] never teaches.

'Explain two ways ... ' for 4 marks is not an IAL question form (that is a 2+2 GCSE pattern); IAL asks 'Explain one...' at 4 marks. Guidance also conflates 'adapting product ranges for local tastes' with Ansoff product development; adapting an existing product for a new geographic market is still market development in Edexcel mark schemes. Ansoff is untaught in content[].

20-mark 'Evaluate the extent to which' matches the tariff and guidance has genuine counter-argument and judgement lines (good). But the context contradicts real-world knowledge and the section's own McDonald's-India example (see accuracyIssues), and there is no levels grid or indicative marks split.

structureIssues: Zero recall exercises (0 reorder, 0 fillin) and 0 diagrams: with 2 blocks of 2 sections each, Learn Mode is exactly 2 steps, each of which is read, read, one MCQ, one written question, explain-it-back, takeaway. No spaced/immediate recall widgets fire at all.

Quiz/content mismatch: 5 of 10 MCQs (indices 1,3,4,6,8) examine terms never taught in content[] (ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric, Ansoff, Porter, niche markets). The PreTest draws 3 random items from this bank, so roughly half of pretests will contain untaught material, which directly feeds the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Block 1 'Standardisation vs Adaptation' has sections on standardisation and glocalisation only; the spec's three named approaches (domestic/ethnocentric, mixed/geocentric, international/polycentric) are the examinable vocabulary and are absent, while takeaway[1] summarises an 'Adaptation' section that does not exist.

Block 2 spends one of two sections on Hofstede (off-spec) and compresses six spec bullets (language, unintended meanings, translations, branding/promotion, social media, different tastes) into one section; social media is never mentioned anywhere in content[].

Section is numbered 4.3.3 and titled 'Global Marketing', but in the IAL WBS14 spec 4.3 is the topic ('Global marketing') with 4.3.1 Marketing, 4.3.2 Niche markets, 4.3.3 Cultural/social factors. The content spans 4.3.1 and 4.3.3 but the numbering suggests only the latter; niche markets (4.3.2) exist only in flashcards/quiz/practice/extras.

Misconceptions: global-standardisation ('always cheaper') and cultural-mistakes-brand-impact ('only translations') are genuine student errors. glocalisation's misconception ('simple middle ground') is filler: it is an assertion that glocalisation is 'harder, not easier' rather than a correction of something students actually write. hofstede-dimensions' is plausible but concerns an off-spec framework.

No 'realExample' or body text provides a verified language/translation/branding failure inside content[]; the only such examples are in flashcards (Nova, mythical) and the KFC anecdote, so the spec bullets most likely to appear in a 4/6-marker have the thinnest, least reliable evidence.

Difficulty ramp is flat rather than sensible: both steps are at the same descriptive level; there is no progression from definitions (approaches) to application (4Ps decisions) to strategic frameworks (Ansoff/Porter) to evaluation, even though the quiz and practice assume the last two.
ialSpecGaps: 4.3.1 (b) Different marketing approaches: domestic/ethnocentric, mixed/geocentric, international/polycentric — not taught in content[] (flashcards/quiz only)
4.3.1 (d) Applying Ansoff's Matrix to global marketing (market development, product development, diversification in an international context) — not taught in content[]
4.3.1 (e) Applying Porter's Strategic Matrix (cost leadership, differentiation, focus) to global marketing — not taught in content[] (one 'link' line in notes only)
4.3.2 (b) Features of global niche markets — not taught in content[]
4.3.2 (c) Application and adaptation of the marketing mix (4Ps) to suit global niches — not taught
4.3.3 (g) Social media as a cultural/social factor in global marketing — not mentioned anywhere in the section

4.3.3 (c)-(f) Language, unintended meanings, inappropriate translations, inappropriate branding and promotion — mentioned in one paragraph of cultural-mistakes-brand-impact but without a reliable worked example (unsure how deep IAL papers go, but a 4/6-mark 'Explain one reason a translation error damages a brand' is a plausible item and is under-supported)
Hofstede's cultural dimensions (taught at length) are NOT a spec requirement for WBS14 — reverse gap
strengths: global-standardisation and glocalisation sections are clear, correctly define the terms, and the 4Ps walkthrough in glocalisation (McArabia / local pricing / local celebrities / local channels) is exactly how IAL application marks are earned.

Misconception on global-standardisation ('savings only matter if the product sells') is a genuine and well-corrected student error; cultural-mistakes-brand-impact's 'not just translation' misconception is also real.
The Fair & Lovely / Glow & Lovely (2020) example is accurate, current and relevant to international-school students in South Asia and the Middle East.
examMatters in cultural-mistakes-brand-impact ('culture affects all 4Ps, not just promotion') correctly targets a common weakness in student answers.

Practice questions 2 and 4 (6-mark Analyse, 20-mark Evaluate) use correct IAL command words and tariffs, and the 20-mark guidance contains a real counter-argument and judgement line rather than a one-sided list.
Flashcards[1-3] define ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric using the spec's exact pairings (domestic/mixed/international), so the vocabulary is available to lift into content[].
extras.evaluation[1] correctly notes Hofstede's IBM-era data limitations; hofstede-dimensions body also flags this rather than presenting the framework as gospel.
topFixes: Add a content section teaching the three spec approaches (domestic/ethnocentric, mixed/geocentric, international/polycentric) plus short sections applying Ansoff's Matrix and Porter's Strategic Matrix to global marketing, and a niche-markets section; until then, remove quiz indices 1,3,4,6,8 from the bank so the PreTest and InlineQuiz only test taught material.

Replace the Hofstede section with a spec-aligned 'Language, translation, branding and social media' section using verified examples (drop the Chevrolet Nova myth from flashcards[11]/common_mistakes[4]; replace the KFC anecdote), and demote Hofstede to the existing extras chain.

Fix quiz index 2 (sachets: accept Product or rewrite the stem to ask about 'price point', e.g. 'selling at a lower unit price to match low incomes') and rewrite quiz index 7's absurd distractors; retire the white-colour trivia item (index 5).

Add recall widgets and one diagram: a fillin on the three approach names (template 'A ___ approach applies the home-market mix abroad; a ___ approach adapts fully per country; a ___ approach mixes the two'), a reorder on the glocalisation decision process (audit culture → decide which 4Ps to standardise vs adapt → test locally → launch), and a standardisation–adaptation spectrum or Ansoff grid diagram.

Convert practice guidance into IAL levels mark schemes (K/A/An/E with level descriptors), change practice[3] to 'Explain one way...' (4 marks), fix the product-development conflation in its guidance, and repair the practice[4] India context so it does not contradict the section's own McDonald's example.

summary: The prose is well written and the real examples (Shell 1973, Kodak 2012, Nadella 2014, $300bn to $2tn) check out, and Lewin/Kotter are explained correctly. But a strong IAL teacher would not use it as-is: the Learn Mode content[] teaches a consultancy-flavoured 'managing change' (Christensen's disruption, Kotter's 8 steps, Shell-style strategic scenarios) while IAL 3.6 actually assesses causes and effects of change, key factors (culture, size, speed, resistance), and 'scenario planning' in the sense of risk assessment, business continuity, succession planning and costs/benefits of contingency planning. Eight of the ten quiz MCQs and one practice question test material the lesson never teaches, so the pre-test/post-test loop measures nothing. There are zero recall widgets and zero diagrams despite the section literally telling students to draw a force field diagram and despite Kotter's 8 steps being a textbook reorder candidate. The section also conflates 'disruptive change' (an external market phenomenon, as it defines it) with step/transformational change (a firm's own response), and uses three different vocabularies across content, notes and flashcards.

accuracyIssues.location: Types of Change > incremental-vs-disruptive-change > examMatters ('use disruptive change when external forces ... make the current model unsustainable')
accuracyIssues.issue: Conflates two different concepts. The body defines disruptive change as something that 'comes from outside the established players' and 'destroys incumbents' (Christensen), i.e. a market phenomenon done TO a firm. examMatters then tells the student the firm should 'use disruptive change' as a management choice. A firm cannot 'use' disruption; it undertakes step/transformational change in response to it. The notes[] compound this with 'Disruptive (step) change' and the flashcards switch to 'transformational change', so three vocabularies for one idea.
accuracyIssues.fix: Teach 'incremental vs step (transformational) change' as the two types of organisational change (matching flashcards and IAL textbooks). Treat disruption as an external CAUSE of change, and reword examMatters: 'step change is needed when external disruption makes the current model unsustainable'.

accuracyIssues.location: Types of Change > drivers-and-scenario-planning > body paragraph 3, flow, keyIdea, misconception; notes[2] 'Scenario Planning'
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Scenario planning' is taught as Shell-style strategic foresight (2-4 futures, best/worst/most-likely/wildcard). In IAL 3.6.3 the heading 'Scenario planning' means identifying key risks through risk assessment (natural disasters, IT failure, loss of key staff), planning for risk mitigation (business continuity, succession planning) and the costs/benefits of contingency planning. A student who answers a 3.6.3 question with Shell scenarios will miss the indicative content entirely. The section's own quiz (Q5, Q6, Q9), flashcards (contingency, business continuity, succession, COVID) and practice Q4 use the spec meaning, so the lesson contradicts its own assessment items.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite the section (ideally as its own block) around risk assessment -> mitigation (business continuity, succession planning) -> cost/benefit of contingency planning. Keep the Shell example as a one-line aside that scenario planning in the wider sense also covers strategic futures.

accuracyIssues.location: Managing Resistance > why-people-resist-change > body paragraphs 1 and 3; block takeaway[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: Two different 'number one' causes in the same section: 'Resistance to change is the single biggest reason organisational change fails' and 'Poor communication is the number one reason change fails'. Both are unevidenced assertions and they contradict each other; the takeaway repeats '#1 cause'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Present poor communication as a major cause of resistance (which in turn causes failure), and drop the 'number one'/'single biggest' superlatives or attribute them.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975 but buried the technology' is the popular myth. Sasson's 1975 prototype is correct and the January 2012 Chapter 11 filing is correct, but Kodak did commercialise digital (DCS line from 1991, EasyShare; it was the top US digital camera seller by units around 2005). The real lesson is that digital could not replicate film's margins and Kodak was late to shift its business model, not that it hid the technology.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword: 'Kodak built the first digital camera prototype in 1975 and later sold digital cameras, but kept protecting its high-margin film business and never rebuilt its model around digital; it filed for bankruptcy in 2012.'

accuracyIssues.location: Managing Resistance > managing-change-models > examMatters ('For top marks, use both models together. Draw Lewin's force field diagram...')
accuracyIssues.issue: Overstates how IAL Business is marked. Levels-based mark schemes for Assess/Evaluate reward knowledge, application to the case, developed chains of analysis and a justified judgement. Using two frameworks or drawing a diagram is not required for the top level, and a diagram earns nothing in itself. Also the section provides no force field diagram (diagrams: 0) while telling the student to draw one.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say: 'One model applied properly to the case beats two recited. If you use Lewin, name the specific driving/restraining forces from the case and weigh them; if you use Kotter, explain which steps the firm has skipped.' Add an actual force field diagram.

accuracyIssues.location: Types of Change > incremental-vs-disruptive-change > examMatters ('Examiners want you to distinguish clearly between the two types')
accuracyIssues.issue: Incremental vs disruptive change is not an IAL 3.6 assessment point; the spec assesses causes of change (organisational size, poor performance, new ownership, transformational leadership, external factors), effects of change, and key factors in successful change. The claim over-promises exam relevance of off-spec content.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reframe examMatters around what the case study is likely to ask: identify the cause of change in the case, whether it is incremental or step change, and its likely effects on stakeholders/competitiveness.

accuracyIssues.location: Managing Resistance > managing-change-models > body paragraph 1 (Kotter's 8 steps)
accuracyIssues.issue: Step names mix Kotter's 1996 and 2014 versions ('Communicate the vision', 'Remove barriers', 'Sustain acceleration', 'Anchor in culture') and differ from notes[1] ('empower', 'build on gains', 'embed in culture'). Not wrong, but inconsistent naming makes the model harder to memorise and any future reorder recall harder to grade.
accuracyIssues.fix: Pick one version (the classic 1996 list is what IAL textbooks use) and use identical wording in content, notes and any recall.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'generated quick wins (Azure growth, Teams adoption)': Teams launched in 2017, three years into Nadella's tenure, so it is not a 'short-term win' in Kotter's sense. Market cap figures ($300bn in 2014, >$2tn by 2021) are correct.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use Office 365/Azure growth in 2014-15 as the short-term wins; cite Teams under 'sustain acceleration'.

quizIssues.question: According to Kotter and Schlesinger, which strategy for overcoming resistance should be used as a LAST resort?
quizIssues.issue: Tests Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies (education/communication, participation, facilitation, negotiation, manipulation/co-optation, coercion), which the content[] never teaches; the lesson teaches Kotter's 8-STEP model, so students will conflate the two Kotters. Answer itself (coercion) is fine as textbook framing, though K&S actually say coercion is appropriate when speed is essential.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is the MOST significant risk highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic?
quizIssues.issue: Odd wording: 'inadequate business continuity planning' is a weakness, not a risk, and 'MOST significant' is opinion with no case context. Business continuity planning is also never taught in content[] (only in flashcards). Distractors (poor marketing, excessive diversification) are nonsense for the stem.

quizIssues.question: Which type of organisational culture is MOST likely to embrace change?
quizIssues.issue: Handy's four cultures are never mentioned in this section's content[] (they belong to 3.4.2). Answer is also arguable: a power culture can change very fast because one person decides; 'task culture' is the textbook answer but 'Power culture' is a defensible distractor, so the question is partly a guess about author intent.

quizIssues.question: A key characteristic of transformational leadership is:
quizIssues.issue: Transformational vs transactional leadership is not taught anywhere in content[] (flashcards only). Correct answer and distractors are fine.

quizIssues.question: Succession planning involves:
quizIssues.issue: Succession planning is not taught in content[]. Question itself is fine.

quizIssues.question: Large organisations tend to change MORE slowly because of:
quizIssues.issue: Effect of organisational size on change (spec 3.6.2) is not taught in content[]. Question itself is fine.

quizIssues.question: The main argument AGAINST extensive contingency planning is:
quizIssues.issue: Costs/benefits of contingency planning (spec 3.6.3c) never taught in content[]. Question is fine; 'It is always unnecessary' and 'Risks can never be predicted' are throwaway distractors.

quizIssues.question: Which pair of leadership styles is correctly contrasted?
quizIssues.issue: Not taught in content[]; options B-D are self-evidently wrong so the item is trivial.

quizIssues.question: Resistance to change is MOST likely to arise from:
quizIssues.issue: Trivial: distractors 'Increased profitability', 'Strong transformational leadership', 'Successful contingency planning' are implausible. Replace with plausible causes vs non-causes (e.g. 'clear communication of the reasons for change' as a distractor).

quizIssues.question: Incremental change is best described as:
quizIssues.issue: Explanation uses 'evolutionary' and 'transformational', terms the content never uses (it says 'disruptive'). Minor terminology drift.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Explain two reasons ... (4)' is not the IAL Business pattern: 4-mark Explain questions ask for ONE reason developed in a chain (knowledge + two linked development/application marks) and are anchored to the case. No context is given. Guidance is a list, not a developed answer.

'Analyse ... (6 marks)': IAL Business papers use 4/8/10/12/20 tariffs with Assess at 8/10/12; a 6-mark Analyse is not an IAL Unit 3 question type (verify against recent WBS13 papers). Guidance content is good and includes a limitation of the model.

10-mark Assess tariff is right, but the stem is generic ('in managing organisational change successfully') rather than anchored to the bank ('...in managing the bank's digital transformation'); IAL stems always reference the case. Guidance is usable and ends with a judgement (necessary but not sufficient).

'Explain the difference between contingency planning and crisis management (4)': 'crisis management' is not on the IAL spec and neither term is taught in content[]; 'Explain the difference' is not an IAL stem. Replace with a contextual 'Explain one reason why [firm] should have a succession plan (4)' or 'Explain one benefit of business continuity planning for [firm] (4)'.

20-mark Evaluate tariff is correct and guidance is thorough (strategies, counter-arguments, context, judgement). Stem is generic ('in a large organisation') instead of naming the insurance company. No levels descriptors, but that is consistent with the rest of the file.

structureIssues: Content/assessment mismatch is the core defect: 8 of 10 quiz MCQs (indices 0,2,3,4,5,6,7,8) and practice index 3 test spec content (Handy cultures, Kotter & Schlesinger, transformational leadership, succession planning, business continuity, size of organisation, contingency-planning costs) that the content[] blocks never teach. The PreTest draws 3 random MCQs from this bank, so most students will be pre-tested on things the lesson then ignores, and the PostTest 'improvement' is noise.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) in a section that contains the best genuine sequence in the whole unit: Kotter's 8 steps. Also no fillin for Lewin's driving/restraining forces. Learn Mode steps therefore have no retrieval practice beyond one MCQ per block.

Zero diagrams, yet managing-change-models > examMatters instructs students to 'Draw Lewin's force field diagram'. A force field diagram (driving arrows vs restraining arrows on a line marked 'current state') is the obvious InlineDiagram and would also make the 'reduce restraining forces' insight concrete.

Only 2 blocks x 2 sections = 2 Learn Mode steps for an entire spec topic (3.6.1-3.6.3). No block covers effects of change, key factors in successful change (culture, size, speed) or risk/contingency planning. Suggested structure: Block 1 Causes and types of change; Block 2 Effects and key factors (culture, size, speed, leadership); Block 3 Managing resistance (K&S strategies + Lewin + Kotter); Block 4 Scenario/contingency planning (risk assessment, business continuity, succession, cost/benefit).

realExample misplaced: drivers-and-scenario-planning carries the Toyota kaizen example, which illustrates incremental change (section 1), not drivers or scenario planning. Section 1 already has Kodak; scenario planning has no example at all despite Shell being mentioned in the body.
