Both sections in block 'Managing Resistance' use the same Microsoft/Nadella example with the same emoji; the second is a near-repeat of the first. One should be swapped for a resistance-specific case (e.g. a failed IT rollout or a factory automation programme).

Block 1 title 'Types of Change' does not describe its second section (drivers + scenario planning); takeaway[1] and [2] are about content the title does not signal. Block 2 title 'Managing Resistance' is fine and its takeaways match.

Blocks have no quizIndices/practiceIndices, so the InlineQuiz/InlinePractice shown at the end of each step cannot be aligned to what the step taught; with this quiz bank the block on Kotter/Lewin may surface a succession-planning MCQ.

Terminology drift across surfaces: content says 'disruptive change', notes[0] says 'Disruptive (step) change', flashcards say 'transformational change', quiz explanation says 'evolutionary'. Students revising across tabs see four labels for two concepts.

Misconceptions: scenario-planning-vs-forecasting and resistance-as-signal are genuine. 'Students assume disruptive change is always better' (section 1) and 'Students present Kotter's 8 steps as rigid and linear' (section 4) are weak/filler for an IAL student; notes[0] 'Students treat all change as equally difficult' is filler.
meta.number is '3.3.6' while the IAL spec heading is 3.6 Managing change (unsure whether the app deliberately prefixes unit number; flagging in case it is a typo that mis-sorts the section).
ialSpecGaps: 3.6.1a Causes of change: 'changes in organisational size', 'poor business performance', 'new ownership', 'transformational leadership', 'market and other external factors' are only partly covered by one paragraph of internal/external drivers; new ownership and transformational leadership are absent from content[] (transformational leadership appears only in flashcards/quiz).
3.6.1b Possible effects of change on competitiveness, productivity, financial performance and stakeholders: not taught anywhere in content[], notes[] or flashcards.

3.6.2 Key factors in successful change: organisational culture, size of organisation, time/speed of change: absent from content[] (culture and size appear only in flashcards and quiz). 'Managing resistance to change' is covered, but Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies (the standard mark-scheme content, and what quiz index 2 tests) are not taught.
3.6.3a Identifying key risks through risk assessment: natural disasters, IT failure, loss of key staff: absent from content[] (flashcards only).
3.6.3b Planning for risk mitigation: business continuity and succession planning: absent from content[] (flashcards only).
3.6.3c Costs and benefits of contingency planning: absent from content[]; only notes[2].takeaway[2] mentions limitations, and quiz index 8 tests it.
(Exact IAL bullet wording recalled from the 2018 WBS13 spec; wording confidence high, numbering of sub-bullets unsure.)
strengths: Real examples are factually sound where checked: Shell and the 1973 oil crisis (Pierre Wack's scenario team), Kodak's 1975 prototype and 2012 bankruptcy, Nadella appointed February 2014, 'know-it-all' to 'learn-it-all', 'mobile-first, cloud-first', market cap roughly $300bn to over $2tn.

Lewin's force field analysis and Kotter's 8 steps are explained accurately and concisely, and the 'it is often easier to reduce restraining forces than to push harder' insight is exactly the evaluative point IAL mark schemes reward.

Misconceptions on scenario planning vs forecasting (drivers-and-scenario-planning) and resistance-as-useful-signal (why-people-resist-change) are genuine student errors and give a ready-made evaluation sentence.
Practice guidance for the 10- and 20-mark questions (indices 2 and 4) gives balanced indicative content, applies to the context and ends with a judgement, so it is usable as a model outline.

The flashcards and quiz, taken as a set, already cover the IAL 3.6 bullets (culture, size, transformational vs transactional leadership, risk types, business continuity, succession planning, cost/benefit of contingency planning). The raw material for fixing the content[] is already in the file.
topFixes: Rewrite 'Drivers of Change and Scenario Planning' (or add a new block) to teach IAL 3.6.3 as the spec means it: risk assessment (natural disasters, IT failure, loss of key staff) -> mitigation (business continuity, succession planning) -> costs vs benefits of contingency planning. Demote Shell-style strategic scenarios to one sentence.

Add a block on effects of change (competitiveness, productivity, financial performance, stakeholders) and key factors in successful change (organisational culture, size, speed of change, transformational leadership) plus Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies, so that quiz indices 0,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 and practice index 3 test material the lesson actually teaches; then set quizIndices/practiceIndices per block.

Fix the disruptive/step conflation: rename the type-of-change pair to incremental vs step (transformational) change across content, notes and flashcards; treat disruption as an external cause; reword the section-1 examMatters that tells firms to 'use disruptive change'.

Add recall widgets and a diagram: a reorder recall for Kotter's 8 steps (genuine procedural sequence; use one consistent wording), a fillin for Lewin's driving/restraining forces, and an InlineDiagram of a force field so the 'draw the diagram' advice is backed by one. Move the Toyota example to section 1 and replace the duplicate Nadella example.

Bring practice questions to IAL form: contextual 'Explain one reason... (4)' instead of 'Explain two'; convert the 6-mark Analyse to an 8-mark Assess; anchor the 10- and 20-mark stems to the bank / insurance company; replace the off-spec crisis-management question with a succession-planning or business-continuity question.

summary: The four Learn Mode sections are well-written, factually mostly sound, and model IAL-style balanced evaluation properly (each benefit is challenged, judgement is made context-dependent). But an IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is: the Learn Mode content[] covers only the 'impact' half of the spec (host/home impacts, transfer pricing) and completely omits 'controlling MNCs' (political influence, legal control, pressure groups, social media), marketing ethics, balance of payments and business culture, while 6 of the 10 quiz MCQs and the PreTest gate draw on exactly that untaught material (Rana Plaza, greenwashing x2, pressure groups, self-regulation, boycotts). Transfer pricing is taught twice in near-identical form across the two blocks, there are zero recall widgets and zero diagrams so the section is passive reading plus one MCQ per block, and the practice set uses non-IAL formats ('Explain two...' for 4 marks; a context-free 20-mark 'global economy' essay). One example is out of date (Amazon Luxembourg routing) and one claim is economically misleading (repatriated profits exceeding the investment 'makes the host country a net loser').

accuracyIssues.issue: 'In extreme cases, repatriated profits exceed the original investment, making the host country a net loser.' This is a fallacy: any profitable long-lived investment eventually returns more than its initial capital; that does not make the host a net loser because the host retains wages, supplier spending, tax and capital stock. It teaches a common student error as fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with: 'Because profits are repatriated, the host economy keeps only the wages, supplier spending and taxes generated locally, not the full value added — so the benefit to the host is smaller than the headline output figure suggests.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] 'Transfer Pricing & FDI Stakeholders' > fdi-stakeholder-analysis > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Present tense 'Amazon routes European sales through a Luxembourg subsidiary, reducing tax paid in countries like the UK, Germany, and France' is out of date: Amazon began booking retail sales through local branches in the UK, Germany, Italy, Spain and France in May 2015. The example as written is ~a decade stale and a well-read student/teacher will know it.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite in past tense ('Until 2015 Amazon booked...') and add that Amazon changed its structure under political pressure, or swap for a current case (e.g. Google/Meta digital services tax disputes) that illustrates the same home/host divergence.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'proposes a global minimum corporate tax rate of 15%' — the 15% minimum (Pillar Two of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework, agreed Oct 2021) is being implemented, in force in the EU, UK, Japan, Korea etc. from 2024, not merely proposed. Also, arm's-length pricing predates BEPS (OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines) rather than being established by it.
accuracyIssues.fix: '...and a global minimum corporate tax of 15% (Pillar Two), which major economies began applying from 2024' and 'reinforces the long-standing arm's-length principle'.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] > transfer-pricing-mechanism > misconception; content[0] > mnc-negative-impacts-ethics > body[2]
accuracyIssues.issue: Transfer pricing is presented as synonymous with tax avoidance ('transfer pricing is a form of legal tax avoidance'). Transfer pricing itself is a neutral, unavoidable accounting practice for any multi-subsidiary firm; it is the manipulation of transfer prices away from arm's length that constitutes avoidance, and where it breaches arm's-length rules tax authorities can reassess and penalise it (i.e. it is not always legal). IAL mark schemes define transfer pricing as the price charged between parts of the same business and then explain how it can be used to reduce tax.
accuracyIssues.fix: Define transfer pricing neutrally first, then: 'Manipulating transfer prices away from arm's length to shift profit is a form of tax avoidance; it is legal only while it stays within what tax authorities accept as arm's length.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Profit was repatriated to shareholders in London and The Hague' while 'local communities suffered' omits that Shell operates in Nigeria through the SPDC joint venture in which the Nigerian state (NNPC) holds 55% and takes the majority of oil revenue. Presenting it as pure extraction by a foreign MNC is misleading and an examiner would expect the governance/state-capture angle, which the section elsewhere claims to emphasise.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add one clause: 'most oil revenue actually went to the Nigerian state through its 55% JV stake, yet little reached the Delta — illustrating that weak host governance, not just the MNC, determined who captured the gains.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'a pattern sometimes called the resource curse' — the resource curse refers to poor development outcomes in resource-dependent economies generally (Dutch disease, rent-seeking), not specifically to MNCs extracting with minimal local benefit. Loose use of an Economics term in a Business section.
accuracyIssues.fix: Drop the term or say 'often linked to the resource curse'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'accounts for roughly a quarter of Vietnam's total exports' was true c.2017-2019; by 2022-2024 Samsung's share was closer to 15-20% as Vietnamese exports diversified. 'over 100,000 workers' is at the top of the reported range (c.90-110k). Not wrong, but a dated snapshot with no date.
accuracyIssues.fix: Anchor the figures to a year ('in 2018 roughly a quarter') or soften to 'around a fifth'.

accuracyIssues.location: flashcards[17] 'UK Modern Slavery Act 2015'; practice[1].guidance 'modern slavery legislation'
accuracyIssues.issue: UK-specific legislation presented without framing for an international cohort; not on the IAL spec and IAL papers do not expect it.
accuracyIssues.fix: Keep as one optional example but label it as a UK example of 'legal control' alongside non-UK equivalents (e.g. EU CSDDD, Australia's Modern Slavery Act 2018).

quizIssues.question: The Rana Plaza disaster in Bangladesh highlighted which issue in MNC supply chains?
quizIssues.issue: Rana Plaza appears nowhere in content[] (only flashcards[1] and common_mistakes). Because PreTest samples 3 random MCQs from this bank and InlineQuiz draws from it, students are examined on material Learn Mode never teaches.

quizIssues.question: What is greenwashing?
quizIssues.issue: Greenwashing is not taught in content[] (flashcards only). Same untaught-material problem; and it duplicates Q9's concept, so 2 of 10 questions test one term that is not in the lesson.

quizIssues.question: Which method of controlling MNCs involves organisations like Greenpeace campaigning against unethical practices?
quizIssues.issue: 'Controlling MNCs' is entirely absent from content[]. Also the stem gives the answer away: 'organisations ... campaigning' maps directly onto 'Pressure group activism'; no thinking required.

quizIssues.question: Why is self-regulation by MNCs often criticised?
quizIssues.issue: Self-regulation/CSR window-dressing is not in content[]. The correct option is also the longest and the only one phrased as a nuanced evaluation, which cues it.

quizIssues.question: A clothing brand markets its products as 'sustainably sourced' but an investigation reveals most materials come from factories with poor environmental records. This is an example of:
quizIssues.issue: Untaught concept (greenwashing) and duplicates Q4. Otherwise the best-written item in the bank (application-level).

quizIssues.question: What is the most likely limitation of using consumer boycotts to control MNC behaviour?
quizIssues.issue: Consumer pressure/boycotts not taught in content[]. Distractors are weak: 'Consumers never care about ethical issues' and 'Boycotts are illegal in most countries' are absolutes no student would pick; correct option is by far the longest.

quizIssues.question: Transfer pricing is used by MNCs to:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option (index 1) is ~3x longer than each distractor and is the only one mentioning 'subsidiaries', a strong surface cue. Stem is also leading ('is used by MNCs to') implying the sole purpose is tax, reinforcing the accuracy issue above.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a negative impact of MNCs on local economies?
quizIssues.issue: 'Crowding out' is discussed only in notes/flashcards, not content[]; correct option is again the longest. Across the bank the longest option is correct in Q1, Q2, Q5, Q7, Q10 — a length heuristic scores ~50%+ without knowledge.

quizIssues.question: Which international initiative aims to prevent MNCs from shifting profits to low-tax countries?
quizIssues.issue: No problem with correctness. Note only: none of the 10 items test host/home stakeholder analysis, balance of payments, technology transfer trade-offs, or the Samsung/Shell/Apple examples that the lesson actually spends its words on.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Explain two benefits...' for 4 marks is not an IAL Business format. IAL WBS14 4-mark questions are 'Explain one [reason/benefit]...' tied to the extract (Knowledge 2 / Application 2). With context: null there is nothing to apply to, so the AO2 marks cannot be earned or modelled. Guidance lists seven possible benefits but gives no mark-scheme structure or model answer.

6-mark 'Analyse' with a scenario is a valid IAL format and the context is realistic. But the guidance overshoots the command word: it asks for counter-arguments and 'whether responsibility lies with the retailer, suppliers or governments' — that is evaluation (AO4), not credited at 6 marks. No levelled mark scheme (Level 1-3 KAA) or model answer.

10-mark 'Assess' with context is correct IAL format (KAA 6 / Evaluation 4) and the guidance is genuinely usable. Only gap: no level descriptors and no model conclusion, so an AI grader or student cannot self-mark reliably.

Same format problem as index 0 ('Explain two reasons', 4 marks, no context). Additionally it tests reasons an MNC locates production in a developing country — that is spec point 'assessment of a country as a production location' (earlier in Unit 4), not this section, and the Learn Mode content does not teach it.

'Evaluate whether the growth of MNCs has been a positive or negative development for the global economy' — 20 marks with context: null. IAL Business 20-mark questions are always data-response, framed around a specific business/country decision in the extract ('Evaluate whether X should...' / 'Evaluate the likely impact of ... on Y'). A context-free 'global economy' essay is an Economics-style framing and cannot earn IAL application marks. Guidance is an unranked pro/con list with no levelled scheme (Level 4 = balanced, contextual judgement) and no model answer.

structureIssues: Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) and 0 diagrams: with block 1 = 2 sections and block 2 = 2 sections, the whole Learn Mode is exactly 2 steps of ~700-800 words of prose each, followed by one InlineQuiz MCQ, one practice question, ExplainItBack and a takeaway. There is no spaced/immediate recall at all, so the section is the passive-reading failure mode the founder worries about (opposite of the 'arbitrary reorder' problem).

Transfer pricing is taught twice: content[0] > mnc-negative-impacts-ethics > body[2] (full mechanism, components example) and content[1] > transfer-pricing-mechanism (full mechanism again, brand-name example, BEPS). The avoidance-vs-evasion misconception is also repeated in notes[1]. Block 2 section 2 (fdi-stakeholder-analysis) then re-sorts block 1's positives/negatives by stakeholder, so roughly half of block 2 is restatement.

No difficulty ramp and no foundation: 'FDI', 'MNC' and 'subsidiary' are used from the first sentence without definition; 'arm's length' is defined only in block 2 after transfer pricing has already been explained in block 1. All four sections sit at the same evaluative level ('net impact depends on governance') rather than definitions -> mechanisms -> evaluation.

Content[] vs assessment misalignment: quiz (6/10 items), flashcards (10/19), common_mistakes (4/6) and extras chains cover controlling MNCs, greenwashing, Rana Plaza, Nestlé, boycotts, social media — none of which appear in content[]. PreTest and InlineQuiz therefore examine students on material the lesson never presents, which is a plausible driver of pre-test demotivation.

examMatters is near-identical across all four sections (variations of 'the net impact depends on the host country's governance capacity, the MNC's industry and the regulatory framework'); the block 2 takeaway[3] repeats block 1 takeaway[2]. The evaluation template is good but repeated four times it reads as filler.

Misconceptions: 'Students assume MNCs always benefit host countries' (mnc-positive-impacts) and 'Students assume all MNCs deliberately exploit host countries' (mnc-negative-impacts-ethics) are mirror images and generic; only the avoidance/evasion and host-only-stakeholder ones are genuine, mark-scheme-relevant errors.

Block 1 title 'MNC Impact & Ethics' promises ethics, but ethics content is one sentence on labour exploitation and one on pollution havens; marketing ethics, child labour and stakeholder conflict (all spec bullets) are absent. Block 2 title 'Transfer Pricing & FDI Stakeholders' bundles two unrelated topics.

Economics framing leaks into a Business section ('current account', 'multiplier effects', 'resource curse', 'global economy' in the 20-marker); IAL Business examiners want business-decision and stakeholder framing.
ialSpecGaps: Controlling MNCs: political influence, legal control, pressure groups, social media — not taught in content[] at all (only flashcards/quiz/common_mistakes)
Ethics — marketing considerations: misleading product labelling, inappropriate promotional activities (greenwashing, Nestlé formula) — absent from content[]
Ethics — supply chain considerations: exploitation of labour and child labour — mentioned in one clause only; no Rana Plaza / DRC cobalt in content[] despite quiz testing them
Ethics — stakeholder conflicts as a framing (shareholders vs workers vs communities) — implicit in fdi-stakeholder-analysis but not framed as ethical conflict
Impact on the national economy: balance of payments (export earnings vs profit repatriation and imported components) — only in flashcards[18]; content[] mentions 'current account' in one clause
Impact on the national economy: business culture — not covered anywhere
Impact on the national economy: consumers (host-country consumers: choice, price, quality) — only home-country consumers are covered

Impact on the local economy: local businesses (crowding out vs supplier opportunities) and local community and environment — covered briefly in fdi-stakeholder-analysis but not developed; wages relative to local averages (MNC wage premium) only in notes misconception
Exact IAL spec numbering for this section (app uses 4.3.4) — unsure; the bullets above are those Edexcel lists under the MNC topic (impact / ethics / controlling MNCs)
strengths: Each section models the IAL evaluative move correctly: state a benefit, challenge it (job quality, whether technology is really transferred, transfer pricing eroding tax), then a context-dependent judgement — this is exactly what Level 4 answers need.

Real examples are specific and largely accurate (Samsung Vietnam, Shell Niger Delta, Apple/Ireland €13bn with the 0.005% figure, OECD $100-240bn BEPS estimate) and the misconception on tax avoidance vs evasion is a genuine mark-scheme distinction.
The home-country vs host-country stakeholder framework (fdi-stakeholder-analysis) is a clean, reusable essay structure that students can lift directly into 10/12/20-mark answers.
Practice[2] (10-mark Assess on transfer pricing with context) is a realistic IAL item with strong guidance, and quiz Q9 is a proper application-level MCQ.
Notes[] and extras chains are coherent, and common_mistakes[] are genuinely exam-relevant (one-sided analysis, vague ethics, overestimating CSR, single-solution control).
topFixes: Add a third block 'Ethics & Controlling MNCs' to content[] (marketing ethics/greenwashing, supply chain labour and child labour with Rana Plaza/DRC cobalt, and the four controls: political influence, legal control, pressure groups, social media) so that the quiz bank, PreTest and flashcards test what the lesson teaches; until then, remove or re-tag quiz Q3, Q4, Q6, Q7, Q9, Q10 so PreTest cannot sample untaught material.

Merge the two transfer-pricing sections into one (define transfer pricing neutrally, then manipulation, then BEPS with Pillar Two as implemented from 2024) and use the freed space for balance of payments, business culture and host-country consumers.

Add recall widgets that are genuinely orderable: a fillin for the transfer-pricing mechanism ('subsidiary in a ___-tax country charges ___ prices to a subsidiary in a ___-tax country so profit is reported where tax is ___') and a reorder for the causal chain 'MNC invests via FDI -> jobs and supplier demand -> skills/technology spill over -> tax revenue -> but profits repatriated'; plus one diagram (stakeholder map host vs home, or a two-subsidiary transfer-pricing flow).

Fix the practice set to IAL formats: 4-mark items become 'Explain one...' with a short extract; replace practice[3] (production-location reasons, wrong spec point); rewrite the 20-marker as a data-response decision ('Evaluate whether [country] should offer tax incentives to attract [MNC]'), and add levelled mark schemes/model answers so AI grading and self-marking have a reference.

Correct the factual issues: delete the 'repatriated profits exceed investment = net loser' sentence, date or replace the Amazon Luxembourg example (structure changed in 2015), change BEPS 15% from 'proposes' to 'implemented from 2024', and add the NNPC 55% JV point to the Shell example.

summary: The prose is competent, correctly-defined, IAL-safe teaching text (scarcity vs shortage, next-best alternative, move-to vs shift-of PPF, four functions of money) and a strong IAL teacher would accept most of the NoteSection bodies. The scaffolding around it is where it fails: 6 of 10 recall widgets are either non-orderable lists, tautological chains, hint-leaking fill-ins or answers that a correct alternative word would fail; the 25-MCQ bank contains five near-duplicate pairs and three questions on concepts the section never teaches (free goods, capital as a factor, entrepreneur's profit) which then feed the demotivating pre-test; the 'Base PPF' SVG is visibly non-concave (slope goes 1.36 to 0.34 then back up) while the checklist tells students to draw it concave; two of three diagrams and 20 of 25 MCQs and 2 of 5 practice questions are never surfaced in Learn Mode because blocks don't reference them; practice mark schemes are point-allocated rather than IAL levels-based; and the examples are heavily UK-domestic (ONS, NHS x2, HS2, Bank of England, 'the UK is a mixed economy') for a Hong Kong/Singapore/Pakistan audience. Fixable to a B+ with targeted edits rather than a rewrite.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
recallAudit.reason: 'Apply ceteris paribus' and 'Isolate the variable of interest' are the same act (ceteris paribus IS how you isolate a variable), so their relative order is arbitrary; and a modeller chooses the variable of interest before/while building the model, so 'Build model' before 'Isolate variable' is equally defensible the other way. The body text never presents this as a procedure. shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. Note the notes[] flow for the same block uses a different 4-step list ('Observe real-world problem / Build simplified model / Apply ceteris paribus / Predict outcome'), so even the author disagrees with the sequence.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification exercise: sort 6 topics into Micro vs Macro (e.g. 'price of coffee', 'UK inflation rate', 'a firm's pricing', 'national unemployment'). Or fillin: 'Economics is a ___ science because it studies ___ behaviour; models hold other variables constant using the assumption of ___ ___' with a word bank instead of letter hints.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'P______' / 'N________' plus the sentence frames 'tested with evidence' / 'value judgements' make blanks 1-2 trivial (section title is 'Positive and Normative Economics'). Blank 3 hint 'o_____' is 6 characters but the stored answer 'ought to' is 8 (incl. space); a student typing 'ought' (the natural single-word fill after 'should, ___, fairer') will likely be marked wrong depending on matcher.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification: present 6 statements (e.g. 'Singapore's inflation was 4.8% in 2023', 'Hong Kong rents are too high', 'Minimum wages reduce youth employment', 'Governments ought to tax sugar') and have the student tag each Positive/Normative. This tests the actual skill IAL Section A MCQs test.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
recallAudit.reason: Genuine causal chain (wants>resources -> scarcity -> choice -> opportunity cost) that the examMatters text explicitly tells students to reproduce. shuffled [3,1,0,2] is a valid non-identity permutation.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Blank 1 'the ___-best alternative' with hint 'n___' is trivial. Blank 2 'It is not the ___ cost': 'monetary' and 'financial' fit equally well semantically; hint 'm____' forces 'money' but that is hint-dependence, not understanding. Blank 3 'Only the ___ alternative counts' expects the two-word 'single best' (hint 'si_________'); 'single', 'second-best' and 'next-best' all fit grammatically and semantically; body text says 'next-best' so a student echoing the taught wording fails.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Scenario fillin: 'A government has $10bn. Ranked options: hospital (1st), school (2nd), road (3rd). It builds the hospital. Opportunity cost = ___' with word bank [the school, the road, the school + the road, $10bn]. Tests the actual misconception the section targets.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: On the PPF curve — productively efficient
Inside the curve — resources wasted or unemployed
Slope of the PPF — shows opportunity cost
recallAudit.reason: Four parallel descriptive facts about a diagram; there is no causal, chronological or procedural relationship between 'on', 'inside', 'outside' and 'slope'. This is exactly the founder-reported complaint. shuffled [1,3,0,2] is a valid non-identity permutation but the exercise is meaningless.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Diagram-linked matching: show the Base PPF SVG (points A-F already exist) and ask 'Tag each point: efficient / inefficient / unattainable'. Or fillin using the diagram's numbers: 'Moving from C (120,150) to D (225,100) gains ___ consumer goods and sacrifices ___ capital goods, so the opportunity cost of 1 consumer good is ___ capital goods'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Template is a verbatim copy of the 'flow' block in the same subsection body ('Investment in education/technology' -> 'Labour productivity rises' -> 'PPF shifts outward' -> 'economic growth'), and as the 'immediate' recall it renders on the same step where that flow is still visible. Hints 'L_____', 'ou_____', 'gr____' remove any residual retrieval.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Sorting exercise: 'Shift of PPF' vs 'Movement to/along PPF' with items: new technology, fall in unemployment, war destroys factories, reallocating workers from farms to factories, discovery of oil, immigration. This directly targets the misconception in the same subsection and mirrors quiz Q3/Q11/Q13.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Specialisation, Division of Labour and Exchange
recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Skills improve and time is saved
Higher output per worker but risk of monotony
recallAudit.reason: Items 3 and 4 are the same thing ('productivity' = output per worker), so their order is arbitrary; item 4 also bolts on an unrelated evaluative clause ('risk of monotony') that is not a downstream consequence of 'productivity rises'. Only steps 1-2 are a real sequence. shuffled [2,3,0,1] valid non-identity.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder with a genuine chain: 'Worker repeats one task' -> 'Dexterity rises and no time lost switching tasks' -> 'Output per worker rises' -> 'Unit costs fall' -> 'Firm can lower price / raise profit'. Or a two-column sort of benefits vs risks of specialisation.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Specialisation, Division of Labour and Exchange
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'double coincidence of ___' and 'medium of ___' are fixed collocations that a student can complete without understanding money; hints 'w____' and 'ex______' remove even that. Blank 3 packs two answers into one field ('value, account') so 'value and account' or reversed order may fail the matcher.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Function-matching: 4 scenarios -> 4 functions of money ('You save HK$5,000 for a laptop next year' -> store of value; 'A menu lists noodles at $8 and rice at $6' -> unit of account; 'You agree to pay the builder in 3 months' -> standard of deferred payment; 'The shop accepts your note' -> medium of exchange). Then a Zimbabwe follow-up: 'Which function fails first under hyperinflation?'

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Market, command or mixed economy answers these
recallAudit.reason: The three fundamental questions have no logical order (only a conventional listing order), and the 4th item is a meta-comment, not a step. A student who understands the material perfectly cannot 'reconstruct' this. shuffled [3,0,2,1] valid non-identity.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Matching: 3 questions -> 3 concrete decisions ('labour-intensive or capital-intensive?' -> How; 'hospitals or missiles?' -> What; 'ration by price or by queue?' -> For whom). Or a sort of features into Free market / Command / Mixed (price mechanism, central planning targets, NHS + private firms, private property, state ownership).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Body text and takeaway teach the functions as 'signalling, incentivising, rationing'; the answers are 'signal / incentive / ration' (mixed parts of speech) so a student who types the taught form 'signalling' or 'rationing' fails. Hint 'in________' is 10 characters but 'incentive' is 9 (hint length mismatch suggests 'incentives'). Template is also a verbatim copy of the subsection's flow block.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Accept stems (signal*/incentiv*/ration*) or use a word bank. Better: scenario-to-function matching using the 2022 oil example already in realExample: 'Price of Brent rises to $120' -> signal; 'Shale firms drill more wells' -> incentive; 'Commuters switch to public transport' -> rationing.

accuracyIssues.issue: The curve is not concave. Sampling the cubic segments gives slope (dy/dx, screen coords) rising to 1.36 just after point C, falling back to 0.34 before D, then rising again to vertical at A: a visible convex bulge between C and D, i.e. decreasing then increasing opportunity cost. The same diagram's checklist item 2 says 'PPF drawn as a concave curve (bowed outward from origin)' and common_mistakes[2] tells students they lose marks for drawing it wrong.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace the S-command path with a single smooth concave cubic through B(0,200), C(120,150), D(225,100), A(300,0), e.g. 'M 80 50 C 230 50, 400 150, 450 330' (as used in scenario 3), then reposition C and D onto that curve.

accuracyIssues.issue: Says China 'operated well inside its PPF' and 'by shifting labour into manufacturing and investing in capital, China moved closer to its frontier'. Investing in capital shifts the frontier outward; China's post-1990 growth was overwhelmingly a PPF shift, not a move to the frontier. The example muddles the exact shift-vs-movement distinction the next subsection's misconception warns about.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either use a clean move-to-frontier example (an economy recovering from recession/unemployment, e.g. Malaysia 1998-2000 post-crisis) or rewrite: 'China did both: reallocating underemployed farm labour moved it toward its frontier, while capital investment shifted the frontier itself'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'A 6-mark answer that names all three with examples will score full marks.' IAL 6-mark 'Explain' items are levels-marked on developed chains of reasoning and (in Section B) application to the extract; naming three functions with generic examples is not guaranteed full marks.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'For a 6-mark explain, take two functions and develop each as a chain (price rises -> signals scarcity -> firms reallocate resources) with reference to the data provided.'

accuracyIssues.location: The Nature of Economics > economics-as-a-social-science > realExample (Bank of England Brexit)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'it assumed ceteris paribus on trade deals, migration and business investment' is not what the BoE's 2018 Brexit scenarios did; those scenarios explicitly varied trade-deal, migration and investment assumptions. The example illustrates the opposite of ceteris paribus.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a genuine ceteris paribus illustration: 'When economists estimate how a $1 rise in petrol prices cuts driving, they hold income, car ownership and public-transport prices constant; in 2022 all of these moved at once, which is why forecasts missed.'

accuracyIssues.location: The Nature of Economics > economics-as-a-social-science > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'When asked why economics is a social science, examiners want three things...' This framing of a specific question type is not something IAL WEC11 papers ask; the risk is students memorising a non-existent question format. Ceteris paribus itself is examined (quiz Q9/Q19 are realistic).
accuracyIssues.fix: Reframe as 'Ceteris paribus is examinable as a 4-mark Section A explanation: define it and explain why a model needs it.'

accuracyIssues.location: Scarcity, Choice and Opportunity Cost > opportunity-cost > realExample (HS2)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'committed £100bn' overstates (approved 2020 estimate ~£98bn; official commitment was lower); and HS2 north of Birmingham was cancelled in Oct 2023 so the example reads as stale to a 2026 cohort. Purely UK-domestic for an international audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap for a regional example students can relate to: Indonesia's Nusantara capital (~$32bn) vs. Jakarta flood defences, or Saudi NEOM (already used above).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'versus just 10 if each worked alone' — Smith wrote each untrained man 'could scarce ... make one pin in a day, and certainly could not make twenty'; the 10 figure is a lower-bound gloss presented as Smith's number.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'versus perhaps 1-20 pins each (under 200 in total) if each worked alone'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Lists three functions of money ('medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account') while the body, examMatters and quiz treat four (adds standard of deferred payment). Inconsistent count in the line students are most likely to memorise.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add 'and standard of deferred payment' to the keyIdea.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'South Korea ~$35,000 vs North Korea ~$1,800' mixes a nominal figure for the South with a PPP-style estimate for the North (Bank of Korea nominal estimates for the North are ~$1,200); direction of the point is right, the precision is spurious.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'roughly 20-30x higher GDP per capita' without false precision, cite Bank of Korea estimates.

accuracyIssues.location: Blocks 1-2 realExamples and misconceptions (ONS, NHS x2, HS2, Bank of England, 'the UK is a mixed economy'); quiz Q0[2], Q17[0], Q17[2]
accuracyIssues.issue: UK GCE-flavoured context for an IAL product whose students sit in HK, Singapore, Malaysia, Pakistan, the Gulf. Not factually wrong, but IAL extracts are deliberately international and these students have no intuition for the NHS or ONS.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace at least half the examples with HK/Singapore/Gulf/South-Asian contexts (HK public housing, Singapore CPF, Pakistan fuel subsidies, Saudi Vision 2030).

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is most likely to be classified as a free good?
quizIssues.issue: Concept 'free good' (vs economic good, zero opportunity cost) is never taught anywhere in content[]; this question can land in the 3-item PreTest gate, which is exactly the demotivating experience the founder describes.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a factor of production classified as 'capital'?
quizIssues.issue: Factors of production are only mentioned parenthetically ('land, labour, capital, enterprise') in the-basic-economic-problem; the physical-vs-financial capital distinction the question hinges on is never taught. Eligible for pre-test.

quizIssues.question: The entrepreneur is rewarded with profit because they:
quizIssues.issue: Rewards to factors of production (rent/wages/interest/profit) and the entrepreneur's risk-bearing role are not taught in content[]. Eligible for pre-test.

quizIssues.question: An outward shift of the PPF could be caused by:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q3 (same correct answer 'improvement in technology', same three distractor concepts). With a 3-random pre-test and a 25-bank, duplicate pairs inflate the odds of a student seeing the same item in pre- and post-test.

quizIssues.question: If an economy is producing on its PPF and decides to produce more capital goods, what is the most likely long-run effect?
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q7 (same scenario, same correct concept 'outward shift in the future').

quizIssues.question: The concept of ceteris paribus in economics means:
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q9 (both test the definition of ceteris paribus; Q19 is the weaker, pure-recall version).

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is an example of a normative economic statement?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q0 (identify the normative statement; same 'should/ought' tell, same UK-inflation distractor pattern).

quizIssues.question: A movement from a point inside the PPF to a point on the frontier represents:
quizIssues.issue: Heavily overlaps Q2 (both test 'inside the PPF = unused/inefficient resources'). Acceptable as a pair but with Q3/Q13, Q7/Q20, Q9/Q19, Q0/Q17 the bank of 25 is effectively ~18 distinct items.

quizIssues.question: Which function of money is most undermined by high inflation?
quizIssues.issue: Option [3] 'Standard of deferred payment' is also directly undermined by high inflation (lenders are repaid in devalued money); 'store of value' is the conventional answer but a strong student can defend [3]. Explanation does not say why [3] is less directly affected.

quizIssues.question: An economy currently producing on its PPF chooses to produce more capital goods and fewer consumer goods. This is most likely to result in:
quizIssues.issue: The capital-goods-now -> PPF-shift-later mechanism is not taught in content[] (only in extras.chains[1], which is paywalled/preview). Question is good; the content should teach the concept it tests.

quizIssues.question: In a free market economy, the allocation of resources is primarily determined by:
quizIssues.issue: Distractors [2] 'Trade unions negotiating' and [3] 'International organisations setting quotas' are implausible; the item is too easy for A-level. Q6 is its mirror (command economy) and is similarly easy.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term opportunity cost (4 marks)': IAL 'Define' items carry 2 marks; the 4-mark guidance awards marks for an example and for 'arises because resources are scarce', which is not how a definition is marked. Either make it 2 marks (definition + reference to 'next best' / 'forgone') or reword as a Section-A-style 'Explain what is meant by opportunity cost, using an example (4)'.

Question asks for 'two reasons why the basic economic problem is relevant to BOTH individuals and governments' but the model answer gives one reason for individuals and one for governments; the answer does not answer the question as worded. Also IAL 6-mark explain questions are data-response and require application to an extract; there is no stimulus. Reword: 'Explain how the basic economic problem affects (a) individuals and (b) governments (6)'.

10-mark 'Assess' allocation is valid for IAL, but the guidance is a point-per-sentence tally ('(2 marks)... (1 mark)') whereas IAL marks 8+ questions with levels (KAA ~6 / Evaluation ~4 for 10 marks). Students revising from this will write lists, not developed chains. Evaluation content ('only two goods', 'does not show what society should choose') is thin and the judgement is generic; no stimulus.

20-mark 'Evaluate' with 'always' in the stem is a realistic IAL essay, but the guidance again tallies points ('3 marks', '2 marks') rather than KAA/Evaluation levels, and the evaluation paragraph (2+2 marks by the guide's own count) is far below the ~8 evaluation marks such a question carries. It never explicitly attacks the word 'always' or reaches a justified judgement. Not linked from any block's practiceIndices, so Learn Mode never shows it despite fitting block 4 exactly.

'Outline' is not an Edexcel IAL Economics command word (Define / Calculate / Explain / Examine / Analyse / Assess / Discuss / Evaluate). Content of the answer is fine. Not linked from any block (fits block 1).

No practice item uses a data extract or a 'Calculate' / 'With reference to Figure 1' stem, although WEC11 Section B is entirely data-response; and no item covers the price mechanism / economic systems block in a way students would meet (e.g. 'Assess the case for a command economy' or 'Explain how the price mechanism rations petrol').

structureIssues: Only 5 of 25 MCQs are reachable in Learn Mode: quizIndices are [0], [1], [2,3], [4] and block 5 'Economic Systems' has no quizIndices at all even though Q6 and Q21 are its questions. The other 20 MCQs exist only for the pre/post-test random draw and the paywalled Quiz tab.

Only 1 of 3 diagrams is reachable in Learn Mode: only block 3 has a diagramRef ('Production Possibility Frontier'). 'Circular Flow of Income' (whose description says it illustrates 'how specialisation and exchange work through markets', i.e. block 4) and 'Economic Systems Comparison' (block 5) are never inlined; and circular flow is Unit 2 (WEC12) macro content, so it is out of place in this section anyway.
practice[3] (20-mark specialisation essay) and practice[4] (assumptions, 4 marks) are unlinked; block 1 and block 4 therefore have no InlinePractice while the questions that fit them sit unused.

Every block has exactly 2 subsections, so each block is a single step carrying: 2 NoteSections + a 'spaced' recall at the top + diagram + InlineQuiz + InlinePractice + ExplainItBack + TakeawayCard + an 'immediate' recall. That is 7-8 interactions on one screen for step 1 of a first-topic section, which is consistent with 167/192 users never leaving step 0. The pairing itself is coherent (social science + pos/norm; scarcity + opp cost; PPF model + shifts; specialisation + money; systems + price mechanism).

The 'immediate' recall of each block's first subsection is often a verbatim copy of a flow block visible on the same step (shifts-of-the-ppf, the-price-mechanism, money-and-exchange), so it measures copying, not recall.

Pre-test draws 3 random MCQs from a bank that includes 3 untaught concepts (Q8, Q15, Q24) and 5 near-duplicate pairs, so a student can be told they 'failed' on material the section will not teach, and the post-test can repeat a pre-test item.

Price mechanism (signalling/incentive/rationing, invisible hand) is IAL 1.2.7 and is likely re-taught in 'price-determination' (1.3.4 in the app's numbering); here it is squeezed into the Economic Systems block with no diagram and no quiz. Consider trimming to the free-market/command/mixed comparison plus the state's role.

Takeaways match their blocks. Block 3 takeaway 4 ('Always label axes, mark the point...') is exam advice rather than content, fine. Block 4 takeaway 2 name-checks the pin factory but the block's quiz Q4 (Smith's three reasons) tests machinery-introduction, which the body never lists.

Misconceptions are mostly genuine student errors (scarcity=shortage; listing all alternatives; move-to vs shift-of; 'UK is a free market'; 'positive = good'; 'invisible hand always optimal'). The economics-as-a-social-science one ('not a real science because it cannot predict') is weaker/filler and its 'Instead write' is just the keyIdea.
Difficulty ramp is sensible (definitions -> PPF diagram -> specialisation/money -> systems), mirroring IAL 1.1.1-1.1.4 order.

The app's section numbering '1.3.1' is not IAL spec numbering (IAL Unit 1 topic 1.1 'Scarcity, choice and potential conflicts'); harmless internally but confusing if students cross-reference the Pearson spec.
ialSpecGaps: 1.1.1 The economic problem: factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise) and their rewards (rent, wages, interest, profit) are not taught as content, only named in one parenthesis, yet quiz Q15 and Q24 test them.

1.1.1: distinction between free goods and economic goods (zero vs positive opportunity cost) not taught; quiz Q8 tests it. (Fairly confident this is in IAL 1.1.1; say 'unsure' on exact bullet wording.)
1.1.1: renewable vs non-renewable resources (in UK 1.1.3; I believe also in IAL 1.1.1) not mentioned. Unsure.

1.1.2 PPF: 'the distinction between capital and consumer goods' and the trade-off between current consumption and future growth (producing capital goods now shifts the PPF later) is tested by Q7/Q20 but only appears in the paywalled extras chain, not in content[].

1.1.2 PPF: 'opportunity cost through marginal analysis' on the PPF (the increasing marginal opportunity cost of successive units) is only one sentence about slope; no worked numeric example despite the Base PPF diagram carrying axis values (120/225/300 and 100/150/200).

1.1.3 Specialisation: 'advantages and disadvantages of specialising in the production of goods and services to trade' (country-level specialisation, dependence on trade) is only a half-bullet; comparative advantage terminology is used in extras but never explained. Unsure whether IAL expects comparative advantage in Unit 1.

1.1.4 Types of economy: 'the role of the state in a mixed economy' (provision of public goods, regulation, redistribution) is a single sentence; no reference to Hayek or Marx alongside Smith, which the spec names.
Economic agents and their objectives (consumers, producers, government) as the parties facing opportunity cost — taught implicitly, never defined.
strengths: Definitions are exam-accurate and echo Edexcel mark-scheme wording: 'next-best alternative forgone', 'unlimited wants / finite resources', 'productively efficient on the curve', 'double coincidence of wants', four functions of money.
Scarcity-vs-shortage and 'only the next-best, not B+C+D' paragraphs (the-basic-economic-problem, opportunity-cost) pre-empt the two commonest Unit 1 errors; common_mistakes[1] and [3] reinforce them.
shifts-of-the-ppf body paragraph 3 and its misconception nail the move-to vs shift-of distinction, and quiz Q3/Q11/Q13/Q23 test it well with plausible distractors (re-employment, reallocation).

Base PPF diagram uses numeric axis values and six labelled points (B,C,D,A on curve; E inside; F outside) — the numbers even give increasing opportunity cost (0.42, 0.48, 1.33 capital per consumer good), so it could support a calculation exercise once the curve shape is fixed.

Two of the recall widgets are genuinely good: the-basic-economic-problem reorder (a real causal chain the examMatters tells students to use) and, structurally, the money functions and price-mechanism fill-ins would be fine with stem-tolerant matching.
Quiz Q7/Q20 (capital goods now -> growth later) and Q23 (pivoted shift) are above-average, exam-realistic PPF items.

Real examples are mostly checkable and correct: Singapore GDP/capita > $80k, South Korea 1960->2000, Zimbabwe 2008 doubling roughly daily, Foxconn Shenzhen, 2022 oil price spike with shale/rationing mechanics.
Every subsection has keyIdea, misconception with 'Instead write:' correction, and examMatters — the note architecture is consistent.
topFixes: Replace the 4 non-genuine recalls (the-ppf-model reorder, free-market-command-and-mixed reorder, economics-as-a-social-science reorder, specialisation reorder) with sort/match exercises (efficient/inefficient/unattainable point tagging; shift vs movement sorting; positive vs normative classification; benefit vs risk sorting), and make fill-in matching stem-tolerant so 'signalling'/'ought' are accepted.

Fix the quiz bank before it feeds the pre-test: delete or rewrite the duplicates (Q13, Q19, Q17, Q20) and either teach free goods / factors of production and rewards in block 2 or remove Q8, Q15, Q24; then wire quizIndices for block 5 (Q6, Q21) and spread the remaining MCQs across blocks.
Redraw the Base PPF SVG as a single concave cubic (it is currently wavy between C and D) and add a one-line worked opportunity-cost calculation from its axis values to the-ppf-model body.
Link the unused assets: practice[4] to block 1, practice[3] to block 4, 'Economic Systems Comparison' diagramRef to block 5; drop or move the Circular Flow diagram to Unit 2.

Rewrite practice guidance as IAL levels-based schemes (KAA + Evaluation, with an explicit judgement on 'always' in practice[3]), make practice[0] a 2-mark Define, fix the practice[1] question/answer mismatch, and swap at least half of the UK-domestic examples (NHS, ONS, HS2, BoE) for HK/Singapore/Gulf/South-Asian contexts.

summary: The prose in blocks 1 and 2 is genuinely good: precise Edexcel terminology (extension/contraction, willing and able, ceteris paribus), real student misconceptions, and correctly drawn diagrams (unit-elastic through origin, elastic cutting P-axis, inelastic cutting Q-axis). But a strong IAL teacher would not ship it as-is: block 3 is Unit 3 (WEC13) content on diminishing marginal returns and returns to scale dressed up as WEC11 1.3.3, and never links short run/long run back to PES, which is the actual spec bullet; the Saudi Arabia oil example is factually backwards (Saudi is the lowest-cost producer and raised output in 2014-16); quiz Q21 marks a wrong answer on a Unit 3 topic; the inline quiz/practice/diagram wiring is sequential (0,1,2) rather than content-matched, so the PES block gets a wheat-shift MCQ and the two PES diagrams are never shown in Learn Mode. Every fill-in leaks its answer via first-two-letters-plus-length hints, and the practice mark schemes are points-based where IAL marks by levels. Fix the wiring, cut/replace block 3, correct the two factual errors, and this becomes a B+/A- section.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the law of supply chain in the right order:
items: Firms expand output and new firms enter
recallAudit.reason: Real causal chain (price -> revenue/unit -> profitability -> output/entry). shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. Weakness: steps 2 and 3 are near-synonyms so the only real decision is first/last, and the identical chain is printed as a flow block in the same step's body immediately above the recall (shown 'immediate' at bottom of step 1), so it is copy-from-screen rather than recall.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the supply curve movements vs shifts:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'mo______', 'ex________', 'sh___' give first two letters plus length; templates '___ along the curve' and '___ of the supply curve' make movement/shift guessable from the collocation alone. Hint 'ex________' is 10 chars but 'extension' is 9 (length mismatch). No word bank with distractors (e.g. contraction/decrease) exists, so the one blank that tests understanding (extension vs contraction) is also given away.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Word-bank fillin with distractors: bank = [extension, contraction, increase, decrease, movement, shift]; templates: 'Price of coffee beans rises 15%: quantity of coffee supplied shows an ___ of supply' / 'A new tax on coffee roasters causes a ___ in supply' / 'A fall in coffee price causes a ___ of supply'. No letter hints.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these supply shift factors in order of explanation:
items: Explain how it affects costs of production
State the direction of the supply curve shift
Show the effect on equilibrium price and quantity
recallAudit.reason: A procedural answer-writing chain that mirrors the section's examMatters and a taught student can reconstruct (factor -> cost mechanism -> shift direction -> equilibrium effect). shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Prompt wording is wrong: these are steps of an explanation, not 'supply shift factors'; rename to 'Put the steps of a supply-shift explanation in order'. Note the section's own diagram scenarios contain no demand curve, so step 4 is never illustrated.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the PES fundamentals:
recallAudit.reason: 'PES = % change in quantity ___ / % change in price' can only be 'supplied' (it is in the acronym); 'PES > 1 means supply is price ___' is answered by the section title context; hints 'su______', 'po______', 'el_____' additionally leak first letters + exact length. Zero discrimination.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Numerical fillin from raw data: 'Price rises from $20 to $25 (___% change); quantity supplied rises from 400 to 440 (___% change); PES = ___ so supply is price ___' with answers 25, 10, 0.4, inelastic. Tests the spec bullet 'use the formula to calculate PES', which nothing in the section currently does with raw figures.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these PES scenarios in order from least to most elastic:
recallAudit.reason: Genuinely orderable but every item contains both its number (0, <1, 1, >1) and its label, so it is a sort-by-number task. shuffled [3,0,2,1] valid. Also omits PES = infinity, which the body teaches as one of 'three special cases'.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder real-world cases from least to most elastic with no numbers in the item text: 'Seats at a sold-out stadium tonight' / 'Fresh strawberries this week' / 'Bottled water from a plant at 60% capacity' / 'E-book downloads'. Or keep numeric but strip labels and add PES = infinity and a decimal (0.4, 1.8) so students must place values, not read words.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the PES determinants:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'Sp___', 'fi______', 'lo__' give first letters + length. 'Supply is most elastic in the ___ run' has one plausible answer anyway; 'Stocks of ___ goods' could take 'final' but the hint disambiguates. Copy of the bullet list two paragraphs above.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Apply-the-determinant fillin with a word bank [elastic, inelastic]: 'A car plant running at full capacity: short-run supply is ___' / 'A warehouse holding 3 months of unsold stock: supply is ___' / 'Coffee trees take 4 years to bear fruit: supply of coffee in year 1 is ___'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the diminishing returns process in the right order:
items: At least one factor of production is fixed
More units of the variable factor are added
Marginal product of each extra worker eventually falls
recallAudit.reason: Sound causal chain, shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. However the whole chain (marginal product, marginal cost) is WEC13 Unit 3 content (costs/diminishing returns), not WEC11 1.3.3, so it recalls material the student should not be revising here.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: If block 3 is kept on-spec, replace with: 'Demand for masks surges' -> 'Momentary period: output fixed, price spikes' -> 'Short run: factories add shifts, some fixed factors' -> 'Long run: new plants and firms enter, supply most elastic', tying SR/LR to PES as the spec requires.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the long-run production concepts:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'va______', 'in________', 'fa___' leak first letters + length. Content is Unit 3 (returns to scale). Additionally, because this is the last section of the last block, under the described recall placement (previous step's last-section recall shown at top of the NEXT step) this recall is likely never surfaced in Learn Mode at all.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Drop with block 3, or if retained make it a bank-based fillin distinguishing 'diminishing returns' vs 'decreasing returns to scale' from scenario descriptions (the one distinction the block claims is exam-critical).

accuracyIssues.issue: Saudi Arabia is presented as raising output above $80 'because expensive extraction methods become profitable' and cutting drilling when prices fell below $30 in early 2016. Saudi Arabia has the lowest lifting costs in the world (roughly $3-10/bbl) and its output is set by OPEC/political strategy; in 2014-16 it famously INCREASED production to record levels (~10.5m bpd) to defend market share while prices collapsed. The example describes US shale/oil-sands behaviour and attributes it to the wrong producer; a student who repeats it in an exam is writing something a well-informed examiner knows is false.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap to US shale: 'The US oil rig count fell from ~1,600 in late 2014 to ~400 in mid-2016 as WTI fell below $30, then recovered as prices rose above $50 — higher-cost shale wells only get drilled when price covers their marginal cost.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[2] 'Short Run vs Long Run' (whole block: short-run-production, long-run-production-and-returns-to-scale, takeaway)
accuracyIssues.issue: Diminishing marginal returns, marginal product, and increasing/constant/decreasing returns to scale are WEC13 (Unit 3, business behaviour: costs and economies of scale) content. The WEC11 supply/PES bullet only requires 'the distinction between short run and long run and its significance for elasticity of supply'. The block never mentions PES or elasticity at all, so it teaches the wrong exam use of the SR/LR distinction and tells Unit 1 students that examiners 'set trap questions' on returns-to-scale terminology in this topic.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace block 3 with an on-spec 'Time and PES' block: momentary / short run (some factors fixed) / long run (all variable) with the existing 'PES Over Time' diagram, and worked example (e.g. chip fabs or housing). Move diminishing returns / returns to scale to the WEC13 costs section.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'increasing returns to scale (also called economies of scale)' and 'decreasing returns to scale (diseconomies of scale)' conflate two concepts. Returns to scale is a physical input-output relationship; economies of scale are falling long-run average cost, which can arise without returns to scale (e.g. bulk-purchasing discounts, financial economies). Mark schemes distinguish them.
accuracyIssues.fix: If retained: 'Increasing returns to scale is one source of economies of scale (falling LRAC); they are related but not identical.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Airbus invested over $25 billion developing the A350' — published estimates are roughly EUR 11-15bn (~US$15bn). The claim that 'doubling the workforce and materials more than doubled the number of planes completed per year' is unverifiable and reads as invented; the A350 ramp-up was actually supplier-constrained (cabin/seat delays 2016-17). The effect described (learning-curve efficiencies) is a learning effect, not returns to scale.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a defensible example or remove with the block. If keeping a returns-to-scale example, use a generic one (a container-ship doubling dimensions carries far more than double the cargo).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Labelling your diagram with arrows showing the direction of change earns additional marks' — IAL mark schemes award diagram marks for labelled axes, correctly labelled original and new curves, and identified original/new equilibrium; arrows are not a mark point. Overclaims how papers mark.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Diagram marks are for labelled axes, labelled S1/S2 (or D), and clearly identified original and new equilibrium price and quantity — arrows help clarity but are not marked on their own.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > factors-that-shift-supply > examMatters; content[0] > factors-that-shift-supply > recall item 4; diagrams[0].scenarios[1..2]
accuracyIssues.issue: examMatters and the recall require 'show the effect on equilibrium price and quantity using a correctly labelled diagram', but neither shift scenario in the section's diagram contains a demand curve or equilibrium, so students are told to do something the section never shows.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add a demand curve and P1/Q1 -> P2/Q2 to the rightward and leftward shift scenarios (or reference the 1.3.4 price-determination diagram explicitly).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Help to Buy' is listed under 'Other factors' affecting housing SUPPLY. Help to Buy was a UK demand-side equity-loan scheme for buyers; it shifts demand, not supply. Teaching it as a supply factor in a supply essay is the exact movement/shift confusion the section warns against.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a supply-side policy (e.g. planning reform, brownfield grants, Affordable Homes Programme) or explicitly frame Help to Buy as demand-side and therefore not a supply factor.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'TSMC's inelastic supply meant prices rose sharply while output barely increased' in 2021. TSMC revenue grew ~25% and wafer shipments rose meaningfully in 2021; price rises were ~10-20%. Direction is right, 'barely increased' overstates.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'output could only grow by a limited amount within existing fab capacity, so prices rose sharply'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'subsidised solar panel manufacturers by over $50 billion' — the commonly cited IEA figure (>$50bn since 2011) is investment in new PV manufacturing capacity, not government subsidy per se. Approximate but presented as a precise subsidy figure.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Chinese state support and over $50bn of investment in manufacturing capacity since 2011 drove module prices down by around 90%'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Ease of factor substitution' is non-standard; Edexcel materials use 'factor mobility / ease of switching production between goods' and also list availability of raw materials, perishability and barriers to entry (which the section's own PES diagram lists but the Learn text omits).
accuracyIssues.fix: Rename to 'factor mobility' and add raw-material availability, perishability and entry barriers to the bullet list so text and diagram agree.

quizIssues.question: A profit-maximising firm would continue to supply output as long as:
quizIssues.issue: correctIndex 0 ('market price exceeds its average total costs') is wrong or at best contestable. A firm continues to supply in the short run as long as price covers average VARIABLE cost (shut-down rule) and produces where P = MC; option 1 ('price is at least equal to its marginal cost') is the textbook supply condition for a price-taking firm. P > ATC is the long-run break-even condition, and a firm with P < ATC but P > AVC still supplies. This is WEC13 Unit 3 theory-of-the-firm content anyway and has no place in a WEC11 supply bank; it can be drawn into the PreTest at random.

quizIssues.question: A subsidy on electric vehicles would:
quizIssues.issue: Ambiguous. Most real EV subsidies (UK plug-in car grant, US tax credit) are paid to buyers and shift DEMAND (option 0). The stem must specify 'a subsidy paid to EV manufacturers' for option 1 to be uniquely correct.

quizIssues.question: If good X and good Y are joint products (produced together), an increase in the price of good X will:
quizIssues.issue: Joint supply is not taught anywhere in content[] (only in a flashcard). Students in Learn Mode are tested on an untaught concept; answer itself is correct.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following would cause a leftward shift of the supply curve for wheat?
quizIssues.issue: Near-verbatim duplicate of Q1 (same stem, same drought answer, same 'fall in price of wheat' distractor). Both can be drawn in the same 3-question PreTest. Option 3 also relies on 'substitute in production' (competitive supply), which the content never teaches.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is most likely to have a perfectly inelastic supply in the short run?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q4 (stadium seats, digital downloads distractor, same explanation). Wastes a slot in a 25-item bank.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following would make the supply of a product more price elastic?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q6 (spare capacity + inventories correct; specialised inputs, short time period, long production distractors reworded).

quizIssues.question: Producer surplus is the area:
quizIssues.issue: Producer surplus is a separate spec point (consumer and producer surplus), not taught in this section's content; appears only in extras chains. Fine as a bank item but should not be PreTest-eligible for this section.

quizIssues.question: Digital goods such as e-books tend to have a very high PES because:
quizIssues.issue: Option 3 'many publishers competing' is a partially defensible answer (number of firms/ease of entry does affect market PES), weakening uniqueness; option 1 is the intended answer and is fine.

quizIssues.question: If wages for factory workers increase, what happens to the supply of manufactured goods, ceteris paribus?
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 3 'Supply increases because firms pass costs to consumers' is incoherent rather than plausibly wrong; replace with 'No change; a movement along the supply curve occurs' to test the movement/shift distinction.

quizIssues.question: A government imposes a specific tax of £2 per unit on a good. This will cause the supply curve to:
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but the 'shift upward by £2' vertical-shift idea is never taught in content[] (only 'taxes shift supply left'); it is the block-3 inline quiz despite block 3 being about SR/LR production. Content/quiz placement mismatch rather than an error.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term price elasticity of supply (4 marks)'. IAL Economics definitions are 2-mark items; the guidance then awards marks 3-4 for 'PES > 1 elastic' and 'PES < 1 inelastic', which is interpretation, not definition. Either make it 2 marks or reframe as 'Calculate and interpret' with data (the spec's calculation bullet is otherwise untested anywhere in the section).

'Evaluate ... UK housing market (20 marks)'. (a) Mark scheme is points-based ('3 marks', '2 marks') whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (KAA and Evaluation levels); students will learn to hunt points rather than build chains and judgements. (b) Guidance lists Help to Buy (demand-side) as a supply factor. (c) Entirely UK-specific (green belt, London, Help to Buy) for an international-school cohort who will get contexts like Malaysian palm oil or Vietnamese rice; no data extract is provided though such a question in WEC11 would be data-response.

'Assess the importance of PES for agricultural markets (10 marks)'. Vague stem (important to whom? for what decision?) unlike real IAL stems which anchor to an extract. Guidance is points-based ('Define PES (1 mark)... Judgement (2 marks)') rather than the KAA/evaluation levels descriptors used for 10-mark Assess; no indication that a diagram or numerical PES value would lift the level.

'Outline two reasons...' — 'Outline' is not a standard Edexcel IAL Economics command word (papers use Explain/State/Define/Analyse/Assess/Evaluate/Discuss). Content and 4-mark allocation (2x[1 id + 1 dev]) are fine.

'Explain two factors that could cause the supply curve for housing to shift left (6 marks)'. Acceptable, but assigned as the inline practice for block 3 (SR/LR production) where it does not belong; block 1 (which teaches shift factors) has no inline practice at all. Guidance omits the diagram the section's own examMatters says is required.

structureIssues: Inline quiz/practice wiring is sequential, not content-matched: content[0].quizIndices=[0], content[1].quizIndices=[1], content[2].quizIndices=[2]. So the PES block's one inline MCQ is Q1 (wheat drought supply shift) and the SR/LR block's is Q2 (specific tax), while the six genuine PES MCQs (Q3,Q4,Q6,Q7,Q8,Q11) are never seen in Learn Mode. Likewise practiceIndices: block 2 -> P0 (Define PES, OK) but block 3 -> P1 (housing shift factors); block 1 has no practice.

Only content[0] has a diagramRef ('Supply Curve'). Diagrams[1] 'PES: Visual Comparison' and diagrams[2] 'PES Over Time: Short Run vs Long Run' — the two diagrams that carry the spec's PES content and are well drawn — are never rendered in Learn Mode. Block 2 should reference 'PES: Visual Comparison' and the SR/LR block should reference 'PES Over Time'.

Block 3 breaks the difficulty ramp and the spec: after supply and PES it jumps to marginal product, diminishing returns and returns to scale (Unit 3 material) without ever mentioning elasticity, while the spec's actual SR/LR bullet is squeezed into one paragraph at the end of factors-influencing-pes. Takeaways for block 3 match the block but not the section's purpose.

Step pairing (2 sections per step within a block; 3-section blocks leave a lone third section) means steps 2 and 4 are single-section steps. Under the described recall placement, a lone section is both 'first' (recall at bottom of its step) and 'last' (recall at top of the next step), so the factors-that-shift-supply reorder and the factors-influencing-pes fillin are probably shown twice back-to-back, while the final section's fillin (long-run) is probably never shown. Worth verifying in LearnModeTab.jsx.

Every fillin recall uses 'first two letters + underscore count' hints, which turns recall into pattern-completion. The same word appears verbatim in the body a few lines above in every case. No word bank/distractors are used anywhere in the section.

Three near-duplicate MCQ pairs (Q1/Q10, Q4/Q16, Q6/Q12) plus three off-section items (Q14 producer surplus, Q20 joint supply, Q21 ATC) in a 25-item bank; the PreTest samples 3 at random, so a student can be pre-tested on untaught Unit 3 content or on two copies of the same question.

Misconceptions are mostly genuine (stock vs supply; price shifts the curve; PES vs PED; inelastic = no change; diminishing returns = total output falls; diminishing returns vs decreasing returns to scale). factors-that-shift-supply's misconception ('students forget to explain the direction') is an exam-technique note rather than a conceptual misconception — mild filler.

Block 1 takeaway 3 ('Costs, technology, taxes, subsidies and firm numbers all shift supply') drops 'external shocks' from the bullet list and the whole section omits related goods in production (joint/competitive supply) and producer expectations, which the quiz then tests.

Section's own examMatters repeatedly insists on showing equilibrium effects on a diagram, but the shift diagrams have no demand curve, and no worked PES calculation from raw prices/quantities appears anywhere in content, recall, quiz or practice.
ialSpecGaps: 'Use the formula to calculate PES' from raw price and quantity data — only a %-given example (10% -> 20%) exists; no worked percentage-change calculation, no quiz or practice item with raw figures.

'Distinction between short run and long run and its significance for elasticity of supply' — the SR/LR block never links to PES; the linkage is one paragraph in factors-influencing-pes. The dedicated 'PES Over Time' diagram is not surfaced in Learn Mode.

Factors that shift supply: the spec list (costs of production, new technology, indirect taxes, subsidies) is covered, but common Edexcel extensions the bank tests — prices of related goods in production (joint and competitive supply), producer expectations, weather/climate for agriculture — are absent from the text.

Diagrammatic effect of a supply shift on equilibrium price and quantity (strictly 1.3.4 price determination, but required by this section's own examMatters and recall) — the shift diagrams contain no demand curve.

Vertical shift of supply by a specific tax / pivot for ad valorem (strictly the indirect taxes and subsidies spec point) is tested in Q2 and in flashcards but not taught in content[]. Exact IAL bullet numbering for supply vs PES within 1.3 — unsure; the substantive bullets above are the standard Edexcel ones.
strengths: Definitions and terminology match Edexcel mark-scheme language exactly: 'willing and able ... at a given price in a given time period', ceteris paribus, extension/contraction for movements, increase/decrease for shifts, PES formula and sign.

Misconceptions in supply-and-the-supply-curve (stock vs supply), movements-along-vs-shifts (price shifts the curve), interpreting-pes-values (inelastic = no change) and short-run-production (total output falls) are real, frequently seen student errors with a correct 'instead write' model sentence.

Diagrams are technically correct: axes labelled Price/Quantity, PES comparison correctly draws unit-elastic through the origin, elastic cutting the price axis, inelastic cutting the quantity axis, and the momentary/SR/LR diagram pivots all curves through the initial equilibrium.
Reorder recalls for the law of supply chain, the explanation procedure and the diminishing-returns chain are all genuine sequences with valid non-identity shuffles.

Most real examples (John Deere GPS, Chinese solar, TSMC fabs, UK housing PES ~0.4, Toyota JIT, Domino's ovens) are apt, international, and correctly illustrate the concept; quiz items Q0-Q8, Q11-Q13, Q15, Q17-Q19, Q22-Q23 are clean, single-answer MCQs with sound explanations.
examMatters for factors-that-shift-supply and factors-influencing-pes correctly stresses chain-of-reasoning and application to the specific market, which is how IAL KAA levels are actually awarded.
topFixes: Rewire block metadata to match content: content[1] quizIndices -> PES items (e.g. Q3, Q7, Q8), practiceIndices -> [0, 2], diagramRef -> 'PES: Visual Comparison'; content[2] diagramRef -> 'PES Over Time'; give content[0] a practice (P1) and keep Q0/Q1.

Replace block 3 with an on-spec 'Time and PES' block (momentary / short run / long run and what each implies for elasticity, using the existing PES Over Time diagram); move diminishing returns and returns to scale to WEC13 costs. Delete or correct Q21 (P >= AVC / P = MC), which is Unit 3 and currently marks a wrong answer.

Correct the factual errors: swap the Saudi Arabia example for US shale rig-count behaviour; fix or drop the Airbus $25bn / 'doubling inputs' claim; remove Help to Buy from the supply-factor mark scheme; soften 'arrows earn additional marks'.

Redesign fill-in recalls: remove first-letters-plus-length hints, use word banks with distractors, and add at least one numerical PES calculation from raw prices/quantities (also as a 4-mark practice item, converting 'Define PES (4)' to 2 marks).

Dedupe the quiz bank (Q1/Q10, Q4/Q16, Q6/Q12), replace with items on joint/competitive supply (after teaching it in factors-that-shift-supply), PES calculation, and SR/LR elasticity; rewrite the 10- and 20-mark practice guidance as IAL levels descriptors (KAA + evaluation) and localise the 20-marker beyond the UK.

summary: The prose (keyIdea/body/misconception) is competent and mostly accurate IAL-level teaching of demand and the three elasticities, and several misconceptions are the real ones examiners see. But the interactive layer is weak: two fill-in recalls are literally uncompletable (duplicate answer words + FillInRecall.jsx:16 filter), every fill-in's word bank is just its own answers so most reduce to trivial 3-word matching, and four of nine reorders order things that have no order. Practice questions are mapped to the wrong blocks (LearnModeTab.jsx sorts practice by marks before indexing, so 'Define PED' lands on the Demand Curve block) and use non-IAL tariffs (Define 4, Analyse 10, Outline 4). Examples are UK-centric and several are fabricated or wrong (Starbucks 'health scare', Waitrose 2008 'dip', PS5 'price cut'), and behavioural economics looks like GCE 1.2.10 content imported into an IAL section. A strong IAL teacher would use the notes but would not trust the exercises or exam-format claims without a rewrite.
