items: Compare marginal benefit vs marginal cost
Choose the option with greatest net benefit
recallAudit.reason: Procedural and reconstructible, but it is a verbatim copy of the body flow with an outcome ('Utility is maximised') appended; low challenge. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Rational Decision Making and Consumer Behaviour
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: BROKEN: answers contain 'utility' twice; FillInRecall.jsx:16 removes every copy of a word from the bank once placed, so blank 2 can never be filled and 'Check answers' stays disabled (allFilled). Also template line 3 literally says 'Marginal utility ___', leaking 'utility'. Word bank is {utility, utility, diminishes}.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in with distinct answers and distractors: 'Total utility rises at a ___ rate because ___ utility ___ with each extra unit' answers [decreasing, marginal, diminishes] with bank including [increasing, total, rises].

recallAudit.blockTitle: Rational Decision Making and Consumer Behaviour
recallAudit.prompt: Put these behavioural economics concepts in order from cognitive shortcut to outcome:
items: Loss aversion distorts their cost-benefit analysis
Decision deviates from the rational model
recallAudit.reason: Anchoring and loss aversion are parallel, independent biases, not sequential stages; a student who understands the topic has no basis to put anchoring before loss aversion. Only first/last are fixed. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Match-the-bias: pair scenario ('sees £999 model first, then £799 feels cheap', 'keeps gym membership never used', 'won't sell shares at a loss') with the named bias (anchoring, habit/inertia, loss aversion).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Bank {ability, income, substitution}; 'ability' only fits blank 1, but income vs substitution effect is a genuine confusion and the template describes each, so the match has some value. Hints 'ab_____','in____','su___________' leak first letters but are opt-in.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these demand curve concepts in the right order:
items: Price of the good itself changes
Movement along the demand curve occurs
Entire demand curve shifts left or right
recallAudit.reason: Two independent cause→effect pairs concatenated; the pair order (movement first vs shift first) is arbitrary, so a student can get it 'wrong' while understanding perfectly. shuffled [1,3,0,2] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the demand shifters:

accuracyIssues.location: Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) > interpreting-yed-values > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Claims Waitrose 'saw sales dip' in the 2008 recession 'confirming' high positive YED. Waitrose sales and market share actually grew through 2008-09 (it launched 'essential Waitrose' in 2009 and gained share). Presented as evidence for a theory it does not support.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a verifiable case (e.g. Aldi/Lidl UK share gains 2008-2012 vs premium ranges, or a non-UK example such as discount retailers in a named Asian market) or make it explicitly hypothetical.

accuracyIssues.location: Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) > yed-definition-and-formula > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'As UK average incomes rose through the 2010s, demand for McDonald's value-menu items stagnated' — UK real incomes were broadly flat 2010-2015 and McDonald's UK sales grew strongly across the decade. Unverifiable and likely false.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a documented inferior-good case (e.g. bus travel or instant noodles vs rising incomes in a named economy) with a source.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'when a viral social-media health scare about coffee emerged, demand for lattes fell at every price' — no such event; a hypothetical is presented in the 'realExample' slot alongside a real Starbucks price.
accuracyIssues.fix: Label as hypothetical or replace the shift half with a real event (e.g. Starbucks Middle East boycott 2023-24 reducing demand at every price).

accuracyIssues.location: Cross Elasticity of Demand (XED) > xed-definition-and-formula > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'When Sony cut the price of the PlayStation 5, demand for PS5 game titles rose sharply… demand for Xbox consoles dipped' — Sony raised PS5 prices in 2022 in most markets; there is no documented cut with these effects. Fabricated evidence.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use printer/ink or console/game as an illustrative relationship without inventing a price-cut event, or cite the 2023 PS5 promotional discounting with sales data.

accuracyIssues.issue: Samsung A-series '20% cut' is unsourced, and 'existing Samsung users upgraded sooner (income effect)' misdescribes the income effect (higher real income → more of the good bought), conflating it with replacement timing.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: lower price raises real income so some buyers purchase a second/better handset (income effect) and some switch from rival brands (substitution effect).

accuracyIssues.location: Rational Decision Making and Consumer Behaviour > why-consumers-may-not-act-rationally (whole subsection) and quiz[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: Heuristics, anchoring, loss aversion, bounded rationality, 'influence of others', habitual behaviour mirror UK GCE spec 1.2.10 'Alternative views of consumer behaviour'. The IAL WEC11 spec (2018) does not list behavioural economics under consumer behaviour (unsure — verify against spec 1.3.2). If off-spec it is time spent on content that cannot be examined.
accuracyIssues.fix: Verify against WEC11 spec; if absent, cut to one short 'beyond the assumption' evaluation paragraph and remove the reorder recall and quiz[1].

accuracyIssues.location: Rational Decision Making and Consumer Behaviour > rational-decision-making > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Examiners often open a paper with a short question on rational decision-making' — WEC11 Section A is five supported multiple-choice items on any topic; there is no such opening question pattern. Invented exam-format claim.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with: rational decision-making appears as an assumption to state in explanation answers and as an evaluation point (behaviour may not be rational).

accuracyIssues.location: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > ped-definition-and-formula > body para 3
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Some examiners ignore the negative sign… check your exam board's convention' — the app is single-board (Edexcel IAL). Edexcel mark schemes accept the negative value and typically show it (e.g. -0.5); telling students to check a convention they cannot check is unhelpful.
accuracyIssues.fix: State the Edexcel convention directly: give the negative sign (or state 'ignoring the sign') and interpret the magnitude.

accuracyIssues.location: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > factors-influencing-ped > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'A common 8-mark question asks you to explain the factors that determine PED' — IAL 8-mark items use 'Examine' and require analysis plus a diagram/evaluation, not a list of factors; 'Explain' items are 4 (sometimes 6) marks.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'a 4-mark Explain question' or describe the 8-mark 'Examine' expectations correctly.

accuracyIssues.location: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > interpreting-ped-values > bullets (Perfectly elastic)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'any price rise above the going price causes demand to drop to zero' — should be quantity demanded, the very distinction the section's own misconception drills.

quizIssues.question: A consumer continues to renew their expensive gym membership despite rarely attending. This is best explained by:
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer 'Inertia and default bias' uses terms never taught in the section (content names heuristics, anchoring, loss aversion, bounded rationality, habit). Also likely off IAL spec. Option 3 'Herding behaviour' is equally untaught.

quizIssues.issue: Consumer surplus is not taught anywhere in this section's content; it belongs to a different WEC11 spec point. As pre-test/post-test/quiz item it measures a different section.

quizIssues.question: If demand for a product is price inelastic, a firm wishing to increase total revenue should:
quizIssues.issue: Options 0 and 3 are both 'Decrease the price…' variants, so only two substantive choices remain; wasted distractor.

quizIssues.question: At the midpoint of a straight-line demand curve, PED is equal to:
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but the varying-elasticity-along-a-linear-curve idea is never taught in the content body (only in diagram 'PED and Total Revenue'); a student who did the reading can only guess.

quizIssues.question: If the cross elasticity of demand (XED) between goods A and B is +2.5, the goods are:
quizIssues.issue: Explanation says 'a price rise in good A leads to a … increase in demand for good B' — reverses the A/B roles that the section's misconception insists on (Qd of A over P of B).

quizIssues.question: The price elasticity of demand for a good is calculated to be -0.4. This means the good has:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicates: 3/10/18 (PED value→inelastic/elastic), 5/20 (YED +2.5/+2.3 luxury), 6/11 (XED sign+strength), 4/14 (inelastic→raise price/TR rises), 2/12/19/24 (shift causes). Bank of 25 has ~15 distinct ideas; pre/post-tests may draw duplicates.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term PED (4 marks)' — IAL 'Define' items are 2 marks; the guidance awards 2 of the 4 marks for explaining elastic vs inelastic, which is not part of a definition. Guidance also says 'PED greater than 1' without absolute value. Additionally, because LearnModeTab.jsx sorts practice by marks before applying practiceIndices, this question is served on Block 1 (The Demand Curve) before PED has been taught.

'Analyse … (10 marks)' — 10 marks in IAL Economics is 'Assess' (level-marked, KAA + evaluation). 'Analyse' is not a 10-mark IAL command word. Guidance gives evaluation 1 mark, which does not match a 10-mark level scheme; and via the sort bug this question lands on Block 5 rather than the YED block.

'Outline two causes … (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word; the 4-mark equivalent is 'Explain'. Guidance is fine. Via the sort bug this is served on Block 2 (PED), where a demand-shift question is off-topic.

'Evaluate … (20 marks)' is the right Section C tariff, but the guidance is a point-based tally (2+3+2+3+2+2+2+2+2) rather than the IAL level-based KAA/Evaluation scheme, gives evaluation only 2 marks, and never requires the TR/elasticity diagram that IAL 20-mark mark schemes reward. It also never appears inline (practiceIndices only reach index 3 of the sorted list).
'Explain two factors (6 marks)' — acceptable IAL-style item; guidance is usable. Via the sort bug it is served on Block 3 (YED) instead of the PED block.

structureIssues: Practice-to-block mapping is broken: LearnModeTab.jsx builds sortedPractice (sorted by marks) and indexes practiceIndices into it, but the JSON's practiceIndices were authored against the unsorted array. Result: Block 1 (Demand Curve) gets 'Define PED', Block 2 (PED) gets 'Outline EV demand shift', Block 3 (YED) gets 'Explain PED factors', Block 5 gets 'Analyse YED'; the 20-mark Evaluate never shows.

Diagrams 'PED Values: Visual Comparison' and 'YED and XED Interpretation' never render in Learn Mode: Block 2 diagramRef 'PED' first-matches 'PED and Total Revenue' (LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104), and Blocks 3/4 have diagramRef null. Half the diagram set is invisible in the primary flow.

Every block has exactly 3 sections, so 2-per-step pairing yields a 2-section step then a 1-section step in every block; the 1-section step then carries diagram + quiz + practice + Explain-It-Back + takeaway + spaced recall + immediate recall — the heaviest step is always the shortest reading, and the rhythm is identical six times.
Inline quiz only ever uses quiz indices 0-7 (quizIndices per block); indices 8-24 are reachable only via pre/post-test and the paywalled Quiz tab.

Block 5 'Significance of Elasticities' largely repeats 'Significance of YED' and 'Significance of XED' subsections already in Blocks 3-4; its reorder recall is a recap of the block's own paragraph order.

Diminishing marginal utility (Block 0) is never connected to the downward-sloping demand curve (Block 1), so the two halves of the section do not link — the spec's reason for teaching DMU here is missing.
Fill-in word banks contain only the answers (FillInRecall.jsx:12), so every fill-in is an n-item matching puzzle with no distractors; two are uncompletable because of duplicate answers.

Filler misconceptions: 'students treat elasticities as purely theoretical' (using-elasticities-for-business-decisions), 'firms should only sell necessities' (significance-of-yed), 'XED only matters for substitutes' (significance-of-xed) are invented rather than observed marking errors; the genuine ones (demand vs Qd, total vs marginal utility, inferior ≠ low quality, price as a shifter, sign of YED) are good.
Several 'flow' blocks present parallel effects as sequences (demand-and-the-demand-curve: 'Income effect → Substitution effect'), reinforcing the same false-sequence habit the reorders have.

examMatters repeatedly asserts paper frequency ('almost every paper', 'often open a paper', 'a common 8-mark question') that does not match WEC11's structure; students in international schools will take these as fact.
ialSpecGaps: Diminishing marginal utility as the explanation for the downward slope of the demand curve (spec links DMU to the shape of the demand curve) — DMU is taught but never applied to the curve.
'Conditions of demand' as the spec term for shift factors — not used; students should recognise the phrase in questions.
PED varying along a straight-line demand curve (elastic above midpoint, inelastic below) — only in a diagram and quiz[7], not in content body.
Significance of elasticities for CONSUMERS (spec: firms, consumers and government) — diagram 3 checklist promises it, content covers only firms and government.
Calculating elasticities from a data table/diagram (IAL routinely gives P/Q tables) — worked example only in prose flows; no table-based practice.

Unsure: exact WEC11 1.3.2 bullet list — if elasticities are a separate spec point the section may be over-packed; if behavioural economics is absent from WEC11 (likely), Block 0 subsection 3 is off-spec.
strengths: keyIdea lines are tight, examinable one-sentence definitions (PED, YED, XED, movement vs shift).

Genuine misconceptions drilled well: demand vs quantity demanded; total vs marginal utility; inferior good ≠ low quality; price is not a shifter; YED sign matters; 'necessities always inelastic' nuance via breadth of definition.
Equi-marginal condition MU_A/P_A = MU_B/P_B is stated correctly with a practical reallocation explanation.
MCQ correctIndex is right for all 25 items; calculation items (3, 16, 18) have correct arithmetic and clear explanations.

Diagram 0 (movement vs shift) has correct axes (Price/Quantity), correct terminology (extension/contraction vs increase/decrease) and a usable checklist; diagram 1 correctly places max TR at unit elasticity.
Government-policy subsection correctly states the revenue-vs-behaviour trade-off of taxing inelastic goods and flags the equity point.
YED/XED interpretation ranges and sign conventions are correct and consistent with Edexcel mark schemes.
topFixes: Unbreak the two uncompletable fill-ins (utility-and-utility-maximisation: [utility, utility, diminishes]; interpreting-ped-values: [elastic, inelastic, inelastic]) — make answers distinct, and add 2-3 distractor words to every fill-in bank (FillInRecall.jsx:12 currently uses answers only).

Fix practice placement: either stop sorting practice by marks before applying practiceIndices (LearnModeTab.jsx sortedPractice) or re-author indices; then retariff to IAL command words (Define 2, Explain 4/6, Assess 10/12, Evaluate 20 level-marked with a diagram) and drop 'Outline'/'Analyse (10)'.

Replace the four non-sequence reorders (behavioural biases, PED-factor 'importance', XED strong-positive vs strong-negative, PED/YED/XED 'order') with sort/classify/match exercises as suggested in recallAudit.
Surface the two hidden diagrams (add diagramRef 'YED and XED' to Block 3 or 4, and either split 'PED Values' out or merge it) and add one sentence linking DMU to the downward-sloping demand curve.

Replace fabricated or wrong examples (Waitrose 2008 dip, McDonald's 2010s, Starbucks health scare, PS5 price cut, Samsung 20%) with verifiable, preferably non-UK cases, and remove invented exam-frequency claims in examMatters.

summary: The prose is fluent, the core externality/public-good mechanics are mostly right, and the misconceptions are largely real student errors, so a teacher would not be embarrassed by most paragraphs. But a demanding IAL examiner would not put it in front of students as-is: one MCQ (Q18) teaches the wrong welfare-loss area and directly contradicts Q5; the Public Goods block insists the market provides 'zero' public goods while the section's own common_mistakes says that is a mistake and its lighthouse example is the textbook counterexample; the welfare-loss block confuses competitive equilibrium with the social optimum; and three of seven blocks (merit/demerit, monopoly, moral hazard) are not on the WEC11 spec while spec bullets (symmetric vs asymmetric information, private vs public goods, social = private + external) go untaught. Learn Mode wiring is also broken: the inline quiz/practice for blocks 4-7 point at the wrong topics, the 'Deadweight Loss' diagramRef matches no diagram, and every reorder recall is a verbatim copy of the flow box shown on the same step, with fill-in hints that spell out the answer (and five hints whose lengths do not match their answers).

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Society gets wrong mix of goods and services
recallAudit.reason: Step 1 is a setting, not an event that causes step 2 ('free market operates' does not cause 'price signals become distorted'; the distortion is caused by an externality/public good etc., which is absent). Steps 3 and 4 are the same statement reworded. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation, but the items are the flow box on the same step verbatim.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in on the definition with no letter hints: 'Market failure = a ___ of resources so the outcome is not ___ efficient' (misallocation / allocatively), or a classify task: sort 6 scenarios into externality / public good / information gap.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Template 'Allocative efficiency requires P = ___' with hint 'M_' leaves only MC; 'When P ≠ MC, market over- or ___' hands over 'underproduces' by symmetry; 'Lost welfare is called ___ loss' with 'de________' is a giveaway. Also hint 'un____________' is 14 chars but 'underproduces' is 13, so the blank is visibly the wrong length.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A short numeric task: 'Market Q = 120, optimal Q = 100, MSC-MSB gap at Qm = $8. Welfare loss = ?' (answer 80) with a follow-up 'is this over- or under-production?'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: External costs fall on third parties
recallAudit.reason: Causal chain a well-taught student can reconstruct (external cost -> MSC>MPC -> overproduction). Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Caveat: items are the on-screen flow box verbatim, so on the 'immediate' placement it is copy-from-screen.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep, but paraphrase the items so they differ from the flow box, or show it only as the 'spaced' recall on the next step.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Consumer acts on private ___ only' + 'be_____' = benefit; 'Third parties bear external ___' + 'co___' = costs; 'MSB is less than ___' + 'MP_' leaves exactly one option. Nothing here tests the concept that distinguishes a consumption from a production externality.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in that tests the distinction: 'For a negative CONSUMPTION externality the ___ curve shifts (benefit/cost), so the socially optimal quantity is ___ (lower/higher) than Qm' with no letter hints.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Market underproduces relative to social optimum
recallAudit.reason: Mirror of the negative-production chain; causal and reconstructible. Shuffled [2,3,0,1] valid. Same verbatim-flow caveat.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep; paraphrase items so they are not identical to the flow box.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Third parties also gain ___ benefits' would accept 'spillover' semantically but hint 'ex______' forces 'external'; 'MSB is greater than MP_' is a one-option blank. Trivial with hints, ambiguous without them.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: 'Vaccination: private benefit = ___, external benefit = ___' as a match-the-example task, or a diagram-labelling task on the Positive Externality of Consumption SVG (which currently is never shown in Learn Mode).

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: No one can be charged for using it
No firm can earn revenue from it
Private market will not provide the good
recallAudit.reason: Causal chain is reconstructible. Shuffled [3,0,2,1] valid. Two caveats: only non-excludability (not non-rivalry) causes 'no one can be charged', so step 1 bundles a non-causal property; and the end item hard-codes the 'will not provide' absolutism the section's own common_mistakes warns against.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep but reword item 1 to 'Good is non-excludable' and item 4 to 'Private market under-provides or does not provide the good'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Good is non-___ so no one pays' + 'ex_________' = excludable; 'Revenue is ___' could be nil/low but 'ze__' forces zero; 'ta_______' = taxation. Two hints are the wrong length (11 vs 10 chars; 9 vs 8), which will confuse the student.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder with paraphrased free-rider chain (non-excludability -> no incentive to pay -> no revenue -> no private supply), which examMatters explicitly says examiners want as a logical chain, and drop the fillin here.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
recallAudit.reason: The body says underconsumption has 'two reasons' (information failure AND positive externalities); items 1 and 2 are parallel causes with no order between them, so a student who understands the content can legitimately put 2 before 1. Only items 3->4 are sequential. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classify task: drag 'teenager underestimates future earnings', 'more educated workforce raises productivity', 'smoker ignores passive smoking harm', 'smoker underestimates addiction' into Information failure vs Externality buckets.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Free market ___ demerit goods' with hint 'ov__________' (12 chars) fits both 'overproduces' and 'overconsumes' (12 chars, and arguably the more correct term for a demerit good). 'Consumer ___ the benefits' also fits 'overestimates'. Hint 'ex____________' is 14 chars but 'externalities' is 13.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Accept synonyms (overconsumes/overproduces; overestimates/overvalues) or reword to 'Free market ___-consumes demerit goods' (over).

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Welfare is lower than it could be
recallAudit.reason: Linear causal chain, reconstructible. Shuffled [1,3,0,2] valid. Very generic and again verbatim from the flow box.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep; paraphrase items.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'One party has ___ information' is naturally answered 'more', 'better' or 'private'; only the hint 'su______' forces 'superior', which is not the term used in Edexcel mark schemes. 'Market for ___' with 'le____' is trivial.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in on the lemons chain that tests mechanism: 'Buyers offer a price reflecting ___ quality -> owners of ___ cars withdraw -> average quality ___' (average / good / falls), accepting synonyms.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Low-risk people exit and market may collapse
recallAudit.reason: Adverse-selection spiral is a true causal sequence. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. Note it only tests adverse selection; moral hazard (half the subsection, and what the paired MCQ Q6/Q19 test) is not recalled.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep; add a second item asking the student to tag each of 4 scenarios 'before contract (adverse selection)' or 'after contract (moral hazard)', which is exactly the distinction examMatters says earns full marks.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Firm has ___ power over price' fits 'monopoly' or 'pricing' as well as 'market'; 'Consumer surplus transfers to ___' fits 'producers', 'the firm', 'the monopolist'; only the letter hints disambiguate. 'price rises above M_' is a one-option blank.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder of the monopoly chain (MR=MC output chosen -> output below competitive level -> P > MC -> surplus transferred + DWL), or move this block out of Unit 1 entirely.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Deadweight loss triangle is the difference
recallAudit.reason: Not a real procedure: item 1 says 'competitive equilibrium' but item 2 compares to 'optimum' (these differ when there is an externality, which is the whole point of the section); items 3 and 4 are the same step restated. A student could defensibly order 2 before 1 or 4 before 3. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A concrete calculation on the Negative Externality diagram: 'Qm = 60, Qopt = 40, vertical MSC-MSB gap at Qm = $10. Welfare loss = ?' (100) plus 'which two curves bound the triangle?' (MSC and MSB/D).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Monopoly: output restricted below ___ level' fits 'efficient', 'optimal', 'socially optimal' as well as 'competitive'; 'Positive externality: market ___' fits 'underconsumes'. Two hints are the wrong length ('un____________' 14 vs 13; 'co__________' 12 vs 11). Item 1 ('triangle to right of social optimum') is a diagram-position fact better tested on the diagram itself.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Interactive diagram task: on the Negative Externality SVG, tap the three points bounding the welfare-loss triangle; on the Positive Externality SVG, tap which side of Qm the triangle lies.

accuracyIssues.location: Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods (body para 4) and block takeaway 'Private markets produce zero public goods — complete failure'
accuracyIssues.issue: Absolutist claim that the free market provides 'zero quantity' of public goods. The IAL spec wording is 'why public goods MAY NOT be provided by the private sector'. The section's own common_mistakes[2] ('Saying public goods cannot be provided by the market') says this exact claim is a mistake and that the issue is under-provision. Internal contradiction that a student will be marked down for repeating.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite to 'the free market will under-provide or fail to provide public goods because firms cannot capture revenue'; change takeaway to 'Private markets under-provide public goods (often not at all)'.

accuracyIssues.location: Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods > realExample (UK lighthouse system)
accuracyIssues.issue: States lighthouses were 'historically funded by the government' and that Trinity House 'collects dues from ports rather than individual vessels'. Historically English lighthouses were largely privately built and financed by light dues levied on ships (Coase 1974 uses this as the canonical counterexample of private provision of a public good); today light dues are charged per ship tonnage on vessels calling at UK/Irish ports into the General Lighthouse Fund, not general taxation. The example undermines the point it is meant to make and is factually wrong.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a clean example (e.g. flood defences / national defence funded from general taxation) or, better, use lighthouses honestly as the 'quasi-public / privately provided' evaluation point.

accuracyIssues.location: Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss > measuring-welfare-loss (body para 1)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'In a perfectly competitive market, total surplus is maximised at the equilibrium where supply meets demand. Any deviation from this point — whether through externalities, monopoly power, or government intervention — reduces total surplus.' With an externality the market equilibrium is NOT the surplus-maximising point; the externality is a property of that equilibrium, not a deviation from it, and moving away from it (a Pigouvian tax) raises welfare. This contradicts the whole Externalities block and the practice[3] model answer.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'Total surplus is maximised where MSC = MSB. When private and social costs/benefits diverge (externalities) or a firm restricts output (monopoly), the market settles away from this point and the lost surplus is the deadweight loss.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Examiners penalise students who draw MSC above MPC for a consumption externality.' Edexcel/IAL mark schemes for demerit-good/cigarette questions routinely accept an external-cost (MSC > MPC) diagram; the IAL spec only requires diagrams for external costs of production and external benefits of consumption. Telling students they will be penalised for the diagram most mark schemes list is misleading about marking.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with: 'Both an MSC>MPC and an MSB<MPB diagram can earn marks for a negative consumption externality provided the labels and the welfare-loss area match your written explanation; be consistent.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Solutions include mandatory insurance, excess charges and no-claims bonuses for moral hazard, and screening, signalling, and regulation for adverse selection.' Mandatory insurance is a remedy for adverse selection (it forces low-risk people into the pool), not for moral hazard.
accuracyIssues.fix: Move 'mandatory insurance' into the adverse-selection list.

accuracyIssues.location: Types of Market Failure > allocative-inefficiency-deadweight-loss (body para 4) and Welfare Loss > measuring-welfare-loss (body para 3)
accuracyIssues.issue: Deadweight loss described as 'the triangle between the supply curve, the demand curve, and the actual quantity traded'. For externalities (the Unit 1 case) the bounding curves are MSC and MSB, not S and D; using S/D language here is what leads students to shade MSC-MPC areas (see quiz Q18).
accuracyIssues.fix: State the bounding curves as MSC and MSB, and only mention S/D for the monopoly/tax case.

accuracyIssues.location: Types of Market Failure > what-is-market-failure (body para 3) and section scope generally
accuracyIssues.issue: Lists 'merit and demerit goods' and 'monopoly power' as key types of market failure. The Pearson IAL WEC11 spec (1.3.1) lists three types: externalities, under-provision of public goods, information gaps. Merit/demerit goods are not Edexcel terminology (AQA/OCR), monopoly as market failure is Unit 3 (WEC13), moral hazard is Unit 4 (WEC14) financial-market failure. Not wrong economics, but presented as the Unit 1 syllabus.
accuracyIssues.fix: Keep the three spec types as the headline list; label merit/demerit, monopoly and moral hazard blocks as 'beyond Unit 1 / useful for Units 3-4' or move them.

accuracyIssues.location: Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss > measuring-welfare-loss > realExample (US sugar programme)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'AEI estimated the annual deadweight loss to the US economy at over 3 billion dollars in foregone consumer and producer surplus.' Published estimates of ~$2.4-4bn are the cost to consumers (much of it a transfer to producers/growers, who gain); net deadweight-loss estimates are far smaller (roughly $0.5-1bn). The example conflates transfer with deadweight loss, which is precisely the misconception the same subsection warns about.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword to 'costs US consumers an estimated $2-4bn a year, part of which is transferred to sugar growers and part of which is deadweight loss'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Attributes '25% more emissions than average cars' to 'Transport for London data'; the widely cited ~25% figure is from the IEA global SUV analysis, not TfL. Unverifiable attribution.
accuracyIssues.fix: Cite IEA or drop the attribution.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Public Health England estimates every pound spent on flu vaccination saves the NHS roughly four pounds' is not a figure I can verify from PHE publications; PHE was also abolished in 2021 (UKHSA). Presented as fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a verifiable stat or drop the number; consider a non-UK example (e.g. measles vaccination herd immunity) for an international cohort.

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[0] and diagrams[1] SVG vs checklist; body text labels
accuracyIssues.issue: SVG y-axis reads 'Price / Cost' while the checklists require 'Costs/Benefits (y-axis)'; SVG labels the free-market quantity 'Qe' while all body text, quizzes and checklists use 'Qm'. Students copying the diagram will not match the text/mark-scheme labels.
accuracyIssues.fix: Relabel SVG axis 'Costs, Benefits' and quantity 'Qm'/'Q1' consistently with the text.

accuracyIssues.issue: The €8.25bn total is correct for the three EC fines (2.42 + 4.34 + 1.49), but the €1.49bn AdSense fine was annulled by the EU General Court in Sept 2024; the example also cites 'the UK's CMA' as the competition authority for an international audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'fined a total of around €8bn, one of which was later annulled on appeal'; mention competition authorities generically or the student's home jurisdictions.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'welfare loss — the area between the social cost and private cost curves over the range of overproduction' is wrong: the MSC-MPC area over Qopt-Qm is the external cost of the overproduced units, not the welfare-loss triangle (MSC-MSB). Same error as quiz Q18.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'the triangle between MSC and MSB from Qopt to Qm'.

accuracyIssues.location: Section-wide realExamples (NHS, CMA, UK tobacco tax, Thames Barrier, Trinity House, TfL)
accuracyIssues.issue: Seven of sixteen real examples are UK-domestic. IAL papers use international data-response contexts and the target cohort is in HK/Korea/Singapore/Malaysia/Pakistan/Sri Lanka/Middle East. Not an error, but reduces relevance and application marks.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap at least half for regional examples (e.g. Jakarta/Delhi air quality, Singapore COE/ERP, Sri Lanka fuel subsidies, Korea national health insurance).

quizIssues.question: The welfare loss (deadweight loss) from a negative externality of production is represented on a diagram by:
quizIssues.issue: The keyed answer 'The area between the MSC and MPC curves, up to the free market quantity' is WRONG: that area (MSC-MPC from 0 to Qm) is the total external cost, not the welfare loss. Q5 in the same bank explicitly keys the correct answer as 'MSC and MPB from Qopt to Qm' and labels 'MPC and MSC from 0 to Qm' as a distractor meaning 'total external cost'. Q18's own explanation ('from the socially optimal quantity to the free market quantity') contradicts its option text. A pre-test can draw Q5 and Q18 together and mark opposite things right.

quizIssues.question: A public good is characterised by:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q2 (same stem meaning, same correct option, same distractor set). Wastes bank capacity and can appear twice in a 3-question pre-test/post-test.

quizIssues.question: The free rider problem arises because:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q3.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is an example of moral hazard?
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q6 (both keyed to the insured-driver example; Q6's explanation already uses it).

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is the best example of a negative externality of consumption?
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q9. Also Q9's keyed answer ('a driver's vehicle emissions') is arguably ambiguous between consumption and production (commercial driving), whereas Q10's passive smoking is unambiguous; keep Q10, drop Q9.

quizIssues.question: Common resources (such as ocean fish stocks) are prone to market failure because they are:
quizIssues.issue: Tests quasi-public goods / common resources / tragedy of the commons, none of which is taught anywhere in content[] (the Public Goods block never defines private goods or quasi-public goods). Fine as a question, but the content must teach it first.

quizIssues.question: Information failure in the market for pensions means that:
quizIssues.issue: Pensions/present bias is not covered in content; distractors 'The government provides too many pension options' and 'Pension providers always make profits' are implausible, so the question is answerable by elimination.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a merit good?
quizIssues.issue: Keyed option bundles two goods ('Healthcare and education'), and 'Designer handbags' is a throwaway distractor; effectively a two-option question. Also tests non-Edexcel terminology.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is least likely to be a cause of market failure?
quizIssues.issue: 'Perfect competition' is answerable without any market-failure knowledge (it is the only item that is not a failure). Trivial.

quizIssues.question: On a negative production externality diagram, the welfare loss is the area between:
quizIssues.issue: Correct and well-explained, but it is wired via quizIndices[5] to the 'Market Power as Market Failure' block, so Learn Mode shows an externality-diagram MCQ after the monopoly step (see structureIssues). Not a content error.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term negative externality (4 marks)' is not an IAL Unit 1 allocation: definitions are 1-2 marks (Section A MCQ-with-explanation gives 1 for the answer + up to 3 for explanation). A 4-mark item in WEC11 is 'Explain'/'Calculate'/'With reference to Figure 1, explain...'. The guidance also awards a mark for 'the good is overproduced', which is analysis, not definition.

'Explain two reasons why public goods would not be provided by the free market (6 marks)' is realistic in size, but the model answer is wrong on mechanism: it attributes the free-rider problem to non-RIVALRY ('Reason 2: Non-rivalry ... This leads to the free-rider problem'). Free riding is caused by non-excludability, as the content itself says (free-rider-problem body para 1). A student copying this scores less than the guidance claims. Also 'would not be provided' hard-codes the absolutist claim.

'Analyse ... (10 marks)' mismatches the IAL command-word ladder: in WEC11 'Analyse' is 8 marks and 10 marks is 'Assess' (levels-based KAA + evaluation). The guidance is point-scored (2+2+2+2+1+1) rather than levels-based, and includes an evaluation mark ('debate about paternalism') that an 'Analyse' question cannot award. Also 'demerit goods' is non-Edexcel terminology; an IAL question would say 'negative externalities of consumption / information gaps'.

'Evaluate ... taxation is the most effective method ... (20 marks)' is a legitimate Section C allocation for WEC11. However the guidance is point-scored to exactly 20 (2+3+2+2+2+2+1+2+2+2) whereas the real mark scheme is levels-based (KAA 12 / Evaluation 8) and expects a diagram (indirect tax shifting MPC to MSC) which the guidance never mentions. Practice content overlaps Unit 1 section 1.4 (government intervention) more than 1.3. It is also wired to the 'Market Power' block via practiceIndices[3], not to Externalities.

'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (the ladder is Define/Calculate/Explain/Analyse/Assess/Discuss/Evaluate). Mark allocation (2+2) is plausible for a 4-mark 'Explain'. It is wired to the 'Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss' block via practiceIndices[4], though it is about information failure.

structureIssues: quizIndices are sequential (block n -> quiz n) rather than topical, so Learn Mode's inline MCQ is off-topic for four blocks: 'Merit Goods & Demerit Goods' gets Q3 (free rider), 'Information Failures' gets Q4 (merit goods), 'Market Power' gets Q5 (negative production externality welfare-loss area), 'Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss' gets Q6 (moral hazard). Q7 (monopolist) is never used. Suggested: Public Goods [2,3], Merit [4,8,14], Info Failures [6,15], Market Power [7], Welfare Loss [5,18-fixed,21].

practiceIndices are similarly misaligned for the last two blocks: 'Market Power' -> practice[3] (Evaluate taxation for negative production externalities), 'Welfare Loss' -> practice[4] (Outline information failure examples). No monopoly or welfare-loss practice question exists.

Block 7 diagramRef 'Deadweight Loss' matches no diagram title (titles: 'Negative Externality of Production', 'Positive Externality of Consumption', 'Public Goods & the Free-Rider Problem', 'Merit & Demerit Goods'), so the InlineDiagram for the diagram-heaviest block renders nothing. Block 2 diagramRef 'Negative Externality' only matches diagrams[0], so the 'Positive Externality of Consumption' diagram (a spec-required diagram) is never shown in Learn Mode; block 4 (Merit/Demerit) has no diagramRef although a matching diagram exists.

Every one of the 8 reorder recalls is the subsection's own flow box (steps + result) verbatim, and the 'immediate' recall renders at the bottom of the same step where that flow box is visible. It is a copy-from-screen task, not retrieval. All 8 fillins carry first-letters+underscore hints that make the blank one-option; 5 hints have the wrong length (allocative-inefficiency 'un____________', free-rider 'ex_________' and 'ta_______', demerit 'ex____________', diagrams-welfare-loss 'un____________' and 'co__________').

Redundant coverage: 'allocative-inefficiency-deadweight-loss' (block 1) and 'measuring-welfare-loss' + 'diagrams-welfare-loss' (block 7) teach the same deadweight-loss idea three times, with block 1 introducing DWL before the student has seen a single externality diagram. Merge block 7 into block 2 (externality welfare loss) and cut block 1 to a definition + the three spec types.

Difficulty ramp/spec fit: blocks 4 (merit/demerit), 5b (moral hazard/adverse selection) and 6 (monopoly) are Unit 3/4 or non-Edexcel material yet sit in the middle of the Unit 1 section; a WEC11 student is told 'examiners expect you to draw a monopoly diagram', which is not examined in Unit 1. Meanwhile the spec's 1.3.4 'symmetric vs asymmetric information' and 1.3.3 'public vs private goods' get no subsection.

2-per-step pairing is coherent (neg prod + neg cons; pos prod + pos cons; merit + demerit; then info failure alone; asymmetric + moral hazard; monopoly alone; measuring + diagrams). No pairing breaks a concept.

Takeaways mostly match their blocks; exceptions: Public Goods takeaway 'Private markets produce zero public goods — complete failure' contradicts common_mistakes[2]; Externalities takeaway 'Government uses taxes and subsidies to close the gap' is the only mention of intervention in a block that otherwise never teaches it.

Misconceptions: most are genuine (public goods = government-provided; education is a public good; merit vs public; moral hazard vs adverse selection; DWL vs fall in consumer surplus; allocative vs productive inefficiency). Filler-ish: 'negative externalities only come from pollution', 'information failure only affects uneducated consumers', 'free riding = laziness', 'monopolies are always bad' (the last is Unit 3 evaluation, not a Unit 1 misconception).

Pre-test gate draws 3 random MCQs from a 25-item bank that contains a wrongly keyed item (Q18), four near-duplicate pairs and two untaught topics (Q20, Q22); a student can be told they were wrong for a correct answer before the lesson even starts.
ialSpecGaps: 1.3.4(a) 'distinction between symmetric and asymmetric information' — symmetric information is never defined or contrasted; only asymmetric is taught.
1.3.3(a) 'distinction between public goods and private goods' — private goods (rival, excludable) are never defined; quasi-public goods / common resources are not taught although quiz Q20 tests them.

1.3.2(a)/(b) explicit 'private cost + external cost = social cost' and 'private benefit + external benefit = social benefit' relationships are only in common_mistakes[0] and quiz Q16, never stated as a taught formula in a subsection body.
1.3.2(d) welfare GAIN from correcting a positive consumption externality (spec wording covers welfare loss and gain areas); content only ever calls the positive-externality triangle a 'welfare loss'.

Unit 1 numbering: the app labels this '1.3.5 Market Failure'; in the 2018 IAL spec market failure is 1.3.1-1.3.4 (types, externalities, public goods, information gaps) — unsure of the app's mapping convention; worth checking that 1.3.1-1.3.4 are not double-covered elsewhere.

Not spec gaps but over-coverage worth flagging: merit/demerit goods (not Edexcel terminology in IAL Unit 1), monopoly as market failure (WEC13 Unit 3), moral hazard/adverse selection (WEC14 Unit 4 financial market failure).
strengths: Externality mechanics are correct and consistently stated across all four externality subsections (MSC>MPC for negative production, MSB>MPB for positive consumption, Qm vs Qopt, triangle bounded by MSC/MSB from Qopt to Qm in body text and diagram checklists).
The two externality SVG diagrams have correct curve placement and detailed, mark-scheme-style checklists (8 items each) that a student could self-assess against.

Most misconceptions are the ones examiners actually see: 'public goods = provided by government', 'education is a public good', 'merit goods = public goods', moral hazard vs adverse selection timing, DWL vs redistributed surplus.
MCQ explanations for Q0-Q9 explain why each distractor is wrong, not just why the key is right — good remediation value.

Real examples are mostly concrete and verifiable (Deepwater Horizon 4.9m barrels, Daraprim $13.50->$750, Akerlof lemons, Harberger 1954, Australia plain packaging 2012, EC Google fines summing to €8.25bn).
examMatters for the free-rider problem ('non-excludability -> no incentive to pay -> no revenue -> no production, link each step') models exactly the chain-of-reasoning IAL analysis marks reward.

extras.evaluation ('market failure is necessary but not sufficient for intervention', 'valuing externalities is subjective', 'merit/demerit classification is value-laden') gives genuine Section C evaluation angles.
topFixes: Fix quiz Q18 (key it to 'MSC and MSB/D from Qopt to Qm') and extras.chains[0]; delete duplicates Q11/Q12/Q19/Q9; then remap quizIndices and practiceIndices so each block's inline MCQ/practice is on-topic (currently blocks 4-7 get the wrong questions and the monopolist Q7 is unused).

Fix the Learn Mode diagram wiring: change block 7 diagramRef from 'Deadweight Loss' to something that matches (or retitle a diagram), add a diagramRef for the Positive Externality of Consumption diagram (spec-required, currently never shown), add 'Merit' ref for block 4; relabel SVG axes 'Costs, Benefits' and Qe->Qm.

Correct the four teaching errors: public goods 'zero quantity / complete failure' (contradicts own common_mistakes and spec 'may not be provided'); the lighthouse example (privately funded via light dues — the classic counterexample); measuring-welfare-loss para 1 (competitive equilibrium is not the optimum under an externality); 'examiners penalise MSC>MPC for a consumption externality'; plus practice[1] attributing free riding to non-rivalry and 'mandatory insurance' filed under moral hazard.

Re-scope to WEC11: add short subsections on symmetric vs asymmetric information, private vs public vs quasi-public goods, and the social = private + external identity; move Market Power (Unit 3) and Moral Hazard/Adverse Selection (Unit 4) into an 'extension' block or out of the section; merge the three deadweight-loss subsections into one.

Rebuild the recalls: stop copying the flow box verbatim (or show reorders only as 'spaced' on the next step); remove first-letter hints or accept synonyms (overconsumes/overproduces, more/better/superior, optimal/competitive); fix the five wrong-length hints; replace the two non-sequential reorders (what-is-market-failure, merit-goods) and the pseudo-procedure (measuring-welfare-loss) with classify tasks or a numeric welfare-loss calculation.

summary: The prose is genuinely good: definitions match Edexcel mark-scheme wording, every block pairs mechanism with evaluation, the examMatters notes are the right ones (elasticity for taxes, opportunity cost for subsidies, quantity-vs-price certainty for permits vs taxes), and the four SVG diagrams are geometrically correct (subsidy = MEB at Qopt, DWL triangles land on the right curves). But what a student actually experiences in Learn Mode is broken by assembly errors: quizIndices are sequential 0-7 so six of eight blocks end with an off-topic MCQ; practiceIndices are applied to a marks-sorted array (LearnModeTab.jsx:82) so all four inline practice questions land in the wrong block and the 20-mark essay never appears; diagramRef "Indirect Tax" never matches the tax diagram so the one diagram examiners most expect is never shown; and all nine reorder recalls are verbatim copies of the flow widget rendered on the same step, so students can copy the order from the screen. The fill-in recalls are a three-word drag bank, which makes six of eight trivial. Practice mark allocations include a 20-mark Evaluate (WEC11 caps at 14) and a 4-mark Define. A strong IAL teacher would happily use the notes but would not put the Learn Mode flow in front of students until the mapping and recall design are fixed.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Indirect Taxes to Correct Negative Externalities
recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Output moves closer to socially optimal level
recallAudit.reason: Real causal chain. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. However it is a verbatim copy of the flow widget in the same section's body, and because it is the block's first section its recall renders 'immediate' at the bottom of the same step, so the answer is visible on screen above it.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep the sequence but extend it so it is not a copy of the flow: add 'Tax incidence depends on PED' and 'Government collects revenue = tax x Q1' steps, or show this recall only in the spaced slot on the next step.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Indirect Taxes to Correct Negative Externalities
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Template item 1 contains the gloss '(hit poorer households harder)' which defines the answer; item 3 '___ market activity' with 'black' in a 3-word drag bank is a collocation, not recall. Bank {regressive, inelastic, black} has no interchangeable slots so it is solved by grammar alone.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Remove the parenthetical gloss; use a bank of 5-6 words including plausible distractors (progressive, elastic, grey, proportional) so the student must choose, not just place.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Output moves closer to socially optimal level
recallAudit.reason: Valid causal chain; shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Same flaw as the tax reorder: identical to the on-screen flow widget in the same step (immediate placement).
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Vary from the flow: e.g. 'Subsidy per unit paid to producers -> producers' costs fall -> S shifts right by subsidy -> consumer price falls to Pc, producer receives Pp -> Q rises to Qopt where MSB = MSC'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Three-word drag bank with three grammatically distinct slots (noun-adjective, noun, verb): solvable without understanding. Not a chain: opportunity cost, overproduction and entrenchment are three separate evaluation points. Hint 'op__________' has 12 characters for an 11-letter answer.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A short MCQ or 5-word bank (opportunity, overproduction, remove, underconsumption, subsidise) so that 'If set too high they cause ___' actually discriminates.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Quantity demanded rises, quantity supplied falls
recallAudit.reason: Valid causal chain; shuffled [2,3,0,1] valid. First three items copy the on-screen flow widget; only item 4 is new.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fine as a sequence; move to spaced slot or add a consumer/producer surplus step so it is not answerable by reading the flow above.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Bank {price, investment, black}: 'lower ___', 'reduce ___', '___ markets' each admit exactly one word by grammar. No economics is tested.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in on the short-run/long-run distinction with a bank including distractors: 'In the ___ run supply is price inelastic so the shortage is small; in the ___ run landlords cut ___ (maintenance/investment) and supply ___ (falls/rises)'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Quantity supplied rises, quantity demanded falls
Government may need to buy up unsold stock
recallAudit.reason: Valid chain; shuffled [3,0,2,1] valid. Copies the on-screen flow (items 1-3). Item 4 is only true for producer-support floors (agriculture), not for minimum unit pricing on alcohol, which the same section uses as its real example.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep, but change item 4 to 'Surplus must be bought, stored, destroyed or exported' and note in body that with alcohol MUP no surplus is purchased.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Minimum ___ is a price floor in the labour market' with 'wage' in the bank is a collocation. The three items (producer income, storage cost, minimum wage) are unrelated facts presented as a chain with arrows.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Replace with an elasticity application: 'If demand is ___ (inelastic), the price floor cuts Qd only slightly, so the surplus is ___ (small) and producer revenue ___ (rises)' with a bank including elastic/large/falls.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Firms trade permits on open market
Emissions fall to cap at lowest overall cost
recallAudit.reason: Genuine procedural sequence; shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. Again duplicates the flow widget on the same step.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Extend to the trading logic: 'Cap set -> permits allocated -> low-abatement-cost firms cut emissions and sell spare permits -> high-abatement-cost firms buy -> total emissions = cap at minimum cost -> cap tightened over time, permit price rises'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Items 1-2 are the best fill-in in the section (quantity/price are swappable in the bank, so it tests the permits-fix-quantity contrast). But item 3's template '___ — fixes price, not quantity' states the answer after the blank, and 'opposite' is the only non-noun in the bank.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Drop item 3's trailing clause: 'A carbon tax does the ___'. Better: make it a 4-blank with bank {quantity, price, quantity, price}: 'Permits fix ___, let ___ vary; taxes fix ___, let ___ vary'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Market fails to provide the good
Good is available free at point of use
Everyone can access regardless of ability to pay
recallAudit.reason: Items 2, 3 and 4 are three descriptions of the same arrangement, not successive causes; 'free at point of use' and 'everyone can access regardless of ability to pay' are near-synonyms and could be swapped. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Copies on-screen flow.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder the free-rider logic, which is a real chain: 'Good is non-excludable -> consumers can benefit without paying -> private firms cannot charge -> no market provision (missing market) -> government provides, funded by taxation'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Two of three answers appear in the section title ('Information Provision and Nudge Theory'); 'choice ___' with 'architecture' in a three-word bank is a collocation. Hints 'in__________' and 'ar___________' are one character too long.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Test the limitation instead: 'Information provision may fail because consumers show ___ (habitual behaviour) and ___ (present bias); a nudge changes the ___ (default) without removing ___ (choice)'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Legal standard or limit is imposed
Firms must comply or face penalties
recallAudit.reason: Items 3 and 4 say the same thing; item 1 is generic preamble that applies to every policy in the section. Nothing here requires understanding regulation specifically. Shuffled [1,3,0,2] valid. Copies on-screen flow.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A matching/fill-in exercise: classify examples (Euro 6 NOx limit, product safety law, merger block) into environmental / consumer-protection / competition regulation; or fill-in on regulation vs tax: 'Regulation gives ___ (certainty) of outcome but treats all firms the same regardless of ___ (abatement cost)'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: With the bank {competition, innovation, instability}, 'removes rules to boost ___' and 'lower costs and encourage ___' both accept competition or innovation (the body itself says deregulation encourages 'entrepreneurship and innovation' and 'increase competition'). A student placing innovation/competition the other way round is marked wrong for a valid answer. Hint 'co__________' is one char too long.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Make slot 1 unambiguous: 'Deregulation removes barriers so new firms can ___ (enter), boosting competition' and slot 2 'reduces ___ (compliance) costs'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Resources are misallocated more than before
recallAudit.reason: Simple but genuine chain; shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. Copies the on-screen flow widget.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Acceptable; make it concrete with a case: 'Rent rising -> rent control imposed below equilibrium -> landlords cut maintenance and withdraw supply -> shortage worse than before -> net welfare loss'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Item 2 'Political ___ favours short-term wins' contains 'short-term' immediately after the blank. Not a chain: three independent causes joined by arrows. Bank slots are grammatically distinct so it is placement-by-grammar. Hints 'im________' and 'sh____________' are one char too long.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reword item 2: 'Elections every few years encourage political ___'. Add the IAL-spec causes (distortion of price signals, excessive administrative costs) as blanks with a larger bank.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Measure the cost of market failure
If intervention costs exceed failure costs, government failure exists
recallAudit.reason: Items 1 and 2 are interchangeable (either cost can be measured first); items 3 and 4 are the same step stated twice. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Copies the on-screen flow.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Replace with an application MCQ or judgement fill-in: give a scenario (e.g. fuel subsidy costing 2% of GDP, smuggling, budget deficit) and ask which costs count as intervention costs and whether government failure has occurred.

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims London taxi licensing 'restricted the number of black cabs', 'keeping fares high and limiting supply'. London has never numerically capped black-cab licences (the constraint is the Knowledge test; fares are set by TfL). The capped-medallion case is New York, not London. Students citing this in an exam would be citing a false fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with New York taxi medallions (numerically capped since 1937, medallion values collapsed after Uber) or keep London but describe the barrier accurately (Knowledge entry requirement, TfL-regulated fares).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'alcohol-specific deaths fell by 13% in the first year' — the Public Health Scotland / Lancet (2023) estimate of a 13.4% reduction covers roughly May 2018 to end-2020 (about 2.5 years), not the first year.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'fell by an estimated 13% over the first two and a half years compared with what was expected'.

accuracyIssues.location: Minimum Prices > how-minimum-prices-work > body para 4 and recall item 4
accuracyIssues.issue: 'The government may need to purchase the surplus itself' is presented as the general consequence of a minimum price, but the section's own example (alcohol MUP) involves no government purchase — retailers keep the higher margin and there is no stockpile. Conflating producer-support floors with demerit-good floors loses the key IAL evaluation point that MUP revenue goes to retailers rather than the government (unlike a tax).
accuracyIssues.fix: Distinguish: for producer-support floors (agriculture) the government buys/stores the surplus; for demerit-good floors (alcohol) there is no purchase, retailers gain the margin, and the government gets no revenue — a reason to prefer an indirect tax.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'UK Plug-in Car Grant subsidised ... by up to 1,500 pounds per car' — the grant was up to £5,000 at launch (2011) and was cut in stages to £1,500 only from December 2021. Stating 'up to £1,500' understates the scheme by a factor of three.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'up to £5,000 per car when launched in 2011, cut in stages to £1,500 before withdrawal in June 2022'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'UK airline deregulation in the 1980s and 1990s allowed easyJet and Ryanair to enter' — the liberalisation that enabled low-cost carriers was the EU 'third package' (1992-97), EU-wide, not a UK policy; Ryanair is Irish.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'EU airline liberalisation (completed 1997) allowed low-cost carriers such as easyJet and Ryanair...'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Nudge theory is increasingly popular in exam questions ... libertarian paternalism' — nudge theory and libertarian paternalism are not in the IAL WEC11 specification (1.2.10 covers habitual behaviour, influence of others, computational weakness). This is UK GCE-flavoured content presented as an IAL exam expectation.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reframe as enrichment: 'Nudges are not named in the IAL spec but can be used as an example of information/choice-based intervention'; remove the claim about exam frequency and the 'libertarian paternalism' label.

accuracyIssues.location: Minimum Prices > how-minimum-prices-work > body para 3 and takeaway 4
accuracyIssues.issue: 'The National Minimum Wage' is a UK proper noun; for an international cohort it should be the generic concept. Also 'Scotland ... the first country in the world' is contestable (Russia set minimum vodka prices in 2010) and 'country' will confuse non-UK students.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'A national minimum wage is a price floor in the labour market'; 'Scotland was the first to introduce a comprehensive minimum unit price for all alcohol'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Invokes 'monopsony labour market' — Unit 3 (WEC13) content, not Unit 1. Fine as a footnote but a Unit 1 student cannot use it.
accuracyIssues.fix: Keep the elasticity-of-demand-for-labour point; drop or flag monopsony as 'Unit 3'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'The 2008 financial crisis was partly caused by government failure through inadequate regulation ... political pressure to expand home ownership' — a contested political narrative presented as fact; weak evidence for an examiner and outside Unit 1 scope.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a cleaner Unit 1 example (e.g. fuel subsidies in Malaysia/Indonesia/Pakistan encouraging over-consumption and smuggling, or India's MSP grain floor producing surplus stocks).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'spending tobacco tax revenue on the NHS' implies hypothecation; UK tobacco duty is not hypothecated. Minor but a marker may query it.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'revenue that could in principle fund healthcare (hypothecation)'.

quizIssues.question: A government introduces a subsidy for solar panel installation. Which of the following is a potential cause of government failure from this policy?
quizIssues.issue: Stem asks for a 'cause' but the keyed option is a distributional consequence (benefits wealthy homeowners). More importantly, regressive distribution is an equity concern, not a net welfare loss; by the IAL definition taught in this very section (government failure = net welfare loss / worse allocation) this is not government failure. Teaches a conflation.

quizIssues.question: A buffer stock scheme to stabilise agricultural prices involves:
quizIssues.issue: Buffer stocks are never taught anywhere in the section (no mention in content, notes or extras) and are not, to my knowledge, in the 2018 IAL WEC11 spec. Because the pre-test draws 3 random MCQs from this bank, a student can be tested on untaught material before the section starts.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best describes the effect of a specific tax on a market with price elastic demand?
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer (producers bear most of the burden, quantity falls significantly) is right, but tax incidence is never explained in this section's body — examMatters only says 'who bears the burden' without teaching it. Tests 1.2.9 content that this section does not cover.

quizIssues.question: A maximum price (price ceiling) set below the equilibrium price will lead to:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q1 (same stem, same keyed idea 'excess demand'). Duplicates inflate pre/post-test scores and reduce bank coverage.

quizIssues.question: Government failure occurs when:
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q4 (identical keyed option wording 'net welfare loss'). Q5 and Q18 also share the identical stem 'Which of the following is an example of government failure?'.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is an advantage of tradeable pollution permits over an indirect tax on pollution?
quizIssues.issue: Keyed option 'guarantee a specific reduction in total emissions' — a cap guarantees a maximum level, not a 'reduction' (if the cap is above current emissions nothing falls; the section's own EU ETS example makes exactly this point). Should read 'guarantee a maximum level of total emissions'.

quizIssues.question: Regulation as a form of government intervention is often criticised because:
quizIssues.issue: Keyed option 'may be avoided through regulatory capture' — regulatory capture weakens or shapes regulation; it does not let firms 'avoid' it. Odd wording that misdefines the term the section teaches.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best explains why information provision alone may not reduce cigarette consumption?
quizIssues.issue: Uses 'present bias and bounded rationality' — not IAL 1.2.10 vocabulary (habitual behaviour, weakness at computation, influence of others). Explanation otherwise good.

quizIssues.question: A minimum price on alcohol set above the equilibrium price is most likely to:
quizIssues.issue: Keyed option 'create excess supply' is correct in the S/D model but sits awkwardly with the real-world MUP example in the body where no surplus stock exists; the explanation does not reconcile the model with the example.

quizIssues.question: A Pigouvian tax on a good with negative externalities aims to:
quizIssues.issue: Overlaps heavily with Q0 (both key on 'internalise the externality / set equal to external cost'). Distractor C 'Generate government revenue' is a genuine secondary aim, so some students will argue it is also true; stem should say 'primary aim'.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' — 20-mark essays are WEC13/WEC14 (Unit 3/4) format. WEC11 Section B tops out at 14 marks (Discuss/Evaluate). Guidance is also point-allocated (2+3+2+2+2+2+2+1+2+2) whereas IAL uses levels-based KAA + Evaluation marking. In addition this question is never surfaced in Learn Mode because practiceIndices only reach sorted positions 0-3.

'Define the term government failure (4 marks)' — in WEC11 'Define' is a 2-mark part (a); a 4-mark part would be 'Explain, with an example, what is meant by...'. Guidance awards a mark for an example, which a 'define' mark scheme would not.
'Outline' is not an Edexcel IAL command word (Define/Explain/Calculate/Analyse/Assess/Discuss/Evaluate/Examine). Content of the guidance is fine for a 4-mark 'Explain two...'.

'Assess ... (10 marks)' is plausible for IAL, but the guidance sums point marks (2+2+1+2+1+1+1=10) instead of showing the KAA/Evaluation level split examiners actually use; the 'judgement' worth 1 mark undervalues evaluation. Also the question wording 'under-consumption of merit goods' is good IAL phrasing — keep.

'Explain two ways in which indirect taxes can be used to correct market failure (6 marks)' — the two 'ways' (consumption externality vs production externality) are the same mechanism applied to two goods; an examiner would expect e.g. specific vs ad valorem, or tax vs the revenue use. Realistic but thin.

structureIssues: quizIndices are sequential [0]..[7] and do not match block content: block 'Subsidies' shows Q1 (maximum price), 'Maximum Prices' shows Q2 (minimum price on alcohol), 'Minimum Prices' shows Q3 (permits vs tax), 'Tradeable Pollution Permits' shows Q4 (government failure definition), 'State Provision' shows Q5 (rent controls as government failure), 'Regulation' shows Q6 (vaccination subsidy). Only blocks 0 (Q0 tax) and 7 (Q7 regulatory capture) are on-topic. Six of eight inline quizzes are off-topic.

practiceIndices are applied to a marks-sorted copy of practice[] (LearnModeTab.jsx:82 sortedPractice, :110-113), so the data indices [0],[1],[2],[3] resolve to: block 'Subsidies' -> 'Define government failure' (worked mode), 'Minimum Prices' -> 'Outline two disadvantages of a maximum price' (guided), 'State Provision' -> 'Explain two ways indirect taxes correct market failure' (guided), 'Government Failure' -> 'Assess subsidies' (independent). Every inline practice is in the wrong block, and the 20-mark essay never appears. Either the data must index the sorted array deliberately or the code must stop sorting before indexing.

diagramRef 'Indirect Tax' on block 0 never matches diagram title 'Tax to Correct Negative Externality' (LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104 requires one string to contain the other), so the tax diagram — the one the section's examMatters says 'examiners expect you to draw' — is never rendered in Learn Mode. The other three refs (Subsidy, Maximum Price, Minimum Price) match.

All nine reorder recalls are verbatim copies of the flow widget in the same section's body, and because each is the first section of its step they render as 'immediate' recalls at the bottom of the same step with the flow visible above. Students can copy the order from the screen; the reorder score in CompletionScreen is therefore meaningless for this section.

Fill-in recalls are a three-word drag bank (FillInRecall.jsx:12). With three grammatically distinct slots, six of eight are solved by grammar without economics. 'Complete the chain:' is used for lists that are not chains (price floors: income/store/wage; causes of government failure: imperfect/short-termism/capture).
Six hint strings are one character longer than the answer (opportunity, information, architecture, competition, imperfect, short-termism) — cosmetic but signals unreviewed generation.

Step structure is monotone: nine steps, each 'How X works' + 'Evaluating X' + MCQ + takeaway + explain-back. There is no ramp; every policy tool is treated at the same depth, and the section never asks students to choose between tools for a given market failure (the actual IAL 12/14-mark skill) until the final block.

Real examples are almost entirely UK (tobacco duty, sugar levy, plug-in grant, NHS, National Minimum Wage, Scotland MUP, UK auto-enrolment, UK buses/airlines, London taxis). For an IAL cohort in HK/SG/MY/PK/LK/Middle East, IAL papers use international contexts; examples like Singapore COE, Malaysian/Indonesian fuel subsidies, India MSP floors, Pakistan wheat support prices, HK public housing would land better.

Misconception filler: 'Maximum Prices > effects-and-evaluation-of-price-ceilings > misconception' ('students assume the government should set it closer to equilibrium') describes a legitimate trade-off, not a misconception; the text concedes the point. Most other misconceptions are genuine (permits 'rich firms pollute as much as they want', 'subsidies always better than taxes', 'information always works').

Block 7 pairing: step 8 = 'What is government failure' + 'Causes'; step 9 = 'Examples and Evaluation' alone. Coherent, but step 9 is where the 20-mark essay should sit and it currently receives 'Assess subsidies' instead.
Takeaways match their blocks. Block 2 takeaway 'Subsidies may achieve affordability without creating shortages' is only supported by one sentence of examMatters, not the body.
ialSpecGaps: Government failure causes named in the IAL spec: 'distortion of price signals' is never stated as a cause (the section lists imperfect information, political short-termism, regulatory capture, unintended consequences); 'excessive administrative costs' is only mentioned in passing in examples-and-evaluation, not taught as a cause.

Tax incidence on consumers vs producers (specific and ad valorem) is referenced in examMatters and tested in Q23 but never taught; the section needs at least a cross-reference to 1.2.9 or a short incidence paragraph tied to the tax diagram's Pc/Pp labels.
Specific vs ad valorem taxes: mentioned in one sentence (parallel vs pivotal shift) with no diagram; the spec expects students to draw both.
Minimum price on demerit goods vs indirect tax comparison (who receives the extra revenue: retailers vs government) — a standard IAL evaluation point, absent.

Choosing between interventions for a given market failure (e.g. tax vs regulation vs permits for pollution; subsidy vs state provision vs information for a merit good) is only partially covered in permits and regulation examMatters; no dedicated comparison content.

Spec numbering: unsure whether IAL 2018 places government failure under 1.3.6 or a separate point; the section merges both, which is defensible, but worth confirming against the WEC11 specification document.
Buffer stock schemes appear in the quiz (Q21) but are not in the section and, as far as I recall, not in the 2018 IAL WEC11 spec — unsure; if they are, they need teaching; if not, remove Q21.
strengths: Core theory is accurate and uses Edexcel mark-scheme vocabulary: tax = MEC at socially optimal output, subsidy = MEB, maximum price must be below equilibrium, minimum price above, government failure = net welfare loss.

Every block pairs mechanism with evaluation, and the evaluation points are the ones IAL examiners reward: PED for tax effectiveness, opportunity cost for subsidies, short-run vs long-run for price ceilings, elasticity for the size of a surplus, quantity-vs-price certainty for permits vs taxes, 'why did the regulation exist' for deregulation.

All four SVG diagrams are geometrically correct: Qopt sits at MSB = MSC, subsidy bracket equals MEB at Qopt, DWL triangles are bounded by the right curves, Pc/Pp labels are present. The tax diagram's MPC+Tax overlaying MSC is exactly what an examiner wants.
Quiz explanations for Q0-Q9 address each distractor individually, which is good formative feedback.

Several misconceptions are real student errors, not filler: permits let rich firms pollute freely; subsidies are 'better than taxes because prices fall'; information provision always works; government failure means never intervene.

examMatters notes are concrete and actionable (label Pc vs Pp on the subsidy diagram; identify the surplus as unemployment in labour-market floors; link each government-failure cause to a specific policy).
The permits reorder and the permits quantity/price fill-in are the best recalls in the section and genuinely test understanding.
topFixes: Re-map quizIndices to block content (e.g. block0 [0,12,14,23]; block1 [6,15,9]; block2 [1,10]; block3 [2,11,17]; block4 [3,16]; block5 [8,20,24]; block6 [7,19]; block7 [4,5,13,18,22]) and fix practiceIndices so each block gets its own question — either index the marks-sorted array deliberately or remove the sort in LearnModeTab.jsx:82 before indexing. Put the essay on block 7.

Change block 0 diagramRef from 'Indirect Tax' to a string contained in the diagram title (e.g. 'Tax to Correct') so the tax diagram renders; consider adding a specific-vs-ad-valorem supply-shift diagram.

Stop reorder recalls duplicating the on-screen flow: either render the first section's recall only as a spaced recall on the next step, or rewrite the nine reorders as longer chains (incidence, revenue, elasticity, Pc/Pp) that are not visible above. Replace the three weak reorders (direct-state-provision, types-of-regulation, examples-and-evaluation) with the free-rider chain, a classification exercise, and a scenario judgement.

Fix practice mark allocations to WEC11 format: 20-mark Evaluate -> 14-mark 'Discuss'/'Evaluate' with a KAA/Evaluation level split in the guidance; 4-mark Define -> 2-mark Define or 4-mark 'Explain, with an example'; 'Outline' -> 'Explain'. Rewrite guidance as levels, not point sums.

Correct the factual/IAL-fit issues: London taxi example (no numeric cap), MUP '13% in the first year', plug-in grant 'up to £1,500', 'UK airline deregulation', nudge-theory exam claim; add the spec-named government-failure causes (distortion of price signals, excessive administrative costs) and swap several UK examples for international ones.

summary: The prose teaching is the strongest part: keyIdeas are precise, the core mechanics (equilibrium adjustment, CS/PS areas, incidence, subsidy shift, government cost = subsidy x new Q) are correct, and most misconceptions are ones students really hold. A strong IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is, for four reasons: the two most diagram-dependent blocks (Indirect Taxes, Subsidies) render no diagram because diagramRef 'Indirect Tax'/'Subsidy' matches no diagram title and no tax/subsidy SVG exists at all; the practice bank is not IAL-shaped (IAL Economics Appendix 6 uses Define 2 / Explain 4 / Analyse 6 / Examine 8 / Discuss 14 / Evaluate 20 and has no 'Assess' or 'Outline'; two of five questions are out of scope, one being a Unit 2 macro essay about the UK); the recall layer is mostly trivial (every fillin word bank is just the three answers, hints leak first letters and length, and 5 of 8 reorders order things that have no order); and two spec bullets (price mechanism in local/national/global markets; effect of demand/supply changes on CS and PS) are untaught while non-spec material (invisible hand, deadweight-loss welfare analysis, Kahneman/Thaler behavioural economics that belongs in 1.3.2) takes four of the fifteen subsections. Several real examples are wrong or dated (London 'rent controls', a CBO sugar-tax score, Glastonbury resale, 59p fuel duty, pre-2003 CAP) and nearly all are UK-centric for an HK/SG/MY/PK audience.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
recallAudit.reason: Items 1 and 2 are two parallel facts with no causal or procedural order (either curve can be described first); only 3 -> 4 is a genuine consequence. shuffled [3,0,2,1] is a valid non-identity permutation.
