recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder the adjustment story instead: 'Price set below Pe' -> 'Qd exceeds Qs (shortage)' -> 'Buyers bid price up' -> 'Qd contracts, Qs extends' -> 'Qd = Qs at Pe'. This is the step-by-step process the examMatters text says examiners want.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Template 'Price below Pe -> ___ exceeds Qs / -> ___ pushes price up / -> Market returns to ___'. FillInRecall.jsx builds the word bank from recall.answers only, so the student drags {Qd, shortage, equilibrium} into three blanks that grammar alone resolves; hints 'Q_', 'sh______', 'eq_________' additionally leak the answers.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin with a distractor bank: 'Price ___ Pe -> Qd ___ Qs -> price is bid ___ -> Qs ___ and Qd ___' with bank {above, below, exceeds, falls short of, up, down, extends, contracts}. That forces the student to choose direction, which is the actual error students make.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
recallAudit.reason: Cause -> shift -> new intersection is a real causal chain and a student can reconstruct it. Weak point: items 3 and 4 are near-synonyms (a new intersection IS the new equilibrium P and Q), so the last swap tests nothing. shuffled [2,3,0,1] valid, not identity.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep, but replace item 4 with the adjustment step: 'Excess demand/supply at the old price' between 2 and 3, and make the last item 'Price adjusts to the new equilibrium'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Willingness to pay minus ___ price / -> Equals consumer ___ / -> Area below ___ curve, above price'. Blank 2 is the subsection title; blank 3 is answered by 'consumer'; bank of three answers plus hints 'ma____','su_____','de____' leaves no decision to make.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin with a CS/PS contrast bank: 'Consumer surplus = area ___ the ___ curve and ___ the price; producer surplus = area ___ the ___ curve and ___ the price' with bank {above, below, demand, supply}. This targets the real confusion listed in common_mistakes[1].

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Area above supply curve, below price
recallAudit.reason: Items 1 and 2 are two independent facts (min price, market price) with no order; item 4 is a diagram description, not a step in a process. Only 'difference' logically follows the two facts. shuffled [1,3,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Numeric fillin (matches IAL QS): 'Minimum acceptable price $150, market price $200, 40 units sold -> producer surplus per unit = $___, total = $___'. Or a diagram-area identification drill: click the PS triangle vs CS triangle.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'CS + PS = total ___ / -> Maximised at free-market ___ / -> Any deviation creates ___ loss'. The three-word bank is the answer set; 'deadweight' is the only word that precedes 'loss', 'equilibrium' the only one after 'free-market'. Hints leak.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Since deadweight-loss welfare analysis is not an IAL 1.3.4 bullet, replace with a recall on spec bullet 2b: 'An increase in supply ___ price, so consumer surplus ___ and producer surplus ___' with bank {raises, lowers, rises, falls, is ambiguous}.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Scarce goods rationed to highest-value buyers
recallAudit.reason: Signalling, incentive and rationing are three simultaneous functions of one price change, not sequential stages. The price rise IS the signal (items 1 and 2 are the same event), and rationing of consumers happens at the moment price rises, not after producers respond; rationing before incentive would be equally defensible. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification drill: give four mini-scenarios (e.g. 'A rise in lithium prices leads mining firms to open new pits', 'At $900 only some fans can afford concert tickets', 'Falling wheat prices tell farmers to plant less') and ask which function each illustrates. Directly matches how the 4-mark Section B questions test this.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Copies the body flow verbatim ('Individuals pursue ___ / Prices guide their ___ / Resources flow to highest-valued ___'); bank is the three answers; 'uses' is the only word that fits the last blank. Hint 'se__________' is also one character short of 'self-interest' (13 chars vs 12 underscores+2) - minor. Also invisible hand is not an IAL 1.3.4 bullet.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Drop or convert into recall of spec bullet 3b: 'In a ___ market (e.g. street food in a city) prices adjust quickly to local conditions; in a ___ market (e.g. crude oil) one price signal coordinates producers on every continent' with bank {local, national, global}.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Output falls and tax revenue collected
recallAudit.reason: Tax -> supply shift -> new equilibrium -> consequences is a real causal chain a student can reconstruct. Minor weakness: items 3 and 4 are simultaneous outcomes. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid, not identity.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: This is the one fillin that discriminates: the bank contains both 'elastic' and 'inelastic', and blanks 2 ('Less ___ side bears more of the tax') and 3 ('___ demand means consumers pay most') accept either grammatically, so a student who thinks 'less inelastic side pays more' gets caught. But hints 'el_____' vs 'in_______' remove the test if the student clicks 'Show hints' (and 'in_______' is shown for both 'incidence' and 'inelastic', which is confusing).
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep the item; remove or generalise hints (e.g. give no hints for this item, or hint by meaning: 'responsive / unresponsive to price').

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Tax raises price and lowers quantity
Consumer and producer surplus both fall
recallAudit.reason: Items 2, 3 and 4 are simultaneous accounting consequences of item 1, not a sequence; 'government gains revenue' before 'DWL remains' is an authorial choice, not a fact. shuffled [1,3,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Area-identification drill on a tax diagram (label CS after tax, PS after tax, tax revenue, DWL), or a numeric fillin: 'Tax $5/unit, quantity falls from 100 to 80 -> tax revenue = $___; consumer price rises $3 so consumer incidence = ___% of the tax'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: 'Government pays ___ to producers / -> Supply curve shifts ___ / -> Price falls, ___ rises': blank 1 is the block title, and with a bank of exactly {subsidy, downward, quantity} grammar resolves every blank. If the bank included 'upward' or 'left' it would test the misconception the section itself flags (students shift supply up).
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Same template with a distractor bank {upward, downward, left, right, price, quantity, tax, subsidy}; or 'Government cost = subsidy per unit x ___ quantity' with bank {original, new}.

recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Output rises toward socially optimal level
But costs taxpayers money via taxation
Net benefit depends on size of externality
recallAudit.reason: This is an argument skeleton (point, effect, counterpoint, judgement), not a causal or chronological sequence; the taxpayer cost is simultaneous with item 1, and it also relies on 'positive externality' and 'socially optimal level', which are 1.3.5 concepts not yet taught in this section. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: An evaluation-paragraph builder is fine as a type, but use content taught here: 'Subsidy lowers price and raises output' -> 'Consumers gain (lower price), producers gain (higher effective price)' -> 'Government pays subsidy x new Q, funded by taxation (opportunity cost)' -> 'Judgement: worthwhile if the gain to consumers/producers exceeds the cost to taxpayers'. Better still, a fillin on incidence of the subsidy (spec 4d): 'If demand is inelastic, most of the subsidy benefit goes to ___'.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Alternative Views of Consumer & Producer Behaviour
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain:
recallAudit.reason: Term-from-definition recall is a reasonable format, but 'Loss ___' can only be 'aversion', leaving a two-way choice between 'anchoring' and 'nudges' that the sentences ('relying on first info seen' vs 'improve choices without removing freedom') resolve by grammar and number. Hints 'an_______', 'av______', 'nu____' make it fully trivial. The terms themselves are not the IAL 1.3.2(1b) list.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Re-key to the spec list: bank {herding, habitual behaviour, inertia, poor computational skills, need to feel valued, framing} with scenario blanks ('Buying the same cereal every week without checking prices = ___').

recallAudit.blockTitle: Alternative Views of Consumer & Producer Behaviour
recallAudit.prompt: Put these in the right order:
items: Consumer faces limited info and time
recallAudit.reason: Constraint -> inability to optimise -> search-until-acceptable is a real causal chain. Items 3 and 4 are the same idea restated (satisficing = stopping at good enough), so the final swap is redundant. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid, not identity.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep but replace item 4 with a consequence ('May end up with a worse phone than the best available') so each step adds information.

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims London has 'rent controls' that keep supply below equilibrium. Private-sector rent control in England was abolished by the Housing Act 1988; London rents are market-set. Also 'many are outbid' describes price adjusting upward, which contradicts the claim of below-equilibrium pricing.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a genuine below-equilibrium case (e.g. Hong Kong public rental housing waiting lists, or a concert ticket sold at a fixed face value below market, e.g. Taylor Swift Singapore 2024 with resale at multiples) and keep the causal story consistent: a price held below Pe -> queue/waiting list -> secondary market.

accuracyIssues.location: Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus > total-welfare-and-efficiency > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'The US Congressional Budget Office estimates deadweight loss when scoring tax proposals. A proposed sugar tax...' - CBO scores federal legislation and does not publish deadweight-loss triangles in scores; there is no federal sugar-tax score of this kind. Worse, the example contradicts the paragraph's own misconception text: a sugar tax targets a negative externality, so it can raise, not reduce, total welfare.
accuracyIssues.fix: Delete. Use a case where the market is competitive and has no externality (e.g. a per-unit tax on an ordinary consumer good) to illustrate DWL, and explicitly reserve 'intervention may raise welfare' for externalities (1.3.5).

accuracyIssues.issue: Glastonbury tickets are non-transferable (photo-ID registration since 2007), so 'resale sites listing tickets at several times the original price' is not what happens; the excess-demand mechanism is right but the illustration is wrong and UK-only for an international audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use an example where resale actually occurs (Coldplay/Taylor Swift Singapore 2024, Cricket World Cup 2023 in India) or the Olympic ticket ballot.

accuracyIssues.issue: Attributes the 2022 oil price rise to 'OPEC production cuts in 2022'. The 2022 spike (Brent ~$128 in March) was driven by Russia's invasion of Ukraine; OPEC+ announced its 2m bpd cut in October 2022 when prices were already falling. The simultaneous-shift lesson is fine but the dates are wrong.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite as: 'In early 2022 the war in Ukraine shifted supply left while post-lockdown recovery shifted demand right' - both shifts raise price, quantity indeterminate.

accuracyIssues.location: Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus > total-welfare-and-efficiency > body[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'No reallocation of resources could make one group better off without making another worse off' is Pareto efficiency, presented as equivalent to maximised total surplus. They are different criteria; many Pareto-efficient allocations do not maximise CS+PS.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'total surplus (CS + PS) is as large as possible; producing more or less would lose some of it' and drop the Pareto phrasing.

accuracyIssues.location: Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus > total-welfare-and-efficiency > keyIdea and block takeaway[2]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Total welfare... is maximised at the free-market equilibrium where no deadweight loss exists' is stated unconditionally; it only holds with no externalities/market failure. The misconception paragraph adds the caveat, but keyIdea and takeaway (the parts students memorise) do not.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add 'in a competitive market with no externalities' to keyIdea and takeaway.

accuracyIssues.issue: '59p per litre on petrol' - UK fuel duty has been 52.95p/litre since March 2022 (57.95p from 2011 to 2022). Not 59p in any period. Also every tax example in the block (fuel duty, 20% VAT, alcohol duty) is UK-only for students in HK/SG/MY/PK/Middle East.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use 'a fixed amount per litre of fuel' without a false number, or use examples students will meet: Singapore's 9% GST / Pakistan 18% sales tax (ad valorem) and excise per stick on cigarettes or per litre of fuel (specific).

accuracyIssues.issue: Describes the EU CAP as paying subsidies 'to keep food production high' with 'subsidised European exports' undercutting developing-country farmers. Since 2003 most CAP payments are decoupled from production (Basic Payment Scheme), and EU export refunds were abolished 2013-15. The description is 1980s-era.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a live per-unit production/consumption subsidy: fertiliser subsidies in India or Pakistan, fuel subsidies in Malaysia/Indonesia, or EV purchase subsidies in China.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'cost German households over 25 billion euros annually through surcharges' - the EEG surcharge peaked around 24bn euros/year (paid by all consumers, with large industrial exemptions) and was abolished in July 2022; present tense 'cost... annually' is out of date.
accuracyIssues.fix: Past tense with 'roughly 20-25bn euros a year until the surcharge was abolished in 2022'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'His [Thaler's] work led the UK government to create the Behavioural Insights Team' - BIT was set up in 2010 (Thaler advised); the Nobel was 2017. Causality/timeline is loose.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Thaler (Nobel 2017) advised the UK's Behavioural Insights Team, set up in 2010, which pioneered nudges such as automatic pension enrolment.'

accuracyIssues.location: Consumer Surplus & Producer Surplus > consumer-surplus > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Those passengers enjoy huge consumer surplus, which is exactly why budget airlines generate such high passenger volumes' - reverses causality (low fares raise quantity demanded; consumer surplus is a result, not the cause of volume) and quotes Ryanair fares in dollars.
accuracyIssues.fix: State it as: 'a passenger willing to pay 100 euros who pays 10 euros gains 90 euros of consumer surplus; summing over all passengers gives the CS triangle.' Or use AirAsia for the target market.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'This is why economists prefer taxing goods with inelastic demand' - normative claim presented as consensus; ignores regressivity, which the section's own extras evaluation ('indirect taxes on necessities can be regressive') raises. Also DWL analysis is UK-GCE-flavoured; IAL 1.3.4 asks for impact on consumers, producers and government, not DWL.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Governments often choose inelastic goods because revenue is stable and quantity falls little - but this makes the tax regressive.'

accuracyIssues.location: Functions of the Price Mechanism > the-invisible-hand > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'examiners expect you to link [the invisible hand] to the three functions' - the invisible hand is not in IAL 1.3.4 (spec bullets are rationing/incentive/signalling and local/national/global markets). ExamMatters overclaims what IAL papers mark.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reframe as background; put the exam emphasis on applying the three functions to a given context and to local/national/global markets.

accuracyIssues.issue: Checklist lists 'For taxes: S+tax curve parallel above S; consumer price Pc, producer price Pp, and quantity Qt labelled' and 'Tax revenue rectangle and deadweight loss triangle', but the diagram has only 'Base Equilibrium' and 'Increase in Demand' scenarios. Diagrams label P*/Q* while the text uses Pe/Qe.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add the tax scenario SVG the checklist describes and align labels to Pe/Qe.

quizIssues.question: If the demand for a good increases while supply remains constant, what happens to consumer surplus?
quizIssues.issue: Keyed answer 'ambiguous' conflicts with (a) the section's own teaching ('When the price rises, consumer surplus shrinks' in consumer-surplus body[1], which points students to 'decreases') and (b) the standard IAL answer for spec bullet 2b: with a rightward demand shift and upward-sloping supply, the CS triangle under the new demand curve is larger, so CS rises. Three contradictory signals on a spec-listed point.

quizIssues.question: In a competitive market, the equilibrium price acts as a rationing mechanism because it:
quizIssues.issue: Keyed answer 'Eliminates both excess demand and excess supply' describes the market-clearing property of equilibrium, not the rationing function (allocating scarce goods to those willing and able to pay). The explanation actually gives the correct definition, which does not match the keyed option text.

quizIssues.question: A subsidy is granted to producers of electric vehicles. Which of the following will NOT result from the subsidy?
quizIssues.issue: The keyed option ('A reduction in government expenditure on transport') is categorically different from the other three (all market outcomes), so it is a giveaway; also it is a claim about a budget line rather than about the subsidy's market effect.

quizIssues.question: In a free market, if the current price is above the equilibrium price, there will be:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q8 (same stem, same keyed answer). Also Q1/Q16 (demand vs supply increase), Q11/Q18 (both 'entirely on the consumer'), and Q5/Q13 (subsidy shift) overlap. With PreTest drawing 3 random MCQs from this bank and each block getting one fixed MCQ, redundancy shrinks effective coverage; there is no MCQ on subsidy incidence direction, ad valorem vs specific revenue, or local/national/global markets.

quizIssues.question: Which diagram best represents the effect of an indirect tax on a market?
quizIssues.issue: Asks 'which diagram' but offers text options; 'shifts up/left by the amount of the tax' is imprecise (the vertical distance equals the tax; the horizontal 'left by the amount' is not meaningful).

quizIssues.question: Market equilibrium is described as stable if:
quizIssues.issue: 'Stable equilibrium' is not an IAL 1.3.4 concept and is not taught anywhere in the section content; a student can only answer by elimination.

quizIssues.question: A subsidy granted to producers of solar panels would:
quizIssues.issue: Explanations for Q10-Q24 are one-liners that do not address distractors, unlike Q0-Q9; inconsistent feedback quality for the InlineQuiz/PostTest.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Evaluate the impact of a significant increase in global oil prices on the UK economy (20 marks)' is a Unit 2 (WEC12) macro essay: the guidance is entirely cost-push inflation, real disposable income, GDP growth and Bank of England monetary policy - none of it taught in 1.3.4, and UK-specific for international students. The 20-mark tariff itself matches IAL 'Evaluate', but the guidance is point-marked ('3 marks', '2 marks') whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (KAA + evaluation levels).

'Assess the effectiveness of the price mechanism... (10 marks)': 'Assess' is not an IAL Economics command word (spec Appendix 6 lists Define 2, Calculate 2/4, Draw 4, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Examine 8, Discuss 14, Evaluate 20) and there is no 10-mark tariff in WEC11. The guidance is point-marked, not levels-marked. Should be 'Examine... (8)' or 'Discuss... (14)', ideally with reference to an extract, and should mention local/national/global markets (spec 3b).

'Outline two effects of a price floor set above the equilibrium price (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an IAL command word, and price floors/minimum wage are 1.3.6 Government intervention, not taught in this section's content (only flashcards mention them). Model answer's 'government may need to purchase surplus output' is fine but off-topic here.

'Define the term equilibrium price (4 marks)': IAL 'Define' is 2 marks. The guidance pads to four separate marking points (definition, no excess, intersection, no tendency to change) which is not how a 2-mark define is credited.

'Explain how a market moves from excess supply to equilibrium (6 marks)': IAL 'Explain' is 4 marks; a 6-mark question is 'Analyse'. The mark scheme awards no marks for a diagram, although a 6-mark Analyse on this topic normally expects one.

Bank-level gap: none of the five questions covers indirect taxes, subsidies, incidence, or CS/PS (half the spec bullets), and there is no Calculate or Draw question despite the QS requirement (>=20% of marks) and the topic being the most diagram-heavy in Unit 1. Additionally LearnModeTab.jsx:80/113 indexes practiceIndices into the marks-sorted list, so Block 3 (Price Mechanism) shows the price-floor question and Block 4 (Indirect Taxes) shows the excess-supply question; the Assess and Evaluate items never appear inline.

structureIssues: No diagram renders for the Indirect Taxes or Subsidies blocks: diagramRef 'Indirect Tax' and 'Subsidy' are matched by substring against diagram titles ('Supply & Demand Equilibrium', 'Consumer & Producer Surplus') in LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104, so neither matches; and no tax/subsidy/incidence/DWL SVG exists anywhere in diagrams[]. Meanwhile examMatters in three subsections tells students tax/subsidy diagrams are compulsory.

Inline quiz mismatch: quizIndices [1] puts Q1 (increase in demand) on the Consumer/Producer Surplus block instead of Q6; quizIndices [4] puts Q4 (cigarette tax incidence) on the Subsidies block instead of Q5/Q13/Q20; the Alternative Views block has no quizIndices although Q7 (bounded rationality) exists.

Inline practice mismatch (practiceIndices index the marks-sorted array): Price Mechanism block gets 'Outline two effects of a price floor'; Indirect Taxes block gets 'Explain excess supply -> equilibrium'; the Assess and Evaluate questions are never surfaced.

2-per-step pairing leaves singleton steps that carry all block widgets: Block 1 = [how-markets, excess-demand] + [changes-in-equilibrium alone + diagram + quiz + practice + explain + takeaway]; Block 2 = [CS, PS] + [total-welfare alone + widgets]; Block 4 = [specific/ad-valorem, incidence] + [welfare-effects alone + widgets]. The heaviest steps are the ones with the least content, and the 'spaced' recall shown at the top of those steps is the previous step's weak reorder (e.g. the producer-surplus $150/$200 ordering).

Block 6 'Alternative Views of Consumer & Producer Behaviour' is misplaced: in the IAL spec it is 1.3.2(1b) 'Reasons why consumers may not aim to maximise utility' with a fixed list (herding, habitual behaviour, inertia, poor computational skills, need to feel valued, framing and bias). The block instead teaches anchoring, loss aversion, availability heuristic, nudges and Simon's bounded rationality, has no diagram, quiz or practice, and reads as an appendix.

Content weighting vs spec: two subsections on deadweight-loss welfare analysis (total-welfare-and-efficiency, welfare-effects-of-taxation) and one on the invisible hand are not IAL 1.3.4 bullets, while spec 3b (price mechanism in local, national and global markets) and 2b (how changes in demand/supply affect CS and PS) have no subsection at all.

Forward references: effects-and-evaluation-of-subsidies (body[0], recall) depends on 'positive externality' and 'socially optimal level', which are 1.3.5 concepts; total-welfare-and-efficiency introduces 'allocative efficiency' without the 1.3.5 framing.

Misconceptions: most are genuine (movement vs shift, CS is not 'saving', PS is not profit, ad valorem drawn parallel, subsidy shifts supply up, tax revenue is not a welfare loss, bounded rationality is not irrationality). Two are exam-technique tips dressed as misconceptions: signalling-incentive-rationing ('Students list the three functions but fail to explain') and behavioural-economics ('proves people are irrational').

Meta says mistakes: 0 but common_mistakes[] has 3 good entries (adjustment process, CS/PS labelling, marking the new equilibrium) - these are not surfaced in Learn Mode. Flashcards include price ceilings/floors/black markets (1.3.6 content).

Takeaways match their blocks and are accurate; difficulty ramp (equilibrium -> surplus -> mechanism -> tax -> subsidy) is sensible, with welfare tools introduced in Block 2 before being reused in Block 4.
ialSpecGaps: 1.3.4 3(b) The price mechanism in the context of different types of markets, including local, national and global markets - not taught anywhere (no subsection, no example, no recall, no MCQ).

1.3.4 2(b) How changes in demand or supply might affect consumer and producer surplus - only a one-line 'when price falls the triangle gets bigger'; no diagram of a shift's effect on CS/PS, and the one MCQ on it (Q14) is keyed 'ambiguous'.

1.3.4 4(d) The incidence of subsidies on consumers and producers - one sentence ('split depends on relative elasticities'); no rule stated (inelastic demand -> consumers capture more of the subsidy), no diagram, no recall; only Q20 tests it numerically.

1.3.4 4(a)/4(c) 'impact on... the government' - tax revenue rectangle and subsidy cost are stated in text/takeaways but never drawn; no Calculate practice on revenue or subsidy cost (IAL QS requirement).

1.3.2 1(b) (if Block 6 is kept here) - the spec list is herding, habitual behaviour, inertia, poor computational skills, the need to feel valued, framing and bias; the block teaches anchoring, loss aversion, availability heuristic, nudges and satisficing instead. Only 'poor computational skills' (via bounded rationality) and 'framing and bias' (via anchoring) are loosely covered.

Assessment format: nothing in the section is shaped like the WEC11 paper (Section A six 1-mark MCQs; Section B five short-answer questions totalling 20; Section C five-part data response of 34; Section D one 20-mark essay from a choice of two) or its command-word tariffs (Define 2, Calculate 2/4, Draw 4, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Examine 8, Discuss 14, Evaluate 20).
strengths: KeyIdeas are precise and examiner-friendly (equilibrium 'no tendency to change'; incidence 'falls on the less elastic side'; subsidy cost = subsidy per unit x new quantity).

Tax Incidence and Elasticity is a genuinely good subsection: correct extremes (perfectly inelastic demand / perfectly elastic supply), correct misconception ('producers always pass on the full tax'), and its fillin is the only recall whose word bank (elastic vs inelastic) actually discriminates.

Most misconceptions are real student errors and give a corrected sentence to write ('when demand shifts right, there is a movement along the supply curve...'; 'producer surplus is not profit'; 'tax revenue is a transfer, not a loss').

MCQs 0-9 have distractor-by-distractor explanations; numeric items Q15 (consumer incidence $3 of $5) and Q20 (producer share $1.50 of $4) match IAL quantitative-skills style; Q12/Q19 correctly test the indeterminate variable under simultaneous shifts.
Extras evaluation points are IAL-grade evaluation: sticky prices/persistent disequilibrium, equity of rationing by price, incidence 'depends on elasticity, not intention' with regressivity.
Block takeaways are accurate one-liners that match their blocks; the two existing diagrams are clean, correctly labelled (P on y, Q on x) and come with useful mark-scheme-style checklists.
topFixes: Add tax and subsidy diagrams (specific parallel shift, ad valorem pivot, consumer/producer incidence shares, tax revenue rectangle, subsidy cost rectangle) and give them titles that the diagramRef substring match will find ('Indirect Tax', 'Subsidy'), so Blocks 4 and 5 stop rendering with no diagram.

Rebuild practice[] to the IAL Appendix 6 tariffs (Define 2 / Explain 4 / Draw 4 / Calculate 2-4 / Analyse 6 / Examine 8 / Discuss 14 / Evaluate 20): delete the UK oil-price macro essay and the 'Outline' price-floor item, add a Calculate on incidence/revenue, a Draw on a subsidy, and an Examine/Discuss on the price mechanism across local/national/global markets; make practiceIndices index practice[] (not the marks-sorted copy) so each block gets an on-topic question.

Fix the recall layer: give every fillin a word bank with distractors (elastic/inelastic, up/down, left/right, demand/supply, original/new) and remove first-letter hints; replace the five non-sequence reorders (equilibrium slopes, producer surplus $150/$200, three price-mechanism functions, tax welfare areas, subsidy evaluation) with classification or diagram-area drills.

Teach the missing spec bullets - 3b price mechanism in local, national and global markets (with Asian/Middle-East examples) and 2b effect of demand/supply shifts on CS and PS - then re-key Q14 to the standard answer; move Block 6 to 1.3.2 and re-key it to the spec's own list (herding, habit, inertia, poor computation, need to feel valued, framing/bias).

Correct or replace the wrong/dated examples (London 'rent controls', CBO sugar-tax score, Glastonbury resale, 59p fuel duty, pre-2003 CAP) and de-UK the examples for the HK/SG/MY/PK audience; fix quizIndices so the CS/PS block shows Q6 and the Subsidies block shows a subsidy MCQ.

summary: The prose is mostly sound: injections/withdrawals, planned vs actual expenditure, the inventory adjustment mechanism, and the multiplier (both formulas, reverse multiplier, evaluation factors) are explained at the right level with real misconceptions. But a strong IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is. It teaches transfer payments as an injection/part of G while its own quiz says they are excluded from GDP; 10 of 24 MCQs (GDP methods, GNI, NNI, PPP, real vs nominal, per capita) belong to 2.1.1 measures and are never taught here yet feed the 3-question pre-test; the inline quizzes surface multiplier calculations in blocks 2 and 3 before the multiplier is taught in block 4; two of four blocks have diagramRefs that match nothing so students never see a diagram for equilibrium or the multiplier; four of five fill-ins are letter-hinted copy exercises and two of five reorders have no genuine order; and blocks 1-2 say the same thing three times. There is also no AD/AS treatment of equilibrium real national output, which is how IAL papers actually test it.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the two-sector circular flow:
items: Households supply factors of production to firms
Firms pay factor incomes to households
Households spend income on goods and services
recallAudit.reason: It is a circle. Starting at 'firms pay factor incomes' or 'households spend' is equally valid; the 'correct' start point is the author's choice, and a student who understands the flow perfectly can still get it 'wrong'. shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification/drag-sort: sort 6 items ('wages', 'labour', 'goods and services', 'consumer spending', 'rent', 'land') into 'real flow' vs 'money flow' and 'households→firms' vs 'firms→households' — this is what the examMatters says examiners want.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the injections and withdrawals:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'go________', 'sa_____', 'ri___' plus the template '___ spending, and exports' make every answer a first-two-letters lookup. 'saving' (Edexcel's usual singular) would also fit line 2 and may be rejected by exact match.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Numeric fill-in: 'I = 40, G = 60, X = 30, S = 50, T = 45, M = 40. Total injections = ___; total withdrawals = ___; national income will ___ (rise/fall).' Tests the balance idea instead of vocabulary.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the injection types from private to public to foreign:
items: Investment (I) — firms spend on capital goods
Government spending (G) — public services and infrastructure
Exports (X) — overseas buyers purchase domestic output
recallAudit.reason: I, G and X are parallel categories with no inherent order; the prompt itself dictates the order ('private to public to foreign'), so the task reduces to matching labels to the prompt's words. shuffled [1,2,0] is a valid permutation.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in with scenario classification: 'Toyota builds a new plant in Thailand → ___ (I/G/X)', 'A Korean tourist pays for a hotel in Singapore → ___', 'Malaysia's government pays teachers' salaries → ___'. Include a transfer-payment distractor so the G-excludes-transfers point is tested.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the withdrawals:
recallAudit.reason: Each template line is the definition of the word ('___ removes income that households choose not to spend' → Savings) and the hints 'Sa_____', 'Ta______', 'Im_____' give the first two letters and exact length. Zero retrieval effort.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in on the paradox-of-thrift chain in the body's flow block: 'If households save more, ___ falls (spending), firms' ___ falls (revenue), so firms cut ___ (output/production) — the paradox of ___.' with no letter hints.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the equilibrium adjustment process:
items: Higher income raises S, T, and M until injections equal withdrawals
recallAudit.reason: Real causal chain with an endogenous-withdrawals ending; each step depends on the previous. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid and not identity.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the equilibrium adjustment:
recallAudit.reason: Template line 2 begins 'If planned spending > output' so line 1's answer 'planned' is printed on screen; 'fa__' and 'in________' give the rest. Also 'Equilibrium: ___ expenditure equals actual output' could take 'aggregate' or 'total' without the hint.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in on the identity-vs-equilibrium distinction (the section's best misconception): 'Actual expenditure ___ (always/sometimes) equals actual output because unsold goods count as ___ investment; the economy is only in equilibrium when ___ expenditure equals output.'

recallAudit.prompt: Order the adjustment to equilibrium when output exceeds planned spending:
items: Firms cut production and lay off workers
Falling income reduces spending until equilibrium is restored
recallAudit.reason: This is the mark-scheme chain examiners credit link by link. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the multiplier process:
recallAudit.reason: 'Recipients ___ a proportion and save the rest' with hint 'sp___' is a copy task; 'withdrawals' fits line 3 as well as 'leakages' and would be marked wrong. No number work despite this being the calculation topic.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Numeric fill-in that mirrors the body's flow: 'Injection = 100m, MPC = 0.6. Round 2 spending = ___m, round 3 = ___m, multiplier = ___, final rise in income = ___m.'

recallAudit.prompt: Order the multiplier calculation steps:
items: Identify MPC or the individual MPW components (MPS, MPT, MPM)
Calculate MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM (or 1 - MPC)
Final change in income = k x initial injection
recallAudit.reason: Procedural sequence a student must actually follow in a calculation question; steps are dependent. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the multiplier evaluation:
recallAudit.reason: '___ lags' with hint 'Ti__' and '___ out occurs when government borrowing raises interest rates' with 'Cr______' are collocation completions, not evaluation.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Judgement fill-in: 'An economy with high import propensity has a ___ (larger/smaller) multiplier; a stimulus during a deep recession has a ___ (larger/smaller) real multiplier than at full capacity; if consumer confidence falls, MPC ___ (rises/falls) so k ___.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] The Circular Flow of Income > three-sector-model > examMatters; and content[1] > injections-explained > body[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: Teaches that transfer payments are government spending (G) and an injection ('these are government spending (injection) even though they are not payment for output'; 'Government spending (G) is expenditure on public services, infrastructure, and transfer payments'). Edexcel IAL treats G in AD as spending on goods and services and excludes transfer payments; quiz[13] in this very section says transfer payments are excluded from GDP. A student following the examMatters would lose the mark quiz[13] awards.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'Transfer payments (pensions, benefits) are NOT counted in G because they are not payment for output — the spending is counted when recipients consume. Examiners often plant this as a trap.' Remove 'transfer payments' from the G definition in injections-explained.

accuracyIssues.location: content[3] The Multiplier and National Income > multiplier-formula > body[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: Defines MPC as 'the fraction of each extra pound of income that is spent on domestic goods'. Edexcel's definition is the proportion of additional income spent on consumption; k = 1/(1-MPC) is the closed-economy version and k = 1/MPW the open-economy version. Redefining MPC to make the two formulas identical is non-standard and could cost a definition mark; it also contradicts the notes[3] MPC definition only loosely.
accuracyIssues.fix: Define MPC conventionally; present 1/(1-MPC) as the simple/closed-economy case and 1/MPW as the version to use when tax and imports are given, and say so explicitly.

accuracyIssues.location: content[3] > multiplier-concept > body flow block ('Workers spend 0.8bn (save 0.2bn)' → 'multiplier = 5')
accuracyIssues.issue: The worked flow uses saving as the only leakage and produces k = 5, then two sections later the misconception scolds students for 'forgetting that MPC must exclude the portions lost to tax and imports'. Internally inconsistent and k = 5 is unrealistic for any IAL case study.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use MPW in the flow (e.g. spend 0.6, withdraw 0.4 as S+T+M) giving k = 2.5, consistent with quiz[3].

accuracyIssues.location: content[3] > multiplier-formula > realExample (UK MPW 0.65, MPS 0.10 + MPT 0.30 + MPM 0.25)
accuracyIssues.issue: Presented as 'an estimated MPW' but these are not published estimates; they are illustrative numbers dressed as fact. Also UK-centric for an international audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Label as 'illustrative' or replace with a genuine estimate (e.g. OBR/IMF fiscal multiplier ranges 0.3-1.0 for the UK) or an Asian economy example (Singapore's high MPM → small multiplier).

accuracyIssues.issue: '$787 billion' was the original CBO score (later revised to ~$831bn); CBO's multiplier range for ARRA components was roughly 0.4-2.5, not '1.5 to 2.5'; the '$1.2-2.0 trillion total impact' is derived from the invented range. Numbers are sloppy for an 'exam-ready' example.
accuracyIssues.fix: State 'about $800bn' and 'CBO estimated component multipliers between roughly 0.4 and 2.5; the higher values applied to direct purchases, the lower to tax cuts for higher earners'.

accuracyIssues.issue: HS2 cost estimates ranged from £45bn to £106bn depending on year/scope, the northern legs were cancelled in 2023, and spending is spread over ~15 years, so 'represents a government spending injection of over 100 billion' is misleading as a single-period injection. UK-only example for an international product.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a bounded, verifiable example relevant to the audience (e.g. Indonesia's Nusantara capital project, Saudi NEOM, or Hong Kong's 2023 consumption vouchers as a G injection with a stated annual figure).

accuracyIssues.location: practice[3] guidance (HDI 'combines GDP per capita, education and life expectancy')
accuracyIssues.issue: HDI has used GNI per capita (PPP), not GDP per capita, since 2010. Would be marked as imprecise.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'GNI per capita (PPP)'.

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[0] main SVG 'Circular Flow of Income' and scenarios[1] 'Full Open Economy'
accuracyIssues.issue: The main diagram shows only the factor-services and factor-income arrows; there is no goods/services flow and no consumer-spending flow, so it fails the section's own examMatters ('label both the real flow and the money flow'). The open-economy scenario collapses 'Factor incomes / Consumer spending' onto one arrow in one direction. The checklist item 'Identify factor markets and product markets correctly' is not represented anywhere.
accuracyIssues.fix: Redraw as the standard four-arrow model (goods and factor services one way, spending and incomes the other), with S/T/M leaving from households and I/G/X entering firms.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > two-sector-circular-flow > realExample (Tesco) and pervasive '£'/'pound' usage in body and diagrams
accuracyIssues.issue: UK-only examples and currency throughout (Tesco, HS2, UK MPW, '£' on diagram axes, 'one billion pounds'). Not wrong, but IAL papers use $ and the audience is HK/Singapore/Malaysia/Pakistan/Middle East.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap to $ and at least half the examples to Asian/Middle-East economies.

quizIssues.question: Equilibrium national income in the circular flow model occurs when:
quizIssues.issue: Option B 'Aggregate demand equals aggregate supply' is treated as a distractor, but in IAL this IS the equilibrium condition for real national output, and quiz[10] in the same bank makes 'AD = AS, or equivalently injections equal withdrawals' the correct answer. Two correct options depending on which question the student saw last; only the phrase 'in the circular flow model' rescues it.

quizIssues.question: National income is in equilibrium when:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option bundles 'AD equals AS, or equivalently injections equal withdrawals' — the 'equivalently' is loose (planned J = planned W is the circular-flow condition; AD = AS is the AD/AS condition) and directly contradicts the explanation in quiz[2]. Pick one framing per question.

quizIssues.question: Transfer payments (such as state pensions and unemployment benefits) are:
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer (excluded from GDP) contradicts the section body and examMatters, which call transfer payments government spending/an injection. Fix the content, not the question.

quizIssues.question: In a simple two-sector (households and firms) circular flow model, the equilibrium condition is:
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer S = I, but the section's two-sector model is explicitly defined as having 'no savings' (misconception in two-sector-circular-flow; diagram scenario says 'no saving'). Students taught this section would answer 'consumption equals investment' or be confused. Either add S and I to the two-sector model or retag the question.

quizIssues.question: The difference between GDP and GNI (Gross National Income) is that:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option's parenthetical 'earnings of citizens overseas minus foreign earnings repatriated' is garbled; net income from abroad = income earned by residents from overseas assets/work minus income paid to non-residents. Also off-topic for this section (belongs to 2.1.1 measures).

quizIssues.question: GDP measured using the expenditure method is calculated as:
quizIssues.issue: Off-topic: GDP measurement methods are not taught anywhere in this section's content[] blocks, yet the question can be drawn into the 3-question pre-test. Same for indices 15, 16, 18, 21, 22, 23 (income method, NNI, PPP, real vs nominal, output method, GDP per capita) and 20 (stock vs flow). 10 of 24 MCQs test untaught material.

quizIssues.question: If the marginal propensity to save is 0.1, the marginal rate of tax is 0.2, and the marginal propensity to import is 0.2, what is the value of the multiplier?
quizIssues.issue: Question is fine; placement is not. quizIndices for block 2 ('Injections and Withdrawals') = [1,2], so this multiplier calculation is the inline quiz two blocks before the multiplier is taught.

quizIssues.question: A government increases its spending by £5 billion. If the multiplier is 2.5, the final increase in national income will be:
quizIssues.issue: Same sequencing problem: block 3 ('Equilibrium National Income') quizIndices = [3], so the second multiplier calculation is shown before block 4 teaches the multiplier. Meanwhile block 4's inline quiz is quiz[4] (basic I/G/X vs S/T/M classification) — too easy for the multiplier block — and quiz[5] (which factor shrinks the multiplier) is never shown because only the first unused index is used.

quizIssues.question: If withdrawals exceed injections in the circular flow, the level of national income will:
quizIssues.issue: 'Become negative' is not a plausible distractor; the item is effectively 3-option.

quizIssues.question: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) exchange rates are used when comparing GDP between countries because:
quizIssues.issue: Off-topic for this section; option D 'They always favour developing countries' is a throwaway distractor.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term circular flow of income (4 marks)' — IAL Economics 'Define' questions carry 2 marks. The 4-mark guidance awards marks for injections and withdrawals, which is not a definition. Should be a 2-mark define or a 4-mark 'Explain'.

'Explain two reasons why national income figures may not accurately reflect the standard of living (6 marks)' — this is 2.1.1 (measures of economic performance / limitations of GDP), not circular flow / equilibrium / multiplier. Because practice is sorted by marks in LearnModeTab.jsx:80, this lands as the inline practice for block 3 'Equilibrium National Income' where it is irrelevant.

'Assess the significance of the multiplier effect for an economy experiencing a recession (10 marks)' — command word and marks fit IAL. But the guidance is a points-based scheme (2+2+2+2+1+1) whereas IAL 'Assess' is levels-marked (KAA levels + evaluation levels). Students should see a KAA/Eval level descriptor, not point tallies. Also no numerical/diagram expectation is mentioned.

'Evaluate the usefulness of GDP as a measure of economic well-being compared with alternative indicators (20 marks)' — off-topic for this section (2.1.1 content); guidance is points-based rather than levels-based; HDI misdescribed as using GDP per capita (should be GNI per capita). It is never surfaced inline (only 4 blocks, 5 practice) so it exists only in the Practice tab.

'Outline the difference between injections and withdrawals (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (use 'Explain'). Content and marks otherwise reasonable and it correctly lands on block 2 after sorting.
No practice question requires a diagram (J/W or AD/AS) or a multiplier calculation with given MPS/MPT/MPM, which are the two most common ways IAL Unit 2 tests this topic.

structureIssues: Heavy redundancy: content[0] section 'three-sector-model' already teaches all three injections, all three withdrawals and the J = W equilibrium rule in full; content[1] then re-teaches 'Injections: I, G, X', 'Withdrawals: S, T, M' and 'The Injections-Withdrawals Balance' as three separate sections. A student reads the same takeaway ('Injections (I, G, X) add to the flow; withdrawals (S, T, M) leak out') at the end of block 1 and again at the end of block 2.

content[2] 'planned-vs-actual' and 'adjustment-to-equilibrium' are the same mechanism told twice (excess demand → inventories fall; excess supply → inventories rise). Merge into one section with both directions and use the freed slot for the AD/AS equilibrium diagram the spec expects.

Broken diagramRefs: content[2].diagramRef = 'National Income Equilibrium' and content[3].diagramRef = 'The Multiplier' match no diagram title ('Circular Flow of Income', 'Injections and Withdrawals Equilibrium') under the bidirectional substring match in LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104. Blocks 3 and 4 therefore render no InlineDiagram; the J/W diagram with its 'ΔY > ΔJ' multiplier scenario is shown at block 2, before the multiplier exists.

Inline quiz sequencing (quizIndices): block 2 → quiz[1] (multiplier calc), block 3 → quiz[3] (multiplier calc), block 4 → quiz[4] (basic classification). Calculations appear two blocks before the concept; the multiplier block gets the easiest question; quiz[2] and quiz[5] are never surfaced.

Pre-test draws 3 random MCQs from a 24-item bank in which 10 items test GDP-measurement content (2.1.1) never taught in this section — a plausible driver of the 'pre-test demotivates' feedback and of step-0 abandonment.

Step pairing: block 2 (3 sections) and block 4 (3 sections) leave a single-section final step carrying diagram + quiz + practice + explain-back + takeaway + two recall widgets — the heaviest step in the section is anchored by the shortest content. Block 1 and 3 (2 sections each) are one step each, so the section has 6 steps but 4 block-end widget dumps.
Takeaways match their blocks, but content[0].takeaway[1-2] duplicate content[1].takeaway[0-2] almost verbatim.

Misconceptions: 'savings as injection / investment as withdrawal', 'investment vs financial investment', 'I = S, G = T, X = M must each hold', 'identity vs equilibrium', 'multiplier is a fixed number', and 'MPC must exclude tax/imports' are genuine and well-phrased. 'Students treat the circular flow as a description of reality' and 'Students describe the adjustment as instantaneous' are filler — not errors students actually make in exams.

Difficulty ramp inside prose is sensible (model → J/W → equilibrium → multiplier → evaluation), but the section never connects to AD/AS: the multiplier is not explicitly linked to the size of an AD shift (spec bullet), and 'equilibrium real national output' is only shown via J/W and Keynesian-cross narrative, never on price-level/real-output axes.
ialSpecGaps: Distinction between income and wealth (flow vs stock) — quiz[20] tests it but no content[] section teaches it (unsure whether IAL keeps the UK 2.4.1 wording, but it appears in IAL textbooks for this topic).

Equilibrium level of real national output shown on an AD/AS diagram (price level vs real output) and using AD/AS to show how the economy moves toward equilibrium — no AD/AS diagram or explanation in this section; equilibrium is treated only through injections/withdrawals and the inventory mechanism.
Significance of the multiplier for shifts in AD (the multiplied horizontal shift of AD) — only implied by quiz[8]; not taught in content[3].

The multiplier ratio as change in real income / change in injection, with calculations from given data (e.g. given ΔY and ΔG, find k) — only the k = 1/MPW direction is drilled; the ratio definition appears only in notes[3] and practice[2] guidance.

Note: the app numbers this 2.3.4 and the notes cross-reference 2.3.2 (AD), 2.3.5 (output gap), 2.3.6 (fiscal policy); I am unsure this matches the official WEC12 numbering (UK GCE uses 2.4 for national income) — worth verifying the spec mapping across the whole unit.
strengths: Planned vs actual expenditure and the accounting-identity-vs-equilibrium misconception (content[2] > planned-vs-actual > misconception) is exactly the distinction IAL examiners reward and is rarely taught this clearly.
The inventory-signal adjustment chain (content[2] > adjustment-to-equilibrium) is written link-by-link the way a mark scheme credits it; its reorder recall is a genuine sequence.

Multiplier coverage is complete for IAL: both formulas, MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM, reverse multiplier, and evaluation via lags, crowding out, spare capacity (Keynesian AS), and confidence. The 'multiplier is not a fixed number' misconception is real.
The 'only totals must balance, not I=S, G=T, X=M individually' misconception (content[1] > injections-withdrawals-balance) is a genuine, frequently-marked error.
Two of five reorders (injections-withdrawals-balance, multiplier-formula) are genuine sequences; all shuffled arrays are valid non-identity permutations.
Diagram 2 (J/W schedule) has correct axes (Y on x, J/W on y), horizontal J and upward-sloping W, and scenarios for both a rise in J and a rise in W with a usable checklist.
Greece austerity and Australia 1991-2019 examples are accurate and internationally relevant.
topFixes: Remove the 10 off-topic GDP-measurement MCQs (indices 12-16, 18, 20-23) from this section's bank (move to 2.1.1) so the pre-test and inline quizzes only test what the section teaches; then re-point quizIndices so multiplier calculations (1, 3, 5) sit on block 4 and classification/equilibrium items (0, 4, 2/6, 9, 11) sit on blocks 1-3.
Fix the transfer-payments error: rewrite three-sector-model.examMatters and injections-explained.body[0] so G excludes transfer payments, consistent with quiz[13].

Repair diagramRefs: set content[2].diagramRef to match a new AD/AS 'Equilibrium real national output' diagram (price level / real output axes) and content[3].diagramRef to 'Injections and Withdrawals Equilibrium' (whose ΔY > ΔJ scenario is the multiplier picture), so blocks 3 and 4 actually show a diagram.

Replace the four trivial letter-hinted fill-ins (three-sector-model, withdrawals-explained, multiplier-concept, multiplier-evaluation) with numeric or judgement fill-ins (J vs W totals; multiplier rounds; larger/smaller multiplier scenarios) and replace the two non-sequence reorders (two-sector-circular-flow, injections-explained) with classification tasks.

Merge the redundant sections (three-sector-model with injections/withdrawals-explained; planned-vs-actual with adjustment-to-equilibrium) and use the space for AD/AS equilibrium and a practice question that requires a multiplier calculation from MPS/MPT/MPM plus a diagram; swap practice[1] and practice[3] (2.1.1 content) out of this section and convert the Assess/Evaluate guidance to levels-based descriptors.

summary: The prose layer (keyIdea/body/misconception/examMatters) is genuinely good: definitions are precise, misconceptions are ones real students hold, and most real examples check out. But the interactive layer that Learn Mode is built on is broken for this section: block.quizIndices are just 0..7, so 5 of the 8 inline MCQs are off-topic (the deflation block gets a cost-push question, the unemployment block gets a current-account question, etc.); the only diagramRef ("Demand-Pull and Cost-Push Inflation") matches neither stored diagram, so no diagram ever renders in Learn Mode and the section has no AD/AS diagram at all despite two examMatters telling students to draw one; the inflation block's inline practice is "Define GDP". Four of twelve reorder recalls ask students to order things with no order (four factor incomes, CPI-vs-RPI differences, the three ILO criteria, the three HDI components), every fill-in has a word bank of exactly its three answers, and only two shuffle permutations are used across all reorders. Content is heavily UK-GCE flavoured (RPI/CPIH, JSA/Universal Credit, council tax, ISAs, Kickstart, BoE) for an IAL audience, and several IAL 2.3.1 bullets (effects of unemployment, money-supply inflation, limitations of CPI, real-wage unemployment, capital/financial account) are not taught, while limitations of CPI and the GDP deflator are tested without being taught. A strong IAL teacher would use the notes but not the exercises as they stand.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the GDP calculation logic in the right order:
items: Count all goods and services produced domestically
Include only final output to avoid double counting
Sum to get total GDP for the time period
recallAudit.reason: Step 1 says count ALL goods and services, step 2 then says only final output; steps 2 and 3 (restrict to final output / value at market prices) are independent filters with no inherent order. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification exercise: given six items (steel sold to a car maker, the finished car, a state pension, a second-hand house sale, a UK-based Japanese-owned factory's output, a British engineer's wages earned in Dubai) sort into 'counts in GDP' / 'does not count'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the real vs nominal GDP chain:
recallAudit.reason: Word bank is exactly the three answers (FillInRecall.jsx builds it from recall.answers), each fits only one blank, and optional hints give first letters plus length. No thinking required.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Numeric fill-in: 'Nominal GDP rises 7%, inflation 3% → real growth ≈ ___%' and 'Nominal GDP $530bn, price index 106 → real GDP = $___bn', with a word/number bank containing distractors (4, 10, 3, 500, 530, 561).

recallAudit.prompt: Put the GDP per capita reasoning in order:
items: Divide by population to get GDP per capita
Compare across countries or over time
Evaluate by considering inequality and distribution
recallAudit.reason: Steps 1-2 are a genuine procedure, but 'compare' and 'evaluate' are essay-structure instructions, not stages of a causal chain; a student could reasonably evaluate before comparing. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Calculation fill-in: 'GDP $3.7tn, population 1.4bn → GDP per capita ≈ $___' plus 'If GDP rises 3% and population rises 4%, GDP per capita ___ (rises/falls) by about ___%'. This also completes the truncated flow in the body.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the output method chain:
recallAudit.reason: Three-word bank, one-to-one grammatical fit ('___ counting' can only be 'double'). Hints 'in___________', 'in________', 'do____' add nothing.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Value-added calculation: farmer sells wheat $1, miller sells flour $2, baker sells bread $5 → value added at each stage ___/___/___ and GDP contribution = $___ (not $___). Bank: 1, 1, 3, 5, 8, 2.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the four factor incomes in order of the factors they reward:
recallAudit.reason: The four factor incomes are parallel categories with no causal, chronological or procedural order. Any order is 'correct' economically; the exercise tests memorising the author's list order. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Matching exercise: pair each factor (labour, land, capital, enterprise) with its reward (wages, rent, interest, profit), plus two decoys (state pension, VAT) that must be left out as non-factor incomes.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the expenditure method formula:
recallAudit.reason: Bank is ['M','consumption','abroad']; the blank in 'GDP = C + I + G + (X - ___)' with hint '_' is a single letter and the only single-letter option. The other two blanks are grammatically forced.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Component calculation with distractors: C=1200, I=300, G=400, X=350, M=450 → GDP = ___ (bank: 1800, 2700, 2600, 1700). Or a classification of spending items into C/I/G/X/M (a family buys a Korean TV → C and M).

recallAudit.blockTitle: Uses and Limitations of GDP Data
recallAudit.prompt: Put the international comparison steps in order:
items: Measure each country's GDP in local currency
Convert to a common currency (e.g. US dollars)
Adjust for price differences using PPP
Compare real GDP per capita across countries
recallAudit.reason: Procedurally it mirrors the body's flow, but in practice PPP conversion replaces market-rate conversion rather than following it, and 'divide by population' is silently folded into step 4. A well-taught student could argue steps 2 and 3 are alternatives. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in with distractors: 'China GDP at market rates ≈ $18tn; at PPP ≈ $___tn because Chinese prices are ___ than US prices, so market rates ___ China's real output' (bank: 30, 12, lower, higher, understate, overstate).

recallAudit.blockTitle: Uses and Limitations of GDP Data
recallAudit.prompt: Complete the GDP limitations chain:
recallAudit.reason: Each template line contains its own answer's context in parentheses ('cash-in-hand, subsistence farming' → informal; 'pollution and deforestation' → environmental); with a three-word bank there is no decision to make.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Sort eight statements into 'GDP overstates welfare' vs 'GDP understates activity' (e.g. deforestation counted as output; unpaid childcare excluded; cigarette sales counted; cash-in-hand plumbing excluded). This tests direction of bias, which examiners actually reward.

recallAudit.blockTitle: Uses and Limitations of GDP Data
recallAudit.prompt: Put the HDI components in order:
items: Measure GNI per capita at PPP (income)
Measure mean and expected years of schooling (education)
Calculate geometric mean for HDI score (0 to 1)
recallAudit.reason: The three HDI dimensions have no order (UNDP itself lists health, education, income — the opposite of this content). Only step 4 is constrained (last). Three of four items are interchangeable, so the 'correct' order is arbitrary. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Matching: pair each HDI dimension with its indicator (income → GNI per capita PPP; health → life expectancy at birth; education → mean & expected years of schooling), with decoys (GDP per capita at market rates, unemployment rate, Gini coefficient) that are NOT in the HDI.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the CPI construction process:
recallAudit.reason: Bank ['basket','weight','100']; '100' is the only numeric token and the only fit for 'base year is set at ___'. Remaining two blanks are forced by grammar.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Weighted-index calculation: two-item basket, food weight 0.4 price +10%, housing weight 0.6 price +5% → inflation = ___% (bank: 7, 7.5, 15, 5). This is the exact skill IAL data-response questions test and the content never demonstrates.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the differences between CPI and RPI in logical order:
items: RPI includes mortgage interest and council tax
CPI uses geometric mean; RPI uses arithmetic mean
RPI typically gives a higher inflation figure than CPI
recallAudit.reason: Items 1-3 are parallel comparison points (basket difference, basket difference restated, formula difference) with no sequence; only item 4 is a consequence and could follow any of them. 'Logical order' is the author's list order. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Two-column sort: drag 'includes mortgage interest', 'geometric mean', 'used for BoE 2% target', 'arithmetic mean', 'includes council tax', 'usually higher' into CPI vs RPI. (Or, given IAL does not require RPI, replace the whole subsection with 'Limitations of CPI' and a sort of limitations into over/understates.)

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the inflation terminology chain:
recallAudit.reason: Bank of three; line 3 ends '-- this is deflation', which defines the blank; 'disinflation' is the only noun that fits line 2. The concept (disinflation ≠ deflation) is important but this format cannot miss.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification: given inflation-rate series (6%→3%, 2%→-1%, -1%→-2%, 3%→5%) label each as disinflation / deflation / accelerating inflation; plus 'CPI 110 → 112.2 gives inflation of ___%' with numeric distractors (2, 2.2, 1.2, 12.2).

recallAudit.prompt: Put the demand-pull inflation process in order:
items: Economy is operating near full capacity
Firms raise prices -- general price level rises
recallAudit.reason: Item 2 is a pre-existing condition, not a consequence of item 1; a well-taught student would defensibly put 'economy near full capacity' first, then 'AD increases'. Items 3-4 are a genuine chain. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reword item 2 as a consequence ('Spending rises faster than firms can expand output') so the chain is strictly causal, or use a sort of causes into demand-pull vs cost-push (tax cuts, oil price rise, depreciation raising import costs, consumer credit boom, wage rises above productivity, government infrastructure spending).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the cost-push inflation chain:
recallAudit.reason: Three-word bank; 'stagflation' is the only term that fits 'called ___'; 'higher ___' takes 'prices'; remainder is 'wages'. Hint 'st_________' redundant.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Diagram-based fill-in on an AD/AS chart: 'SRAS shifts ___ (left/right), price level ___ (rises/falls), real output ___ (rises/falls)' with both directions in the bank; contrasted with the same for demand-pull.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the effects of inflation on savers in order:
items: Interest rate on savings is below inflation
recallAudit.reason: Item 3 is a condition, not an effect of item 2; it belongs logically alongside item 1 (or before it). Only 1→2 and (1,3)→4 are genuine. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Winners/losers sort: drag 'fixed-rate mortgage borrower', 'pensioner on fixed annuity', 'saver at 1% with 9% inflation', 'worker with strong union', 'exporter', 'government with large nominal debt' into 'gains from unexpected inflation' / 'loses'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the causes of deflation:
recallAudit.reason: Template line 1 reads 'Demand-side deflation is caused by falling aggregate ___' — the sentence names its own answer; line 3 'Demand-side deflation is harmful; supply-side deflation can be ___' forces 'beneficial'. Three-word bank makes it trivial regardless.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification: label scenarios as demand-side or supply-side deflation (Japan 1990s after asset bubble; falling computer prices from chip productivity; 1930s US bank failures; cheaper solar panels from mass production) and state whether output rises or falls in each.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the deflationary spiral stages in order:
items: Consumers delay spending expecting further price falls
Firms cut output, reduce investment and lay off workers
Falling incomes reduce spending further -- cycle repeats
recallAudit.reason: Strict causal chain a well-taught student can reconstruct from mechanism; each step is the consequence of the previous. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the deflation consequences chain:
recallAudit.reason: '___ trap' can only be 'liquidity', '___ lower bound' only 'zero', leaving 'debt'. Three-word bank.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Real-debt calculation: 'You owe $100,000; prices and your income fall 10%. The nominal debt is $___; the real burden has ___ (risen/fallen)'. Bank: 100,000, 90,000, 110,000, risen, fallen.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the ILO unemployment definition criteria in order:
items: Person is available to start within two weeks
Person is classified as ILO unemployed
recallAudit.reason: The three ILO criteria are simultaneous conditions with no order; only item 4 (conclusion) is constrained. Three of four items are interchangeable. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification: sort people into employed / ILO unemployed / economically inactive / claimant-count-only (a furloughed worker; a 19-year-old full-time student; a discouraged worker who stopped searching; a jobseeker with savings above the benefit threshold; a part-timer wanting full-time hours = underemployed).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the types of unemployment:
recallAudit.reason: Mapping definitions to the three type names is a legitimate, if easy, recall task and each answer fits only its own line. Weakened by the three-word bank and by hints 'Fr________/St________/Cy______' that spell the answers when revealed; add 'Seasonal' and 'Real-wage' as distractors.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the demand-side unemployment policy chain in order:
items: Government increases spending or cuts taxes
Firms increase output and rehire workers
recallAudit.reason: Clear cause→policy→transmission→outcome chain that follows from understanding. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the four components of the current account:
recallAudit.reason: Each line's parenthetical defines the blank ('physical products like cars and oil' → goods; 'finance, tourism, consulting' → services; 'transfers, aid, remittances' → secondary). Three-word bank.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Sort transactions into the four current-account components (Pakistani worker in Dubai sends money home; Singapore Airlines sells a ticket to a tourist; Hyundai exports cars; a UK pension fund receives dividends from a US firm; foreign aid received; interest paid on foreign-held government bonds), then compute the overall balance from four given sub-balances.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the current account deficit chain in order:
items: Imports of goods and services exceed exports
Country must attract capital inflows to finance it
Evaluate: sustainable if investment-led, risky if consumption-led
recallAudit.reason: Items 1-3 are a genuine chain, but item 4 is an instruction to the student ('Evaluate:'), not a stage in the process; mixing meta-commentary into a sequence is confusing. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Replace item 4 with a consequence ('Persistent deficit puts downward pressure on the exchange rate / raises external debt') to keep it causal, or convert to a two-way sort: 'reasons a deficit is worrying' vs 'reasons it may not be'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the current account surplus analysis:
recallAudit.reason: Three-word bank, each blank grammatically forced ('___ earnings exceed import spending' → export; 'invested ___' → abroad; 'weak ___ demand' → domestic).
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Effect-direction fill-in with both directions in the bank: 'A large surplus puts ___ (upward/downward) pressure on the exchange rate, which makes exports ___ (more/less) competitive over time; it may signal ___ (strong/weak) domestic demand.'

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Gross Domestic Product (GDP)' > gdp-definition > body[2] and realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: GNI is described as 'income earned by a country's citizens wherever they work' / 'income earned by British citizens abroad'. GNI is based on residence/ownership of factors (GDP + net primary income from abroad), not citizenship. A Japanese citizen resident in the UK contributes to UK GNI.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace 'citizens' with 'residents' and add the identity GNI = GDP + net primary income from abroad.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Inflation' > rpi-vs-cpi > bullets[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'CPI -- excludes housing costs' is wrong: CPI includes rents, utilities and household services; it excludes owner-occupier housing costs (mortgage interest, council tax). The misconception box repeats 'the CPI excludes housing costs'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'excludes owner-occupiers' housing costs such as mortgage interest payments and council tax'.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Inflation' > rpi-vs-cpi > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'In 2023, RPI was 1.2 percentage points higher than CPI' understates the gap (2023 annual averages ≈ 9.7% RPI vs 7.3% CPI, ~2.4pp; monthly gaps were 2-4pp). Regulated rail fares in England were decoupled from RPI from 2023 (5.9% rise vs 12.3% RPI), so 'use the RPI to set annual fare increases... resisted by the Treasury' is dated. UK season-ticket cost given in '$'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either update to the actual 2023 gap and note fares are now set below RPI, or replace with a non-UK example (e.g. an index-linked bond or pension).

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Inflation' > rpi-vs-cpi > body[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'RPI will be reformed to align with the CPI in 2030' — the announced reform (Feb 2030) aligns RPI with CPIH, not CPI.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'aligned with CPIH from 2030'.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Inflation' > rpi-vs-cpi (whole subsection) and takeaway[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: RPI vs CPI vs CPIH, the formula effect and 'CPIH is now the ONS headline measure' are UK GCE (Edexcel A-level 2.1.2) material. The IAL WEC12 2.3.1 spec asks for measurement of inflation using CPI and the limitations of CPI (unsure whether RPI is named); international students in HK/Singapore/Pakistan will not meet RPI in their papers, while 'limitations of CPI' (which IS tested here in Q3 and practice P2) is never taught.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace the subsection with 'Limitations of the CPI' (substitution bias, quality change, representative household, basket lag, excludes owner-occupier costs), keeping RPI as a one-line aside.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Inflation' > cpi-construction > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Claim that the ONS 'added oat milk and electric vehicle charging to the CPI basket in 2024, while removing coal' does not match the widely reported 2024 changes (added air fryers, vinyl records, gluten-free bread, spray oil; removed hand sanitiser, sofa beds). Could not verify oat milk/EV charging; likely fabricated.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use verifiable 2024 additions (air fryers, vinyl records) or generic phrasing, and cite the ONS basket release.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Consumer Price Index (CPI) and Inflation' > cpi-construction > body[2]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'subsequent CPI values show the percentage change in prices relative to that base' — index values show the price level relative to base; the % change since base is (index − 100), and the inflation rate is the year-on-year % change. Students routinely confuse these.
accuracyIssues.fix: State: an index of 112 means prices are 12% above the base year; the inflation rate is the % change between two years' index values.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Inflation: Causes and Effects' > demand-pull-inflation > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: US 2021-22 inflation is called 'a textbook case of demand-pull inflation' while the same paragraph notes supply chains were disrupted; energy/supply shocks were a major cost-push component. Presenting a contested mixed case as pure demand-pull is misleading and a 'Discuss' question would expect both.
accuracyIssues.fix: Frame as 'largely demand-pull, combined with cost-push from supply-chain and energy shocks' — which also models the evaluation examiners want.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'The deflationary spiral was only broken when the government intervened with massive fiscal stimulus under the New Deal' is contested history; leaving the gold standard and monetary expansion in 1933 are the mainstream explanation for the end of US deflation. Stated as fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'was broken after the US left the gold standard in 1933, allowing monetary expansion, alongside New Deal spending'.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Balance of Payments: Current Account' > current-account-deficit > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'The United States has run a current account deficit every year since 1982' — the US recorded a small surplus in 1991. 'over $800 billion in 2022' understates the 2022 deficit (≈$970bn-$1.0tn).
accuracyIssues.fix: 'in almost every year since the early 1980s, reaching roughly $1 trillion in 2022'.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Uses and Limitations of GDP Data' > limitations-of-gdp > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: 'A common 8-mark question asks you to evaluate GDP as a measure of living standards' — in IAL WEC11/12, 8-mark items are 'Analyse'/'Explain' (KAA only); evaluation marks appear at 10 ('Assess'), 12 and 14 ('Discuss'). Telling students to write evaluation for 8 marks misdirects effort.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'A 10- or 12-mark Assess question...'; and note 8-mark Analyse requires chains of reasoning, not judgement.

accuracyIssues.issue: UK GDP 'approximately $3.1 trillion in 2023' — 2023 UK GDP was ≈$3.3tn (2022 was ≈$3.1tn). Minor.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use '$3.3 trillion in 2023' or drop the number.

accuracyIssues.issue: Flow ['Total GDP rises by 3%', 'Population rises by 4%'] stops before the conclusion; a flow with no consequence step teaches nothing.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add 'GDP per capita falls by roughly 1%'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Almost every real example and institution is UK-specific (ONS, Bank of England 2% target, JSA/Universal Credit, council tax, cash ISAs, Kickstart, UK rail fares, 'EU contributions'), with UK sums written in '$'. For an IAL cohort in HK/Korea/Singapore/Malaysia/Pakistan this is both less relatable and occasionally wrong-looking (a '$200,000' UK mortgage).
accuracyIssues.fix: Mix in regional examples (Singapore CPI basket, Pakistan 2023 inflation ~38%, HK LFS unemployment, Malaysia/Korea current-account surpluses, Sri Lanka 2022 deflation-to-hyperinflation) and use local currency or 'about $X equivalent'.

accuracyIssues.location: Block 'Uses and Limitations of GDP Data' > limitations-of-gdp > body[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: 'the informal sector can be 30-60% of true economic activity' in developing countries — the upper end is an outlier; typical estimates are 25-40% of GDP.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'often 25-40% of GDP, and higher in some cases'.

quizIssues.question: The CPI is likely to overstate the true rate of inflation because:
quizIssues.issue: Explanation states 'CPI does NOT include mortgage interest payments (that's CPIH)'. Wrong: CPIH adds owner-occupiers' housing costs via rental equivalence, not mortgage interest; it is the RPI that includes mortgage interest payments. Also 'substitution bias' (the key) is never taught anywhere in the content, so the pre-test/inline draw can present an untaught concept.

quizIssues.question: If nominal GDP rises from $500bn to $530bn while the GDP deflator increases from 100 to 106...
quizIssues.issue: Key (0%) and arithmetic are correct, but the GDP deflator and the formula real = nominal/deflator×100 are never taught in content (only 'base-year prices' and the approximation nominal − inflation). Untaught skill; same for index 10.

quizIssues.question: If nominal GDP is $500 billion and the GDP deflator is 125, real GDP is:
quizIssues.issue: Correct key ($400bn) but relies on the untaught deflator formula; the section's common_mistakes tip mentions it, content[] does not.

quizIssues.question: A sustained fall in the general price level caused by a collapse in aggregate demand is best described as:
quizIssues.issue: Uses 'malign/benign deflation' whereas the content teaches 'demand-side (bad) / supply-side (good) deflation' — terminology mismatch a student cannot map from the notes. 'Cost-push deflation' is a nonsense distractor rather than a plausible misconception.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is NOT included in the measurement of GDP?
quizIssues.issue: Identical stem to index 12 with a different key (transfer payments vs unpaid housework). Both can appear in the same pre-test/post-test draw; students perceive a contradiction.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is NOT included in the measurement of GDP?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate stem of index 0 (see above). Merge into one question with both exclusions as options is impossible (two correct answers), so reword one stem, e.g. 'Which is excluded because it is not a market transaction?'.

quizIssues.question: A current account deficit on the balance of payments means:
