quizIssues.issue: Key wording 'the value of imports of goods, services, and transfers exceeds the value of exports' treats transfers as imports and omits primary income; sloppy for a definition question the content itself defines carefully (four components).

quizIssues.question: A country's current account balance worsens. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
quizIssues.issue: Option 0 'An appreciation... making exports cheaper' is internally impossible, so options 0 and 1 (both 'appreciation') let the student eliminate by spotting the contradiction rather than by economics. Option 2 (depreciation) can worsen the balance short-run (J-curve) — acceptable at IAL but not airtight.

quizIssues.question: Cost-push inflation is most likely to result from:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of index 5 (both key on a global oil price rise with AD-side distractors). Wastes one of only 25 slots while HDI, PPP, effects of inflation, the deflationary spiral/liquidity trap, current account surplus and the three GDP methods have no MCQ at all.

quizIssues.question: The UK's current account deficit is MOST likely to worsen if:
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 'The UK government reduces spending on imports' is oddly worded (governments do not 'spend on imports' as a policy lever). Explanation asserts depreciation improves the current account without the elasticity caveat.

quizIssues.question: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures:
quizIssues.issue: Distractors (total output, unemployment, balance of payments) are not plausible; pure definition recall. Same for indices 16, 22, 23 — four near-free marks inflate post-test scores.

quizIssues.question: Which component of the UK's current account is typically in surplus?
quizIssues.issue: UK-specific factual recall; an IAL student in Karachi or Seoul has no reason to know the UK's component balances. Better framed with data given in the stem.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term GDP (4 marks)' — in IAL Economics 'Define' items carry 2 marks; the scheme awards marks for the three measurement methods, real vs nominal, and 'most widely used indicator', none of which a define mark scheme credits. Teaches students to pad definitions. This is also the item that surfaces inside the Inflation block in Learn Mode (practiceIndices [0] → sortedPractice[0]).

'Evaluate... (20 marks)' — WEC12 (Unit 2) papers have no 20-mark essay; the top tariff is 14 ('Discuss') with 12 'Assess'. 20-mark 'Evaluate' is a WEC13/WEC14 format. The scheme is also point-tallied (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) whereas IAL marks 10+ questions on KAA/Evaluation levels, so the 'model answer' misrepresents how marks are earned.

'Assess the usefulness of CPI (10 marks)' — tariff and command word match IAL 'Assess', good. But the scheme credits limitations (unrepresentative basket, quality change, excludes mortgage costs) that the content never teaches, and it is point-based rather than levels-based. Never surfaces in Learn Mode (no block references index 3 of sortedPractice).
'Outline two types of unemployment (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (use 'Explain'). Scheme is otherwise sensible (2×2). Correctly surfaces on the Unemployment block.
'Explain two limitations of GDP per capita (6 marks)' is well-pitched and the scheme is usable. Only issue: it never appears in Learn Mode because no block's practiceIndices reference it.

structureIssues: Inline quiz mapping is broken: block.quizIndices are simply [0],[1],...,[7] and LearnModeTab.jsx:106-108 uses them literally, so block 2 'Uses and Limitations of GDP' shows Q2 (malign deflation), block 4 'Inflation: Causes and Effects' shows Q4 (structural unemployment coal miner), block 5 'Deflation' shows Q5 (cost-push oil), block 6 'Employment and Unemployment' shows Q6 (UK current account), block 7 'Current Account' shows Q7 (LFS vs claimant count). Only blocks 0, 1 and 3 get a topically relevant MCQ.

No diagram ever renders in Learn Mode: block 4 diagramRef 'Demand-Pull and Cost-Push Inflation' matches neither stored diagram title ('CPI Basket of Goods', 'Types of Unemployment') under the substring test at LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104, and blocks 3 and 6 (which those diagrams fit) have diagramRef null. The section has no AD/AS diagram at all, yet demand-pull and cost-push examMatters both instruct students to shift AD/SRAS on a diagram (and never state the axes: price level / real output).

Inline practice mapping: block 4 (Inflation) practiceIndices [0] resolves to sortedPractice[0] = 'Define GDP (4 marks)'; block 6 → 'Outline two types of unemployment' (correct). P1, P2, P3 (the 6/10/20-mark items) never surface in Learn Mode, so students never meet an Assess/Evaluate question in the guided flow.

Every block has exactly 3 sections, so 2-per-step pairing yields [s1,s2] then a lone [s3] step that also carries diagram+quiz+practice+ExplainItBack+takeaway — 16 steps with an uneven 'light, heavy' rhythm. Recall scheduling side-effect (LearnModeTab.jsx:345-359, 397-402): the lone section's recall is shown as 'immediate' at the bottom of its step and again as 'spaced' at the top of the very next step, i.e. 8 recalls (gdp-per-capita, expenditure-method, HDI, measuring-inflation, effects-of-inflation, consequences-of-deflation, causes-and-policies, current-account-surplus) appear twice back-to-back while the middle section's recall appears once and nothing is actually spaced.

recall.shuffled uses only two permutations across all 12 reorders ([2,0,3,1] ×7 and [3,1,0,2] ×5); ReorderRecall.jsx:9 applies them verbatim, so the displayed order is predictable and a student can learn 'swap positions' patterns.

Fill-in word banks are exactly the three answers (FillInRecall.jsx:12), so all 12 fill-ins are 3-item drag-drops with grammatically forced slots; combined with letter-count hints they cannot discriminate understanding.

Terminology drift between layers: content teaches 'demand-side / supply-side deflation', quiz Q2 tests 'malign / benign'; content teaches real GDP via base-year prices, quiz Q1/Q10 test the GDP deflator formula; content never mentions substitution bias but Q3 keys on it. The pre-test draws randomly from all 25, so the gate can be failed on untaught material (consistent with the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis).

Sequencing/scope: HDI (Unit 4 development in IAL) sits inside the GDP-limitations block; the Deflation block spends a full subsection on liquidity trap and QE (policy, later units) while the Unemployment block omits the effects/costs of unemployment entirely, so block depth is inverted relative to the spec.

Takeaways match their blocks well and misconceptions are largely genuine student errors (GDP=wealth; disinflation=deflation; deficit always bad; cutting rates always fixes deflation). Two are filler: 'cost-push inflation only comes from oil prices' and 'GDP is useless'.

Difficulty ramp is flat rather than rising: every subsection follows the same template (definition, flow, example, misconception) with no calculation practice until the quiz, so the numeracy the spec demands (index numbers, real growth, per-capita, weighted CPI) is never scaffolded in the notes.
ialSpecGaps: Effects/costs of unemployment on consumers, firms, workers, government and society — entirely absent (block 6 covers measurement, types and policies only).
Growth of the money supply as a cause of inflation — not mentioned (IAL 2.3.1 lists demand-pull, cost-push and money supply growth).
Limitations of the CPI as a measure of inflation (substitution bias, quality change, representative household, basket lag, sampling) — not taught, though tested in Q3 and practice P2.
Effects of inflation on the government and on firms' competitiveness/investment in depth — only savers/borrowers/workers covered; government (fiscal drag, debt erosion, tax revenue) missing.

Real-wage inflexibility (classical) unemployment and the significance of migration and skills for employment — not taught; the 'cutting wages' misconception dismisses the real-wage view rather than explaining it.
Employment rate, economic inactivity rate and the significance of changes in them; underemployment gets a single bullet.
Capital and financial accounts as the counterpart to the current account — mentioned only in passing as the financing source; no structure of the BoP.
Relationship between current account imbalances and other macro objectives, and interconnectedness of economies through trade — not taught.

Value vs volume, index numbers and calculating rates of change/growth from data (a core WEC12 data-response skill) — no worked calculations in the notes; the deflator formula appears only in the quiz.
Weighted-average construction of the CPI with a numerical example — process described in words only.
Unsure: whether IAL 2.3.1 names RPI/CPIH or HDI at all; both are covered here in depth and may be over-coverage of UK-GCE material rather than gaps.
strengths: All 25 MCQ keys are correct and the arithmetic in Q1/Q10 is right.

Definitions in keyIdea/body are exam-precise (final goods, within borders, time period; ILO three criteria; four current-account components; disinflation vs deflation) and examMatters mostly describe real marking behaviour (exclude transfers, avoid double counting, name all four CA components, don't call disinflation deflation).
Misconception boxes are overwhelmingly genuine student errors with a usable 'Instead write:' correction.

Most real examples are accurate and well chosen: India total vs per-capita GDP, China market vs PPP, 1973 OPEC and UK 1975 inflation, UK CPI 11.1% Oct 2022, Japan's lost decade, Germany's surplus, US stimulus ≈$800bn.
Two reorder recalls (deflationary spiral; demand-side policy chain) are genuine causal sequences and model exactly the chain-of-reasoning IAL analysis marks reward.
Block takeaways summarise their blocks faithfully; the two stored diagrams (CPI basket weights, Types of Unemployment) are clear and have useful checklists, even though Learn Mode never shows them.
Deficits-not-always-bad / surpluses-not-always-good and demand- vs supply-side deflation are handled with the two-sided judgement examiners want.
topFixes: Repair the block-level wiring: set quizIndices by topic (e.g. block2 → [12,18,21,23], block4 → [5,13,17,9], block5 → [2,22], block6 → [4,7,14,16,19,20], block7 → [6,8,15,24]), point practiceIndices so the 6/10/14-mark questions appear on the matching blocks, add diagramRef 'CPI Basket' to block 3 and 'Types of Unemployment' to block 6, and build an AD/AS diagram (axes: price level / real output) for block 4 so its diagramRef resolves.

Replace the four non-orderable/arbitrary reorders (factor incomes, CPI-vs-RPI differences, ILO criteria, HDI components) with matching/classification exercises, and give fill-ins distractor words plus numeric calculation blanks (real GDP, per-capita, weighted CPI, value added) instead of three-word banks with letter hints.

Close the spec gaps most likely to be examined in WEC12: add an 'Effects of unemployment' subsection, money-supply growth as an inflation cause, 'Limitations of the CPI' (replacing most of RPI-vs-CPI), real-wage unemployment, and a short capital/financial account explainer; swap several UK examples for Asian/Middle-East ones.

Fix the practice set to WEC12 tariffs and marking: Define = 2 marks, drop 'Outline' for 'Explain', convert the 20-mark Evaluate into a 14-mark Discuss (or label it Unit 4 style), and rewrite the 10/14-mark schemes as levels (KAA + Evaluation) rather than point tallies.

Correct the factual slips: Q3 explanation (CPIH does not include mortgage interest; RPI does), 'CPI excludes housing costs', GNI 'citizens' → residents, US CA 'every year since 1982', 2023 RPI–CPI gap and rail-fare claim, the unverified ONS 2024 basket example, and reframe 2021-22 US inflation and the 1930s New Deal claim as mixed/contested.

summary: The prose is mostly competent, exam-aware and pitched at the right level: definitions are correct, the movement-vs-shift distinction is drilled properly, and the misconceptions are genuine student errors rather than filler. But a strong IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is. There are real content faults (consumption is called "the most volatile component" in one keyIdea while investment is called that everywhere else; the 2022 UK inflation example mislabels Bank of England rate rises as the "interest rate effect" that explains AD's slope; the car-industry accelerator example says sales were still rising when UK registrations actually fell; "narrowly avoided a recession" is false for 2023; UK figures are quoted in dollars). The Learn Mode experience is worse than the notes: none of the 3 diagrams render inline because diagramRef strings do not substring-match any diagram title, the inline quiz for the "Shifts" block is a multiplier calculation the student has not yet met, 10 of 14 recall widgets are trivial, hint-leaking, or not genuinely orderable, and the 3-subsection multiplier block duplicates the national-income section (same subsection ids) while several actual 2.3.2 spec bullets (gross/net investment, saving vs consumption, animal spirits, protectionism, non-price factors, G over the trade cycle) are absent. Practice items use non-IAL command/mark pairings ("Define" 4, "Outline" 4, "Analyse" 10), demand Unit 4 content (Marshall-Lerner, J-curve) in a WEC12 mark scheme, and the 20-mark scheme adds to 22.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the AD formula and components:
recallAudit.reason: Blank 1 is a single letter ('_') in a formula printed two lines above; blank 2 hint 'co_________' for 'consumption' when the bullet 'C (Consumption)' is on screen in the same step; blank 3 'tr_______' gives the answer (and is 9 chars for an 8-letter word). Nothing here requires understanding.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification exercise: sort 8 items into C / I / G / (X-M) / not in AD -- e.g. state pension payment, teacher salary, firm buys a lathe, household buys Apple shares, tourist spending by foreigners, a Korean firm buys German machinery. This directly targets the transfer-payment and financial-investment misconceptions the section itself flags.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the interest rate effect on consumption in order:
items: Saving becomes less attractive; borrowing becomes cheaper
Households increase spending on credit-financed goods
Consumption rises, shifting AD to the right
recallAudit.reason: Clear causal chain with a unique order; shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. Note: near-duplicate of the factors-shifting-ad-left reorder (same chain in reverse), so one of the two adds little.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the determinants of investment:
recallAudit.reason: Hints 'ca_____', 'bo________', 'co________' give first two letters plus exact length; 'capital goods' and 'cost of borrowing' are stock collocations lifted verbatim from the paragraph in the same step. Also note the accepted answer 'confidence' for blank 3 is the only word that fits but the claim it tests ('often more important than interest rates') is an evaluative opinion, not a fact.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder of the interest-rate-to-investment chain is already in the body as a flow; better: a 'which determinant?' matcher -- give 5 mini-scenarios (firm's CFO reads a gloomy forecast; central bank cuts rates; new robotics tech launched; bank tightens lending criteria; export orders from the US double) and ask the student to name the determinant and the direction of I.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the exchange rate effect on net exports in order:
items: Export prices fall in foreign currency terms
Import prices rise in domestic currency terms
recallAudit.reason: Steps 2 and 3 happen simultaneously -- there is no causal reason export-price falls precede import-price rises, so a student who swaps them is marked wrong for a correct understanding. The chain also skips the actual causal link (price change -> quantity of X demanded rises / quantity of M demanded falls). Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Merge steps 2-3 into one ('Exports cheaper abroad, imports dearer at home') and insert the missing quantity step: depreciation -> relative prices change -> quantity of exports demanded rises and quantity of imports demanded falls -> (X-M) rises -> AD shifts right. That is a unique 4-step causal chain.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the three effects explaining the AD curve's slope:
recallAudit.reason: 'we____', 'mo___', 'tr___' with exact lengths make each blank a one-guess fill; the three names are also printed in bold in the paragraph on the same step. Mapping mechanism-to-name is a fair recall target, but the hints remove the recall.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep the mechanism-to-name mapping but drop letter hints, or invert it: give the effect name and blank the variable ('Lower price level -> real value of ___ rises -> C rises'; 'Lower price level -> demand for ___ falls -> interest rates fall -> I rises'; 'Lower price level -> ___ become more competitive -> (X-M) rises').

recallAudit.prompt: Put the movement along AD in the correct order:
items: Wealth, interest rate and trade effects activate
Total quantity of real output demanded changes
This is shown as a movement along the existing AD curve
recallAudit.reason: Items 1-3 are a chain but so abstract ('changes', 'activate', 'changes') that ordering is by grammar not economics; item 4 is a meta-statement about how it is drawn, not an event. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. This is the section's self-declared 'single most common mistake' and the recall does not test the mistake at all.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Classification: 8 events -> 'movement along AD' / 'AD shifts left' / 'AD shifts right' (e.g. general price level rises; central bank cuts rates; deflation; consumer confidence falls; income tax cut; currency appreciates; trading partners boom; price level falls). This is exactly the skill examMatters says examiners test.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the AD rightward shift chain:
recallAudit.reason: The subsection title is 'Factors That Shift AD to the Right' and the last blank is 'AD shifts to the ___' (hint 'ri___'); 'Consumption (C) ___' with hint 'ri___' in a rightward-shift chain can only be 'rises'. Hint 'di_________' is 11 chars for the 10-letter 'disposable'.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Chain with a non-obvious link: 'Income tax cut of $10bn -> disposable income rises by $10bn -> C rises by MPC x $10bn = $___ (MPC 0.8) -> AD shifts right by less than the tax cut because part is ___ (saved)'. Ties the shift to the multiplier block that follows.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the interest rate rise effect on AD in order:
items: Central bank raises the base interest rate
Cost of borrowing rises for households and firms
AD curve shifts to the left
recallAudit.reason: Unique causal order; shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. But it is the mirror image of the determinants-of-consumption reorder two steps earlier, so the student is effectively doing the same exercise twice. Consider swapping one for an appreciation or confidence-collapse chain.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the multiplier process in order:
items: Initial injection of spending (e.g. government investment)
Recipients earn income and spend a proportion
Their spending becomes income for others
Process continues but diminishes due to leakages
recallAudit.reason: Genuine process order (injection -> income -> re-spending -> diminishing rounds); shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid. Fine.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the multiplier formula:
recallAudit.reason: Blank 1 (MPC vs MPS/MPW/MPM with hint 'M__') is a reasonable discriminator, but blank 2 is the exact worked example from the paragraph above (MPC 0.8 -> 5) and blank 3 'im_____' for 'imports' is given away by hint and by the flow 'saving, taxation and ___'. Two of three blanks are copy-from-screen.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep blank 1. Replace blank 2 with a fresh calculation not in the body (MPC 0.75 -> k = ___; or MPS 0.1, MPT 0.2, MPM 0.2 -> MPW = ___ -> k = ___). Replace blank 3 with an interpretation: '$20m injection with k = 2.5 raises national income by $___m'.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the factors affecting multiplier size in order of logic:
items: Identify the three leakages: saving, tax, imports
Higher leakages mean a larger MPW
A larger MPW gives a smaller multiplier
Near full capacity, the multiplier effect is mostly inflationary
recallAudit.reason: Item 1 is an instruction ('Identify...'), not an event; item 4 (spare capacity) is a separate determinant unrelated to the leakage chain in items 1-3, so it has no logical position. 'In order of logic' signals the author knew this was not a sequence. Shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid. Because this is a single-section step, the Learn Mode recall logic shows this widget at the bottom of step 6 AND at the top of step 7 -- the weakest recall in the section is the one shown twice.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Comparison/calculation: 'Economy A: MPS 0.1, MPT 0.2, MPM 0.3. Economy B: MPS 0.2, MPT 0.3, MPM 0.1. MPW(A) = ___, MPW(B) = ___, k(A) = ___, k(B) = ___. Which has the larger multiplier and why?' This is the form IAL calculation questions take.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the accelerator principle:
recallAudit.reason: Blank 2 'Faster growth causes investment to ___' accepts only 'surge' (hint 'su___'); 'rise', 'increase', 'grow' are all economically correct and a student typing them is marked wrong for a vocabulary choice. Blank 3 'sl_______' is 9 chars for the 8-letter 'slowdown'. Blank 1 'rate of ___ of GDP' with 'ch____' is trivial.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Numeric accelerator table (the form examiners use): capital-output ratio 2; output 100 -> 110 -> 115 -> 115. Net investment each year = ___ , ___ , ___. Then: 'In year 3 output still rose but investment ___ (fell) because the growth rate ___ (slowed)'. Makes the 'rate of change' insight concrete instead of a word-guess.

recallAudit.prompt: Put the multiplier-accelerator boom cycle in order:
items: Accelerator triggers a surge in investment
Investment spending feeds back through the multiplier
recallAudit.reason: It is explicitly a cycle ('feeds back'), so there is no unique start: beginning at 'Investment spending feeds back through the multiplier' -> 'GDP growth accelerates' -> 'Accelerator triggers investment' -> 'Consumer spending rises' is equally valid. Shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Anchor with an exogenous trigger so the start is unique: 'Government launches a $50bn infrastructure programme -> multiplier raises incomes and C -> GDP growth rate accelerates -> accelerator: firms raise net investment -> that investment is a further injection, multiplied again'. Alternatively a fillin distinguishing the two mechanisms (multiplier: spending -> ___ ; accelerator: change in ___ -> investment).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the accelerator limitations:
recallAudit.reason: 'spare capacity', 'business confidence', 'access to finance' are the bold bullet headings on the same step; hints 'sp___', 'co________', 'ac____' give the rest. Zero retrieval demand.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Application: for each scenario say whether the simple accelerator's prediction holds and which limitation explains any failure -- (a) growth 2%->4%, factories at 95% utilisation; (b) growth 2%->4%, factories at 60% utilisation; (c) growth 2%->4% but banks have frozen lending; (d) growth 4%->2%.

accuracyIssues.location: Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-consumption > keyIdea
accuracyIssues.issue: States consumption 'is the largest and most volatile component of AD'. Investment is the most volatile component (as the next subsection's keyIdea, the block takeaway 'Investment is the most volatile', and block 5's takeaway all say). Consumption is the largest and the most stable. Direct internal contradiction on a fact IAL examiners test.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'it is the largest and most stable component of AD; investment is the most volatile.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims 2022 UK inflation caused a movement along AD via three effects and lists 'pushed the Bank of England to raise interest rates (interest rate effect)'. The interest-rate effect behind AD's slope is the money-demand mechanism; a central bank raising the policy rate is a discretionary monetary tightening that SHIFTS AD left. The example therefore confuses the exact distinction the subsection exists to teach, and 2022 inflation was a cost-push (SRAS) episode, which the example never mentions.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a supply-shock framing: 'When energy costs pushed SRAS left in 2022, the higher price level moved the economy up along AD: real wealth fell, and UK goods became less competitive. Separately, the Bank of England's rate rises shifted AD left -- do not confuse the two.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Says UK car investment fell in 2017-18 'even though car sales were still at historically high levels' and that a 'slowdown in growth, not an actual decline' triggered it. UK new-car registrations peaked in 2016 (~2.69m) and fell in both 2017 (-5.7%) and 2018 (-6.8%), so demand actually declined. The example contradicts the mechanism it is meant to illustrate.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either reframe honestly ('demand fell, and investment fell far more than proportionately -- from about £2.5bn in 2015 to under £0.6bn in 2018') or pick a case of decelerating-but-positive growth (e.g. a hypothetical numeric table, or China's investment slowdown as GDP growth eased from 10% to 6-7% in 2012-2015).

accuracyIssues.location: Shifts in Aggregate Demand > factors-shifting-ad-left > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'The economy narrowly avoided a recession' after the 2021-23 rate rises. The UK entered a technical recession in H2 2023 (Q3 -0.1%, Q4 -0.3%), confirmed by ONS in Feb 2024.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'The UK slipped into a shallow technical recession in the second half of 2023.'

accuracyIssues.location: Shifts in Aggregate Demand > factors-shifting-ad-right > realExample; The Multiplier > multiplier-definition > realExample; The Multiplier > multiplier-formula > body para 2
accuracyIssues.issue: UK amounts given in dollars: furlough 'over $70 billion' (CJRS cost ~£70bn), London 2012 'approximately $9 billion' (public budget was £8.9bn, i.e. ~$14bn), and 'households spend 80p of every extra $1 earned' mixes pence and dollars in one sentence. Also multiplier-formula body says 'each extra pound' then '$10 million'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use one currency per example; for UK examples use £, or convert consistently. Fix '80p of every extra $1' to '80 cents of every extra $1' (or 80p per £1).

accuracyIssues.location: Shifts in Aggregate Demand > factors-shifting-ad-right > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Furlough described as a 'massive fiscal expansion [that] shifted AD sharply to the right' in a year AD collapsed and GDP fell ~10-11%. Furlough was a wage subsidy/transfer that sustained C; it limited the LEFTWARD shift rather than shifting AD right. The section has just told students transfers are not G, then uses a transfer-type scheme as the G example.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'The scheme supported household incomes and therefore C, so the leftward shift in AD was far smaller than it would otherwise have been' -- and note explicitly that it worked through C, not G.

accuracyIssues.location: The Multiplier > multiplier-formula > body para 1 vs quiz Q21
accuracyIssues.issue: Body defines MPC as 'the proportion of each extra pound ... spent on domestic goods and services' and says k = 1/(1-MPC) is 'equivalent' to 1/MPW. Under that definition it is; but quiz Q21 marks '1/(1-MPC)' WRONG for an open economy with government. The section teaches one thing and tests the opposite.
accuracyIssues.fix: Teach the standard IAL treatment: in the simple model MPC + MPS = 1 so k = 1/(1-MPC) = 1/MPS; with government and trade, k = 1/MPW = 1/(MPS+MPT+MPM). Drop the 'on domestic goods' qualifier, and reword Q21's stem or distractor accordingly.

accuracyIssues.location: Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-consumption > body para 1
accuracyIssues.issue: 'disposable income -- the income left after taxes and benefits' reads as if benefits are deducted. Disposable income = income after direct taxes are deducted AND benefits/transfers added.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'disposable income -- income after direct taxes have been deducted and state benefits added.'

accuracyIssues.location: Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-investment > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Apple's R&D expense (FY2023 ~$29.9bn) is used as the example of investment immediately after defining I as 'spending by firms on capital goods'. R&D is largely operating expense, not capital-goods spending in the national-accounts sense; 'even when borrowing costs are elevated' is irrelevant because Apple self-finances.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use capital spending: e.g. TSMC's ~$30bn+ annual capex on fabs, or Samsung's Pyeongtaek/Taylor fab investment, both driven by expected demand rather than interest rates -- and better matched to the IAL audience.

accuracyIssues.location: The Accelerator Effect > accelerator-definition > body para 2
accuracyIssues.issue: 'investment responds to the change in the change -- not the level of GDP but its rate of growth'. The accelerator says the LEVEL of net investment depends on the change in GDP (first difference); the CHANGE in investment depends on the change in the change. Conflating the two will confuse strong students.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'The level of net investment depends on the change in GDP. So when the growth rate slows, the required addition to capital falls, and investment falls even though GDP is still rising.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'This is why Singapore relies more on trade policy than fiscal stimulus.' Singapore ran fiscal packages of ~20% of GDP in 2020 and conducts monetary policy via the exchange rate (MAS), not 'trade policy'. Unsupported claim in an example aimed squarely at the target audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'This is one reason Singapore's fiscal packages have to be very large to have a domestic effect, and why it manages the economy mainly through the exchange rate and supply-side policy.'

accuracyIssues.location: Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-gov-spending-net-exports > examMatters; practice[2] guidance
accuracyIssues.issue: J-curve and Marshall-Lerner are WEC14 (Unit 4) content. Telling WEC12 students examiners 'expect' the J-curve, and awarding 4 of 10 marks for it in a Unit 2 practice scheme, misrepresents what this paper marks.
accuracyIssues.fix: Remove J-curve/Marshall-Lerner from 2.3.2, or flag them as 'Unit 4 extension' without mark weight.

accuracyIssues.location: Components of Aggregate Demand > determinants-of-gov-spending-net-exports > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'The UK's net export position temporarily improved' after the 2016 depreciation. Export volumes were widely noted as barely responding and the current account did not improve meaningfully; the claim is contested at best.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Economists expected net exports to improve, but export volumes responded weakly -- a useful evaluation point about the limits of a depreciation.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 2008-09 example says the wealth effect 'should have boosted spending' but 'was overwhelmed'. It muddles a movement along AD (price effects) with a large leftward shift (confidence collapse) without naming that distinction, one step before the subsection that teaches it.
accuracyIssues.fix: State explicitly: 'the slope effects still applied, but the whole AD curve shifted left because of the confidence collapse -- a shift dominated a movement.'

accuracyIssues.location: Components of Aggregate Demand > ad-formula-and-components > body vs common_mistakes[0].examTip
accuracyIssues.issue: Consumption share given as '60-70% of AD' in body, '63%' in realExample and '60-65%' in common_mistakes. Minor inconsistency.
accuracyIssues.fix: Standardise on 'roughly 60-65% in most developed economies'.

quizIssues.question: In an open economy with government, the multiplier formula is:
quizIssues.issue: Distractor [2] '1/(1-MPC)' is presented as wrong, but the section body defines MPC as spending 'on domestic goods and services' and states k = 1/(1-MPC) is 'equivalent' to 1/MPW. Under the section's own teaching two options are correct.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is NOT counted in the government spending (G) component of AD?
quizIssues.issue: Answer depends on knowing that 'Jobseeker's Allowance' is a UK unemployment benefit and that 'NHS' is a health service. International IAL students (HK, Korea, Pakistan) may not know either; the item then tests UK civics not economics.

quizIssues.question: If the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is 0.6, what is the value of the multiplier?
quizIssues.issue: Assigned as the inline quiz for block 3 'Shifts in Aggregate Demand' (quizIndices [2]) -- a multiplier calculation shown one block BEFORE the multiplier is taught. Also near-duplicate of Q11.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following would cause a leftward shift of the AD curve?
quizIssues.issue: Assigned as the inline quiz for block 5 'The Accelerator Effect' (quizIndices [4]); the accelerator questions Q7 and Q15 never appear inline. Near-duplicate of Q12.

quizIssues.question: The paradox of thrift states that:
quizIssues.issue: Paradox of thrift is not taught anywhere in this section's content, notes or extras (only named in passing in extras.evaluation[1]). Can appear in the 3-question pre-test gate.

quizIssues.question: In the circular flow model, which of the following correctly identifies the three injections?
quizIssues.issue: Circular-flow injections/withdrawals are not taught in this section's content (they belong to and are taught in national-income); only a diagram exists. Eligible for the pre-test gate.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a withdrawal (leakage) from the circular flow of income?
quizIssues.issue: Same as Q9: tests content taught in national-income, not here.

quizIssues.question: Keynes used the term 'animal spirits' to describe:
quizIssues.issue: 'Animal spirits' is in the IAL spec (2.3.2 investment) and is worth testing, but appears only in the investment examMatters, never in body text. Teach it in the body.

quizIssues.question: If the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is 0.8, the value of the multiplier is:
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q2 with the body's own worked example (0.8 -> 5). Four near-duplicate pairs exist (Q2/Q11, Q3/Q17, Q4/Q12, Q6/Q24) in a 25-item bank.

quizIssues.question: The AD curve slopes downward because, when the price level falls:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option is the only long, three-clause answer; guessable by length. Split into three parallel-length options or test one effect at a time (as Q13 and Q20 already do).

quizIssues.question: Consumer confidence is most likely to increase consumption spending because:
quizIssues.issue: Odd stem ('Consumer confidence is most likely to increase consumption spending because'); should be 'A rise in consumer confidence is likely to increase consumption because'.

quizIssues.question: A depreciation of the pound sterling would most likely shift the AD curve to the right because:
quizIssues.issue: Option [2] 'It reduces the cost of imported raw materials' is the opposite of what a depreciation does, so it is not a plausible distractor; and pound-specific framing again for an international cohort.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term aggregate demand (4 marks)': IAL definitions are 2-mark items; the scheme awards a mark for 'downward-sloping curve', which is not part of a definition. Should be 2 marks (definition + components/formula), or reworded to 'Explain what is meant by aggregate demand' if 4 marks.

'Analyse ... (10 marks)': in IAL WEC12 'Analyse' is an 8-mark question; 10 and 12 marks are 'Assess'/'Discuss' with evaluation. The scheme awards 4 of 10 marks for Marshall-Lerner and the J-curve, which are Unit 4 (WEC14) content, and lists point-by-point marks where IAL uses levels-based marking for 8+ mark items. No AD diagram is required, which an examiner would expect in KAA.

'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' is a realistic Section C item, but the guidance's itemised marks sum to 22, and IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (KAA and evaluation levels, with a diagram expected), not 2-3 marks per point. 'Bank of England' framing again UK-specific; IAL essays are usually country-neutral or refer to the extract's country.

'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (Define/Explain/Analyse/Assess/Discuss/Evaluate/Calculate/Draw/Examine). Reason 2 (multiplier) explains the SIZE of the shift, not why it shifts right, so it is a weak second 'reason'.

'Explain two factors ... in the UK (6 marks)' is a usable IAL-format item with a workable 3+3 scheme. Only issue: UK framing; IAL data-response questions anchor to the extract's country. Low priority.

Set-level gap: none of the 5 items has a data stimulus (IAL Unit 2 is data-response heavy) and none is a calculation (e.g. 'Calculate the value of the multiplier / the change in national income' 2-4 marks), which is the most predictable question form on this topic. Only 2 of 5 items ever reach Learn Mode (sortedPractice[0] and [1] = the two 4-mark items), so the 10- and 20-mark items are never practised inline.

structureIssues: Inline diagrams never render: block 2 diagramRef 'Aggregate Demand Curve' and block 3 diagramRef 'Shifts in Aggregate Demand' do not substring-match any diagram title ('The AD Curve', 'The Multiplier Effect', 'Circular Flow of Income with AD Components') under the match in components/LearnModeTab.jsx:97-104 (t.includes(ref) || ref.includes(t)). Blocks 4 and 5 have no diagramRef even though 'The Multiplier Effect' exists. Net: 0 of 3 diagrams appear in Learn Mode for this section.

quizIndices are assigned sequentially [0],[1],[2],[3],[4] rather than by topic: block 'Shifts in AD' shows Q2 (multiplier calc, untaught yet), block 'The Accelerator Effect' shows Q4 (AD leftward shift). Only 5 of 25 MCQs are used inline; the two accelerator MCQs (Q7, Q15) are never used.

The 3-subsection 'The Multiplier' block duplicates national-income's 'The Multiplier and National Income' block (national-income uses ids multiplier-concept / multiplier-formula / multiplier-evaluation; this section uses multiplier-definition / multiplier-formula / multiplier-size-determinants -- 'multiplier-formula' is the same id in both files). IAL puts the multiplier under 2.3.4 National income. A student following the unit does the multiplier twice, and if any client-side state is keyed by subsection id it may collide.

Pre-test gate draws 3 random MCQs from a 25-item bank that includes circular-flow (Q9, Q18) and paradox-of-thrift (Q23) items not taught in this section, plus UK-institution items (Q8). A first-time learner can be gated on material the section never teaches -- consistent with the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Recall placement side-effect: single-section steps (multiplier-size-determinants, step 6) get their recall shown as 'immediate' at the bottom of that step AND as 'spaced' at the top of the next step, so the not-orderable 'order of logic' reorder is the one widget students meet twice in a row.

Misconception duplication: ad-formula-and-components and determinants-of-gov-spending-net-exports carry the same transfer-payments misconception almost verbatim. Otherwise misconceptions are genuine (MPC<1, 'AD falls' vs 'shifts left', micro substitution reasoning, multiplier != government revenue, accelerator vs multiplier).

Audience fit: 11 of 14 realExamples are UK-centric (house prices, Brexit, furlough, Bank of England, London 2012, OBR, UK car makers, UK 2008, UK 2020) for a HK/Korea/Singapore/Malaysia/Pakistan/Sri Lanka/Middle East cohort; only Apple and Singapore are non-UK. Not wrong for IAL marking, but a mismatch with the product's audience and its own 'international' positioning.

2-per-step pairing is coherent (formula+C; I+G/NX; shape+movements; right+left; concept+formula; size; accel def+cycle; limitations). Block takeaways match their blocks. Difficulty ramp (components -> curve -> shifts -> multiplier -> accelerator) is sensible, but the accelerator gets 3 of 14 subsections -- disproportionate for a topic that is at most an evaluation point, while spec bullets are missing (see ialSpecGaps).
Diagram SVGs hard-code light text (#e8ecf5) with a transparent background: legible only on a dark theme. If the app supports a light theme the axes and labels vanish.
ialSpecGaps: 2.3.2(a) relative importance of the components of AD -- only a UK % breakdown; no discussion of why C dominates, why I matters despite its size, or how composition differs (e.g. export-led Singapore/Korea vs consumption-led economies).

2.3.2(b) the distinction between saving and consumption (saving as the residual of disposable income; APC/APS/MPC/MPS) -- not taught in the consumption subsection; MPC only appears later inside the multiplier block.
2.3.2(c) gross vs net investment (depreciation/replacement investment) -- not taught, yet the accelerator block relies on 'net investment' undefined.
2.3.2(c) distinction between investment and saving -- only a one-clause aside ('does not include financial investments like buying shares').

2.3.2(c) influences on investment: 'Keynes and animal spirits' (examMatters only, never in body; tested by Q5), 'demand for exports', 'access to credit' (only as an accelerator limitation), 'influence of government and regulations' -- missing from the investment subsection.
2.3.2(d) government expenditure: G over the trade cycle (automatic stabilisers, counter-cyclical spending) -- one sentence only; fiscal policy link is thin.

2.3.2(e) net trade: effect of domestic real income on imports (income -> M), degree of protectionism, non-price factors (quality, design, reliability) -- missing; only exchange rate, relative inflation and foreign income are covered.
Multiplier ratio/process/MPC-MPS-MPT-MPM/calculation belong to 2.3.4 National income in the IAL spec; present here as a duplicate rather than a gap.
Accelerator: unsure whether the 2018 IAL WEC12 spec requires it explicitly under 2.3.2; treat as extension, not core, and reduce its weight.
strengths: Definitions are correct and examiner-phrased: AD as 'total planned expenditure ... at a given price level over a given time period'; transfer payments correctly excluded from G; axis labels 'Price Level' / 'Real GDP' on all AD diagrams match Edexcel mark-scheme expectations.
Movement-along vs shift is taught explicitly, flagged as the most common diagram error, and reinforced in misconception, takeaway and common_mistakes -- exactly what IAL markers penalise.
Three slope effects (wealth, interest-rate, trade) are stated with mechanisms, and the micro-substitution misconception is called out.

examMatters blocks are genuinely useful exam craft: 'name the factor, the component, the direction'; 'say AD shifts left, not AD falls'; 'show working for multiplier calcs'; 'evaluate multiplier size via leakages and spare capacity'.
Misconceptions are real student errors (MPC<1, 'AD falls', multiplier as government revenue, accelerator vs multiplier), not filler.
Multiplier worked example ($100m -> $80m -> $64m) and diagram 2's round-by-round bars are a good concrete treatment; quiz calculation items (Q2, Q3, Q11, Q17) have correct arithmetic.
Reorder recalls for interest-rate chains and the multiplier process are genuine sequences with valid, non-identity shuffles.
topFixes: Fix Learn Mode wiring: set diagramRef strings that substring-match the diagram titles ('The AD Curve' for block 2, reuse its shift scenarios for block 3, 'The Multiplier Effect' for block 4) and reassign quizIndices by topic (block 3 -> Q4/Q12/Q16, block 4 -> Q3/Q21/Q24, block 5 -> Q7/Q15) so students stop seeing a multiplier calculation before the multiplier is taught. Also route the 10- and 20-mark practice items into Learn Mode.

Correct the content errors: consumption is NOT the most volatile component (determinants-of-consumption keyIdea); rewrite the 2022-inflation example so BoE rate rises are a shift, not the 'interest rate effect'; fix the car-industry accelerator example (sales fell); replace 'narrowly avoided a recession'; use one currency per example and fix '80p of every extra $1'; align the multiplier formula teaching with Q21.

Replace the 10 non-genuine recalls with application exercises: movement-vs-shift classifier (movements-along-ad), C/I/G/X-M classifier (ad-formula), MPW->k calculation comparison (multiplier-size-determinants), numeric accelerator table (accelerator-definition), scenario-based limitation matcher (limitations); drop leading-letter hints everywhere.

Remove or shrink the duplicated multiplier block (it lives in 2.3.4 national-income with overlapping ids) and use the space for missing 2.3.2 spec bullets: saving vs consumption and MPC/MPS, gross vs net investment, animal spirits and access to credit in the investment body, G over the trade cycle, protectionism and non-price factors for net trade. Cut the accelerator to one subsection.

Rebuild practice to IAL format: Define (2), Explain (4/6), Analyse (8) with a diagram, Assess (10/12), Evaluate (20) with levels-based guidance that sums correctly; add a short data extract and a 'Calculate the multiplier / change in national income' item; strip Marshall-Lerner and J-curve from the WEC12 mark scheme. While there, swap most UK-only examples (and Q8's NHS/JSA) for country-neutral or Asian/Middle-East cases to match the audience.

summary: The explanatory prose (keyIdea/body/misconception) is accurate on core AD/AS theory, uses the correct IAL axis labels, and the misconceptions are mostly real ones — a teacher would happily use the notes text. But the interactive layer is weak: 5 of 7 fill-ins are trivial three-word matching tasks (the word bank is the answer list), two fill-ins have double-blank template lines that the FillInRecall renderer cannot display (the second blank is silently dropped and a compound token like "rises, rises" lands in the first), three of six reorders are the same generic "draw/identify/read off" procedure, inline quiz/practice items are attached to the wrong blocks, the quiz bank is ~14 distinct questions padded to 25 by duplicates, and several real-world examples are wrong or contradict the section's own teaching (the 2022 UK manufacturers example, the "UK in 2019 close to equilibrium" example, "classical economics had not predicted stagflation"). The section also spans three IAL spec areas (2.3, 2.4.3, 2.5.2) under a "2.3.3" label and repeats stagflation/classical-vs-Keynesian material across blocks. Good bones, unreliable scaffolding.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the SRAS logic:
recallAudit.reason: FillInRecall.jsx builds the word bank from recall.answers, so the student drags 3 given words into 3 slots; 'wages' is the only word that fits '___ are sticky', 'profit' the only fit for '___ margins', 'output' for 'expanding ___'. It is a matching task with no discrimination. The flow chain immediately above ('wages are fixed', 'Profit margins widen', 'Firms expand output') contains the exact words.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in with a 6-word bank including distractors (wages, prices, profit, cost, output, demand) and a line that forces the movement-vs-shift distinction, e.g. 'A rise in the general price level causes a ___ along SRAS, not a ___' (movement/shift).

recallAudit.prompt: Order these SRAS shift factors from cause to effect:
items: Raw material and transport costs rise
SRAS shifts left at every price level
Output falls and price level rises
recallAudit.reason: Genuine causal chain (supply cut -> input costs -> curve shift -> equilibrium outcome) that a student can reconstruct from understanding. shuffled [2,0,3,1] is a valid non-identity permutation. Minor: the prompt says 'shift factors' but the items are chain steps, not factors.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the classical LRAS reasoning:
recallAudit.reason: Three distinct bank words, each fits exactly one slot ('___ adjust fully' = wages, 'return to ___' = normal, 'LRAS is ___' = vertical). 'normal' is a weak target word copied from the flow chain's own odd phrasing ('Real profit margins return to normal').
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in contrasting SR and LR: 'In the short run ___ are fixed so SRAS slopes ___; in the long run ___ factor prices adjust so LRAS is ___ at ___' with bank {wages, all, upward, vertical, Yf, horizontal, prices}.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the sections of the Keynesian AS curve from left to right:
items: Horizontal section — spare capacity, output rises without inflation
Upward-sloping section — bottlenecks cause rising costs
Vertical section — full capacity, only price level can rise
recallAudit.reason: Real spatial/logical order on the diagram (spare capacity -> bottlenecks -> full capacity). shuffled [1,2,0] valid and not identity. Only 3 items so it is easy, but it targets the exact misconception the section names (drawing Keynesian AS as a flat line).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the LRAS determinants:
recallAudit.reason: Bank words are unmistakable by slot ('Technological ___' can only take 'progress', 'Higher ___ investment' only 'capital'). Template line 1 'More or better ___ increases the economy's labour capacity' is awkward English. Hint 'ed________' is 10 characters for a 9-letter word.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Sorting/classification recall: given 6 events (oil price rise, immigration of skilled workers, VAT rise, new broadband network, minimum wage rise, competition policy reform) place each as 'shifts SRAS' or 'shifts LRAS' — this targets common_mistakes[0] (confusing SRAS and LRAS shifts), which no recall currently tests.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the steps to finding macroeconomic equilibrium:
items: Draw the AD curve sloping downward
Draw the SRAS curve sloping upward
Read off the equilibrium price level and real GDP
recallAudit.reason: Whether AD or SRAS is drawn first is arbitrary; the remaining two steps are the only forced order. It tests drawing procedure, not economics. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Reorder of the market-clearing logic: 'Price level is above equilibrium' -> 'Planned output exceeds planned expenditure' -> 'Firms accumulate stocks and cut prices' -> 'Price level falls until AD = AS'. Or a fill-in asking what is read off each axis (price level / real GDP) with distractors 'price' and 'quantity', which is the axis-label error examMatters warns about.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the equilibrium change analysis:
recallAudit.reason: Template lines 1 and 2 each contain two '___' but answers[] supplies one compound token per line. FillInRecall.jsx line 79 does `const [before, after] = part.split('___')`, so the second blank and the text after it are dropped: the student sees 'AD shifts right → price level [rises, rises] and real GDP' with no second slot, and the word bank shows chips reading 'rises, rises' and 'rises, falls'. The rendered line is confusing and the third word ('stagflation') is a giveaway with 'st' hint. Hint 'st__________' is 12 chars for an 11-letter word.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Split into one blank per template line (four lines: PL after AD-right, GDP after AD-right, PL after SRAS-left, GDP after SRAS-left) with bank {rises, falls, unchanged}, so the same word can legitimately go in several slots and the student must actually decide direction.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the demand-side shock transmission mechanism:
items: External event triggers a change in C, I, G, or X-M
AD curve shifts left or right
New intersection with AS at different price level and output
Economy moves to new short-run equilibrium
recallAudit.reason: Items 3 and 4 describe the same thing (a new intersection IS the new equilibrium), so their order is arbitrary; the chain is content-free ('left or right', 'different'). shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: A concrete chain: 'Stock market crashes' -> 'Household wealth falls' -> 'Consumption (C) falls' -> 'AD shifts left' -> 'Real GDP falls and price level falls'. Mirrors the section's own flow block and is reconstructible from causation.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the supply-side shock analysis:
recallAudit.reason: 'left' is the only direction word in the bank so slot 1 is automatic; line 2 has the same double-blank/compound-token render bug as changes-in-equilibrium ('price level [rises, falls] while real GDP' — second blank dropped); 'dilemma' is the only remaining word. Hint 'di______' is 8 chars for a 7-letter word.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fill-in that tests the policy dilemma itself: 'Raising AD after a negative supply shock restores ___ but worsens ___; cutting AD lowers ___ but deepens the ___' with bank {output, inflation, recession, unemployment, price level}.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the AD/AS analysis framework:
items: Determine whether it shifts AD, AS, or both
Draw the diagram with the correct shift(s)
Read off the new price level and real GDP and evaluate
recallAudit.reason: Each step logically depends on the previous, so it is orderable, but it is the third 'procedure' reorder in this section (after ad-as-equilibrium and demand-side-shocks) and tests exam method rather than economics. shuffled [3,1,0,2] valid — the same permutation as ad-as-equilibrium.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Keep it if the other two procedure reorders are replaced; otherwise swap for a both-curves chain using the Brexit example: 'Sterling depreciates' -> 'Imported inputs cost more (SRAS left) and exports cheaper (AD right)' -> 'Price level rises' -> 'Effect on real GDP ambiguous'.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the output gap definitions:
recallAudit.reason: Three distinct words with one obvious slot each. Note the body text says positive gaps put 'upward pressure on wages and prices' while the template wants 'inflationary pressure' — harmless with a word bank but shows the template was not written against the body. Hint 'in___________' is 13 chars for a 12-letter word.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Diagram-reading recall: given the base AD/AS diagram (diagrams[2] already shows Y* < Yfe), ask the student to pick which of 'positive gap / negative gap / full employment' applies and which direction SRAS will move under classical adjustment.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the self-correcting mechanism from start to finish:
items: Negative output gap — actual GDP below potential
Unemployment puts downward pressure on wages
Falling wages shift SRAS to the right
recallAudit.reason: Textbook causal chain, exactly what IAL 'explain the self-correcting mechanism' answers require. shuffled [2,0,3,1] valid (third use of this permutation in the section).

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the classical vs Keynesian comparison:
recallAudit.reason: Correct core vocabulary, but with a 3-word bank the only decision is flexible-vs-sticky and the template ('___ downward') makes it obvious. Hint 'in____________' is 14 chars for a 12-letter word.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Widen the bank to {flexible, sticky, rigid, vertical, horizontal, intervention, stimulus} and add a line 'Keynesians therefore favour ___ policy to shift ___' so the student must attach the view to its policy conclusion.

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims UK manufacturers in early 2022 saw margins boosted and expanded production because wages lagged output prices. 2022 was a cost-push squeeze (energy/input costs rose faster than output prices; UK manufacturing PMI fell below 50 from mid-2022 and output declined). The example illustrates the opposite of what happened.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with a neutral or historically clear case of a price-level rise raising SR margins (e.g. post-2020 reopening in the US where output prices rose ahead of contracted wages, with a caveat), or drop the real example and use a stylised firm-level illustration.

accuracyIssues.issue: Says the UK in 2019 'was operating close to macroeconomic equilibrium'. An economy is always at AD=AS equilibrium; what is meant is full-employment equilibrium. The section's own misconception two lines later warns that equilibrium is not the same as full employment, so the example teaches the misconception it is correcting.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword: 'was operating close to its full-employment level of output (a near-zero output gap), so the AD/SRAS intersection sat close to LRAS'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'a combination that classical economics had not predicted' — stagflation contradicted the Keynesian Phillips-curve consensus of the 1960s; monetarists/classical economists (Friedman, Phelps) are the ones credited with anticipating it. Attribution is reversed.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'a combination the Keynesian Phillips-curve consensus had not predicted, and which strengthened monetarist arguments'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Defines the LRAS position as 'the maximum output achievable when all resources are fully and efficiently employed'. Block 4 then teaches positive output gaps where actual GDP exceeds potential, and the classical-lras misconception itself says output can be above Yf in the short run. 'Maximum' is inconsistent with a positive output gap; IAL uses 'full-employment / normal-capacity output'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use 'the economy's full-employment (normal capacity) level of output — the level sustainable in the long run' and reserve 'no more output can be produced' for the vertical section of the Keynesian curve.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] 'Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)' > sras-shape-and-slope > body[1] and takeaway[3]; diagrams[0] annotations 'Spare capacity (flatter section)' / 'Near full capacity (steeper section)'
accuracyIssues.issue: Describes and draws SRAS as steepening toward full capacity with spare-capacity and bottleneck reasoning. That is the Keynesian LRAS story taught in block 1; in IAL materials SRAS is the upward-sloping curve explained by sticky input costs. Presenting both with the same shape/rationale blurs the SRAS vs Keynesian-LRAS distinction that Q3/Q9/Q10/Q20 then test.
accuracyIssues.fix: Draw SRAS as a simple upward-sloping line justified only by fixed factor costs; move the flat/steep/vertical explanation exclusively to keynesian-lras. Delete takeaway 'Near full capacity the SRAS curve becomes steeper'.

accuracyIssues.location: content[3] 'AD/AS Analysis of Macroeconomic Events' > demand-side-shocks > realExample vs applying-adas-to-events > body[2]
accuracyIssues.issue: COVID-19 is presented as 'a massive negative demand shock' (AD left), then two sections later the section says 'a pandemic can reduce both AD and SRAS'. Internally inconsistent; the second is the correct IAL framing. Also the '9.7%' GDP fall is one of several ONS vintages (first estimate -9.9%, later revisions -9.3%, -11.0%, -10.4%).
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a clean demand-only example for demand-side-shocks (e.g. the 2008–09 collapse in consumer and investment confidence) and keep COVID for the both-curves case; cite the GDP fall as 'around 10% (ONS estimates have been revised several times)'.

accuracyIssues.location: content[4] 'Short-Run vs Long-Run Adjustment' > output-gaps > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: States US actual GDP in late 2021 was 'above its pre-pandemic trend'. US real GDP had regained its pre-pandemic level by Q2 2021 but remained below the pre-pandemic trend line through 2021; CBO's output gap only turned modestly positive in 2022. The example also measures the gap against 'trend' rather than 'potential' — the section defines it against potential.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'pushed demand ahead of the economy's capacity to supply (labour shortages, record job openings), opening a positive output gap by 2022' and drop the 'above pre-pandemic trend' claim.

accuracyIssues.location: content[4] 'Short-Run vs Long-Run Adjustment' > self-correcting-mechanism > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Mixes 'return to pre-crisis GDP level' with 'return to Yf' (potential grows over time, so regaining the 2008 level is not closing the gap), and credits 'the government's fiscal stimulus' when UK policy from 2010 was fiscal consolidation; the stimulus was 2008–09 only.
accuracyIssues.fix: Reword: 'UK output stayed below estimated potential for around five to six years after 2008; the Bank of England's QE and the 2008–09 fiscal stimulus were justified by critics of the classical view who argued adjustment was too slow.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'OPEC's ... cuts in 2023 pushed crude above $90' is broadly right (Brent peaked ~$97 in Sept 2023 after OPEC+ cuts) but 'contributing to persistent cost-push inflation across advanced economies' overstates it — 2023 was a year of falling inflation; the major oil-driven cost-push episode was 2022.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use 2022 (Brent >$120 after the invasion of Ukraine) or soften to 'slowed the fall in inflation in late 2023'. Write 'OPEC+'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'shifted AD right (cheaper exports boosted net trade)' — post-2016 UK export volumes did not respond measurably (the 'missing export boom'); the documented effect was the SRAS-left/inflation-to-3% channel. Fine as a theoretical both-curves illustration but the AD-right leg is asserted as fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'in theory shifted AD right via cheaper exports, though the export response was weak in practice, while the imported-cost effect clearly shifted SRAS left'.

accuracyIssues.location: content[2] > ad-as-equilibrium > examMatters; content[0] > sras-shape-and-slope > examMatters; common_mistakes[2].examTip
accuracyIssues.issue: Repeated language of examiners 'deducting' or 'penalising' marks, and 'Diagram marks are usually 2-4 marks'. IAL Economics marking is positive and levels-based for 8/10/12/14/20-mark questions; a diagram contributes to the KAA level rather than carrying a fixed 2–4 marks. Students may wrongly think a wrong axis label loses marks already earned.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rephrase as 'you will not be credited for a diagram whose axes read price/quantity' and 'a correct, labelled AD/AS diagram is expected to reach the higher KAA levels'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'unemployment is above its natural rate' — natural rate of unemployment is not Unit 2 IAL vocabulary and is undefined here.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use 'unemployment is higher than at full employment'.

accuracyIssues.location: Notation: content uses 'Yf'; diagrams[1], diagrams[2] and quiz Q2/Q6 use 'Yfe'
accuracyIssues.issue: Inconsistent label for full-employment output between text, diagrams and quiz.
accuracyIssues.fix: Standardise on one label (IAL papers commonly use Yfe or YFE).

quizIssues.question: In the short run, an increase in aggregate demand when the economy has significant spare capacity will primarily lead to:
quizIssues.issue: Frames the question as 'in the short run' but the keyed answer (large output rise, little price change) assumes the horizontal Keynesian LRAS section. On the section's own SRAS model (upward sloping, sticky wages) an AD rise in the short run raises both P and Y. A strong student could defend option 0/1 depending on model; the stem should name the Keynesian model.

quizIssues.question: Stagflation refers to a situation where:
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q4 (same construct, same correct idea, near-identical distractors). With PreTest/PostTest drawing 3 random items from this bank, duplicates inflate pre/post overlap.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following would cause the LRAS curve to shift to the right?
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q5: same correct answer (education/training) and two identical distractors (consumer confidence, interest-rate cut).

quizIssues.question: A leftward shift of the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve could be caused by:
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q1 (wage-cost rise; distractors fall in oil prices / productivity rise repeated).

quizIssues.question: Supply-side improvements that shift LRAS to the right tend to:
quizIssues.issue: Duplicate of Q8 with the same keyed option text '(non-inflationary growth)'. Also, both Q8 and Q19 key 'reduce the price level' as a general tendency; in practice a rightward LRAS shift lowers inflationary pressure rather than the price level — Q8's explanation concedes this but the option does not.

quizIssues.question: If LRAS shifts right while AD remains unchanged, the economy will experience:
quizIssues.issue: Keyed option contains the parenthetical '(non-inflationary growth)', a label giveaway that makes it the only 'textbook-sounding' option. Remove the parenthetical.

quizIssues.question: If an economy is at macroeconomic equilibrium where AD intersects SRAS to the left of LRAS, this indicates:
quizIssues.issue: Near-duplicate of Q18 (negative output gap definition). Q18 distractor 'Government spending exceeds tax revenue' and Q24 distractor 'hyperinflation' are implausible, so both reduce to two-option items.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor that determines the position of the LRAS curve?
quizIssues.issue: Overlaps Q12 (LRAS determined by supply-side factors, not price level/AD). Acceptable individually but adds to the bank's redundancy.

quizIssues.question: In the Keynesian model, the aggregate supply curve is horizontal at low levels of output because:
quizIssues.issue: Same construct as Q3 and Q20 (spare capacity → output up, prices flat). Distractors 'The government is controlling prices' and 'Inflation is always zero in the short run' are not plausible, so the item is effectively binary.

quizIssues.question: According to Keynesian economics, the economy can settle at an equilibrium below full employment because:
quizIssues.issue: Distractor 3 'Workers always demand wages above the equilibrium level' is close to the real-wage-rigidity argument some Keynesians make; the word 'always' is the only thing making it wrong. Fine, but a strong student could argue it.

quizIssues.question: A recession is typically shown on an AD/AS diagram by:
quizIssues.issue: Keyed answer is fine, but the stem says 'typically' while the section itself teaches that a leftward SRAS shift also produces falling output (stagflation). No SRAS-left distractor is offered, so it is unambiguous only by omission.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term LRAS (4 marks)' — IAL Economics uses 'Define' for 2-mark items; 4-mark Section A/B items are 'Explain ...'. The guidance also awards marks for 'LRAS is vertical in the classical model' and 'shifts are caused by ...', which are not part of a definition. Mark allocation and mark scheme do not match IAL practice. Because LearnModeTab sorts practice by marks, this LRAS question is the inline practice for the SRAS block.

'Outline two factors ... (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (IAL uses 'Explain one/two ...'). Content of the guidance is fine (1 mark identification + 1 mark development each), so only the command word needs changing.

'Assess ... (10 marks)' matches the IAL Unit 2 Section B 10-mark 'Assess' slot, but the guidance is written as additive points (2+2+2+1+1+1+1 = 10). IAL 10-mark Assess is levels-marked (KAA up to 6 + evaluation up to 4); students need level descriptors (define/apply/analyse chain + two-sided evaluation + judgement), not a points tally. No diagram is required in the guidance although an LRAS-shift diagram is the expected KAA vehicle.

'Evaluate ... (20 marks)' matches the Section C essay format, but again the guidance is an additive 20-point tally rather than the levels-based KAA + evaluation scheme, does not require AD/AS diagrams, and the question compares 'AS increase' generically without distinguishing SRAS from LRAS (the model answer silently switches to LRAS). Question is a reasonable essay; scheme needs rewriting as levels with an explicit diagram expectation.

'Explain the difference between a movement along and a shift of SRAS (6 marks)' — acceptable command/mark pairing and a usable model answer. However, none of the five practice questions is data-response style ('With reference to Figure 1...'), which is how every Section B AD/AS question is asked in WEC12; there is no application practice at all.

structureIssues: Inline quiz-to-block mapping is wrong: content[1] (LRAS) has quizIndices [1] which is an SRAS-shift question; content[2] (Equilibrium) gets Q2 (classical LR effect of AD, really LRAS material); content[4] (SR vs LR adjustment) gets Q5 (LRAS determinants). Only blocks 0 and 3 get a topically matching inline MCQ. Q7/Q23/Q24 (self-correction, sticky wages, output gap) are never shown inline.

Inline practice mapping is by mark size, not topic: LearnModeTab.jsx line 80 sorts practice by marks, so practiceIndices [0..4] resolve to Define-LRAS(4) on the SRAS block, Outline-LRAS(4) on the LRAS block, Explain-SRAS-movement-vs-shift(6) on the Equilibrium block, Assess-supply-side(10) on the Events block, Evaluate(20) on the Adjustment block. The mark ramp is sensible but three of five are off-topic for their block.

Two blocks get no inline diagram: diagramRef 'AD/AS Shifts' (content[3]) and 'Self-Correcting Mechanism' (content[4]) match no diagram title via the substring test in LearnModeTab.jsx lines 97-104 (titles are 'Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS)', 'LRAS: Classical vs Keynesian', 'AD/AS Equilibrium: Multiple Scenarios'). There is no diagram anywhere of the self-correcting mechanism (SRAS shifting to close a gap), which is the most diagram-dependent idea in the section. Renaming content[3].diagramRef to 'AD/AS Equilibrium' would collide with content[2] (usedDiagrams set), so a fourth diagram is needed.

Recall duplication caused by odd section counts: blocks 1, 3 and 4 have 3 sections, so the third section is a solo step. For a solo step, the 'immediate' recall (first section of the step) and the next step's 'spaced' recall (last section of the previous step) are the same object — lras-determinants fillin and applying-adas-to-events reorder are each shown twice back-to-back (LearnModeTab.jsx lines 345-402).

Content repetition across blocks: stagflation is taught with near-identical flow chains in changes-in-equilibrium and supply-side-shocks; the AD-right analysis appears in changes-in-equilibrium and demand-side-shocks; classical vs Keynesian appears in block 1 (shapes) and block 4 (adjustment) with examMatters in keynesian-lras and classical-vs-keynesian-adjustment saying the same thing. Block 3 ('AD/AS Analysis of Macroeconomic Events') is largely a restatement of block 2 and could be merged, cutting the section from 13 to ~10 subsections — relevant given 75% of users never leave step 0.

Three of six reorders are the same generic exam-procedure list (ad-as-equilibrium, demand-side-shocks, applying-adas-to-events); only sras-shifts, keynesian-lras and self-correcting-mechanism test economics. Recall 'shuffled' arrays reuse two permutations ([2,0,3,1] x3, [3,1,0,2] x2), so a student who notices can solve by pattern.

Fill-in data shape not supported by the renderer: changes-in-equilibrium template lines 0-1 and supply-side-shocks template line 1 contain two '___' with a single compound answer ('rises, rises'); FillInRecall.jsx destructures split('___') into [before, after], dropping the second blank. Five of seven hints have character counts that do not match the answer length (education, stagflation, dilemma, inflationary, intervention).

Section scope vs label: titled '2.3.3 Aggregate Supply' but covers IAL 2.3.1-2.3.3 (AS characteristics, SRAS, LRAS) plus 2.4.3 (equilibrium real national output, blocks 2-3) plus 2.5.2 (output gaps, block 4). Students cross-referencing the spec will not find macro equilibrium or output gaps under 2.3.3.

Takeaways match their blocks, with one exception: content[0] takeaway 'Near full capacity the SRAS curve becomes steeper' encodes the SRAS/Keynesian-LRAS conflation noted under accuracy. Misconceptions are mostly genuine student errors (higher prices shift SRAS; government spending shifts LRAS; Keynesian AS drawn flat; equilibrium = desirable; output gap = recession); the classical-vs-keynesian-adjustment one ('Keynesians say markets never work') is a straw man rather than an observed error.
Difficulty ramp is sensible (SRAS -> LRAS -> equilibrium -> shocks -> adjustment) and pairing classical-lras with keynesian-lras in one step is the right pedagogical choice.
ialSpecGaps: 2.3.3 LRAS factor 'changes in relative productivity' (productivity relative to other economies) — not taught; productivity appears only as a diagram annotation and a quiz distractor.
2.3.3 LRAS factor 'demographic changes and migration' — only the word 'immigration' inside one bullet in lras-determinants; no treatment of ageing populations, participation rates or emigration.

2.3.3 LRAS factor 'changes in government regulations' — only 'deregulation' listed inside the 'Institutional factors' bullet with no explanation of the mechanism (compliance costs, labour-market rules).
2.3.3 LRAS factor 'competition policy' — named in one bullet, never explained (how contestability raises efficiency/potential output).
2.3.1 'distinction between movement along and shift of the AS curve' is taught for SRAS only; not stated for LRAS (e.g. that there is no 'movement along' a vertical LRAS).
2.5.2 (if output gaps are intended to live here) 'difficulties of measuring output gaps' — not taught; the section presents potential output as observable.

Unsure: whether the spec's 2.4.3 expectation of showing 'equilibrium in the short run and long run' with SRAS and LRAS on one diagram is examined via the Keynesian curve as well — the section only shows LR adjustment on the classical diagram.
strengths: Core theory in keyIdea/body is accurate and uses IAL-correct terminology: sticky input costs as the SRAS rationale, vertical classical LRAS at full-employment output, three-section Keynesian curve, movement-vs-shift rule stated explicitly (sras-shifts body[3]).
Axis labels are correct everywhere (Price Level / Real GDP) in all three diagram sets and the sras-shape-and-slope examMatters explicitly warns against 'price/quantity' — a real IAL marking point.

Misconceptions are mostly genuine and phrased as 'instead write:' corrections a student can copy: 'higher prices shift SRAS', 'government spending shifts LRAS', 'Keynesian AS is a horizontal line', 'equilibrium is automatically desirable', 'negative output gap = recession'.
Two reorders (sras-shifts OPEC chain; self-correcting-mechanism) and the keynesian-lras left-to-right reorder are exactly the causal chains IAL 'explain' answers require.

Diagram set 3 (AD/AS Equilibrium scenarios) is well built: base diagram shows Y* < Yfe with a labelled negative output gap, and the four scenarios (demand-pull, cost-push, LRAS growth, recession) have P1/P2, Y1/Y2 and a stated outcome box — matching the examMatters advice to label both P and Y before and after.
Practice questions 2 and 3 use correct IAL mark/command pairings (Assess 10, Evaluate 20) and the 20-mark model answer has a two-sided structure with a context-dependent judgement.

Real examples that are accurate and usable: 1973 oil crisis (quadrupling, UK inflation >25%), South Korea LRAS growth, Ukraine-war gas shock and >10% eurozone inflation, US 9.1% CPI in June 2022, UK 2019 inflation near 2% with unemployment at a multi-decade low.
topFixes: Fix the fill-in data shape and renderer mismatch: split every template line to one '___' (changes-in-equilibrium, supply-side-shocks), replace compound tokens like 'rises, rises' with single words, and widen word banks beyond the answer list (add 2-3 distractors) so the 5 trivial fill-ins become real decisions; correct the five hint lengths.

Re-map inline quiz and practice to their blocks: set content[1].quizIndices to LRAS items (5/12/13/21), content[2] to 2/3/24, content[4] to 7/23/18; either stop sorting practice by marks in LearnModeTab.jsx line 80 or reorder practiceIndices so the SRAS block gets the SRAS movement-vs-shift question and the LRAS block gets the LRAS definition/outline; change practice[0] to a 2-mark 'Define' and practice[4] to 'Explain two factors'.

Add a fourth diagram titled to match 'Self-Correcting Mechanism' (negative gap closing via SRAS shift right, positive gap via SRAS left) and rename content[3].diagramRef so blocks 3 and 4 stop rendering without a diagram.

Correct the wrong/contradictory real examples: replace the 2022 UK manufacturers SRAS example, reword 'UK 2019 close to macroeconomic equilibrium' to 'close to full-employment output', fix the 'classical economics had not predicted stagflation' attribution, and use a demand-only case (2008-09 confidence collapse) instead of COVID in demand-side-shocks since applying-adas-to-events later says COVID shifted both curves.

De-duplicate: merge block 3 into block 2 (stagflation and AD-right analysis are taught twice), replace the two generic procedure reorders (ad-as-equilibrium, demand-side-shocks) with concrete causal chains, prune the quiz bank duplicates (Q11=Q1, Q13=Q5, Q14=Q4, Q19=Q8, Q24~Q18) and rewrite Q20 to name the Keynesian model; remove the 'SRAS steepens near capacity' takeaway so SRAS and Keynesian LRAS stay distinct.

summary: The prose is generally accurate, well-pitched and IAL-appropriate in scope (four objectives, fiscal, monetary incl. QE, market-based vs interventionist supply-side, SRPC/LRPC), and a teacher would be broadly comfortable with the notes text. But the Learn Mode experience built around it is broken in ways the student will feel: none of the four diagrams renders (diagramRef 'fiscal-policy-ad' etc. never substring-matches titles like 'Fiscal Policy: AD/AS Impact'), the inline quiz at the end of 'Macroeconomic Objectives' is a Phillips-curve question four blocks before the Phillips curve is taught, practice questions are attached to the wrong blocks because practiceIndices index a marks-sorted array, and the 20-mark essay is never shown. Of the 17 recalls, 3 reorders are non-orderable or arbitrary and all 9 fillins are trivially solvable from a 3-word bank where each slot accepts exactly one word grammatically. There are a handful of factual slips (UK 1970s unemployment never exceeded 10%; the UK has never had a 2% growth target), inconsistent lag figures (12-18 / 12-24 / 18-24 months), and mark schemes that use point-marking and UK framing rather than IAL levels-based marking. Fixable to a B+ with mostly structural/plumbing work rather than rewriting.

recallAudit.prompt: Complete the chain: 'Target growth rate for developed economies ≈ ___% per year → Balances expansion with economic ___ → Too fast risks inflation, too slow risks ___'
recallAudit.reason: Word bank is only the 3 answers (FillInRecall.jsx:12). Slot 1 is the only numeric slot; 'economic ___' only accepts 'stability'; the remainder goes to slot 3. Solvable by grammar with zero economics. Hint '2-_' also leaks the answer outright. The three lines are not a causal chain.
recallAudit.suggestedReplacement: Fillin with a real chain and a 5-word bank containing plausible distractors, e.g. 'Real GDP grows faster than ___ output → ___ output gap → demand-pull ___ pressure' with bank {potential, positive, negative, inflationary, deflationary}.

recallAudit.prompt: Order the reasoning for a 2% inflation target:
items: Give central bank room to cut real rates
