quizIssues.issue: The shutdown rule (P < AVC short run, P < AC long run) is not taught in content[] — it exists only in diagrams[3], common_mistakes[3] and a flashcard, and diagrams[3] is never surfaced in Learn Mode (see structureIssues). Distractor D 'MC > MR at all output levels' is nonsensical rather than plausibly wrong.

quizIssues.question: The marginal cost curve intersects the average cost curve:
quizIssues.issue: 'the average cost curve' is ambiguous — MC cuts both AVC and ATC at their minima; harmless here since B is the only defensible answer, but the stem should say 'average total cost'. Option C 'Where AC equals AFC' is an implausible distractor.

quizIssues.question: X-inefficiency occurs when:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option says 'operates above its LRAC curve' — X-inefficiency is normally described as operating above the (short- or long-run) AC curve; content[3] says 'above its minimum cost curve'. Minor inconsistency in terminology between quiz and content.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term marginal revenue (4 marks)' — IAL Economics definitions carry 2 marks (or are embedded in a 4-mark supported MCQ). The guidance pads the definition with two non-definitional points ('For a perfectly competitive firm MR = price', 'for a firm with market power MR < price') to reach 4, teaching students that definitions earn marks for extra content they do not.

'Outline the conditions... (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (it is a Business one); Economics uses Explain/Analyse/Discuss/Assess/Evaluate. Also the shutdown rule it examines is not taught in content[].

'Assess... (10 marks)' — acceptable mark allocation, but the guidance is scored 2 marks per point (5 x 2) rather than the levels-based KAA + Evaluation scheme IAL uses for 10-mark Assess questions. Only one weak 'judgement' line; no counter-view (e.g. increasing returns at low output, the possibility that the firm is in a range of constant returns, the assumption that all other factors are fixed). Would not reach the top level as written.

'Evaluate... always harmful to consumers (20 marks)' — good IAL-style essay title. But the guidance again allocates marks per point ('(3 marks)', '(2 marks)') instead of KAA/Evaluation levels, and never asks for a diagram (monopoly diagram showing P > MC and the supernormal profit rectangle is expected for top-level KAA). Also note this 20-marker is never surfaced in Learn Mode (see structureIssues).

'Explain two types of economies of scale (6 marks)' — reasonable question, model answer fine, but economies-of-scale types are not taught in content[], so students meet this in the 'guided' practice slot with no supporting content.

structureIssues: Zero recall widgets: none of the 8 subsections has a `recall` object, so Learn Mode shows no reorder/fill-in retrieval at all for this section — the only active element per step is one MCQ + one written question. Given the section is diagram- and rule-heavy, the natural recalls are missing: a genuine sequence exists for the profit-max four-step method (MC=MR → Q* → P* from AR → compare AR to ATC) and for the supernormal-profit-entry chain (TR>TC → entry → supply up, price down → normal profit); fill-ins for 'MR = a − 2bQ', 'MC cuts ATC at its ___ point', 'shut down in SR if P < ___'.

No block carries diagramRef / quizIndices / practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:86 `hasRefs` is false and the legacy fallback runs. Consequences computed from utils.js: (a) matchDiagramsToBlocks only places diagrams[0] 'Revenue Curves' on block 0 and diagrams[1] 'Short-Run Cost Curves' on block 1; diagrams[2] 'Long-Run Average Cost Curve' and diagrams[3] 'Short-Run and Long-Run Shutdown Points' share no title word with 'Profit' or 'Efficiency' and are NEVER shown in Learn Mode. (b) distributeItems(10 MCQs, 4 steps) puts quiz[0..3] on steps 0..3: quiz[1] (MR = 0, revenue) lands on the Cost block, quiz[2] (diminishing returns) on the Profit block, quiz[3] (MC cuts AC) on the Efficiency block; quiz[4..9] never appear. (c) sortedPractice by marks = [Define MR 4, Outline shutdown 4, Explain EoS 6, Assess dim. returns 10, Evaluate 20]; steps get Define MR (worked, block Revenue — fine), Outline shutdown (guided, on Cost block — topic untaught), Explain EoS (guided, on Profit block — untaught, wrong block), Assess diminishing returns (independent, on Efficiency block — wrong block); the 20-mark essay never appears.

Every block has exactly 2 sections, so the whole section is 4 steps, each ~900-1000 words (2 full sections + diagram + MCQ + practice + Explain-it-back + takeaway). Each step is simultaneously first- and last-in-block, so the spaced/immediate recall scaffolding has nothing to attach to. Recommend splitting into 6-8 blocks (Revenue; Revenue by market structure; SR costs; LR costs + economies of scale; Profit + shutdown; Profit max; Efficiency) so that each step is one idea and the last-of-block activities are topical.

Block 4 'Efficiency' (allocative, productive, dynamic, X-inefficiency) is IAL 3.3.3 'Market structures and contestability' content, not 3.3.2; it belongs after perfect competition/monopoly are taught. Meanwhile the 3.3.2 bullets actually missing (economies of scale types, shutdown points) are absent — the block budget is spent on the wrong topic.

content[] vs the rest of the section is internally inconsistent: notes[] has 8 headings including 'Long-Run Cost Curves' (which does cover EoS types) and 'Alternative Objectives on a Diagram' (3.3.1 material), common_mistakes[3] covers the shutdown rule, flashcards cover economies of scope and accounting vs economic profit — none of which the Learn Mode content teaches. A student who only uses Learn Mode is under-prepared for this section's own quiz.

Difficulty ramp inside Block 1 is inverted for weaker students: the twice-gradient/elasticity/MR-negative material (subsection 1) precedes the simpler price-taker vs price-maker distinction (subsection 2). Teaching AR = MR = P for a price taker first, then introducing the downward-sloping AR/MR, is the conventional and easier order.

Takeaways match their blocks and are accurate. Misconceptions are real ones (MR below AR in PC, diminishing returns vs diseconomies, normal profit = 'no profit', profit max vs revenue max, 'monopoly always bad'); only the first ('MR falls because the firm sells more') is slightly contrived. Flow chains are genuine causal sequences — these would convert well into reorder recalls.
ialSpecGaps: Economies and diseconomies of scale as a full topic: types of internal economies (technical, managerial, purchasing/bulk-buying, financial, marketing, risk-bearing), external economies of scale, causes of diseconomies (communication, coordination, motivation) — only one sentence in content; tested in quiz[4], quiz[5], practice[1].

Short-run and long-run shutdown points (P < AVC shut down in SR; P < AC exit in LR; firm's SR supply curve = MC above AVC) — tested in quiz[7], practice[4], diagrams[3], common_mistakes[3], but not taught in content.

Calculation of TR, TC, AC, MC, profit from numerical data/tables — the IAL data-response regularly asks for calculations; no numeric worked example anywhere in content (quiz[0] is the only calculation).

Law of diminishing marginal productivity via marginal and average product (MP/AP curves and their link to MC/AVC) — content asserts diminishing returns raise MC but never shows product curves or a numeric example.

Loss-making firm diagram (AR < ATC) and the profit/loss rectangles for a price maker — profit-max subsection describes the four-step method but the only shaded-profit diagram (diagrams[3]) is perfect-competition and is not surfaced in Learn Mode.
Distinction between accounting profit and economic profit (in flashcards only) — unsure whether explicitly on the IAL 3.3.2 spec; include as low priority.
Efficiency content (allocative, productive, dynamic, X-inefficiency) is IAL 3.3.3 — not a gap, but a misplacement; check that section 3.3.3 does not duplicate it.
strengths: Core theory is correct and phrased in Edexcel mark-scheme language: TR/AR/MR definitions, MR = a − 2bQ, MC cuts ATC at minimum with the batting-average analogy, normal profit inside TC, MC = MR four-step diagram method, LRAC as envelope of SRAC with MES.

examMatters fields give concrete, correct diagram-drawing instructions (MR intercept at half AR intercept; label elastic/inelastic portions; LRAC tangent to SRACs; label MES; show P = MC and min ATC).
Misconceptions are authentic student errors with a corrected 'Instead write' sentence — good exam-technique scaffolding.

Diagrams are correctly labelled (Revenue/Cost on the vertical axis, Quantity/Output on the horizontal; MC through AVC min then ATC min; AFC hyperbola; shutdown scenarios) and each has a usable checklist; diagrams[3]'s three-scenario shutdown diagram is excellent — it just never reaches Learn Mode.
Quiz MCQs: all 10 correctIndex values are correct, distractors are mostly plausible, explanations are accurate and teach the reasoning (e.g. quiz[0], quiz[7]).

Practice[3] 20-mark essay title ('supernormal profits are always harmful to consumers') is a realistic IAL Section C style question with a two-sided model answer and a source/persistence-based judgement.
extras chains are genuine causal sequences and evaluation points are relevant (non-profit-max objectives, diseconomies, non-permanent barriers).
topFixes: Add diagramRef, quizIndices and practiceIndices to each block (and split into 6-8 single-idea blocks) so Learn Mode stops using the legacy fallback: today diagrams[2] (LRAC) and diagrams[3] (shutdown), quiz[4..9] and the 20-mark essay never appear, and the MCQs/practice that do appear sit on the wrong block.

Add two teaching subsections for the untaught-but-tested 3.3.2 content: 'Economies and diseconomies of scale' (internal types, external, causes of diseconomies, link to LRAC/MES) and 'Shutdown points' (P < AVC in SR, P < AC in LR, MC above AVC as supply curve), wiring diagrams[3], quiz[4/5/7] and practice[1/4] to them.

Replace the two factually wrong real examples: British Airways (airline pricing is the opposite of what is stated) and OpenAI (has never earned supernormal profit). Also qualify 'competitive pressure forces firms to be productively efficient' to perfect competition only.

Add recall objects: reorder recalls from the existing flow chains (profit-max four-step method; supernormal-profit-entry chain; MC < ATC → average falls → MC crosses at min) and fill-ins for MR = a − 2bQ / MC cuts ATC at ___ / shut down if P < ___ — the section currently has zero retrieval practice.

Rewrite practice mark schemes to IAL format: 2-mark definition (not 4), replace 'Outline' with 'Explain', and present the 10-mark Assess and 20-mark Evaluate guidance as levels-based KAA + Evaluation with an explicit diagram requirement, instead of '(2 marks)' per bullet.

summary: The eight prose subsections are the strongest part: definitions match Edexcel mark-scheme wording, the flows are genuine causal chains, and the misconceptions are real student errors rather than filler. A strong IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is, for four reasons: (1) it covers only part of the IAL 'Market structures and contestability' topic (monopsony, natural monopoly, X-inefficiency, barrier-to-entry types, concentration ratios, predatory/limit pricing and non-price competition are all absent from content[] while four of the twelve MCQs test exactly those gaps, so the 3-question pre-test has roughly a 75% chance of containing at least one untaught item); (2) two of the five diagrams (PC long-run and monopolistic-competition long-run) do not actually draw a tangency, and the monopoly diagram's MR=MC point, Pm and Qc markers are off the curves, while the two long-run diagrams the examMatters text calls 'the key diagram skill' never appear in Learn Mode because the blocks have no diagramRef; (3) with no diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices the legacy fallback pairs the Oligopoly block with a perfect-competition MCQ and a contestable-markets practice question, and the 20-mark essay is never surfaced; (4) there are zero recall widgets, so the section has no retrieval practice at all, and the examples are uniformly UK-centric (Tesco/Morrisons, Thames Water/Ofwat, Avanti, CMA, Ryanair) for an audience in HK/Korea/Singapore/Pakistan/Middle East, with one 'Top-band 25-mark essays' reference that is UK GCE, not IAL.

accuracyIssues.issue: The SVG does not draw a tangency. AC path (M110,100 Q200,195 280,165 Q340,152 440,185) has its minimum at roughly x=240,y=172 and then rises to a hump near x=320 before falling again at high output (an AC curve that falls at high output is malformed). At the marked 'tangency' E (225,148) the AR line is at y≈158 and AC at y≈171, so AR sits ~13px above AC — the picture shows supernormal profit, exactly what the section's own examMatters says 'examiners penalise'. 'Qeff' is drawn at x=295 but the AC minimum is at x≈240, so the 'Excess Capacity' bracket is measured to the wrong point.
accuracyIssues.fix: Redraw with AR genuinely touching AC at one point left of AC's minimum; place Qeff at the true AC minimum; MC through AC minimum; keep AC monotonically rising after its minimum.

accuracyIssues.issue: Same defect: AC path (M110,120 Q200,220 270,170 Q320,155 430,200) has its minimum near x≈226,y≈186, then rises to y≈166 near x≈305 and falls again. The AR = MR = P line at y=160 lies above AC everywhere (AR > AC), so the diagram depicts supernormal profit, not the 'tangent at minimum AC, normal profit only' the checklist claims; E at (270,160) is not on the AC curve (AC at x=270 is y=170).
accuracyIssues.fix: Draw AC as a clean U whose minimum lies exactly on the AR line at Q*, with MC passing through that same point.

accuracyIssues.issue: Markers are not on the curves. MR line (90,40)->(270,280) and the MC segment through (200,200)-(280,100) intersect at ≈(205,193), but the MR=MC dot is at (210,170) — ~23px above the intersection. Pm on AR at x=210 should be y≈122 but is drawn at 108. AR=MC (competitive output) is at ≈(244,145) but Qc/the DWL apex is placed at (290,153), where AR is at y≈177 and MC at y≈88 — so the shaded DWL triangle (210,108)-(290,153)-(210,170) is not the area between AR and MC. This is the diagram examMatters calls 'the most important in the entire unit' and it IS the one shown in Learn Mode (block 2 via title-match fallback).
accuracyIssues.fix: Compute Qm from the actual MR/MC intersection, read Pm from AR at that x, place Qc where MC cuts AR, and build the DWL polygon from those three computed points.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Airlines like Ryanair and easyJet lease aircraft rather than buying them' — Ryanair overwhelmingly owns its fleet (bulk Boeing 737 purchases; leasing is a small minority), and easyJet owns roughly two-thirds. The factual hook used to illustrate low sunk costs is wrong for the named firms.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use carriers that genuinely lease most of their fleet and fit the audience (e.g. IndiGo, AirAsia, Cebu Pacific use heavy operating-lease/sale-and-leaseback models), or drop the leasing claim and cite route-switching and low exit costs only.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Top-band 25-mark essays' — 25-mark essays are UK GCE A-level (Papers 1/2/3). IAL WEC13 Section C essays are 20 marks; Section B data-response sub-questions top out at 12. Presents UK-GCE exam format as IAL.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to 'Top-band 20-mark Section C essays (and 12-mark Assess questions)'.

accuracyIssues.location: Contestable Markets > evaluating-market-structures > body[0], misconception, flow step 'Perfect competition: static efficiency but no dynamic', and Block 4 takeaway[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: States as fact that perfect competition has 'zero dynamic efficiency, meaning no innovation, no new products, and no technological progress'. This is an absolute an examiner would mark as unbalanced: PC firms can earn short-run supernormal profit, and the stronger theoretical reason is perfect information (innovations are instantly copied), not merely 'no funds'. IAL mark schemes phrase it as 'may lack dynamic efficiency'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Soften to 'is unlikely to be dynamically efficient' and add the perfect-information/no-incentive argument alongside the no-funds argument.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'UK supermarket industry — dominated by Tesco, Sainsbury's, Asda, and Morrisons' — Aldi overtook Morrisons as the UK's fourth-largest grocer in September 2022; the 'big four' framing is out of date. Also entirely UK-centric for an international-school audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use a regional example (e.g. Hong Kong's ParknShop/Wellcome duopoly, Singapore's FairPrice/Sheng Siong/Dairy Farm, or global mobile-network oligopolies) or update to Tesco/Sainsbury's/Asda/Aldi with a date.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'members like Iraq and Nigeria frequently exceed their production quotas' — Iraq (and OPEC+ member Kazakhstan) are the commonly cited over-producers; Nigeria has repeatedly produced BELOW its quota in 2022–24 because of theft and under-investment. Nigeria is the wrong illustration of cheating.
accuracyIssues.fix: Cite Iraq and (OPEC+) Kazakhstan, or keep it generic: 'several members have repeatedly pumped above quota'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Pharmaceutical patents grant companies like Pfizer a 20-year monopoly on new drugs' — patents run 20 years from filing, but 8–12 of those are typically consumed by trials and approval, so effective market exclusivity is far shorter. Imprecise in a way that weakens the static-vs-dynamic evaluation.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'a patent lasting 20 years from filing (typically 8–12 years of actual market exclusivity)'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Tells students to 'draw two side-by-side diagrams' for third-degree PD but diagrams[] contains no price-discrimination diagram, so the skill is described and never shown.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add a two-market (elastic/inelastic) third-degree PD diagram with common MC and MR=MC in each market.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Thames Water ... 15 million customers' — Thames Water currently states c.16 million; minor, but also a purely UK example with a UK regulator (Ofwat) for a non-UK audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Update the figure or swap to a regional regulated utility (e.g. CLP Power in Hong Kong under the Scheme of Control, SP Group in Singapore).

accuracyIssues.issue: Teaches first-, second- and third-degree discrimination. The IAL spec requires third-degree only; the extra taxonomy adds load without exam payoff (not wrong, just off-spec weight).
accuracyIssues.fix: Keep third-degree as the main content; mention the other degrees in one sentence as 'not required for IAL'.

quizIssues.question: The shutdown point in the short run occurs where:
quizIssues.issue: Tests the short-run shutdown point, which is not taught anywhere in content[] of this section (only in notes[1]); it belongs to the revenue-costs-profits section. Because the pre-test samples 3 random MCQs from this bank, students can be pre-tested on untaught material. Answer/explanation are correct.

quizIssues.question: A natural monopoly is characterised by:
quizIssues.issue: Natural monopoly is never taught in content[] (appears only in practice[2] guidance and common_mistakes). Correct answer and explanation are fine, but the item is untaught in Learn Mode.

quizIssues.question: A monopsony buyer will tend to:
quizIssues.issue: Monopsony is entirely absent from content[], notes[] and flashcards for this section, yet is an IAL spec bullet and a pre-test candidate. Explanation also mislabels: it says 'MCL' (marginal cost of labour) and 'marginal benefit' although the question is about a generic input buyer — should be 'marginal cost of the input (MC of purchasing) = MRP'.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is an example of a strategic (artificial) barrier to entry?
quizIssues.issue: The structural-vs-strategic barrier taxonomy and limit pricing are never taught in content[]. Distractor 'High natural resource requirements' is oddly worded (reads as a paraphrase of economies of scale rather than a distinct barrier).

quizIssues.question: Which market structure is most likely to achieve dynamic efficiency?
quizIssues.issue: Correct option combines two structures ('Monopoly or oligopoly — because ...') and is the only compound option, a tell. Option D (contestable market forces innovation) is a defensible answer in the evaluation literature, so the item rewards recall of the section's line rather than economics. Low-quality item rather than wrong.

quizIssues.question: Allocative efficiency is achieved when:
quizIssues.issue: Placed (via fallback) as the inline MCQ on step 0, before allocative efficiency is defined anywhere in the flow — efficiency definitions only appear in the final subsection. Item itself is correct.

practiceIssues.issue: 20-mark 'Evaluate the usefulness of game theory' guidance awards marks for 'game theory explains real-world phenomena such as price rigidity — the kinked demand curve model' — the kinked demand curve is NOT a game-theory model, and common_mistakes[2] in this very section warns students not to conflate them. The model answer commits the section's own listed mistake. Also point-based (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) whereas IAL 20-markers are levels-marked (KAA + evaluation levels); no indication of the KAA/evaluation split.

'Define the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market. (4 marks)' — 'Define' is not used with 4 marks in IAL and one does not 'define characteristics'. IAL would phrase this as 'Explain two characteristics ... (4)' or as a Section A MCQ-plus-explanation (4). Guidance is fine content-wise.

'Outline two characteristics of a contestable market. (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word. Guidance's 'Characteristic 2: the threat of hit-and-run competition disciplines incumbents' is a consequence, not a characteristic; the second characteristic should be low/zero sunk costs or equal access to technology/information for entrants (guidance buries sunk costs inside characteristic 1).

'Explain two conditions ... (6 marks)' — IAL uses 'Explain' at 4 marks and 'Analyse' at 6/8; 6-mark 'Explain' is a mismatch. Guidance merges 'separate markets' and 'prevent arbitrage' into one condition while the section teaches three, and awards a mark for 'monopolies and oligopolies are therefore where PD is most common', which is not a condition.

'Assess whether monopoly is always less efficient than perfect competition. (10 marks)' — command/marks correct for IAL. Guidance is point-scored (2+2+2+2+1+1) but IAL 10-mark Assess is levels-marked (KAA 6 / Eval 4); no diagram is required or credited even though the comparison is diagram-driven. Also introduces X-inefficiency and natural monopoly, neither taught in content[].

Set-level: no question requires a diagram, no question has a data/extract stimulus, and the IAL Section A format (MCQ + 3-mark explanation) is absent — for the most diagram-heavy topic in Unit 3 this misses the main skill IAL papers test. Also, via the no-index fallback, sortedPractice places 'Outline contestable market' on the Oligopoly step and 'Assess monopoly' on the Contestable step, and the 20-mark essay is never shown in Learn Mode.

structureIssues: Zero recall widgets (meta.reorder = 0, meta.fillin = 0; no section has a 'recall' key). Learn Mode's spaced/immediate retrieval layer renders nothing for this section — the flow is read → one MCQ → one practice per block. The flows (e.g. perfect-competition 'supernormal profit → entry → supply up → price falls → normal profit', game-theory 'cartel → temptation → cheat → collapse') are genuine causal sequences that would make good reorder exercises.

No block has diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:114-118 uses the legacy fallback. matchDiagramsToBlocks (components/learn-mode/utils.js:31) title-matches: diagrams[0] PC short-run → block 0, diagrams[2] Monopoly → block 2, diagrams[4] Kinked → block 1; diagrams[1] 'Perfect Competition — Long-Run Equilibrium' and diagrams[3] 'Monopolistic Competition — Long-Run Equilibrium' find no unused block and are NEVER shown in Learn Mode — even though perfect-competition.examMatters ('practise showing the shift from short-run supernormal profit to long-run normal profit') and monopolistic-competition.examMatters ('the key diagram skill is drawing the long-run tangency') name those exact diagrams. Block 3 (Contestable Markets) gets no diagram.

Quiz fallback (distributeItems, utils.js:12-13): 12 items ≥ 4 steps so quiz[0..3] land on steps 0..3: step 1 (Oligopoly) shows 'In the long run in perfect competition...', step 2 (Monopoly) shows 'shutdown point', step 3 (Contestable) shows the monopolistic-competition excess-capacity item. The kinked-demand (4), price-discrimination (5), Nash (7) and contestability (8) MCQs — the ones that match blocks 1–3 — never appear inline.

Practice fallback: sortedPractice by marks = [Define PC 4, Outline contestable 4, Explain PD 6, Assess monopoly 10, Evaluate game theory 20]; steps 0–3 get items 0–3, so the Oligopoly step gets the contestable-markets question, the Contestable step gets the monopoly Assess, and the 20-mark game-theory essay (the only one matching block 1) is never surfaced. getPracticeMode then makes the mismatched Oligopoly item the 'guided' one.

Sequencing: allocative/productive/dynamic efficiency are used from perfect-competition (step 0) onward but only defined in evaluating-market-structures (step 3, last subsection). IAL orders Efficiency (3.3.1) before the structures. The 'Spectrum of Market Structures' overview exists in notes[0] but not in content[], so Learn Mode opens cold on perfect competition with no map of the four structures.

Pre-test gate: 3 random MCQs from a 12-item bank in which 4 items (shutdown point, natural monopoly, monopsony, barrier types) test material absent from content[]; P(at least one untaught item) = 1 − C(8,3)/C(12,3) ≈ 75%. This directly feeds the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis for this section.

Pairing coherence is otherwise fine: (PC, mon comp), (kinked, game theory), (monopoly, PD), (contestability, efficiency evaluation). Block 3 takeaway[2] ('statically inefficient but dynamically efficient') previews block 4's content rather than summarising block 3 — minor. Difficulty ramp is sensible; monopoly-before-oligopoly would be the more conventional order but the current one works.

Misconceptions are genuine student errors (normal ≠ zero profit; monopolistic competition ≠ monopoly; oligopoly ≠ always high prices; collusion ≠ always succeeds; PD ≠ always harmful; contestable ≠ merely low entry barriers). 'monopolies always bad' (monopoly-equilibrium-welfare) and 'PC always ideal' (evaluating-market-structures) overlap and could be differentiated (e.g. replace the latter with 'students draw monopoly price from the MR curve').

Real examples are 100% UK (wheat aside): Tesco/Sainsbury's/Asda/Morrisons, Thames Water/Ofwat, Avanti West Coast, CMA, Ryanair/easyJet. For the stated audience (HK, Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Middle East) none of these are recognisable; IAL examiners accept any country's examples.
ialSpecGaps: Monopsony (IAL 3.3 'Monopsony'): characteristics; costs and benefits to firms, consumers, employees and suppliers — entirely absent from content[], notes[] and flashcards, though quiz[9] tests it.
Natural monopoly (under Monopoly): continuously falling LRAC, MES vs market size, why competition is wasteful — absent from content[] (only in quiz[6] and practice[2] guidance).
Efficiency (IAL 3.3 'Efficiency'): X-inefficiency is never defined or taught; efficiency definitions only appear in the last subsection rather than framing the section.
Oligopoly: calculation and interpretation of n-firm concentration ratios — absent from content[] (defined once in notes[3]).
Oligopoly: types of price competition — price wars, predatory pricing, limit pricing — absent (limit pricing appears only as quiz[10]'s answer).
Oligopoly: non-price competition (advertising, branding, loyalty schemes, quality) and reasons firms prefer it — absent (one 'link' line in notes[2]).
Oligopoly: overt vs tacit collusion and the factors making collusion more/less likely (number of firms, similar costs, stable demand, detection/enforcement) — only lightly touched.
Monopoly: costs and benefits of monopoly to firms, employees and suppliers (spec asks for all stakeholder groups) — only consumers/society covered.
Monopoly: third-degree price discrimination diagram and explicit costs/benefits to producers AND consumers — evaluation is present, diagram is absent.
Contestability: types of barriers to entry and exit (legal, sunk costs, economies of scale, brand loyalty, predatory behaviour) — no taxonomy of barriers taught anywhere in content[].

Perfect competition: short-run loss-making equilibrium and shutdown decision (P ≥ AVC) — not in content[] (may belong to the revenue-costs-profits section; unsure of IAL placement, but quiz[2] tests it here).

Unsure: the kinked demand curve is given a full subsection and diagram, but I do not recall it as an explicit IAL oligopoly bullet (the explicit bullets are concentration ratios, collusive/non-collusive behaviour, game theory, price and non-price competition). Worth verifying against the WEC13 spec before keeping it at this weight.

Unsure: app numbering '3.3.3' does not correspond to IAL spec numbering, where Market structures and contestability is its own topic heading with ~7 sub-bullets (Efficiency, Perfect competition, Monopolistic competition, Oligopoly, Monopoly, Monopsony, Contestability); the app's 3.3.1/3.3.2 are Business growth and Revenues/costs.
strengths: Definitions and mechanisms in keyIdea/body are accurate and use mark-scheme phrasing: price taker AR=MR=P; long-run PC at P=MC and min ATC; monopolistic competition tangency left of min ATC with excess capacity; MR<AR because price falls on all units; MC=MR then price from AR; three PD conditions; sunk (not fixed) costs as the contestability criterion; hit-and-run entry.

Every 'flow' block is a genuine causal chain (entry → supply → price → normal profit; cartel → cheat → collapse; MC=MR → price from AR → P>MC → DWL) — ideal raw material for reorder recalls if the section ever gets them.

Misconceptions are real ones teachers see (normal vs zero profit; 'monopolistic' ≠ monopoly; kinked demand explains stickiness not price setting in notes[3]; collusion always succeeds; PD always harmful), each with an 'Instead write' line that models exam wording.

Evaluation is built in rather than bolted on: static vs dynamic efficiency trade-off, PD can raise output, monopoly may be dynamically efficient, contestability shifts focus from structure to behaviour — these are the exact evaluation lines IAL 10/12/20-mark schemes reward.

Diagram checklists (diagrams[i].checklist) are well written and exam-oriented ('Price Pm read from the AR curve (not the MR curve)', 'MC and MC' both pass through the MR gap'); the kinked-demand SVG is geometrically correct (MC and MC' both inside the gap).

Practice command/mark pairs for the two big questions (Assess 10, Evaluate 20) match IAL, and the 10-mark model answer includes the right evaluation moves (natural monopoly, Schumpeter, X-inefficiency, judgement).
Quiz distractors are generally plausible and explanations teach the 'why' (e.g. quiz[0] explanation distinguishes allocative, productive, normal profit and MR=0).
topFixes: Add diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices to all four blocks so Learn Mode stops using the legacy fallback: block0 → diagrams 'Perfect Competition — Long-Run' (and/or short-run) + quiz [1,3] + practice [0]; block1 → 'Kinked Demand' + quiz [4,7] + practice [3]; block2 → 'Monopoly' + quiz [5] + practice [1,2]; block3 → quiz [8] + practice [4]. This fixes the mismatched inline MCQs/practice and surfaces the two long-run diagrams and the 20-mark essay.

Fix the three broken diagram SVGs: redraw PC long-run and monopolistic-competition long-run so AR is genuinely tangent to a clean U-shaped AC (currently AR sits above AC and Qeff is not at min AC), and recompute the monopoly diagram's MR=MC, Pm, Qc and DWL polygon from actual curve intersections. Add a third-degree PD two-market diagram that examMatters already promises.

Close the spec gaps that the quiz already tests: add subsections (or a fifth block) for Monopsony (characteristics, stakeholder costs/benefits), Natural monopoly, X-inefficiency (moved to a short 'Efficiency' opener before perfect competition), barrier-to-entry types, and n-firm concentration ratios; then either remove quiz[2] (shutdown) or teach it. This alone removes the ~75% chance the pre-test contains untaught items.

Add recall exercises (currently zero): reorder recalls from the existing flows (perfect-competition entry chain; game-theory cartel-collapse chain; monopoly MC=MR→AR→DWL chain; contestability hit-and-run chain) and fillin recalls for the three PD conditions and the PC/mon-comp long-run conditions.

Correct the factual/exam-format errors: Ryanair/easyJet 'lease rather than buy' (wrong — use IndiGo/AirAsia or drop), '25-mark essays' → 20-mark IAL Section C, Nigeria as OPEC over-producer → Iraq/Kazakhstan, Morrisons in the 'big four' → Aldi (2022), soften 'zero dynamic efficiency' in PC; remove the kinked-demand-as-game-theory point from practice[3]'s model answer; and swap at least half the UK examples for HK/SE-Asia/Middle-East equivalents.

summary: The prose is mostly accurate and the monopsony / NMW / bilateral-monopoly material is explained at a level a strong IAL teacher would accept; the MCQ bank is sound (all 10 correctIndex values verified correct). But the section as delivered in Learn Mode is hobbled: no block carries diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, so the legacy fallback drops the monopsony diagram entirely, surfaces only quiz[0..2] (including an untaught elasticity question), and shows the trade-union practice question one step before unions are taught. There are zero recall widgets across six subsections, one keyIdea contradicts the spec (wage differentials are 'not' market failure), the monopsony SVGs have geometry errors (Wm not on the supply curve, Qmin on neither curve), and two practice questions use command-word/mark pairings that do not exist in IAL Economics. Fixable, but a teacher would not put it in front of students in its current Learn Mode form without the routing and diagram fixes.

accuracyIssues.location: content[2] 'Trade Unions and Wage Differentials' > wage-differentials > keyIdea
accuracyIssues.issue: States wages differ 'not because markets are failing'. The IAL spec explicitly lists geographical and occupational immobility as market failure in labour markets, and the same section's own body calls discrimination 'unjustified' and immobility a 'friction' that stops differentials being competed away. A student who writes 'wage differentials are not a market failure' in an exam loses the evaluation.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite keyIdea: 'Wages differ because of compensating differentials, human capital and barriers to entry (efficient reasons) AND because of discrimination and labour immobility (labour-market failures that stop differentials being competed away).'

accuracyIssues.issue: Geometry is wrong: the Wm marker is drawn at y=215 but the supply line passes x=230 at y≈193, so the 'wage read off the supply curve' is ~22px below the supply curve, exaggerating the exploitation gap. Qc is marked at x=280 while S=MRP actually intersect at x≈263. A student copying the construction learns to drop below S rather than onto it.
accuracyIssues.fix: Place the Wm point on S at (230,193) and Qc/Wc at the true S=MRP intersection (~263,171); regenerate the exploitation bracket accordingly.

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[1] 'Monopsony Labour Market' > scenarios[1] 'Minimum Wage in Monopsony' (svg comment + Qmin marker)
accuracyIssues.issue: SVG comment says new employment is 'where Wmin = MRP on demand curve'. For a minimum wage set below Wc (which is what the label says), employment is at the kink where the horizontal Wmin section meets the original supply curve (x≈242), not where Wmin meets MRP (x≈287). The Qmin marker is at x=268, which lies on neither curve. Direction of the arrows (↑W, ↑Q) is still correct.
accuracyIssues.fix: Redraw with Qmin at the kink (Wmin ∩ S) and change the note to: 'With Wmin below Wc, the supply curve is horizontal at Wmin up to S; MCL = Wmin along that section, so the firm hires up to the kink — more than Qm.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'creates a horizontal section of the supply curve up to that wage' is muddled — the horizontal section is AT the minimum wage, extending up to the quantity where it meets the original supply curve. The mechanism (MCL = Wmin along the flat section) is the exam point and is not stated.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'The minimum wage makes the supply curve horizontal at Wmin up to the point where it meets the original supply curve. Along that section MCL = Wmin, so the firm no longer has to raise everyone's pay to hire one more worker and expands employment.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] 'Demand and Supply of Labour' > demand-for-labour-mrp > body[2] and flow step 4
accuracyIssues.issue: 'MRP shifts right and more workers are hired at a higher wage' conflates firm and market. A firm in a competitive labour market is a wage-taker: a rightward shift of its MRP raises its employment at the given wage; the wage only rises when the MARKET demand curve shifts. The section never distinguishes firm (horizontal supply, W = MRP) from industry.
accuracyIssues.fix: Split: 'For the individual firm (wage-taker) a rightward MRP shift means more workers hired at the going wage; if MRP rises across all firms, market demand shifts right and the market wage rises.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'The backward-bending supply curve is a favourite diagram question' overclaims. The IAL WEC13 labour market content is framed around the supply of labour to an occupation/market (upward-sloping); the individual backward-bending curve is not a listed spec diagram (unsure of exact wording, but it is not in the spec bullets I know). The Notes tab for the same subsection says the opposite: 'Most exam questions focus on the market supply curve'. Risk: students draw a backward-bending curve for a market supply question.
accuracyIssues.fix: Align with the Notes tab: 'Market supply to an occupation slopes upward — draw this for wage-determination questions. The backward-bending individual curve is a supporting concept for explaining incentives/income vs substitution effects, not the default diagram.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'the union can raise wages with little or no job loss' understates the standard result: against a monopsonist, a union wage set up to the competitive wage RAISES employment (same mechanism as the NMW paragraph in monopsony-power). Stopping at 'no job loss' loses the strongest evaluation point.
accuracyIssues.fix: '…a union wage set between Wm and Wc raises both wages and employment, exactly like a minimum wage in monopsony; only if the union pushes above Wc does employment fall.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Determinants of the ELASTICITY of demand for labour (share of labour in total cost, substitutability with capital, PED of the product, time) are never taught anywhere in content, yet quiz[2] tests them and the trade-unions section relies on 'elasticity of demand for labour' to size the employment loss.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add a short paragraph or bullets block on determinants of wage elasticity of demand (and of supply) for labour to demand-for-labour-mrp or competitive-labour-markets.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'exploitation that a minimum wage can actually fix' — a NMW only removes exploitation if set at Wc; between Wm and Wc it reduces it. Minor overstatement.
accuracyIssues.fix: '…exploitation that a minimum wage set between Wm and Wc can reduce (and remove if set at the competitive wage).'

accuracyIssues.location: All six realExample entries (AI engineers/Google-OpenAI, NHS junior doctors, EU 2004 UK construction, NHS nurses, RMT 2022-23, City of London)
accuracyIssues.issue: All examples are UK/US. They are factually sound (2004 A8 accession, RMT strikes 2022-23 with Network Rail and TOCs, NHS monopsony over nurses, AI engineer pay >$200k) but none speak to HK/SG/MY/PK/Gulf students who sit IAL. Not an error; an audience mismatch.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap at least two: e.g. Singapore/HK foreign domestic worker market (monopsony-like MOM quotas), Gulf kafala construction labour supply, Malaysia's 2022 NMW rise, Korean surgeon vs nurse differentials.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is most likely to make the demand for labour wage inelastic?
quizIssues.issue: Correct (index 2) and distractors are fine, but the determinants of elasticity of demand for labour are not taught in any content[] subsection. Because no block has quizIndices, the legacy fallback (components/learn-mode/utils.js distributeItems) shows quiz[0], quiz[1], quiz[2] at steps 0/1/2, so this untaught question is the inline MCQ on the Trade Unions & Wage Differentials step.

quizIssues.question: A profit-maximising firm in a competitive labour market will hire workers up to the point where:
quizIssues.issue: Under the fallback this MCQ lands on step 1 (Wage Determination / monopsony), not step 0 where MRP = W is taught. Distractor 'Total Revenue Product (TRP) equals total cost' is not a real IAL term — a made-up option rather than a plausible misconception (better: 'MPP equals the wage rate' or 'ARP equals the wage rate').

quizIssues.question: A national minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage will:
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer and explanation are good, but two distractors use 'Definitely' — test-wise students eliminate absolutes without knowing the economics. Never surfaces in Learn Mode (fallback stops at quiz[2]).

quizIssues.question: Which of the following would shift the supply of labour to the right in a particular occupation?
quizIssues.issue: Stem says 'a particular occupation' but distractors 'increase in income tax rates' and 'increase in welfare benefits' are economy-wide effects, and income tax is ambiguous (income vs substitution effect). Still unambiguous which option is correct; wording slightly off-target.

quizIssues.question: In a monopsony labour market, compared to a competitive market, the employer pays:
quizIssues.issue: No error. Note only: this and quiz[6] are the section's key MCQs and neither is reachable inline in Learn Mode because blocks lack quizIndices.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define … (4 marks)': in IAL Economics 'Define' is a 2-mark command word; 4-mark parts are 'Explain…'. Guidance pads a definition into 4 point-marks including an example, which does not reflect how a define question is marked.

'Outline two ways … (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word. Guidance cites 'closed shops' — outlawed in the UK since 1990 and irrelevant to international contexts; use 'restricting entry via professional accreditation' or industrial action instead. Also, via the marks-sorted fallback this question is shown on step 1 (Wage Determination), before trade unions are taught on step 2.

20-mark Evaluate: guidance mark tallies sum to 18 (2+3+2+2+2+2+2+1+2), not 20; it is written as point-marking whereas IAL 20-markers are level-marked (KAA 12 / Evaluation 8) with a supported judgement; and it never tells the student to draw the monopsony diagram, which is essential for KAA at Level 3-4 on this question. Never surfaces in Learn Mode (fallback shows only the three lowest-mark questions).

10-mark Assess: guidance is point-marked (2+2+2+2+1+1) rather than KAA 6 / Eval 4 levels; no diagram instruction; the question premise ('usefulness of MRP theory in explaining wage determination') is a reasonable UK-style essay, but MRP theory's explicit place in WEC13 is unsure — a more spec-central 10-marker would be 'Assess the likely effects of a national minimum wage on a labour market' with a diagram. Never surfaces in Learn Mode.
'Explain two factors … (6 marks)' is plausible. Minor: IAL Unit 3 'Explain' parts are commonly 4 marks and 6/8-markers are 'Analyse'; no diagram or data reference expected here, which is fine.

structureIssues: No block has diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:86 takes the legacy fallback. matchDiagramsToBlocks (utils.js:31) scores by title-word overlap: 'Competitive Labour Market Equilibrium' matches block 0 ('Demand and Supply of Labour') on 'labour' and consumes it; 'Monopsony Labour Market' then scores 0 against 'Wage Determination' and 'Trade Unions and Wage Differentials' and is NEVER shown. The single most examined diagram in the section is invisible in Learn Mode.

distributeItems fallback assigns quiz[0], quiz[1], quiz[2] to steps 0/1/2: step 1 (monopsony) gets the MRP = W question, step 2 (unions/differentials) gets the untaught elasticity question. quiz[5..9] (monopsony, NMW, differentials, immobility) never appear inline.

Practice fallback sorts by marks then takes the first three: step 0 = Define derived demand (worked), step 1 = Outline trade unions (guided) — shown BEFORE trade unions are taught in step 2 — and step 2 = Explain wage differentials. The Assess (10) and Evaluate (20) questions never reach Learn Mode.

Zero recall objects across all six subsections: the spaced/immediate recall mechanism has nothing to show, so the only retrieval in the whole section is three inline MCQs. This section has several genuinely orderable chains that should be recalls (monopsony construction; NMW-in-monopsony mechanism; derived-demand chain; union wage above equilibrium → move up MRP → lower employment).

Block 2 pairing is incoherent: 'Trade Unions' is the bilateral-monopoly counterpart to monopsony and belongs with block 1; 'Wage Differentials' belongs with supply-side immobility. Suggested: Block 1 = competitive market + NMW in a competitive market; Block 2 = monopsony + trade unions/bilateral monopoly; Block 3 = wage differentials + immobility + government policy.

Firm vs market never distinguished: no subsection shows the perfectly competitive firm facing a horizontal labour supply (W = ACL = MCL) hiring where W = MRP, so the jump to 'MCL above supply' in monopsony has no baseline diagram to contrast against.

NMW in a COMPETITIVE labour market (wage floor → excess supply → unemployment) is never taught, yet monopsony-power > misconception refers to 'the standard unemployment prediction' as if it had been, and flashcard 'What is the national minimum wage' states it. The student meets the exception before the rule.

trade-unions > body flow is a list of three parallel cases (competitive / monopsony / bilateral monopoly), not a causal chain — misuse of the flow type; would confuse a reorder recall if one were later generated from it.

demand-for-labour-mrp > misconception ('firms hire workers because they need them') is filler. Real student errors here: confusing a movement along MRP (wage change) with a shift (product demand / productivity); writing MRP = MPP × price when the product market is imperfectly competitive; treating diminishing returns as workers being 'worse'.

supply-of-labour > examMatters directly contradicts the Notes-tab examMatters for the same subsection (backward-bending 'favourite diagram' vs 'most questions focus on the market supply curve'). Students switching tabs see opposite advice.
Difficulty ramp is otherwise sensible (demand/supply → competitive → monopsony → unions → differentials) and each block's takeaway list faithfully summarises its two subsections.
ialSpecGaps: Elasticity of demand for labour and its determinants (labour share of cost, substitutability, PED of product, time) — not taught; tested in quiz[2].
Elasticity of supply of labour and its determinants (training period, qualifications, mobility, time) — not taught beyond one sentence.
National minimum wage in a competitive labour market (wage floor, excess supply, unemployment diagram) — only the monopsony case is covered.

Government intervention to reduce labour market failure: maximum wages, public-sector wage setting, policies to tackle geographical/occupational immobility (housing, retraining, relocation grants) — only appears in quiz[9].

Current labour market issues listed in WEC13 3.4.3 (from my recollection of the spec — treat as 'probable'): skills shortages, ageing population/retirement age, young workers, flexible/temporary/zero-hours working, migration — only migration is touched, via one flow and one misconception.
Diagram for the individual firm in a perfectly competitive labour market (horizontal supply to the firm, W = MRP) versus the industry — not taught.
Discrimination as a labour-market failure — one sentence only; no analysis of how it distorts demand for labour.

Unsure: whether WEC13 explicitly requires MRP = MPP × MR theory (the 2018 spec wording I recall is 'demand for labour as derived demand' plus factors influencing demand). Content leans heavily on MRP; not wrong, but examMatters 'Examiners expect you to draw the MRP curve' may overclaim.

Section numbering: the app labels this 3.3.4; in the WEC13 spec I recall the labour market as topic 3.4 (3.4.1 demand, 3.4.2 supply, 3.4.3 wage determination). Unsure — flag for verification against the current spec PDF.
strengths: Monopsony explained with the correct hiring rule (MCL = MRP, wage from S), correct reason MCL lies above S, and the NMW-in-monopsony result stated correctly — the key evaluation point on this topic.
Bilateral monopoly / indeterminate wage is taught, which is genuinely top-band evaluation for IAL.
Misconceptions in monopsony-power, trade-unions, competitive-labour-markets (immigration) and supply-of-labour are real student errors with usable 'instead write' phrasing.
All 10 quiz correctIndex values verified correct; explanations are accurate and teach the reasoning, not just the answer.

Competitive-market SVGs (diagrams[0], both scenarios) are geometrically correct with equilibria at true intersections, and every diagram uses the correct IAL axis labels (Wage Rate / Quantity of Labour).
Real examples are factually true (2004 EU enlargement and UK construction, RMT 2022-23, NHS nurse monopsony, AI engineer pay).
Practice guidance for the 10- and 20-mark questions contains genuine two-sided argument and a judgement, not one-sided lists.
topFixes: Add diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices to all three blocks (block 0: 'Competitive Labour Market', quiz [0,1], practice [0]; block 1: 'Monopsony', quiz [5,6], practice [3]; block 2: 'Wage Differentials', quiz [7,8,9], practice [1,4]) so the monopsony diagram actually renders and inline MCQs/practice match what was just taught.

Write recalls for all six subsections — reorder for the monopsony construction (faces whole market supply → must raise wage for all → MCL above S → hire where MCL = MRP → pay wage from S), reorder for NMW-in-monopsony, fillin for 'MRP = MPP × MR; hire until MRP = W', fillin for bilateral monopoly/indeterminate wage.

Fix wage-differentials keyIdea ('not because markets are failing') and add a short NMW-in-competitive-market paragraph plus determinants of elasticity of demand/supply for labour, so the misconceptions and quiz[2] rest on taught content.
Repair the two monopsony SVGs: put Wm on the supply curve, Qc at the true S=MRP intersection, Qmin at the Wmin ∩ S kink, and correct the 'Wmin = MRP' construction note.

Bring practice in line with IAL command words and marking: Define → 2 marks (or 'Explain', 4); drop 'Outline'; make the 20-mark guidance total 20, structure as KAA/Evaluation levels, and require the monopsony diagram.

summary: The prose is genuinely good: definitions are exam-usable, every subsection has a mechanism-led keyIdea, a real example, a misconception and an 'it depends on' evaluation frame, and the takeaways match their blocks. But a strong IAL teacher would not ship it as-is. The section has zero recall exercises (so Learn Mode's retrieval loop is empty), no block carries diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, and the entire Trade Blocs block (types of bloc, trade creation/diversion) has no quiz MCQ, no practice question and no diagram, even though its own examMatters tells students to 'show trade creation and diversion on a diagram'. There are content errors a teacher would catch (Brexit example says the UK 'lost tariff-free access to EU markets'; trade diversion is attributed solely to the CET; 'common market' never appears; MNC in notes vs TNC in every quiz/practice item), one diagram has overlapping boxes, and the indicators chart presents invented index values on a numeric axis. Quiz distractors are mostly 'the opposite of the truth', so the 10 MCQs are far easier than IAL Section A.

accuracyIssues.issue: States 'After Brexit, the UK lost tariff-free access to EU markets'. Wrong: the UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (in force 1 Jan 2021) keeps zero tariffs and zero quotas on goods meeting rules of origin. What the UK lost was frictionless access (customs declarations, rules-of-origin checks, SPS and regulatory non-tariff barriers). The 'trade diversion in reverse' framing is also muddled and not a term a marker will recognise.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'After Brexit the UK left the EU customs union and single market. Goods still trade tariff-free under the 2021 TCA, but new customs, rules-of-origin and regulatory checks raised trade costs, and UK-EU goods trade fell relative to trend. This shows that a bloc's gains come from removing non-tariff as well as tariff barriers.' Or replace with a clean trade-diversion example (e.g. EU CET on agricultural imports diverting sourcing to higher-cost EU producers).

accuracyIssues.location: Trade Blocs > trade-creation-diversion > body[1] and flow steps
accuracyIssues.issue: Trade diversion is defined as occurring 'when the common external tariff (CET) forces a country to switch imports from the cheapest global supplier'. The mechanism is the preferential removal of tariffs between members (so a higher-cost member becomes tariff-free while the lower-cost outsider still faces the pre-existing tariff). Diversion happens in free trade areas without any CET. The flow ('Countries form customs union > CET applied to non-members (diversion)') hard-wires this misconception.
accuracyIssues.fix: Define: 'Trade diversion occurs when removing tariffs between members causes a country to switch from a lower-cost non-member supplier (which still faces the external tariff) to a higher-cost member supplier.' Note that a CET affects the size of diversion, not whether it can occur.

accuracyIssues.issue: Tells students to 'Show trade creation and diversion on a diagram', but the section contains no such diagram (the 3 diagrams are an indicators line chart, an FDI flow chart and a costs/benefits balance). Students are told to do something the section never teaches.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either add a standard trade creation/diversion diagram (price/quantity, domestic S and D, world supply at Pw, world+tariff at Pw+t, partner supply at Pp between them, with creation and diversion areas labelled) or remove the diagram instruction and replace with a textual analysis chain.

accuracyIssues.issue: Uses only 'single market' for the third level of integration. The Edexcel IAL spec and mark schemes use 'common market' (free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary/economic union). 'Common market' appears nowhere in the section. 'Economic union' is also omitted.
accuracyIssues.fix: Write 'A common market (also called a single market, e.g. the EU single market) adds free movement of factors of production...' and mention economic union as CU + common market + coordinated fiscal/monetary policy.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'less national sovereignty over trade, fiscal, and monetary policy' overstates: a monetary union removes independent monetary policy and a customs union removes independent trade policy, but fiscal policy is only constrained (e.g. Eurozone Stability and Growth Pact), not surrendered.
accuracyIssues.fix: '...less sovereignty: trade policy in a customs union, monetary policy in a monetary union, and constraints on fiscal policy in a full economic union.'

accuracyIssues.issue: 'more likely when ... the bloc is large and diverse' is imprecise. Standard analysis (Viner): creation dominates when pre-union tariffs were high, the CET is low, the bloc is large, and members' economies are competitive/overlapping (so cheaper members can replace higher-cost domestic producers). 'Diverse' (complementary) economies tend to produce less creation.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace 'large and diverse' with 'large and made up of economies that produce similar goods, so cheaper members can replace inefficient domestic producers'.

accuracyIssues.location: Multinational Corporations > both subsections; quiz[3..8]; practice[1,2,4]
accuracyIssues.issue: Content body defines and uses 'multinational corporation (MNC)' throughout; every quiz item and practice question uses 'transnational corporation (TNC)' with no bridge sentence. IAL papers use TNC. A student reading the notes then the quiz meets an undefined acronym.
accuracyIssues.fix: In why-mncs-invest-abroad body[0] write 'A transnational corporation (TNC), also called a multinational corporation (MNC), ...' and use TNC consistently in keyIdea/takeaways to match the exam.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'The World Bank estimates that globalisation helped lift over one billion people out of extreme poverty between 1990 and 2015.' The World Bank reports the fall in extreme poverty (about 1.9bn to about 0.74bn, roughly 1.1bn fewer); it does not attribute that to globalisation. Presenting the causal attribution as a World Bank estimate is misleading.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'World Bank data show the number in extreme poverty fell by over one billion between 1990 and 2015, much of it in export-led economies such as China and India.'

accuracyIssues.issue: Layout bug: the 'Reasons for FDI' column occupies x=10-140, y=100-257, while the 'Positive (+)' impact boxes occupy x=60-230, y=153-273. They overlap in the region x=60-140, y=153-257, so four reason labels and four positive-impact labels render on top of each other and the diagram is unreadable.
accuracyIssues.fix: Move the Positive/Negative impact columns below the reasons column (e.g. reasons y=100-260, impacts y=280+ with the canvas taller) or put reasons across the top row and impacts in two columns underneath.

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[0] 'Indicators of Globalisation Over Time' (svg + checklist)
accuracyIssues.issue: The chart has a numeric y-axis ('Index (1980 = 100)', gridlines at 100-500) but the plotted values are invented: trade/GDP ends at roughly index 340 (real world trade/GDP went from about 38% to about 55-60%, i.e. index about 150) and FDI flows end at roughly 480 (real global FDI inflows grew from about $54bn to about $1tn, index well over 1000). Presenting made-up numbers on labelled axes invites students to quote them. Also not a diagram an IAL student would draw, yet it carries a 'draw it' checklist.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either use real indexed series (World Bank/UNCTAD) with a source line, or remove the numeric gridlines and label it 'illustrative trend'. Drop or rewrite the checklist as a 'what the data show' list.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'over 3,000 direct jobs' at Toyota Burnaston: Toyota Manufacturing UK's roughly 3,000 headcount covers Burnaston plus the Deeside engine plant; Burnaston alone is roughly 2,500. Minor, and a UK developed-country host example sits oddly in a subsection whose keyIdea and practice questions are about developing host countries.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'around 3,000 jobs across its Burnaston and Deeside plants', or swap for a developing-country host example (e.g. Samsung in Vietnam, roughly a fifth of Vietnam's exports) that matches the exam framing.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'containerisation cut shipping costs by over 90%' is a frequently repeated but unsourced figure; the well-documented claim is a very large fall in port handling costs and ocean freight rates since the 1950s.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'containerisation cut the cost of moving goods by sea dramatically (port handling costs fell by well over 90%)' or drop the number.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a key characteristic of globalisation?
quizIssues.issue: All three distractors are simply the opposite of the truth ('decrease', 'decrease', 'reduced'), so the item is answerable without knowing anything. Also tests 'characteristics/indicators' (trade/GDP, FDI, migration) which the content body never teaches (only diagram 0 does).

quizIssues.question: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) has contributed to globalisation primarily by:
quizIssues.issue: Distractors A, C ('protectionist') and D ('single global currency') are implausible; no near-miss such as 'setting a common external tariff' or 'providing loans to developing countries' (IMF/World Bank confusion, the real student error).

quizIssues.question: A transnational corporation (TNC) is most likely to undertake foreign direct investment (FDI) in a developing country in order to:
quizIssues.issue: Uses 'TNC' which the notes never define (notes say MNC). Distractors A, C, D are nonsensical for the stem; an IAL-standard distractor would be e.g. 'to benefit from a stronger host-country currency' or 'to increase the home country's exports'.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a positive impact of FDI on a recipient developing country?
quizIssues.issue: Option C 'race to the bottom' and option D 'dependency on volatile foreign capital inflows' use terms not taught in the content body ('race to the bottom' appears only in extras and diagram 2; 'volatile capital inflows' nowhere).

quizIssues.question: One benefit of globalisation for consumers in developed countries is:
quizIssues.issue: Correct option C is by far the longest and the only one with an economic mechanism ('lower-cost producers increase competition'); D 'Guaranteed employment security' is absurd. Trivially easy.

quizIssues.question: Globalisation is most likely to increase income inequality within developed countries because:
quizIssues.issue: Options A, C, D are not causal explanations at all ('All workers receive equally higher wages', 'Governments always redistribute', 'TNCs are required to pay the same wages'), so only B is even grammatically a reason. Absolutes ('all', 'always') signal wrong answers.

quizIssues.question: The concept of a 'race to the bottom' in the context of globalisation refers to:
quizIssues.issue: Tests a term that the content body never introduces (only extras[evaluation][2] and diagram 2 mention it). A student who completed Learn Mode has not met it.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is the most valid evaluative point about the overall impact of globalisation?
quizIssues.issue: Answer is the only hedged/balanced option ('depends on country-specific factors'); students learn to pick the 'it depends' option without understanding. Not testable knowledge. Also the section has zero MCQs on the Trade Blocs block (types of bloc, CET, trade creation vs diversion), so any inline quiz shown at the end of that block cannot test it and the pre-test/post-test never sample it.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term globalisation (4 marks)': IAL definition parts are normally 2 marks (or 4 marks as 'explain what is meant by... with reference to the extract'). The guidance awards 1 mark each for four sentences, two of which are causes ('facilitated by reductions in trade barriers...') rather than the definition, which is not how Edexcel marks a definition (2 marks for the definition, remaining marks for application/data).

'Assess the impact of FDI on developing countries (10 marks)': command word and marks fit IAL, but the guidance is point-scored (2+2+2+2+1+1) with only 1 mark for judgement. IAL 10-mark 'Assess' is levels-marked, KAA 6 / Evaluation 4; a student following this guidance under-weights evaluation by a factor of four. No reference to a data extract, whereas real 10-mark Section B questions require application to the extract.

'Evaluate the view that globalisation has been more beneficial than harmful for developing countries (20 marks)': good IAL Section C question, but guidance again point-scores (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) instead of the levels-based KAA 12 / Evaluation 8 structure; it should signal that a Level 4 KAA needs developed chains of reasoning and that evaluation needs a supported judgement, not a tally of 2-mark facts.

'Outline two reasons why TNCs may use transfer pricing (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an Edexcel IAL Economics command word (the paper uses Define, Calculate, Explain, Analyse, Examine, Assess, Discuss, Evaluate, To what extent). Reason 2 (avoiding tariffs/exchange controls) is beyond IAL expectations. Should be 'Explain two reasons... (4)' with tax minimisation and profit repatriation/limits on host-country tax.

'Explain two ways in which TNCs contribute to globalisation (6 marks)': acceptable, but the content body never teaches TNCs as a cause of globalisation (they are framed only as an effect/actor in block 2), so the student has not been taught the answer. Whole set: no question on trade blocs, trade creation/diversion or types of integration (block 3 untested), and no 8-mark 'Examine' item, which IAL Section B always contains.

structureIssues: Zero recall exercises (meta.reorder=0, meta.fillin=0): Learn Mode's 'spaced' top-of-step and 'immediate' bottom-of-step retrieval widgets never appear in this section. Obvious candidates exist: reorder = the integration ladder FTA > customs union > common market > monetary union (genuine sequence); fillin = trade creation/diversion definitions; fillin = the four causes of globalisation.

No block carries diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices, so InlineDiagram/InlineQuiz/InlinePractice cannot be matched to the block being studied; whatever fallback the code uses, block 3 (Trade Blocs) has no quiz MCQ, practice question or diagram anywhere in the section, so its end-of-block widgets are necessarily off-topic.

Trade Blocs block is placed under 'Causes and Effects of Globalisation' (spec 4.1) although the IAL spec puts trading blocs and the WTO under 'Trade and the global economy' (app section 4.3.2, which currently has no trade-bloc block). A student revising by spec point will not find trade blocs where the spec puts them; either move the block or cross-reference it in both places.

Each block has exactly two subsections, so the whole section is 3 steps; a 6-subsection, 3-step section with no recalls is very thin for a topic that carries a 20-mark essay. Blocks 1 and 2 could each gain a third subsection (block 1: characteristics/indicators of globalisation, which quiz[0] and diagram 0 assume; block 2: the type-of-FDI distinction greenfield vs M&A that common_mistakes[1] relies on).

Quiz and extras test vocabulary the content body never introduces: 'race to the bottom' (quiz 4, 8; practice 3 guidance; extras), 'characteristics of globalisation' (quiz 0), 'greenfield vs M&A FDI' (common_mistakes[1]), 'TNC' (all quiz/practice). Learn Mode students hit these cold.

Misconception quality is mixed: types-of-trade-bloc (FTA vs customs union = CET) is the classic real error and is well handled; benefits-costs ('entirely good or entirely bad') and costs-of-mncs ('MNCs are always bad') are the same generic 'be balanced' filler stated twice. The notes[] misconception for the same subsection ('students treat globalisation as entirely new') is a different, better one and is not surfaced in Learn Mode.

Stakeholder framing absent: IAL question stems ask for impact on 'governments', 'producers', 'workers', 'consumers', 'the environment'; the content is organised as benefits vs costs with governments and producers never addressed as stakeholders (diagram 2's 'TNC influence on policy' is the only mention of governments).

Takeaways match their blocks well and the ramp (causes > effects > MNC benefits > MNC costs > bloc types > creation/diversion) is sensible; the 2-per-step pairs are coherent (each pair is a benefit/cost or definition/application couple). This is the section's structural strength.
ialSpecGaps: Characteristics of globalisation (rising trade/GDP, FDI and capital flows, TNC growth, migration, integration of financial markets): not taught in content body; only implied by quiz[0] and diagram 0.

Impact of globalisation on governments (tax competition/'race to the bottom', reduced policy autonomy, tax base erosion) and on producers (access to larger markets, cheaper inputs, global supply chains, competition): spec lists impacts on 'individual countries, governments, producers and consumers, workers and the environment'; governments and producers are not covered as stakeholders.
Growth of TNCs as a factor contributing to globalisation (spec lists TNCs among the causes): TNCs appear only as an effect/actor in block 2; practice[1] asks it but the body never teaches it.
Deindustrialisation in developed economies as an effect (flashcards teach it; content body does not).
'Common market' as the spec term for the third level of integration, and 'economic union' as a level: absent (unsure whether IAL requires economic union explicitly).
Trade creation and trade diversion diagram: examMatters demands it, none provided. Unsure whether the IAL spec requires the diagram, but the concepts sit under spec 4.2 trading blocs, not 4.1.
Brain drain / migration effects on source and host countries: flashcards mention brain drain; content body only mentions migration in a misconception (unsure whether IAL 4.1 or 4.5 expects this).
strengths: Definitions are exam-ready and precise: globalisation (causes-of-globalisation body[0]), FDI/TNC motives, transfer pricing, trade creation (trade-creation-diversion body[0]) and the FTA vs customs union distinction (types-of-trade-bloc misconception) would all earn definition marks.
Every subsection ends with a usable evaluation frame ('depends on domestic institutions / host-country governance / level of CET') that maps directly onto IAL Level 3-4 evaluation.

Real examples are mostly accurate and current: China WTO 2001 and largest exporter within a decade, Bangladesh garments (about 4m workers, over 80% of exports), Starbucks 2012 transfer-pricing backlash, NAFTA to USMCA.
Takeaway cards summarise their own block faithfully and the block ordering has a sensible difficulty ramp from definition to mechanism to evaluation.
All 10 quiz correctIndex values are correct, no item has two defensible answers, and explanations address each distractor.
practice[3] is a genuine IAL Section C 20-mark 'Evaluate the view' question with a for/against/judgement outline and a country example (South Korea).
Diagram 3 (costs vs benefits balance) makes the 'benefits diffuse, costs concentrated' distributional point, which is a high-value evaluation hook examiners reward.
topFixes: Add recall exercises to every subsection (currently zero): a reorder for the integration ladder (FTA > customs union > common market > monetary union), fillins for trade creation vs diversion and for the four causes of globalisation, and a fillin for TNC motives; and set diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices on each block so inline widgets match the block.

Give the Trade Blocs block its own assessment: at least 3 MCQs (FTA vs CU, trade creation vs diversion scenario, effect of a lower CET), one 'Explain'/'Examine' practice question, and either a real trade creation/diversion diagram or delete the 'show it on a diagram' instruction in examMatters.

Fix the content errors: Brexit realExample ('lost tariff-free access' is false; TCA is zero-tariff), define trade diversion by preferential tariff removal rather than 'the CET forces', add the spec term 'common market', and introduce TNC = MNC in block 2 so the quiz/practice vocabulary matches the notes.

Repair diagram 1 (FDI reasons/impacts): the Reasons column and the Positive-impacts column overlap (x 60-140, y 153-257) and render on top of each other; and either source real indexed data for diagram 0 or remove its numeric gridlines.

Rewrite practice guidance in IAL levels form (KAA/Evaluation split, e.g. 6/4 for 10-mark Assess, 12/8 for 20-mark Evaluate), replace 'Outline' with 'Explain', cut 'Define... (4 marks)' to 2 marks, and add an 8-mark 'Examine' item so the set mirrors a Section B ladder.

summary: The four subsections that exist (BoP, exchange rate systems, exchange rate determination, Marshall-Lerner/J-curve) are accurate, well-sequenced within themselves and pitched correctly for IAL, with genuine misconceptions and a properly labelled currency-market diagram. But the section is titled as the whole of IAL topic 4.3 and teaches roughly half of it: there is no content on international competitiveness at all (block 2 is titled "Competitiveness" yet contains none), nothing on measures to correct a current account imbalance, revaluation/devaluation terminology, competitive devaluation, or the growth/inflation/employment/FDI effects of exchange rate changes. As a result 6 of 12 quiz MCQs and 1 of 5 practice questions test material a Learn Mode student has not been taught. There are zero recall widgets and no diagramRef on either block, so the five good diagrams likely never appear in the Learn Mode flow. A strong IAL teacher would use the existing prose but would not consider this a complete 4.3 resource.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] 'Balance of Payments and Exchange Rates' > balance-of-payments > body[0] and keyIdea
accuracyIssues.issue: States the BoP 'has two main components: the current account and the financial account' and keyIdea says 'the current and financial accounts must always sum to zero'. IAL spec 4.3.1(a) and Edexcel mark schemes name three accounts (current, capital, financial) plus net errors and omissions; the section's own diagram 3 ('Balance of Payments Structure') and quiz[1] explanation both show the three-account identity. Internally inconsistent and imprecise for a 'Define/components' question.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite to: 'three components: current account, capital account (very small: capital transfers, non-produced assets) and financial account'; keyIdea: 'current + capital + financial accounts (+ errors and omissions) sum to zero'.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] 'Competitiveness' > marshall-lerner-j-curve > body[0] (also extras.chains[2].steps[2] and quiz[4] option text)
accuracyIssues.issue: 'If demand is inelastic on both sides, depreciation worsens the current account' conflates 'each elasticity < 1' with the actual failure condition '|PEDx| + |PEDm| < 1'. Two inelastic demands (e.g. 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2) still satisfy Marshall-Lerner. The sentence immediately after the correct formula teaches a wrong shortcut.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'If the sum of the elasticities is less than one, depreciation worsens the current account...'

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims post-Brexit sterling depreciation produced 'a textbook J-curve' with UK exports 'gradually becoming more competitive' over two years. The UK current account deficit actually narrowed sharply in late 2016 (5.2% of GDP in 2016 to ~3.5% in 2017, driven largely by primary income valuation effects), and the widely discussed empirical finding is the absence of an export volume response (exporters raised sterling prices/margins). Presenting a contested, arguably counter-example as 'textbook' is misleading; a teacher who knows the data will object.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with an international-context example relevant to IAL students and where the mechanism is cleaner, e.g. Sri Lanka 2022 (rupee fell ~45%; fuel/food import demand inelastic so import bill rose first) or Turkey 2018-21 (lira depreciation, initial widening then narrowing of trade deficit). Soften wording to 'consistent with a J-curve'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Most major economies operate some version of a managed float' / 'Most countries operate a managed float'. Under IMF AREAER classification USD, EUR, GBP, JPY are free-floating; managed floats/soft pegs are common among emerging economies, not 'major economies'. Two different claims (major economies vs countries) in the same block.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Most large advanced economies float freely with occasional intervention; many emerging economies (China, India, Singapore) operate managed floats or pegs.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > balance-of-payments > realExample and marshall-lerner-j-curve > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: Two of four real examples are UK-centric (UK deficit, Brexit) for an audience sitting IAL in HK, Korea, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Middle East. IAL Unit 4 data-response extracts are almost always non-UK developing/emerging economy contexts.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap one for e.g. Pakistan's persistent current account deficit financed by IMF/foreign borrowing, or Singapore's managed float against a basket (MAS), which also directly illustrates spec bullet 4.3.2(d) on intervention.

accuracyIssues.issue: Long-run determination via PPP and 'productivity differentials' (Balassa-Samuelson) is beyond the IAL spec; not wrong, but the term PPP is only defined in a flashcard, never in content, so a student meets it undefined here.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either add a one-line definition of PPP in the paragraph or trim to relative inflation rates, which is the spec factor.

quizIssues.question: The J-curve effect occurs because, in the short run after a depreciation:
quizIssues.issue: The correct option is the only one that contains a stated consequence ('so the current account initially worsens'), which any student who knows the J-curve shape can pattern-match without knowing the cause; it also repeats the 'inelastic = ML fails' conflation. Strip the consequence clause from the option.

quizIssues.question: Which term correctly describes a deliberate decrease in a fixed exchange rate by the government?
quizIssues.issue: Devaluation vs depreciation is never taught in content[] (only in notes/flashcards/common_mistakes). A Learn Mode student can be served this in the pre-test or inline quiz with no supporting text. Question itself is fine.

quizIssues.question: A depreciation of the exchange rate is likely to:
quizIssues.issue: The inflation effect of depreciation is not taught in any content[] section (only in diagram 4 text). Coverage gap rather than a question defect. Option 3 'Have no effect on inflation if the economy has spare capacity' is a reasonable distractor.

quizIssues.question: Unit labour costs (ULC) are calculated as:
quizIssues.issue: Unit labour costs never appear in content[]. Block 2 is titled 'Competitiveness' but has no competitiveness content. Question and explanation are correct.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is most likely to improve a country's international competitiveness in the long run?
quizIssues.issue: Factors influencing competitiveness (spec 4.3.3b) are not taught in content[]; only extras.chains[3] touches it. Question fine.

quizIssues.question: A persistent current account surplus in one country can be problematic for the global economy because:
quizIssues.issue: Global trade imbalances (spec 4.3.1d) are not taught in content[]. Explanation's phrase 'Global trade is a zero-sum game in terms of balances' is loose: the sum of balances is an accounting identity, not a game; students may repeat 'zero-sum' in essays and lose precision marks.
