quizIssues.question: A country with high unit labour costs relative to its competitors is likely to experience:
quizIssues.issue: Tests relative ULC, untaught in content[]. Distractor 1 ('surplus due to expensive high-quality exports') is close to a real evaluation point (Germany: high wages but strong non-price competitiveness) but the stem says ULC not wages, so it is defensibly wrong; acceptable.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term ... (4 marks)': IAL Economics 'Define' questions carry 2 marks (definition + development/example). The guidance awards 1 mark each for describing four components, which is a 'components' or 'explain' scheme, not a definition scheme. Reframe as 'Define ... (2 marks)' or 'Explain the four components of the current account (4 marks)'.
'Explain two causes ... (6 marks)': IAL uses 'Explain' at 4 marks and 'Analyse' at 6 marks. The 3+3 point scheme is usable but the command/mark pairing will mis-calibrate students' expectations.

'Assess ... (10 marks)': command/marks correct. Guidance is a points-based tally (1+2+2+2+2+1) whereas IAL 10-mark 'Assess' is levels-based (KAA 6 + Evaluation 4). Guidance never tells the student a J-curve or currency-market diagram earns KAA credit. Model answer content is otherwise good.

'Evaluate ... (20 marks)': command/marks correct. Guidance again presents an itemised 20-point tally (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) that does not reflect IAL levels marking (KAA 12 + Evaluation 8). No diagram expectation, no context/application requirement, no explicit 'judgement with justification' which Level 4 evaluation requires. Example of 'small open economies' pegging is good.

'Outline two measures ... (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (should be 'Explain'). The topic (measures of competitiveness) is not taught anywhere in content[]. Guidance uses 'real effective exchange rate' where the spec bullet 4.3.3(a) names 'relative export prices' and 'relative unit labour costs'; REER is acceptable but the spec term should appear.

structureIssues: Block 2 is titled 'Competitiveness' (content[1].title) but its two sections are exchange-rate-determination and marshall-lerner-j-curve; there is no section on international competitiveness. Its takeaways do not mention competitiveness either. Retitle to 'Exchange Rate Movements and Their Effects' and add a genuine competitiveness block.

Zero recall widgets in a section with two genuine causal chains already written as flow blocks (balance-of-payments flow: imports exceed exports -> CA deficit -> financed by financial account surplus -> capital inflows; exchange-rate-determination flow: Fed raises rates -> capital attracted -> demand for dollars rises -> dollar appreciates). Both are ideal reorder recalls; ML condition is an ideal fillin ('|PED_ + PED_| > _'). Learn Mode currently offers no retrieval practice at all.

Neither block has a diagramRef (content[0] and content[1] keys are title/sections/takeaway only), although diagrams[] contains five relevant diagrams including the currency-market S/D diagram that examMatters explicitly tells students to draw. If InlineDiagram matches by diagramRef substring, no diagram is ever shown in Learn Mode for this section. Add diagramRef 'Balance of Payments Structure' to block 1 and 'Exchange Rate Determination' (or 'J-Curve') to block 2.

No quizIndices/practiceIndices on either block, so the inline quiz/practice at the end of block 1 (BoP + systems) may draw ML/ULC questions the student has not reached, and the pre-test draws 3 of 12 where 6 test untaught material.

Ordering: exchange-rate-systems (block 1) explains 'if demand for a currency falls, it depreciates automatically' before exchange-rate-determination (block 2) teaches what determines currency demand. Swap so determination precedes systems, or move systems to block 2 after determination.

Step weight: each block is a single 2-section step; block 1 step carries 7 paragraphs + 1 flow + 2 examples + 2 misconceptions before any interaction. With no recalls and no diagram, this is a long passive read, consistent with the product-wide step-0 drop-off.

Misconceptions are genuine student errors (deficit = failing; floating always better; strong currency always good; depreciation auto-fixes deficit). The stronger, more exam-relevant one recorded in common_mistakes (devaluation vs depreciation terminology) is absent from content[] and would be a better misconception for exchange-rate-systems.
extras.chains and notes[] contain competitiveness content (ULC, non-price factors, REER) that never made it into content[]; the Learn Mode path is thinner than the Notes tab for the same section.
ialSpecGaps: 4.3.1(a) Components of the BoP: capital account not taught in content (text says two components).
4.3.1(c) Measures to reduce a current account imbalance (expenditure-switching, expenditure-reducing, supply-side policies) - not taught anywhere in content[].
4.3.1(d) Significance of global trade imbalances - not taught in content[] (only quiz[9]).
4.3.2(b) Distinction between appreciation/revaluation and depreciation/devaluation - absent from content[] (only notes/flashcards/quiz[5]).

4.3.2(d) Government intervention in currency markets via foreign currency transactions and interest rates - only implied in the fixed-rate paragraph; no explicit treatment of how a central bank buys/sells reserves or uses rates to defend a rate.
4.3.2(e) Competitive devaluation/depreciation and its consequences - not taught (one line in diagram 4 only).

4.3.2(f) Impact of exchange rate changes on economic growth, employment/unemployment, inflation and FDI flows - not in content[]; only diagram 4 text. Only the current-account impact (ML/J-curve) is taught.
4.3.3(a) Measures of international competitiveness: relative unit labour costs, relative export prices - not taught (tested in quiz[7], quiz[11], practice[4]).
4.3.3(b) Factors influencing international competitiveness (exchange rate, productivity, wage costs, regulation, non-price factors) - not taught in content[] (extras chain only).
4.3.3(c) Significance of international competitiveness: benefits of being competitive, problems of being uncompetitive - not taught.

Note: sub-numbering 4.3.1/4.3.2/4.3.3 is from memory of the 2018 IAL spec; the section id '4.3.3' with the full 4.3 title suggests the app's numbering differs. Bullet content is stated with reasonable confidence; exact lettering unsure.
strengths: Prose accuracy is high for what is covered: BoP financing identity, floating vs fixed trade-offs, hot money and interest rate differentials, Marshall-Lerner formula and J-curve mechanism are all stated the way IAL mark schemes expect.

examMatters for exchange-rate-determination gives the exact axis labels (exchange rate on y, quantity of currency on x) and the correct shift directions; diagrams[0] and its two scenarios match this and are correctly labelled ($/GBP, Quantity of GBP).
All four misconceptions are real student errors with a concrete 'instead write' sentence a student can copy into an essay.
Real examples that are used are factually sound apart from the Brexit overclaim: China's daily fix and band, US Fed 2022-23 dollar strength, UK deficit >5% of GDP.

Quiz correctIndex is right on all 12 items and explanations are teaching-quality (e.g. quiz[3] stresses it is the SUM of elasticities; quiz[5] cleanly separates devaluation/depreciation/deflation/disinflation).
Practice[2] and practice[3] use correct IAL command words and mark sizes (Assess 10, Evaluate 20) with sensible content in the guidance.
Flow blocks are genuine causal chains, not decorative lists.
topFixes: Add the missing content: a real 'International Competitiveness' section pair (measures: relative ULC and relative export prices; factors; significance) and an 'Effects of Exchange Rate Changes' section (inflation, growth, employment, FDI, competitive devaluation, revaluation/devaluation terminology), plus 'Correcting a current account deficit' in block 1. This makes quiz[5..11] and practice[4] teachable and closes ~8 spec bullets.

Wire the blocks into Learn Mode: add diagramRef ('Balance of Payments Structure' on block 1; 'Exchange Rate Determination' on block 2, J-curve on the new effects block) and quizIndices/practiceIndices so inline quiz and practice match what the step taught.

Add recall widgets from existing flows: reorder on 'Imports exceed exports -> CA deficit -> financed by financial account surplus -> capital inflows' and 'Fed raises rates -> capital attracted -> demand for $ rises -> $ appreciates'; fillin on '|PED_x| + |PED_m| > __' with word bank {exports, imports, 1, 0}.

Fix precision errors: three BoP accounts (not two) in body[0]/keyIdea; 'sum of elasticities < 1' instead of 'inelastic on both sides' in the ML paragraph; replace the Brexit 'textbook J-curve' example with an international one (Sri Lanka 2022 or Turkey 2018-21) worded as 'consistent with'.

Realign practice to IAL conventions: Define 2 marks, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Assess 10/12, Evaluate 14/20; drop 'Outline'; rewrite guidance for the 10- and 20-markers as levels descriptors (KAA + Evaluation) rather than point tallies, and state the diagram expected.

summary: The prose in content[] is genuinely good A-level writing: correct RPI-X arithmetic, Averch-Johnson, monopsony/NMW logic, real student misconceptions, and strong evaluative framing. But an IAL teacher would not put it in front of students as-is. Three of the ten MCQs (Laffer curve, occupational immobility, poverty trap) are not 3.3.5 content and, because the pre-test samples 3 random MCQs, there is a ~71% chance a student's very first interaction with the section is an off-topic question. The blocks carry no diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, so the legacy fallback places an RPI-X quiz and a 'Define privatisation' practice question on the Competition Policy step before either is taught. Two of the three diagrams have geometric errors (the price-cap diagram draws the regulated price below AC, i.e. a loss-making firm, and marks MC=MR ~30px from the true intersection; the 'privatisation' diagram is a competitive supply-shift that contradicts the section's own claim that privatising a natural monopoly creates a private monopoly). Several spec bullets (quality standards, performance targets, competitive tendering, promotion of small business, deregulation, protecting suppliers) are absent from content, there are zero recall exercises, the material is entirely UK/EU-framed for an international cohort, and one examMatters tells students this is a '25-mark essay topic' (UK GCE tariff; IAL tops out at 20).

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] Regulation of Monopoly > privatisation-nationalisation > examMatters
accuracyIssues.issue: "This is a classic 25-mark essay topic" — 25-mark essays are UK GCE 9EC0 Papers 1/2 Section C. IAL WEC13 essays (Section C) are 20 marks; the highest IAL tariff is 20 ('Evaluate'). Sets wrong exam expectations for the target audience.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to "classic 20-mark 'Evaluate' essay in WEC13 Section C" and structure the advice around 12 KAA + 8 Evaluation marks.

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[0] 'Price Regulation of a Monopoly (RPI-X Price Cap)' svg
accuracyIssues.issue: Geometry contradicts the intended teaching. The regulated price line Preg is at y=170 while the AC curve at Qreg (x=268) is at y≈115 — i.e. AC is ABOVE Preg, so the regulated firm is drawn making a loss, with no mention of this anywhere in checklist/description (the SVG comment even says 'above AC'). Also the MC=MR point is marked at (200,226) but the MC and MR paths actually intersect near (232,228), so the Qm/Pm dashed lines hang in space. The AC is U-shaped, not the falling LRAC of a natural monopoly, which is the case regulators actually price-cap.
accuracyIssues.fix: Redraw: natural-monopoly falling LRAC with MC below it; show P=MC cap (allocatively efficient but loss-making, needs subsidy) vs P=AC cap (normal profit, no subsidy). Make dashed lines hit the true MC=MR intersection. Add a checklist item on whether Preg covers AC.

accuracyIssues.issue: Represents privatisation as a rightward supply shift in a competitive S/D market ('new entry + efficiency gains'). This directly contradicts content[1] > privatisation-nationalisation body[1] ('privatising a natural monopoly simply replaces a public monopoly with a private one') and conflates privatisation with deregulation — exactly the confusion common_mistakes[1] warns against. E1 is also mis-plotted (S1 and D cross near (272,165), not (260,150)).
accuracyIssues.fix: Retitle to 'Deregulation / increased contestability' and keep S-shift only for that case; for privatisation use the monopoly diagram (Pm vs regulated/competitive price). Fix E1 coordinates.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] Competition Policy > cma-merger-control (whole section) and all six realExamples
accuracyIssues.issue: Entire section is built around the UK CMA (SLC test, Sainsbury's-Asda, Ofwat, Ofgem, British Rail, UK NLW, UK rent controls). IAL spec 3.3.5 says 'competition authorities' generically and IAL extracts are frequently non-UK. International students (HK, SG, KR, MY, PK, ME) are given no local hook and may think UK institutional names are required.
accuracyIssues.fix: Frame as 'competition authorities (e.g. the UK CMA, Singapore CCCS, Korea KFTC, Hong Kong Competition Commission, Pakistan CCP)'. Swap 2-3 examples: CCCS fined Grab/Uber S$13m over their 2018 merger; KFTC fined Google ₩207bn in 2021 over Android; Pakistan CCP cement cartel.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] Regulation of Monopoly > price-cap-regulation > body[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: "This is superior to rate-of-return regulation" is asserted as fact. It is an argument (RPI-X trades investment risk for cost incentives); the same section's examMatters correctly tells students to evaluate the two. Also the spec's own terms 'price regulation' and 'profit regulation' never appear in body text (only in quiz[1]).
accuracyIssues.fix: "Economists generally argue this is superior to profit (rate-of-return) regulation because..." and introduce 'price regulation = RPI-X; profit regulation = rate-of-return' explicitly.

accuracyIssues.issue: examMatters instructs 'Always draw both diagrams — competitive and monopsony', but the section only supplies the monopsony diagram; there is no competitive labour-market NMW diagram showing the excess supply gap.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add a competitive-market NMW diagram (W_min above W_e, L_d < L_s, unemployment gap labelled) so the instruction is actionable.

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[1] 'Minimum Wage in a Monopsony Labour Market'
accuracyIssues.issue: MCL is drawn from (100,240) with slope -1 while ACL starts at (100,270) with slope -0.59 — different W-axis intercepts and slope ratio 1.7, not the textbook 'same intercept, twice the slope'. Lm is marked at x=198 but MCL and MRPL actually cross at x≈211. The description says the NMW 'flattens the MCL curve' but the post-NMW kinked MCL (horizontal at Wmin to Lmin) is not drawn.
accuracyIssues.fix: Start MCL and ACL from the same intercept with MCL twice as steep; snap Lm to the true intersection; draw the horizontal Wmin segment as the new MCL up to Lmin.

accuracyIssues.issue: "individual directors can face criminal prosecution and prison sentences" is placed in a generic penalties paragraph. In the UK the criminal cartel offence (Enterprise Act 2002) applies to cartels only, not to abuse of dominance; and the '10% of worldwide turnover' cap is UK/EU-specific.
accuracyIssues.fix: "In the UK/EU fines can reach 10% of worldwide turnover, and in the UK individuals involved in cartels can be prosecuted."

accuracyIssues.issue: "privatisation in utilities was always accompanied by the creation of regulators like Ofgem, Ofwat, and Ofcom" — Ofgem (1999) and Ofcom (2003) post-date the privatisations; the original regulators were Oftel (1984), Ofgas (1986), Ofwat (1989), Offer (1990).
accuracyIssues.fix: "...creation of sector regulators (Oftel, Ofgas, Ofwat — today's Ofcom and Ofgem)" or simply 'independent sector regulators'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Ofwat switched from RPI to CPIH indexation from 2020 (PR19), so 'using an RPI–X framework' is dated; historically water used RPI+K to fund investment.
accuracyIssues.fix: "Ofwat sets five-year price controls of the RPI-X / CPIH-X type" — or use a non-UK example (e.g. Singapore's or Malaysia's utility price controls).

accuracyIssues.issue: Flow ends 'Merger blocked or approved with conditions' with result 'Competition protected', omitting the most common outcome (unconditional clearance) — mildly contradicts the section's own misconception ('most mergers are approved').
accuracyIssues.fix: Final step: 'Cleared unconditionally / cleared with remedies / blocked'.

quizIssues.question: The Laffer curve suggests that:
quizIssues.issue: Not 3.3.5 content (fiscal policy / macro). With the pre-test drawing 3 random MCQs from this bank, students can be tested on it before seeing anything on government intervention in firms. Also appears in inline quiz rotation for a section that never mentions it.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is an example of a measure to reduce occupational immobility?
quizIssues.issue: Belongs to 3.3.4 Labour Markets (labour immobility policies), not taught anywhere in this section's content[]. Off-topic for pre-test and inline quiz.

quizIssues.question: The poverty trap (benefits trap) occurs when:
quizIssues.issue: Welfare/tax content (macro / UK-style 'poverty trap'), not in 3.3.5 and not taught in this section. Off-topic for pre-test.

quizIssues.question: A government introduces competitive tendering for waste collection services. Which of the following is the most likely intended benefit?
quizIssues.issue: On-spec (3.3.5 'competitive tendering for government contracts') but competitive tendering is never taught in content[] — the term does not appear in any section body. Students are quizzed on untaught material. Fix the content, keep the question.

quizIssues.question: Under the RPI-X price regulation formula, a firm subject to a cap of RPI - 3% when inflation is 4%...
quizIssues.issue: Question itself is fine, but because blocks lack quizIndices the legacy distributeItems() fallback places quiz[0] on step 0 (Competition Policy) — RPI-X is not taught until block 2. Also the bank has no MCQ at all on Block 1 content (mergers/SLC, cartels, predatory pricing, abuse of dominance).

practiceIssues.issue: "Define the term 'privatisation'. (4 marks)" — IAL definition items are 2 marks and only appear in Units 1/2; WEC13 has no 'Define' questions (Section A is MCQ + 4-mark explanation). The scheme awards a mark for naming UK examples (BT 1984, British Gas 1986), which a definition would not credit. Also lands on Learn step 0 (Competition Policy) via the marks-sorted fallback, before privatisation is taught.

"Outline two problems associated with regulatory capture (4 marks)" — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word. 'Problem 1' is just the definition of regulatory capture restated ('regulator acts in the interests of the industry'), not a problem caused by it, so the two 'problems' collapse into one.

10-mark 'Assess' tariff is correct for IAL. But the model answer is point-marked (2+2+1+2+1+1+1) whereas IAL 10-markers are levels-based with 6 KAA + 4 Evaluation; only ~2 marks of the model are evaluative. No diagram is expected despite examMatters demanding both NMW diagrams. Definition assumes NMW is 'set above the market equilibrium wage', pre-judging the analysis.

20-mark 'Evaluate' tariff is correct. But IAL 20-markers are 12 KAA + 8 Evaluation; the model gives evaluation ~4 marks. 'Regulatory capture suggests that even under public ownership, interest groups can influence policy' misapplies the term (capture is of a regulator by regulated private firms; the public-ownership risk is political interference / producer capture). 'Water and rail have significant positive externalities' is loose — the case is natural monopoly/essential service, not externalities.

Acceptable 6-mark 'Explain two...' with 3+3 KAA scheme. Minor: cites only the UK CMA; add 'or the relevant national competition authority'. Also note the set has no extract-based ('With reference to Extract A') or 'Analyse'-with-diagram question on price regulation, the most diagram-dependent bullet in the spec.

structureIssues: Zero recall exercises (0 reorder, 0 fillin) — the section has no retrieval practice at all between steps; the only checks are 3 inline MCQs. Obvious candidates exist: a fillin on RPI-X arithmetic; a reorder on the merger-control procedure (notification → Phase 1 → SLC test → Phase 2 → remedies/decision), which is a genuine procedural sequence; a reorder on the Averch-Johnson chain (guaranteed return on capital → incentive to over-invest → inflated capital base → productive inefficiency).

No block carries diagramRef / quizIndices / practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:117-121 falls back to distributeItems()/matchDiagramsToBlocks(). Result (3 steps, 1 block each): step 0 'Competition Policy' gets quiz[0] (RPI-X arithmetic) + practice 'Define privatisation' — both untaught at that point; step 1 'Regulation of Monopoly' gets practice 'Outline regulatory capture' (taught in block 3); step 2 gets 'Explain two objectives of competition policy' (block 1). All three inline practice items are on the wrong block.

diagrams[2] 'Effects of Privatisation and Deregulation' shares no title word with any block title ('Competition Policy', 'Regulation of Monopoly', 'Government Failure and Minimum Wages'), so matchDiagramsToBlocks() never places it — it is invisible in Learn Mode and only visible on the Diagrams tab.

Pre-test contamination: 3 of 10 MCQs are off-topic (Q5 Laffer, Q6 occupational immobility, Q7 poverty trap); P(at least one off-topic in a 3-question pre-test) = 1 - C(7,3)/C(10,3) ≈ 71%. This is a concrete mechanism behind the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis for this section.

Block 3 'Government Failure and Minimum Wages' pairs two unrelated topics into one step. Government failure is Unit 1 content used here as an evaluation lens (fine) and minimum wage is 3.3.4 Labour Markets content; neither is a 3.3.5 bullet. The spec's own 3.3.5 hook for labour is 'protect suppliers and employees: restricting monopsony power of firms', which is only obliquely covered.

The section is not organised around the spec's logic (why intervene → tools: mergers / monopoly control / promoting competition & contestability / protecting suppliers & employees → impacts on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice → limits: regulatory capture, asymmetric information). There is no summary of 'impact on prices/profit/efficiency/quality/choice' (spec 3.3.5b), so a student cannot easily answer the standard 'assess the impact of X on consumers/firms' data-response question.

Difficulty ramp is inverted: the most technical material (RPI-X vs rate-of-return, Averch-Johnson, information asymmetry) sits mid-section, while the closing block depends on 3.3.4 prerequisites (MRPL, MCL, ACL) that are assumed rather than recapped.

Takeaways match their blocks and misconceptions are genuine student errors (dominance vs abuse; RPI-X 'prices always fall'; privatisation 'always improves efficiency'; always-draw-competitive-model) — these are good. Flashcards drift off-section (consumer sovereignty, contestable market, deadweight loss, dynamic efficiency are 3.3.3), low priority.
ialSpecGaps: 3.3.5a control of monopolies: quality standards and performance targets — not mentioned anywhere in content[] (only price regulation and, via quiz[1], profit regulation).
3.3.5a promote competition and contestability: promotion of small business — absent.
3.3.5a promote competition and contestability: deregulation — appears only in flashcards, common_mistakes[1] and diagrams[2]; never taught in content[].
3.3.5a promote competition and contestability: competitive tendering for government contracts — only in quiz[8]; not taught.

3.3.5a protect suppliers and employees: restricting monopsony power of firms (as buyers, e.g. supermarket-supplier codes) — only the NMW/labour-monopsony angle is covered; the supplier-protection angle is absent.

3.3.5b impact of government intervention on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice — no explicit treatment; partially implied in RPI-X and privatisation sections but never framed as the spec's five impacts.
3.3.5c limits to intervention: regulatory capture and asymmetric information — covered (government-failure-intervention; price-cap-regulation body[2]; quiz[9]). No gap.
Unsure: whether IAL 3.3.5 explicitly lists 'nationalisation' under protecting suppliers/employees (I believe it does, and it is covered).
strengths: RPI-X mechanics, the worked 3%-2%=1% example, Averch-Johnson effect and the 'setting X correctly / information asymmetry' evaluation are accurate and pitched exactly at IAL level (content[1] > price-cap-regulation).

Monopsony vs competitive NMW analysis (content[2] > minimum-wage-intervention) is correct, and the 'net effect is an empirical question / depends on market structure' framing is precisely the evaluation examiners reward; quiz[3] tests it well.
Misconceptions are real ones teachers see: dominance ≠ abuse; RPI-X does not mean nominal prices fall; privatisation alone ≠ efficiency; government failure ≠ leave markets alone.
Real examples are factually correct where checked: Sainsbury's-Asda blocked 2019; Google Android €4.34bn July 2018; BR privatisation 1994-97; UK NLW introduced April 2016.

Practice tariffs for the 'Assess' (10) and 'Evaluate' (20) items match IAL conventions; extras.evaluation paragraphs (Schumpeter/dynamic efficiency, Card & Krueger, ownership vs regulatory framework) are strong evaluation material.
Quiz explanations explain why each distractor is wrong (e.g. quiz[0], quiz[2], quiz[6]), which is good feedback design.
topFixes: Replace quiz[5] (Laffer), quiz[6] (occupational immobility), quiz[7] (poverty trap) with on-spec MCQs on mergers/SLC, predatory pricing vs abuse of dominance, and quality standards/performance targets; then add quizIndices, practiceIndices and diagramRef to each block so pre-test and inline items match what the step teaches.

Fix the diagrams: redraw diagrams[0] as a natural-monopoly price-cap diagram (falling LRAC, P=MC vs P=AC caps, Preg not below AC, MC=MR dashed lines at the true intersection); retitle/replace diagrams[2] so privatisation is not shown as a competitive supply shift; add the competitive-market NMW diagram the examMatters demands; draw the kinked post-NMW MCL in diagrams[1].

Add the missing spec content as a new block ('Promoting competition and contestability': deregulation, competitive tendering, promotion of small business; 'Protecting suppliers': monopsony buyers) plus a short 'impact on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice' summary table; consider moving the minimum-wage subsection to 3.3.4.
Add recall exercises: fillin on RPI-X (RPI 5%, X 2% → ?%), reorder on merger-control procedure and on the Averch-Johnson causal chain.

De-UK and de-GCE the exam framing: change '25-mark essay' to '20-mark Evaluate'; say 'competition authorities (e.g. CMA, CCCS, KFTC, HK Competition Commission)'; add 2-3 Asia/ME examples (CCCS Grab-Uber 2018 fine, KFTC Google 2021); rewrite practice mark schemes as IAL KAA + Evaluation levels, fix 'Define (4 marks)' and 'Outline'.

summary: The four prose sections that exist (comparative advantage, benefits of free trade, protectionism, WTO) are accurate, well-pitched IAL prose with real misconceptions and sensible examMatters, and 13 of 14 MCQs have a defensible single correct answer. But the section is only half a topic: terms of trade, trading blocs/trade creation-diversion and patterns of trade are absent from content[] yet are tested by 7 of 14 MCQs, 1 of 5 practice questions, 2 of 5 diagrams and a third of the flashcards, so the pre-test, step-1 inline quiz (quiz[1], ToT calculation) and step-1 inline practice (practice[4], ToT deterioration) all ask about things never taught. Learn Mode has zero recall widgets, only 2 steps, and because the blocks carry no diagramRef/quizIndices the legacy word-overlap fallback (components/learn-mode/utils.js:31-57) matches diagram titles on the word "the", putting the Tariff diagram at the end of "The Case for Free Trade" and never showing the Comparative Advantage, ToT or Trading Blocs diagrams at all. The numerical CA diagram also fails to demonstrate a gain from specialisation (world output goes from 70W+30C to 40W+50C). A strong IAL teacher would use the prose but would not accept this as a complete section for the spec area.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] 'Protectionism and the WTO' > methods-of-protectionism > body[3] flow.result
accuracyIssues.issue: Result reads 'Net welfare loss — producer gains are smaller than consumer losses plus government revenue'. That inequality is trivially true and is not the welfare argument. The net loss exists because consumer surplus lost (a+b+c+d) exceeds producer surplus gained (a) PLUS government revenue (c). As written it teaches the wrong comparison.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change to: 'Net welfare loss — the consumer surplus lost exceeds the producer surplus gained plus the tariff revenue; the difference is the two deadweight-loss triangles.'

accuracyIssues.location: diagrams[0] 'Comparative Advantage: Numerical Example' (Gains from Specialisation panel + checklist[2])
accuracyIssues.issue: Before: 70 wheat + 30 cars. After full specialisation: 40 wheat + 50 cars. That is +20 cars but -30 wheat, so the panel does NOT show 'total world output increases' as the checklist demands; a student cannot tell whether the world is better off. Full specialisation by the country with absolute advantage in both goods is the classic case where partial specialisation is needed.
accuracyIssues.fix: Have Country A partially specialise: A produces 30 wheat + 35 cars, B produces 40 wheat + 0 cars → 70 wheat + 35 cars (same wheat, +5 cars). Or change the numbers so full specialisation dominates on both goods (e.g. A 100W/50C, B 60W/10C gives 100W+50C? no — pick numbers such as A: 80W or 80C, B: 60W or 20C so B's full wheat + A's full cars gives 60W+80C vs 70W+50C before).

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] 'The Case for Free Trade' > comparative-advantage > realExample
accuracyIssues.issue: 'Bangladesh has a comparative advantage in textiles due to low labour costs' explains comparative advantage with an absolute-cost argument, which is exactly the confusion the same section's misconception warns against. Comparative advantage in garments comes from a low opportunity cost (abundant low-skilled labour with few higher-value alternative uses), not from low wages per se.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rephrase: 'Bangladesh's abundant low-skilled labour gives it a low opportunity cost of producing labour-intensive garments; Germany's capital and skilled labour give it a low opportunity cost in precision machinery.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] > the-wto > body[1] (dispute settlement 'jewel in the crown', 'binding legal process')
accuracyIssues.issue: Presents the dispute settlement mechanism as fully functional. Since December 2019 the Appellate Body has had no quorum because the US blocked appointments, so panel rulings can be appealed 'into the void' and are not enforceable. This is the single most examinable current limitation of the WTO and it is absent from body, examMatters and takeaway.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add one sentence: 'Since December 2019 the Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals because the US blocked new appointments, so losing parties can appeal into the void — sharply weakening enforcement.'

accuracyIssues.issue: An improvement is a rise in the index relative to the previous period, not an index above 100. An index of 95 rising to 98 is an improvement; 105 falling to 102 is a deterioration. The '>100 / <100' gloss teaches a wrong test.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with 'index rises over time' / 'index falls over time' and drop the 100 threshold.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > benefits-free-trade > realExample ('intra-EU trade grew by an estimated 60%')
accuracyIssues.issue: Unsourced, undated figure. Published estimates of the single market's effect on intra-EU goods trade range widely (Mayer, Vicard & Zignago 2019 put it near a doubling; other EC estimates are lower). Without a source or date a student cannot use it credibly in application.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either attribute it ('the European Commission estimates…') or use a verifiable fact such as the size of intra-EU trade as a share of members' total trade (~60% of EU goods trade is intra-EU).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'one representing lost consumer surplus (production inefficiency) and one representing lost consumer surplus (consumption inefficiency)' — the same phrase is used for both triangles. The production-inefficiency triangle (b) is the extra real resource cost of producing Q1→Q2 domestically instead of importing, not simply 'lost consumer surplus'.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'triangle b = production inefficiency (resources wasted producing at above world cost); triangle d = consumption inefficiency (consumer surplus lost on units no longer bought).'

accuracyIssues.location: flashcards[17] 'What is a non-tariff barrier?' vs quiz[12] explanation and content[1] methods-of-protectionism body[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: Flashcard defines an NTB as 'any trade restriction that is not a tariff — e.g., quotas…' while quiz[12]'s explanation says a quota is 'not a non-tariff barrier in the strict sense' and the content lists quotas and NTBs as separate tools (matching the IAL spec's four categories). Internal inconsistency the student will hit on the same section.
accuracyIssues.fix: Align the flashcard with the spec: list tariffs, quotas, subsidies and NTBs as four categories; give NTB examples as standards, licensing, customs delays, embargoes.

accuracyIssues.location: meta.number '4.3.2' / meta.title 'Trade and the Global Economy'
accuracyIssues.issue: In the 2018 IAL Economics (WEC14) specification the trade content (specialisation and trade, terms of trade, trading blocs and WTO, restrictions on free trade) sits under 4.1 'Causes and effects of globalisation', and 4.3 is poverty and inequality. Numbering does not match the spec students and teachers use to navigate. Unsure of the exact sub-numbering, but 4.3.2 is not trade.
accuracyIssues.fix: Check the section number against the WEC14 spec table of contents and renumber.

quizIssues.question: If a country's export price index rises from 100 to 120 and its import price index rises from 100 to 110, what has happened to its terms of trade?
quizIssues.issue: Correct (109.1) but terms of trade are never taught in content[] — the formula appears only in diagrams[3], flashcards[14] and extras. Because the block has no quizIndices, distributeItems() makes this the ONLY inline MCQ on step 1 (Protectionism + WTO), so the Learn Mode quiz for that step tests an untaught concept.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is the key feature that distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but trading-bloc types are not in content[] (only diagrams[4] and flashcards). Can appear in the pre-test before anything is taught.

quizIssues.question: Trade diversion occurs when:
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but trade creation/diversion is not in content[] (only extras.chains[2], flashcards and common_mistakes[2]).

quizIssues.question: According to the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis, developing countries that rely on primary commodity exports will experience:
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer, but Prebisch-Singer is not taught here and in IAL sits with growth/development (primary product dependency) rather than this section. Explanation reason (3) 'developed countries add value through manufacturing and capture more gains' is not one of the hypothesis's stated mechanisms (low YED for primaries, technological substitution, asymmetric market power/wage bargaining).

quizIssues.question: A depreciation of the exchange rate will improve a country's trade balance if:
quizIssues.issue: Marshall-Lerner is exchange-rate/BoP content (a different spec sub-topic and app section), not taught anywhere in this section. Minor precision: the condition is that the sum of the ABSOLUTE values of the elasticities exceeds 1.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of trading bloc membership?
quizIssues.issue: Option C 'the ability to set independent trade policy with non-member countries' IS retained in a free trade area (the diagrams[4] text says exactly that: 'Each keeps own external tariffs'). The question says 'trading bloc' generically, and the explanation has to hedge 'particularly a customs union or above'. A well-taught student can argue C is a benefit of FTA membership over customs-union membership. Restrict the stem to 'customs union'.

quizIssues.question: A country's terms of trade have 'improved' but its export revenue and trade balance have both worsened. Which explanation is most likely?
quizIssues.issue: Good discriminating question, but relies on ToT + PED reasoning that content[] never introduces.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is the best example of a non-tariff barrier to trade?
quizIssues.issue: Explanation classifies a quota as 'not a non-tariff barrier in the strict sense', contradicting flashcards[17] which gives quotas as the first NTB example. Answer is still defensible because of 'best example', but the section is inconsistent with itself.

quizIssues.question: Country X can produce 60 units of food or 30 units of machinery...
quizIssues.issue: Options and explanations across the bank contain literal '—' HTML entities (e.g. option D here, explanation of quiz[1], [3], [4], [10]). If options are rendered as plain text these show as raw '—'. Verify the InlineQuiz/PreTest renderer decodes entities.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term comparative advantage (4 marks)'. IAL Economics 'Define' items are 2 marks (definition + a development/example). The guidance awards marks for Ricardo's policy prescription and 'consume beyond PPF', which are analysis, not definition, and would not appear in an Edexcel define mark scheme. Should be 2 marks, or reworded as 'Explain, using a numerical example, what is meant by comparative advantage (4)'.

'Explain two economic effects of imposing a tariff (6 marks)'. IAL 'Explain' is normally a 4-mark item; 6 marks would be 'Analyse'/'Examine'. More importantly the guidance never asks for or references the tariff diagram, while the section's own examMatters says examiners 'love tariff diagrams'; a WEC14 answer on tariff effects is expected to use it. The two effects also ignore government revenue and deadweight loss, the two things the diagram exists to show.

'Assess the economic impact of the formation of a customs union (10 marks)'. Mark allocation is right for Assess, but customs unions, trade creation and trade diversion are not taught in content[] — a student who has only done Learn Mode cannot attempt it. Guidance is points-based (2+2+1+2+1+2) whereas IAL 10-markers are levels-marked (KAA 6 + Evaluation 4); tell the student that.

'Evaluate the view that free trade is always preferable to protectionism (20 marks)'. Command word/marks fine and the question is realistic. Guidance is presented as a points tally summing to 20, which misrepresents IAL 20-mark essays (levels-based: KAA 14 + Evaluation 6 in the 2018 spec). Evaluation is only 4 of the 20 allocated marks in the guidance and there is no diagram (tariff welfare) or real-world application, which the top level requires.

'Outline two factors that may cause a deterioration in a country's terms of trade (4 marks)'. 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (Edexcel uses Define/Calculate/Explain/Analyse/Examine/Discuss/Assess/Evaluate). Terms of trade are not taught in content[], yet because practice is sorted by marks this is practice index 1 and therefore the inline practice on step 1 in Learn Mode. Guidance is fine in substance.

structureIssues: Coverage vs assessment mismatch: content[] teaches only comparative advantage, benefits of free trade, protectionism tools/arguments, and the WTO. Terms of trade (quiz 1,6,11; practice 4; diagrams[3]; flashcards[14]; extras.chains[3]), trading blocs / trade creation-diversion (quiz 2,3,9; practice 2; diagrams[4]; flashcards[10-13]; extras.chains[2]; common_mistakes[2]) and Marshall-Lerner (quiz 8) are assessed but never taught. 7/14 MCQs and 2/5 practice questions are untaught.

Only 2 Learn Mode steps (block 0: comparative-advantage + benefits-free-trade; block 1: methods-of-protectionism + the-wto). Each pair is coherent, but the whole spec area is compressed into two screens; the protectionism section crams four tools, four arguments for, four against and a tariff flow into three paragraphs with no explanation of the tariff diagram in the body.

Zero recall objects (meta.reorder 0, meta.fillin 0) so Learn Mode offers no retrieval practice beyond one MCQ per step and the completion screen's recall score is always 0/0. This section has genuinely orderable chains that would suit reorder (tariff imposed → domestic price rises to Pw+t → domestic supply Q1→Q2, demand Q4→Q3 → imports shrink → DWL b+d) and clean fill-ins (CS loss = a+b+c+d, PS gain = a, revenue = c).

Blocks have no diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, so LearnModeTab.jsx:117-119 uses the legacy fallback. matchDiagramsToBlocks (components/learn-mode/utils.js:31-57) keeps any word longer than 2 chars, so 'the' in 'The Effect of a Tariff (Welfare Analysis)' matches 'The Case for Free Trade' (score 1) and the TARIFF diagram is placed at the end of step 0 before protectionism is taught; 'The Effect of a Quota' then matches 'Protectionism and the WTO' on 'the'. The Comparative Advantage numerical diagram, the ToT diagram and the Trading Blocs diagram never appear in Learn Mode. Fix by adding diagramRef ('Comparative Advantage' / 'Tariff') to the blocks and adding a stopword filter to normalize().

distributeItems (utils.js:9-23) with 14 quiz items and 2 steps gives step 0 → quiz[0] (fine) and step 1 → quiz[1] (ToT calculation, untaught). Practice sorted by marks gives step 0 → practice[0] Define CA (4), step 1 → practice[4] Outline ToT (4). So the protectionism/WTO step's assessment never touches protectionism or the WTO.

PreTest draws 3 random from the 14-item bank (PreTest.jsx:9); with half the bank untaught, the expected pre-test contains ~1.5 questions the student cannot have learned, which reinforces the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis for this section specifically.

Takeaways do match their blocks (block 0: CA / static vs dynamic gains / frictions; block 1: protectionism DWL / WTO principles / regionalism). Block 1 takeaway 1 'arguments for it are often abused' is a value judgement stated as a takeaway; better to state the evaluation criterion (temporary, targeted, credible exit).

Misconceptions are real student errors (absolute vs comparative; benefits without limits; tariffs save jobs; WTO enforces free trade), not filler — good. But the comparative-advantage realExample (low labour costs) undercuts the first one.

Difficulty ramp is sensible (concept → gains → intervention → institutions) but ends at the WTO without returning to the numerical/diagrammatic skills the examMatters fields promise ('practise until this is automatic') — there is no worked tariff-diagram walk-through or numerical CA exercise in the flow.
ialSpecGaps: Terms of trade: definition, calculation (index of export prices / index of import prices × 100), factors influencing the ToT, and impact of changes on an economy — entirely absent from content[] (only in diagrams/flashcards/extras/quiz).

Trading blocs: types (free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary union) with examples, and costs and benefits of regional trade agreements including trade creation and trade diversion — absent from content[].

Possible conflicts between regional trade agreements and the WTO — one sentence in the-wto body[2] plus extras.evaluation[2]; not developed (rules of origin, MFN exception under GATT Article XXIV, 'spaghetti bowl').
Patterns of trade: changes in trade patterns between developed and emerging economies, the role of relative exchange rates and trading blocs in shaping patterns — absent.

Absolute advantage: defined only in a flashcard and in passing inside the misconception; no numerical worked example of comparative advantage in the body (only diagrams[0], which is not surfaced in Learn Mode).

Impact of protectionist policies on consumers, producers, governments, living standards and equality — the tariff welfare analysis is only in the diagram; distributional effects (living standards, equality, effect on developing-country exporters) are not covered.
Subsidies to domestic producers: listed as a tool but never analysed (no subsidy diagram, no welfare analysis).

Limitations of the theory of comparative advantage beyond listing assumptions (e.g. increasing costs, dynamic/created comparative advantage, transport costs, externalities) — only in extras.evaluation[0], not in content.
Numbering: unsure of exact sub-numbers, but in WEC14 this material sits under 4.1 (Causes and effects of globalisation), not 4.3.2.
strengths: Prose in all four sections is accurate, examiner-literate and appropriately pitched: correct definition of comparative advantage via opportunity cost, terms-of-trade range for mutual gain, static vs dynamic gains, four WTO principles, Doha/regionalism critique.

Misconceptions are genuine and each ends with an 'Instead write:' sentence a student can lift into an answer (e.g. methods-of-protectionism: tariffs save jobs in the protected sector but destroy jobs elsewhere).
examMatters fields describe real IAL demands: numerical CA tables, the full tariff diagram checklist, static/dynamic evaluation, WTO effectiveness structure.
Real examples are accurate and current (US-China 2018-20 tariffs ~$360bn with consumer incidence; Airbus-Boeing WTO dispute; Smoot-Hawley; Doha 2001).

MCQ bank is technically sound: all 14 correctIndex values are correct, distractors are plausible and several items (q4 DWL vs transfers, q10 quota rent, q11 harmful ToT 'improvement') discriminate at A/A* level. Explanations teach, not just confirm.

Tariff and quota diagrams (diagrams[1], [2]) are correctly labelled (Price/Quantity, Pw, Pw+t, Q1-Q4, areas a-d) with checklists that mirror mark-scheme expectations, including the 'quota rent is not government revenue' point.
Extras chains and evaluation points (dynamic comparative advantage, infant-industry capture, spaghetti bowl) are exactly the evaluation material a 20-mark answer needs.
topFixes: Add two content blocks (or split into separate sections): 'Terms of Trade' (formula, causes, impact, harmful vs beneficial improvement) and 'Trading Blocs' (FTA→CU→common market→monetary union, trade creation vs diversion, conflict with WTO) so that quiz 1,2,3,6,9,11, practice[2] and [4], diagrams[3] and [4] are taught before they are tested; move quiz[8] (Marshall-Lerner) to the exchange-rate section.

Add diagramRef, quizIndices and practiceIndices to both blocks (block 0: diagramRef 'Comparative Advantage', quiz [0,13,5], practice [0]; block 1: diagramRef 'Tariff', quiz [4,10,12,7], practice [1,3]) and add a stopword filter to normalize() in components/learn-mode/utils.js:33 so 'the' can never match a diagram to a block.

Fix diagrams[0] so specialisation shows an unambiguous output gain (partial specialisation by Country A: 30W+35C, B: 40W → 70W+35C) and rewrite the tariff flow result in methods-of-protectionism to 'consumer surplus lost exceeds producer surplus gained plus tariff revenue'.

Add recall widgets: a reorder on the tariff causal chain (tariff → Pw+t → domestic supply expands/demand contracts → imports fall → DWL b+d), a fillin on tariff welfare areas (CS loss = a+b+c+d / PS gain = a / revenue = c / DWL = b+d), and a fillin on the opportunity-cost calculation from the CA table.

Realign practice with IAL conventions: 'Define' 2 marks; 'Explain' 4 marks with the tariff diagram required; replace 'Outline' with 'Explain'; present 10- and 20-mark guidance as levels (KAA + Evaluation) with an explicit diagram and application requirement, and add the Appellate Body paralysis to the WTO section as the key contemporary limitation.

summary: The prose is clean, the definitions are exam-usable, and the Lorenz/Gini and equity-efficiency material is pitched correctly for IAL. But a strong IAL teacher would hesitate: the body covers only 4 subsections and skips several explicit spec bullets (income vs wealth distinction, causes and measures of poverty, inequality between countries, impact of development/Kuznets, significance of capitalism) that the quiz, flashcards and diagrams nonetheless test, so the pre-test and inline quiz can ask about things the Learn flow never teaches. The body repeatedly conflates relative poverty with inequality (the exact error its own common_mistakes block warns against), the World Bank poverty line is mislabelled and out of date, and 8 of 10 MCQs can be answered by picking the longest option. There are zero recall widgets and no diagramRef on either block, so the retrieval and diagram mechanics of Learn Mode are inert for this section.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] 'Types of Poverty' > absolute-relative-poverty > body[0] and keyIdea; diagrams[1] label '(fixed: $2.15/day)'; practice[0].guidance; notes[0]; flashcards[0]
accuracyIssues.issue: '$2.15 per day (2022 PPP)' is wrong on two counts: the $2.15 line was expressed in 2017 PPP (adopted Sept 2022), and in June 2025 the World Bank raised the international poverty line to $3.00/day at 2021 PPP. As of 2026 the section teaches a superseded figure with a mislabelled base year.
accuracyIssues.fix: State '$3.00 per day (2021 PPP, World Bank, updated June 2025; previously $2.15 at 2017 PPP)'. Update diagram label, practice[0] guidance, notes and flashcard consistently; note that examiners accept either recent figure.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > absolute-relative-poverty > body[1], body[2], flow.steps[3], realExample ('meaning relative inequality worsened dramatically'), takeaway[1]
accuracyIssues.issue: Relative poverty is treated as a synonym for inequality. 'Relative inequality' is not a term; a rising Gini driven by the top decile pulling away does not by itself raise relative poverty (share of households below 60% of median), which depends on the median and the bottom of the distribution. The section's own common_mistakes[0] says students must not 'confuse relative poverty with inequality', yet the body does exactly that.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite the China example: 'absolute poverty collapsed while the Gini rose from ~0.30 to ~0.47 — inequality widened; relative poverty (below 60% of the rising median) also stayed high because rural incomes lagged'. In body[1]/flow, say 'relative poverty may rise if incomes at the bottom grow more slowly than the median' rather than 'if the rich gain more'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'tax policy changes that reduced top marginal rates from 91% to 37%' is paired with a 1965–2023 window, but the US top federal rate was 70% in 1965 (91% ended in 1963). The CEO-pay ratio figures (20:1 → 350:1) are EPI's realized-compensation series (EPI reports ~21:1 in 1965 and ~290:1 in 2023, 344:1 in 2022), so 'around 350:1 in 2023' is loose.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use 'from 70% in 1965 to 37% today' and '~21:1 in 1965 to roughly 290–340:1 in 2022–23 (EPI)'. Also drop 'rising returns to human capital at the top' as the explanation for CEO pay; EPI attributes it mainly to stock-based pay and governance, which the example already mentions.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Poverty traps arise when the withdrawal of benefits as income rises creates effective marginal tax rates above 80%' presents an arbitrary threshold as the definition. A poverty trap exists whenever the effective marginal rate is high enough to remove the incentive to earn more; 80% is an illustration, not a criterion. flashcards[9] separately describes 'no better off working than not working', which is the unemployment trap, not the poverty trap.
accuracyIssues.fix: Define: 'a poverty trap occurs when benefit withdrawal plus tax means a low-income household keeps very little of each extra pound earned (effective marginal rates can approach or exceed 70–80%)'. Distinguish unemployment trap (better off not working) from poverty trap (little gain from working more).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Top marginal tax rates exceed 55%' is true for Denmark (~55.9%) but not Sweden (~52% after the 2020 abolition of the austerity tax). Presented as a joint fact about both.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Top marginal income tax rates are around 52% in Sweden and 56% in Denmark'.

accuracyIssues.issue: Body says most countries' Gini falls 'between 0.25 and 0.65'; quiz[5] explanation says '0.25 to 0.60'. Minor internal inconsistency a student will notice.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use one range (0.25–0.65) in both places.

accuracyIssues.issue: Not an IAL exam diagram (no mark scheme asks for it) but the checklist is written as if it is ('Draw ... Label the axes'). The relative-poverty line is also not drawn at 60% of the median (at the right edge it is ~72% of the median's height above the origin).
accuracyIssues.fix: Relabel the checklist as 'understanding points' rather than drawing instructions, or redraw so the green line is visibly 60% of the blue line's height.

quizIssues.question: (applies to the whole bank) A country experiences rapid economic growth but the Gini coefficient rises from 0.35 to 0.42...
quizIssues.issue: Answer-length cue across the bank: in 8 of 10 MCQs (indices 0,1,2,3,4,6,8,9) the correct option is the longest, usually by a wide margin. A test-wise student can score ~80% without reading the stems. Since the PreTest samples 3 of these, the pre/post-test delta is unreliable.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best distinguishes relative poverty from absolute poverty?
quizIssues.issue: Explanation claims 'relative poverty exists primarily in developed countries'. By construction relative poverty (below 60% of median) exists in every society; it is simply more relevant as a policy measure where absolute poverty is rare. Teaches a subtly wrong idea in the feedback.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is most likely to reduce absolute poverty in a developing country?
quizIssues.issue: Three distractors are transparently harmful (raise taxes on essentials, cut education, cut minimum wage) and the key is the only positive-sounding option. Zero discrimination between strong and weak students.

quizIssues.question: According to the Kuznets hypothesis, as a country develops economically, inequality will:
quizIssues.issue: Kuznets is never mentioned in content[] body text — it appears only in diagrams[2] and flashcards[10]. The Learn flow (and the PreTest, which samples this bank) can test a concept the section has not taught. Distractor D ('market forces maintain equilibrium') is filler.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a cause of inequality between countries rather than within countries?
quizIssues.issue: Distractor D contains the phrase 'within a country', which flags it as wrong on wording alone. 'Inequality between countries' as a topic is not taught in the body (only one flow result line mentions it).

quizIssues.question: How might a civil war affect poverty in a developing country?
quizIssues.issue: Content body never discusses conflict or causes of poverty; the question tests general knowledge, not the section. Distractor B ('GDP is unaffected by conflict') is not plausible.

quizIssues.question: In a free market economy, which of the following is the most significant reason why inequality tends to increase over time without government intervention?
quizIssues.issue: Distractors A, C and D are absurd ('Free markets prevent any individual from earning above-average income'; 'profits are always distributed equally among workers'). Only one option is even coherent. Also tests 'significance of capitalism for inequality', which appears only in extras.chains[3], not the taught body.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the difference between absolute poverty and relative poverty (4 marks)' is not an IAL construction — 'Define' is a 2-mark command; a 4-mark contrast question would be 'Distinguish between…' or 'Explain the difference between…'. Guidance still cites $2.15 (out of date) and offers a UK-specific 60% example without noting OECD's 50%.

'Explain two causes of income inequality within a country (6 marks)' is realistic for IAL Unit 4 Section A/B. Guidance is point-marked (1+1+1 per cause), which matches IAL short-answer marking. No issue beyond the fact that 'skill-biased technological change' in the answer is not developed in the body text.

'Assess the usefulness of the Gini coefficient… (10 marks)' — correct IAL command/mark pairing. But the guidance allocates discrete marks (2+2+1+2+2+1) whereas IAL 'Assess' questions are levels-marked (KAA and Evaluation levels), so the model answer misrepresents how marks are earned and never mentions the level descriptors or a diagram (a Lorenz sketch is an easy application mark).

'Evaluate the view that globalisation has increased inequality between developed and developing countries (20 marks)' — realistic Section C essay, but the guidance is again point-allocated (2+3+2+2+3+2+2+2+2) rather than IAL levels (KAA up to 12, Evaluation up to 8 on the 20-mark grid). Content of the answer (IP rights, terms of trade, East Asia catch-up) leans on globalisation sub-topics not taught in this section, and no 'in context' data reference is modelled.

'Outline two economic effects of poverty on a developing country (4 marks)' — 'Outline' is not an IAL Economics command word (papers use Define/Explain/Analyse/Assess/Discuss/Evaluate). Content-wise fine, but the body never covers 'effects of poverty' (savings gap, human capital), so this is untaught.

structureIssues: Zero recall widgets in the section (meta.reorder=0, meta.fillin=0), so the spaced/immediate recall mechanic of LearnModeTab never fires here. Obvious candidates exist in the data already: notes[1].flow ('Rank population by income' → 'Plot cumulative income share' → 'Calculate Gini = A/(A+B)') is a genuine procedure suitable for reorder; the Gini formula and 0/1 endpoints are ideal fillin material.

Neither block carries diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices (content[0] and content[1] have only title/sections/takeaway). InlineDiagram matches by diagramRef substring, so none of the 3 diagrams (including the exam-critical Lorenz curve) appears inside the Learn flow; students only meet it if they visit the Diagrams tab.

Coverage vs testing mismatch: quiz[4] (Kuznets), quiz[7] (between-country causes), quiz[8] (civil war/poverty), quiz[9] (capitalism), practice[3] (globalisation and between-country inequality), practice[4] (effects of poverty) and 8 of 18 flashcards (HDI, wealth tax, minimum wage, equity vs equality, income vs wealth, Kuznets, between-country causes, education) test material absent from content[] body. The PreTest can therefore gate on untaught content, which plausibly feeds the observed step-0 abandonment.

Only 4 subsections for a spec point with ~8 bullets; two steps total. Block 1 (poverty types + Lorenz/Gini) and Block 2 (causes + consequences/redistribution) pair coherently, but the ramp is flat: nothing on measures of poverty (headcount, poverty gap, MPI), income-vs-wealth distinction, or development/Kuznets before the causes block.

Misconceptions: absolute-relative-poverty ('growth automatically reduces all poverty') is a real student error. lorenz-curve-gini ('Gini is a perfect measure') is filler — the real student errors are swapping the axes, reading Gini 0.4 as '40% poor', and drawing the Lorenz curve above the diagonal (common_mistakes[1] already names the axis error and should be promoted into the section). causes-inequality ('caused only by effort or talent') is ideological rather than an exam misconception. consequences-redistribution is really an evaluation point restated as a misconception.

Takeaways match their blocks (Block 1 takeaway[0-3] and Block 2 takeaway[0-3] all trace to body text). Block 2 takeaway[3] name-checks the Laffer curve, which gets one sentence in the body — thin support for a takeaway.

The examMatters fields are good and IAL-consistent (chains of reasoning, define both terms, Gini = A/(A+B)), but three of four end with the same 'this earns the highest marks / top marks' formula, which reads as template output.
ialSpecGaps: Distinction between income inequality and wealth inequality (spec bullet explicitly requires it; only flashcards[17] covers it, body never does)
Measures of absolute and relative poverty beyond the $-a-day line: headcount ratio, poverty gap, Multidimensional Poverty Index (only extras.evaluation[2] mentions MPI)
Causes of changes in absolute and relative poverty (unemployment, low wages, lack of education/health, conflict, demographic change, benefit levels) — body only covers causes of inequality
Causes of inequality between countries (institutions, colonial legacy, capital/infrastructure, primary-commodity dependence) — flashcards[5] and quiz[7] only
Impact of economic change and development on inequality (Kuznets hypothesis, structural change, technology) — diagrams[2] and quiz[4] only, no body teaching
Significance of capitalism for inequality (returns to capital vs labour, factor ownership) — extras.chains[3] and quiz[9] only
Unsure: whether the IAL spec lists 'measures of inequality' beyond Lorenz/Gini (e.g. income share ratios, Palma) — practice[2] guidance mentions income share ratios without teaching them
strengths: Definitions of absolute poverty, relative poverty, Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient (content[0] both sections; notes[0], notes[1]) are precise, mark-scheme-ready and correctly worded (cumulative % population on x, cumulative % income on y, Gini = A/(A+B), 0–1 range).

diagrams[0] Lorenz curve is exam-correct: axes labelled properly, 45° line labelled 'Line of Perfect Equality', areas A and B marked, formula stated, two curves for comparison, and the checklist mirrors what an IAL mark scheme rewards.

Flow chains are genuine causal chains (e.g. causes-inequality flow: globalisation → skilled workers sell globally → unskilled face competition → gap widens) and match the IAL emphasis on chains of reasoning.

consequences-redistribution examMatters gives a real evaluation lever (some redistribution, e.g. education, improves both equity and efficiency; poorly designed benefits create poverty traps) that goes beyond the textbook trade-off.
Real examples (China 1978–2020, South Africa vs Denmark Gini, Scandinavian model) are broadly accurate, memorable, and international rather than UK-centric — appropriate for IAL cohorts.
Quiz explanations consistently address every distractor, not just the key.
Practice[2] 'Assess' 10 marks and practice[3] 'Evaluate' 20 marks use correct IAL command-word/mark pairings and the model answers have a genuine judgement paragraph.
topFixes: Add body subsections for the untaught spec bullets (income vs wealth inequality; measures and causes of poverty incl. headcount/poverty gap/MPI; inequality between countries; Kuznets/impact of development; capitalism and inequality) so the quiz bank, PreTest and flashcards test what the Learn flow actually teaches.

Fix the relative-poverty/inequality conflation in absolute-relative-poverty (body[1], body[2], flow, realExample 'relative inequality', takeaway[1]) so it agrees with common_mistakes[0]; say inequality rose (Gini) and relative poverty depends on the bottom vs the median.

Rewrite MCQ distractors so the correct option is not the longest (currently 8/10), replace the absurd distractors in quiz[3] and quiz[9] with plausible near-misses, remove the 'within a country' giveaway in quiz[7], and correct quiz[1]'s 'relative poverty exists primarily in developed countries' explanation.

Add recall widgets and diagram hooks: a reorder on the Lorenz→Gini procedure (from notes[1].flow), fillins on the Gini formula/endpoints and the two poverty definitions, and set diagramRef: 'Lorenz' on content[0] and 'Kuznets' on content[1] so InlineDiagram renders.

Update the poverty line to $3.00/day (2021 PPP, June 2025) everywhere ($2.15 '2022 PPP' is mislabelled and superseded), fix the US 91%→70% top-rate claim, and recast practice[2]/[3] guidance as IAL levels-based marking (KAA/Evaluation) while replacing the non-IAL 'Define the difference' and 'Outline' command words.

summary: The Learn Mode content and the assessment layer of this section were clearly written to two different briefs. The four taught subsections (public goods, merit goods, a one-paragraph-each tour of fiscal/monetary/supply-side, income redistribution + UBI) are mostly Unit 1/Unit 2 revision and cover almost none of IAL 4.3.5 (public expenditure types, progressive/proportional/regressive tax, deficit vs debt, structural vs cyclical, automatic stabilisers, crowding out, TNC/transfer-pricing controls, policy problems). Meanwhile all 12 MCQs, 4 of 5 practice questions, all 5 diagrams and all 4 extras chains DO target the spec, so a student is pre-tested, inline-quizzed and post-tested on material the section never teaches. Neither block carries diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices and there are zero recall widgets, so Learn Mode is two flat text steps with orphaned diagrams. Prose quality, the quiz bank and the extras are individually good; a strong IAL teacher would not put the Learn Mode in front of students for this spec point without rewriting the content blocks around the spec.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] 'Market Failure and the State' > public-goods, merit-goods-redistribution (whole block)
accuracyIssues.issue: Public goods and merit goods are Unit 1 market-failure content (IAL 1.3.3 public goods, 1.3.4 information gaps), not 4.3.5 'Role of the state in the macroeconomy'. Presenting them as the first half of this spec point misdirects revision. Note also Edexcel IAL does not use the term 'merit good' in its spec (it uses information gaps/externalities); the term is fine as vocabulary but should not be framed as the examiner's expected answer.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace block 1 with spec content: public expenditure (capital/current/transfer payments; size and composition as % of GDP; effects on growth, living standards, crowding out, taxation, equality) and taxation (progressive/proportional/regressive; effects of direct and indirect tax changes on incentives, revenue/Laffer, distribution, output/employment, price level, trade balance, FDI).

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] > fiscal-monetary-supply-side > body[1] ('rates cannot fall below zero (the zero lower bound)')
accuracyIssues.issue: Stated as a hard fact; the ECB, BoJ, SNB and Danish central bank all ran negative policy rates 2014-2022. For an international audience this is a visible error.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'rates cannot fall much below zero (the effective lower bound); some central banks experimented with slightly negative rates, with limited effect.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > merit-goods-redistribution > body[1] ('compulsory education until age 18')
accuracyIssues.issue: England-specific (participation age to 18 in England only; Scotland/Wales/NI and most IAL markets differ). Presented as a general fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use 'compulsory schooling laws (e.g. to age 16-18 depending on the country)'.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > merit-goods-redistribution > examMatters ('Show the divergence between private benefit and social benefit on a diagram')
accuracyIssues.issue: Instructs students to draw an MPB/MSB diagram, but the section supplies no such diagram (all 5 diagrams are Laffer/deficit/crowding-out/AD-AS/tax incidence), and this diagram is not what 4.3.5 questions ask for.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either remove the instruction or point to the correct spec diagrams for this section (Laffer curve, AD/AS policy effects, tax incidence).

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] > income-redistribution-policies > examMatters ('Draw a diagram showing how benefit withdrawal creates a near-flat relationship between gross and net income')
accuracyIssues.issue: This gross-vs-net income diagram is not an Edexcel IAL diagram and no mark scheme rewards it; the section provides no version of it. Students following this advice waste exam time.
accuracyIssues.fix: Replace with: 'Explain the poverty trap using effective marginal tax rates in words; if a diagram is asked for in this topic it will be the Laffer curve or an AD/AS shift.'

accuracyIssues.issue: UBI is not on the IAL spec at all; a full paragraph plus the block's only 'misconception' and a takeaway are spent on it, while spec items (regressive/proportional taxes, transfer payments as a category of public expenditure) are not defined in the taught content.
accuracyIssues.fix: Cut UBI to one evaluative sentence; use the space to define progressive/proportional/regressive taxes with a worked example.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] > fiscal-monetary-supply-side > keyIdea/body (no mention of exchange rate policy or direct controls)
accuracyIssues.issue: Spec 4.3.5(d) explicitly lists 'fiscal policy, monetary policy, exchange rate policy, supply-side policies and direct controls in different countries'. Presenting only three tools as the complete set is misleading for this unit.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add exchange rate policy (devaluation, managed floats, e.g. China/PBoC) and direct controls (price controls, capital controls, import quotas) with one-line trade-offs each.

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > public-goods > body[1] and flow ('Complete market failure — zero private provision')
accuracyIssues.issue: Overstated: pure public goods can have some private/club provision (private lighthouses historically, private security, open-source software), and quasi-public goods exist. The notes[] section correctly mentions quasi-public goods; the learn body omits it.
accuracyIssues.fix: '…market failure: little or no private provision; quasi-public goods (roads, beaches) sit between the two.'

accuracyIssues.location: content[0] > merit-goods-redistribution > realExample (NHS) ; content[1] > fiscal-monetary-supply-side > realExample (BoE) ; content[1] > income-redistribution-policies > body[0] ('UK's 20%/40%/45%') and realExample (Universal Credit)
accuracyIssues.issue: All four real examples and the tax-band illustration are UK-specific. The facts are correct (BoE 0.1% Dec 2021 to 5.25% Aug 2023; CPI peak 11.1% Oct 2022; UC 55% taper, six benefits, five-week wait), but for an international-school audience IAL papers use global contexts; nothing here from Asia, the Middle East or developing economies.
accuracyIssues.fix: Swap at least two examples: e.g. Singapore's progressive income tax with 0% lowest band vs Hong Kong's flat-ish 15-17% cap; Pakistan/Sri Lanka IMF fiscal-deficit conditions; Bank of Korea/HKMA rate cycles.

accuracyIssues.location: content[1] > fiscal-monetary-supply-side > body[2] ('may worsen inequality in the short run')
accuracyIssues.issue: Generalises a criticism of market-based supply-side policies to all supply-side policies; interventionist ones (education, infrastructure) usually reduce inequality.
accuracyIssues.fix: 'Market-based policies (deregulation, lower top taxes) may worsen inequality; interventionist ones are costly and slow.'

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is classified as a transfer payment?
quizIssues.issue: Correct and well-explained, but 'transfer payment' vs current/capital expenditure is never defined anywhere in content[] (only in this explanation). As a pre-test item it is unanswerable from the section.

quizIssues.question: According to the Laffer Curve, what happens if a government increases its tax rate when it is already above the revenue-maximising rate (t*)?
quizIssues.issue: Option 3 'Tax revenue doubles due to the higher rate' is a throwaway distractor; and the stem reads 'above the revenue-maximising rate' which nearly gives away 'decreases'. Weak discrimination.

quizIssues.question: What is the key distinction between a fiscal deficit and the national debt?
quizIssues.issue: Correct. Not taught in content[] (deficit/debt distinction appears only in diagrams[1] and practice[4]).

quizIssues.question: Automatic stabilisers help moderate economic fluctuations because:
quizIssues.issue: Correct. 'Automatic stabilisers' never appear in content[]; only in practice[1] guidance and flashcards.

quizIssues.question: Crowding out is most likely to occur when:
quizIssues.issue: Correct. Crowding out is not mentioned in content[]; taught only in diagrams[2]/extras chain 2.

quizIssues.question: The structural deficit is defined as:
quizIssues.issue: Correct. Structural vs cyclical deficit absent from content[].

quizIssues.question: Which statement best describes how TNCs use transfer pricing to reduce their tax liability?
quizIssues.issue: Correct. Transfer pricing/TNC control absent from content[]; also the correct option is by far the longest, a common tell.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following was NOT a key policy response to the 2008 financial crisis?
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but a history-recall item rather than an economics-reasoning item, and the explanation cites the UK VAT cut; international students may not know it. Consider reframing as 'Which policy would be contractionary during a recession?'

quizIssues.question: A government faces inaccurate economic data, time lags, and external shocks. Which problem does this combination most directly create for policymakers?
quizIssues.issue: Correct, but the three distractors all contain 'will always'/'no effect' absolutes, making the answer guessable without knowledge. Spec item (problems facing policymakers) is absent from content[].

quizIssues.question: When demand for a good is highly price inelastic, the imposition of an indirect tax will result in:
quizIssues.issue: Correct assuming supply is not perfectly inelastic; stem should say 'relative to supply' for rigour. Tax incidence not taught in content[].

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best explains why the OECD agreed a global minimum corporation tax rate of 15%?
quizIssues.issue: Correct. Minor: it was agreed by the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework (c.136 jurisdictions), not 'the OECD' alone. Content[] never mentions it.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term fiscal policy (4 marks)' does not match IAL command-word conventions: 'Define' is a 2-mark item; 4 marks would be 'Explain'. The guidance then awards marks for expansionary/contractionary/supply-side uses, which are not part of a definition.

'Explain two reasons… (6 marks)': IAL 'Explain' items are typically 4 marks; 6 marks is usually 'Analyse'. Content is good (progressive tax as automatic stabiliser is a strong point) but the mark tariff is off.

'Assess… (10 marks)': tariff acceptable, but the guidance is a points-based scheme (2+2+1+2+2+1) whereas IAL marks 10+ items with levels (KAA + Evaluation). Students will over-focus on ticking points. Also the topic (Laffer validity) is the ONLY practice question whose concept appears in content[] (one paragraph).

'Evaluate… TNCs… sustainable economic growth (20 marks)': realistic 4.3.5(d)/4.3.3 essay and tariff correct, but the guidance is points-based, not levels-based, and content[] never teaches TNCs, transfer pricing or limits on government control, so the student cannot answer it from the section.
'Outline two differences… (4 marks)': 'Outline' is not an Edexcel IAL Economics command word (use 'Explain' or 'Distinguish between'). Deficit vs debt is not taught in content[].

structureIssues: Content/assessment mismatch is the defining fault: 0 of 12 MCQs, 4 of 5 practice questions, 5 of 5 diagrams and 4 of 4 extras chains cover 4.3.5 spec material that the four content[] subsections never teach; conversely nothing in quiz/practice tests public goods, merit goods, poverty traps or UBI. Pre-test (3 random MCQs) and post-test therefore measure nothing the section teaches.

Neither block has diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices (content[0] and content[1] keys are only title/sections/takeaway). InlineDiagram cannot substring-match any of the 5 diagrams, so Learn Mode shows none of them; inline quiz/practice selection falls back to arbitrary items unrelated to the block just read.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) in a section whose spec is full of genuine sequences (crowding-out chain, automatic-stabiliser chain, deficit-to-debt accumulation, transfer-pricing mechanism) and definitional contrasts ideal for fillin. Learn Mode is two text-only steps.

Block ordering/difficulty ramp: block 1 is AS-level Unit 1 content (easy, off-spec), block 2 jumps to a compressed whole-course policy overview. There is no build from 'what the state spends and taxes' through 'public finances' to 'policy in a global context', which is the spec's own ramp.

Subsection fiscal-monetary-supply-side compresses three policy tools into three paragraphs with a flow only for monetary tightening; spec 4.3.5(d) needs five tools (adds exchange rate policy, direct controls) plus TNC controls plus policymaker problems. This one subsection would need to become a block.
Takeaways match their blocks, but block 2 takeaway 4 (UBI) elevates an off-spec idea to a headline point.

Misconceptions: public-goods vs publicly-provided (real, good), merit vs public goods (real), fiscal/monetary interchangeable (plausible), 'UBI solves poverty without trade-offs' (filler; not a misconception IAL students hold or are examined on). A real 4.3.5 misconception (deficit = debt; falling deficit = falling debt; indirect taxes are neutral) is only in the quiz explanations.

notes[] (4 titles) mirror the content[] topics, so the Notes tab has the same spec gap; flashcards[] include 'demerit good', 'moral hazard', 'principal [sic] of equity in taxation' which are not taught in either.
ialSpecGaps: 4.3.5(a) Public expenditure: distinction between capital expenditure, current expenditure and transfer payments — not taught (only in quiz[0] explanation).
4.3.5(a) Reasons for the changing size and composition of public expenditure in a global context (ageing populations, demand for services, crises) — absent.

4.3.5(a) Significance of differing levels of public expenditure as a proportion of GDP: productivity and growth, living standards, crowding out, level of taxation, equality — absent (crowding out only in diagrams/extras).
4.3.5(b) Taxation: distinction between progressive, proportional and regressive taxes — only 'progressive' taught; regressive appears only in quiz[8]; proportional nowhere.

4.3.5(b) Economic effects of changes in direct and indirect tax rates on: incentives to work, tax revenues (Laffer), income distribution, real output and employment, price level, trade balance, FDI flows — only Laffer and incentives touched; tax incidence/price level only in diagrams[4]/quiz[10]; trade balance and FDI absent.
4.3.5(c) Public sector finances: automatic stabilisers vs discretionary fiscal policy — absent from content.
4.3.5(c) Fiscal deficit vs national debt; structural vs cyclical deficits — absent from content (diagram[1], quiz[2],[5], practice[4] only).
