4.3.5(c) Factors influencing the size of fiscal deficits and national debt; significance of their size (interest payments, crowding out, credit ratings, intergenerational equity, inflation risk) — absent.
4.3.5(d) Use of exchange rate policy and direct controls in different countries — absent.

4.3.5(d) Measures to control global companies' (TNCs) operations: regulation of transfer pricing; limits to government ability to control TNCs — absent from content (extras chain 4, quiz[6],[11], practice[3] only).
4.3.5(d) Problems facing policymakers when applying policies: inaccurate information, risks and uncertainties, external shocks — absent from content (quiz[9] only).
Unsure: whether IAL 4.3.5 expects the loanable-funds crowding-out diagram (diagrams[2]) — it is not a listed spec diagram; AD/AS and Laffer are the safer choices.
strengths: Quiz bank is factually correct across all 12 items (verified correctIndex on every one), covers the spec breadth well (public expenditure categories, Laffer, deficit/debt, automatic stabilisers, crowding out, structural deficit, transfer pricing, tax incidence, Pillar Two, policy problems) and explanations are examiner-quality with the distinguishing reasoning spelled out.

Extras chains and evaluation paragraphs are genuinely evaluative and spec-aligned (Laffer limits, conditions for crowding out, BEPS/Pillar Two limits) — strong raw material for the 12/20-mark questions.
Diagram checklists are precise and correct (Laffer peak t*, tax wedge Pc/Pp with deadweight loss, AD/AS with LRAS shift, deficit-as-flow vs debt-as-stock) with useful two-scenario contrasts.
Real-example facts that are given are accurate (BoE 0.1% to 5.25% Dec 2021-Aug 2023, CPI peak 11.1%; UC 55% taper, six benefits, five-week wait; UK 1970s 83% top rate).
Prose is clear, mechanism-first (e.g. free-rider chain, poverty-trap chain via effective marginal tax rates), and the public-good vs publicly-provided misconception is a real one handled well.
practice[3] (Evaluate TNC control, 20 marks) is a realistic IAL Unit 4 essay with balanced for/against and a proportionality judgement.
topFixes: Rewrite content[] to the 4.3.5 spec: Block 1 'Public expenditure and taxation' (capital/current/transfer; size as % GDP effects; progressive/proportional/regressive; effects of direct vs indirect tax changes incl. Laffer and incidence). Block 2 'Public sector finances' (automatic stabilisers vs discretionary; deficit vs debt; structural vs cyclical; factors and significance). Block 3 'Policy in a global context' (five tools incl. exchange rate policy and direct controls; TNC/transfer-pricing controls and limits; inaccurate information, uncertainty, external shocks). Move public/merit goods to the Unit 1 sections.

Wire the assessment layer to the blocks: add diagramRef ('Laffer'/'Tax Incidence' to block 1, 'Fiscal Deficit' to block 2, 'AD/AS'/'Crowding Out' to block 3), quizIndices ([0,1,8,10], [2,3,5,4], [6,7,9,11]) and practiceIndices so the inline quiz/practice and pre/post-test measure what was just taught.

Add recall widgets, one per subsection, using genuine sequences already in extras: reorder 'crowding out' (deficit → bond sales → demand for loanable funds up → interest rate up → private I falls), reorder 'automatic stabiliser in recession' (incomes fall → tax take falls, benefits rise → AD cushioned), fillin 'deficit is a ___ (flow); debt is a ___ (stock); a ___ (surplus) is needed to reduce debt', fillin regressive/proportional/progressive definitions.

Fix practice tariffs and formats to IAL: practice[0] 'Define fiscal policy (2 marks)' or 'Explain… (4 marks)'; practice[1] to 4 marks or 'Analyse (6)'; practice[4] 'Distinguish between/Explain' not 'Outline'; convert practice[2] and [3] guidance to levels-based KAA/Evaluation descriptors.

Internationalise examples and remove UK-only framing (NHS, council housing, 20/40/45 bands, England's age-18 rule, ECB-contradicting 'cannot fall below zero'): add e.g. Singapore/Hong Kong tax structures, an IMF-programme fiscal deficit case (Pakistan/Sri Lanka), and a non-UK central bank cycle; cut UBI to one sentence.

summary: The prose is well written and mostly accurate, the flows are genuine causal chains, and the six misconceptions are real ones a teacher would recognise. But as a Learn Mode section it is hollow: there are zero recall exercises, no block carries a diagramRef/quizIndices/practiceIndices, so the five good diagrams (HDI, Harrod-Domar, Lewis, Prebisch-Singer, strategies) never appear inline and the inline quiz has no mapping to the block just read. Five of the twelve MCQs (Lewis turning point, capital flight, Dutch disease x2, foreign currency gap) test material the Learn content never teaches, and the pre-test gate draws from that same bank. One-third of the section (Sustainability: EKC, green growth, Paris, CBDR) is very likely off the WEC14 4.3.6 spec while listed spec items (Lewis model, foreign currency gap, capital flight, demographics, property rights, privatisation, floating/managed exchange rates, joint ventures, tourism, Fairtrade, debt relief, NGOs) are absent from the taught content. A strong IAL teacher would use the notes and diagrams but would not trust the section as spec coverage.

accuracyIssues.issue: States the Paris Agreement 'committed 196 countries to limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius'. The Agreement commits parties to hold warming 'well below 2C' and to 'pursue efforts' toward 1.5C. The $100bn/yr climate-finance pledge originated at Copenhagen (2009) and was reaffirmed in the Paris decision text, not established by the Agreement; OECD reports it was first met in 2022, so 'consistently fallen short' is dated.
accuracyIssues.fix: Rewrite: 'The Paris Agreement (2015) commits 196 parties to keep warming well below 2C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5C, via nationally determined contributions. The $100bn a year climate-finance pledge (made in 2009, reaffirmed at Paris) was missed every year until 2022.'

accuracyIssues.location: Growth vs Development > growth-vs-development > misconception + takeaway[1] vs body[2]
accuracyIssues.issue: Misconception and takeaway assert 'growth is necessary for development but not sufficient' as the model answer, while body paragraph 3 says 'targeted investment in health and education can improve development outcomes even at relatively low GDP levels' (Kerala/Sri Lanka/Cuba cases). The section contradicts itself and presents a contested evaluative claim as fact.
accuracyIssues.fix: Change the model phrasing to 'growth usually enables development but is not sufficient; some states (Sri Lanka, Kerala) raised HDI with modest growth by prioritising health and education' and keep the body's nuance.

accuracyIssues.issue: South Korea is presented as the real example of 'market-led strategies' with 'strategic trade liberalisation', but its take-off (1960s-80s) combined export promotion with heavy import protection, directed credit and state-picked chaebol; trade liberalisation came later (1980s-90s). The hedge in the last clause does not stop a student writing 'South Korea = trade liberalisation success' in an exam.
accuracyIssues.fix: Use Vietnam (Doi Moi 1986, WTO accession 2007) or Chile's post-1975 liberalisation as the market-orientated example and keep South Korea as the mixed/interventionist case in the next section, which already uses India.

accuracyIssues.location: Development Strategies > both sections (classification vs spec)
accuracyIssues.issue: The section classifies SAPs as market-led and aid as interventionist. The IAL spec lists market-orientated strategies (trade liberalisation, FDI promotion, subsidy removal, floating exchange rates, microfinance, privatisation), interventionist (human capital, protectionism, managed exchange rates, infrastructure, joint ventures with TNCs, buffer stocks) and 'other' (industrialisation/Lewis, tourism, primary industries, Fairtrade, aid, debt relief), with IMF/World Bank/NGOs under international institutions. Diagram 4 ('Development Strategies Comparison') already uses the spec taxonomy; the Learn text does not.
accuracyIssues.fix: Re-map the two strategy sections to the spec's three-way taxonomy and add the missing named strategies (see ialSpecGaps); use the spec term 'market-orientated' consistently.

accuracyIssues.issue: Claims 'Examiners expect you to ... evaluate the Environmental Kuznets Curve' and green-growth section claims examiners 'want you to evaluate whether green growth is achievable'. I am not aware of EKC, green growth, natural capital or CBDR appearing in WEC14 4.3.6; these examiner expectations look invented. (Sustainability is assessed in Unit 2 as a cost of growth, not here.)
accuracyIssues.fix: Verify against the WEC14 spec; if not listed, demote this block to an optional 'stretch/context' card and replace examMatters with a truthful note ('may be used as evaluation of growth strategies; not a stand-alone question topic').

accuracyIssues.issue: keyIdea lists 'low human capital, and geography' as barriers, but the body never explains either (they appear only in the Notes tab). keyIdea promises content the step does not deliver.
accuracyIssues.fix: Either add a short paragraph on human capital/demographics/geography (landlocked, disease burden) or trim the keyIdea to what is taught.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'forest cover rising from 21% in 1987 to over 60% today' overstates; most sources put current cover around 52-59%. The 99% renewable electricity figure is fine.
accuracyIssues.fix: Say 'to well over half today (around 55-60%)'.

accuracyIssues.issue: 'mean and expected years of schooling' is described as one dimension correctly, but the text never notes the HDI is a geometric mean of three normalised indices or its limitations (ignores inequality, environment, freedom). Limitations are a standard IAL mark-scheme point (common_mistakes[1] even says so) and are nowhere in the Learn content.
accuracyIssues.fix: Add one paragraph: how HDI is calculated (geometric mean, 0-1) and three limitations (averages hide inequality; excludes environment/political freedom; GNI PPP data quality).

accuracyIssues.issue: 'Foreign aid can fill the savings gap identified by the Harrod-Domar model' is fine, but the section never introduces the foreign currency gap, which is the second gap aid/FDI fills and is a named spec item (and quiz Q4 option D relies on it).
accuracyIssues.fix: Add the 'two-gap' framing: savings gap and foreign currency (exchange) gap, and note capital flight as the leakage that widens both.

quizIssues.question: In the Lewis Dual-Sector Model, the 'Lewis turning point' occurs when:
quizIssues.issue: Correct answer (B) is right, but the Lewis model is never mentioned in any of the six Learn subsections; it exists only in diagram 2, flashcards and extras. Students hit this in the pre-test and inline quiz having never been taught it.

quizIssues.question: Capital flight is most harmful to developing countries because it:
quizIssues.issue: Correct (B), but 'capital flight' is never defined or explained in Learn content (it appears only in practice Q1 guidance). Untaught item in the quiz bank.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following best explains the 'Dutch disease' effect in resource-rich developing countries?
quizIssues.issue: Correct (B), but distractors C ('Dutch colonial trade policies') and D ('immigration from the Netherlands') are jokes, not plausible errors; the item is effectively a two-option question. Dutch disease is also never taught in Learn content (only in extras chains) and is already tested by Q4.

quizIssues.question: Which of the following is a valid criticism of using foreign aid to promote development?
quizIssues.issue: Correct (C), but relies on Dutch disease and the 'foreign currency gap' (option D), neither of which is taught in the section. Duplicates Q11's concept.

quizIssues.question: Which development indicator would best capture the structural transformation of an economy from subsistence agriculture to manufacturing and services?
quizIssues.issue: Correct (C) but 'Percentage of adult MALE labour force employed in agriculture' is an odd, dated gendered indicator; a student may reasonably reject it because it excludes women. Use 'share of the labour force employed in agriculture'.

quizIssues.question: In the Harrod-Domar model, if a country has a savings ratio of 12% and a capital-output ratio of 3, the predicted rate of economic growth is:
quizIssues.issue: Correct (B, 4%). Distractor '0.25%' is mis-scaled (3/12 = 25%, not 0.25%), so it does not capture the real inversion error. Also the g = s/k formula is never given in the Learn text (only in diagram 1, which never renders inline).

quizIssues.question: The IMF's structural adjustment programmes (SAPs) have been criticised primarily because they:
quizIssues.issue: Correct (C). Explanation says option B 'describes the World Bank, not the IMF' which is a loose characterisation (World Bank also does short-term crisis lending via IDA/IBRD instruments); minor.

practiceIssues.issue: 'Define the term HDI (4 marks)' - IAL Economics 'Define' items are 2-mark knowledge questions; a 4-mark stem would be 'Explain what is meant by' or a data-linked 'With reference to Figure 1, define ... and calculate ...'. The guidance awards a mark per component list-item, which is not how a definition is marked.

'Explain two constraints on economic development (6 marks)' is a plausible Section B 6-marker but IAL 6-markers are almost always 'With reference to Extract A, explain ...' (application marks). Guidance bundles 'capital flight and corruption' as one constraint, and capital flight is never taught in the Learn content.

'Assess the usefulness of the Harrod-Domar model (10 marks)' - command/marks correct. But the model answer is point-allocated (2+2+1+2+2+1) whereas IAL 10-markers are levels-marked (KAA 6 + Evaluation 4). Students will learn to write lists rather than a chained argument plus weighted judgement. The g = s/k formula the answer opens with is never stated in the Learn text.

'Evaluate ... market-oriented vs interventionist strategies (20 marks)' - command/marks correct for a Section C essay. Guidance is point-allocated rather than levels (KAA/EV) and lists 'World Bank and IMF conditional lending' under interventionist strategies, which is wrong (conditionality pushes market-orientated reform). Spec spelling is 'market-orientated'.

'Outline two roles of the IMF (4 marks)' - 'Outline' is not a Pearson IAL Economics command word (it is a Business one); IAL would use 'Explain two roles' or 'State/Identify'. The IMF's roles are not taught in this section's Learn content (only SAPs are mentioned), and the app's spec map already assigns IMF/World Bank to 4.3.5.

structureIssues: Zero recall exercises (meta reorder=0, fillin=0). None of the six subsections has a 'recall' object, so Learn Mode's spaced/immediate recall widgets never fire and the section has no retrieval practice at all between reading and the inline quiz.

No block has diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices (all null). Consequence: the five diagrams (HDI, Harrod-Domar, Lewis, Prebisch-Singer, strategies comparison) never render inline in Learn Mode, and the inline quiz/practice picked for each block is not tied to that block. Block 3 (Sustainability) has no quiz question and no practice question covering it at all, so whatever is shown after that step is off-topic.

Pre-test gate draws 3 random MCQs from a 12-item bank in which 5 items (Q3 Lewis, Q4 aid/Dutch disease, Q7 capital flight, Q11 Dutch disease, Q10 H-D assumptions) test content the section never teaches. A student can legitimately score 0/3 before starting, which matches the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Each block has exactly two sections, so the whole section is 3 steps. Each step is ~900-1000 words of prose (2 x 3 paragraphs + flow + example + misconception + examMatters) before any interaction. No difficulty ramp inside a step; the interactive elements are all stacked at the end.

Takeaways match their blocks (checked all 12 bullets) - good. But Block 1's takeaway bullet 3 names 'debt' and bullet 4 'multi-dimensional intervention' while the body's flow only shows the savings-gap loop; the debt/commodity/institution links are asserted, not shown.

Notes tab is broader than Learn content (geography, human capital, disease burden, Washington vs post-Washington Consensus) and diagram 4 uses the spec's strategy taxonomy, whereas the Learn text uses a different (SAP/aid) classification. A student switching tabs sees two different maps of the same topic.

Misconceptions: growth-vs-development, barriers-as-checklist, market-led-universal, dismiss-all-intervention and sustainability-means-no-growth are genuine student errors. 'Students present green growth as a cost-free solution' is filler - no IAL question elicits that error. Every misconception uses the identical 'Wrong - ... Instead write:' template, which reads as generated.

Lewis model and Prebisch-Singer are 'taught' only through a diagram (which cannot render inline) and a quiz question. Lewis is a named spec strategy ('industrialisation: the Lewis model') and should have its own subsection, not be relegated to extras.

Sequencing: Block 3 (sustainability) is the least spec-relevant content but is placed last, where completion-rate data shows the fewest students arrive; meanwhile the spec's core 'other strategies' and 'international institutions' bullets have no block at all.
ialSpecGaps: Measures of development beyond HDI: HDI limitations, other indicators (e.g. MPI, IHDI, Gini, % in agriculture, access to clean water) - only Q0 and Q9 touch this; not taught.

Factors influencing growth and development: foreign currency gap; capital flight; demographic factors (population growth, dependency ratio); access to credit and banking; infrastructure (mentioned only as a strategy); education/skills; absence of property rights (one phrase only); non-economic factors (wars, political instability, geography) - taught only in the Notes tab, not in Learn content.
Market-orientated strategies missing: removal of government subsidies; floating exchange rate systems; privatisation (appear in diagram 4 only).
Interventionist strategies missing: development of human capital as a strategy; managed exchange rates; promoting joint ventures with global companies (diagram 4 only).

Other strategies missing entirely: industrialisation via the Lewis model (diagram/quiz only), development of tourism, development of primary industries, Fairtrade schemes, debt relief (flashcards only).
Role of international institutions and NGOs: World Bank, IMF (beyond SAPs), NGOs - absent from Learn content; app's spec map puts IMF/World Bank in 4.3.5 but practice Q4 tests it here.

Unsure: whether sustainability / Environmental Kuznets Curve / green growth is in WEC14 4.3.6 at all - I believe it is not (sustainability of growth is a Unit 2 cost-of-growth point). If confirmed, Block 3 is off-spec and should be cut or demoted.
strengths: HDI facts are precise and correct: three dimensions, mean + expected schooling, GNI per capita PPP, 0.8 threshold; diagram 0 correctly shows goalposts (20-85 years, $100-$75,000) and the geometric mean.
Harrod-Domar is stated correctly (g = s/k) and Q2 (12%/3 = 4%) and Q10 (S = I assumption) are exam-realistic; the poverty-trap flow in barriers-development is a genuine causal chain.
Prebisch-Singer explanation (Q1 and diagram 3) correctly gives the Engel's Law / YED / substitutes / material-intensity reasoning, which is exactly what WEC14 mark schemes reward.
India Licence Raj example (1947-1991, ~3.5% 'Hindu rate of growth', 1991 liberalisation) is accurate and is a good balanced ISI case; the interventionist examMatters gives a usable essay structure.
Real examples for Equatorial Guinea (high GDP per capita, low HDI) and DRC (resource curse) are accurate and exactly the kind of divergence examples examiners want.
